# Nava-vraja-mahima. Vol. 4

## Preface

The title of the book you are now reading, Nava-vraja-mahima, when rendered in English becomes “The Glories of New Vraja-dhama.” I originally conceived of it as a booklet, meant to guide devotees visiting the holy places of New Vraja-dhama, ISKCON’s rural community in Hungary.  
As you must have noticed, the book has grown in size since its inception and would now likely require a small handcart for eager pilgrims to be able to transport it from one pastime place to another! Nonetheless, it still serves its original purpose of extolling New Vraja-dhama by praising its presiding Deities, Radha-Syamasundara, and by narrating the Supreme Lord Krsna’s pastimes in His eternal abode, Sri Vrndavana-dhama.  
Texts that glorify the holy abodes (dhamas) of the Lord are called dhama-mahatmyas. Two prime examples of this genre of devotional literature are Rupa Gosvami’s Sri Mathura-mahatmya and Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya. Both of these books establish the sanctity of the dhamas they depict — Vrndavana and Navadvipa respectively — by citing Puranic praise of the dhamas themselves as well as the pastime places within their boundaries. There is, however, an interesting difference between the two. Sri Mathura-mahatmya is an unordered compendium of scriptural references to the pastime places it describes, while Sri Navadvipa-dhama- mahatmya chronicles the Lord’s pastimes and the places at which they occurred by following the sequence in which pilgrims visit those places as they circumambulate the dhama. Thakura Bhaktivinodaalso recounts the personal spiritual reflections he gleans from cir­cumambulating Navadvipa in an appendix to Sri Navadvipa-dhama- mahatmya that he calls Sri Navadvipa-bhava-taranga.  
Despite their stylistic differences, the transcendental benefit readers derive from these two types of mahatmyas is the same. They act as practical guidebooks to the dhama, and at the same time they aid pilgrims in immersing their thoughts in the Lord's glories. For that reason, devotees who do not travel to the dhama can also derive transcendental benefit by circumambulating the holy places in their minds as they meditate on both the Lord’s pastimes and the dhama's glories as they are recounted in sacred texts of this nature.  
Nava-vraja-mahima is a mahatmya in the style of Sri Navadvipa-dhama-mahatmya in that it includes an account of my own personal circumambulation, or parikrama, of New Vraja-dhama and the realisations that came to me as a result. In fact, as I visit the pastime places in New Vraja-dhama — more commonly known to the people of Hungary as Krsna Valley — I sometimes reflect on similar parikramas I have undertaken in Bhauma Vrndavana, recount histories of how New Vraja-dhama was established and developed, or express my own devotional aspirations. This personal approach is primarily an attempt to please the devotees of New Vraja-dhama, who requested me to describe the parikrama not as a passive observer but as a participant who shares his adventure with the reader.  
Amongst many possible readers, this personal adventure is especially intended to be shared with the residents of and visitors to New Vraja-dhama, for whom this book will naturally be of greatest interest. Those readers who are not a part of that particular audience may rightly question what New Vraja-dhama is and how its glorification can be relevant to persons who live outside Hungary or who may never visit.  
As its name suggests, New Vraja-dhama is modelled after the original Vraja-dhama, Bhauma Vrndavana, Krsna’s eternal home as it appears on earth. The inspiration to establish New Vraja-dhama came from my spiritual master, His Divine Grace A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acarya of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. In the 1960s in America, Srila Prabhupada established New Vrndavana and envisioned it to be a self-sufficient community, dependent upon agriculture and cow protection, as well as a place of pilgrimage in the West. New Vraja-dhama is therefore our humble attempt to fulfil the desire of His Divine Grace that such places of pilgrimage be established throughout the world.  
In the introduction to this book and in the essay entitled ‘‘The Truths of the Dhama,” the reader will find a detailed history of how and why New Vraja-dhama came to be, along with a philosophical study of the spiritual principles that make it a holy place. I cannot overstate how important it is for the reader to carefully go through these parts of the book in order to clearly understand the spiritual foundations upon which New Vraja-dhama and Nava-vraja-mahima rest.  
What benefit will those who do not visit New Vraja-dhama gain from reading this book? The answer is threefold.  
Nava-vraja-mahima contains extensive and very detailed narrations of Krsna’s pastimes at all the major places in Vrndavana, as well as at many lesser-known places. Extensive research went into compiling — from the Vedas, Upanisads, Puranas, Samhitas, and other Vedic histories, as well as from the commentaries of our previous acaryas and other sources — the information it contains. Altogether, the text and the accompanying references offer the reader a unique opportunity to delve deeply into Krsna’s pastimes in Bhauma and Goloka Vrndavana and better get to know the Supreme Lord and His loving associates.  
Second, although the topographical orientation, distances, and occasionally the sequence of New Vraja-dhama’s parikrama differ from the same in Bhauma Vrndavana, the book also serves as an in-depth guide for pilgrims to use in visiting the pastime places of Sri Krsna’s original earthly abode.  
Third, through the glorification of New Vraja-dhama, this book testifies to the greatness of Srila Prabhupada’s achievement in spreading the potency of Vrndavana throughout the world.  
Now, allow me to clarify a few points about certain expressions and literary devices used in the text, about the structure of the volumes, and about the actual parikrama route of New Vraja-dhama.  
The expression “Krsna’s pastimes in New Vraja-dhama” is not meant to imply that Krsna manifests His eternal pastimes here in the way that He does, creation after creation, in Bhauma Vrndavana. Rather it means that the pastime places in New Vraja-dhama correspond to the original places in Bhauma Vrndavana or Goloka Vrndavana. Largely due to the uncommon format of the text (which I will discuss elsewhere in this preface) and because of the correspondence between the pastime places in both dhamas, it was sometimes necessary to refer to the pastimes associated with those places in a way that may make it sound as if they happened in New Vraja-dhama.  
If I say, for example, “At this place, called Aghavana, Krsna killed Aghasura,” it means “Krsna killed Aghasura in the Aghavana of Bhauma Vrndavana, which is commemorated by the place of the same name here in New Vraja-dhama.” Similarly, phrases such as “At this place Radha and Krsna enact Their rasa dance” should be taken to mean “At the Rasa-sthali of Goloka Vrndavana, the divine couple enact Their eternal rasa dance. The place called Rasa-sthali in New Vraja-dhama commemorates that original place.”  
The reason I use such expressions, aside from literary necessity, is to emphasise the importance of New Vraja-dhama and its stature as a place of pilgrimage. Again, the reader will find the philosophical and spiritual reasoning and supporting scriptural evidence for employing this convention in the introduction and the essay on dhama-tattva that follow this preface.  
Another literary device found in this book — as well as in other books describing the holy dhama — is that I sometimes speak about New Vraja-dhama as if I were directly seeing the unmanifest (aprakata) abode and pastimes of the Lord. These expressions are not declarations of my existential position; rather, they are poetic expressions of my deep feelings for the subject matter and the places themselves. I qualify such statements here to avoid causing misunderstandings that might blur the line between the manifest and unmanifest features of the dhama, merging them in a way that could be taken as contrary to authorised dhama-tattva.  
When, in describing the dhama, authors weave between manifest and unmanifest realities in this way, it often causes the features of the aprakata realm or the pastimes Krsna is relishing there to seem as if they are part of the world visible to conditioned souls. But devotees well versed in the principles of dhama-tattva will have no difficulty following these transitions between the manifest and unmanifest realms, whereas others may either not notice them or find them confusing.  
Our great acaryas may express themselves in such ways due to the overwhelming bliss they feel at seeing the aprakata-dhama and the eternal pastimes going on there. Or, in the case of those who are not on the fully realised platform of our great acaryas, authors may be making a conscious endeavour to emphasise the divinity that underlies the features of the dhama that conditioned souls are able to perceive.  
In writing Nava-vraja-mahima, poetic inspiration would sometimes impel me to describe the features of the dhama not in terms of what I was seeing with my eyes — for I cannot see that which is unmanifest — but in terms of the aprakata counter-whole as I have heard about it from scripture and as I contemplate it in relation to New Vraja-dhama. Readers who notice such expressions in the pages of this book should take them in this light, not as my personal realisation of the unmanifest dhama in the way of the great acaryas.

**\* \* \* \***

Parikrama is the traditional way of visiting Vrndavana. When Krsna sent Uddhava to Nandagrama with messages for the Vraja-vasis, He directed His cousin along a specific route and pointed out places to note along the journey. Thus Uddhava relished parikrama by travelling from Mathura to Nandagrama, as did Krsna by describing the journey to him.  
On His only visit to Vrndavana, Caitanya Mahaprabhu spent the first month of His two-month stay touring through Vraja’s twelve forests. And even though Lord Caitanya is Krsna Himself, He requested the help of a guide and followed the established route of His time.  
With the rediscovery of Krsna’s pastime places, the Vraja-mandala parikrama has evolved into what is currently called caurasi-krosa parikrama, or circumambulation of the one hundred and sixty-eight- mile dhama, the longest version of which takes almost two months to complete. Today, often during the holy month of Karttika, hundreds of devotees relish walking barefoot from place to place on ISKCON’s Vraja-mandala parikrama, living in the meadows or fields of Vraja, and absorbed in hearing about Krsna and chanting His names.  
For Hungarian devotees who cannot go to Bhauma Vrndavana, who cannot stay there for thirty days or more, or who would like to go on parikrama every year but cannot afford to go to India so often, the Nava-vraja-mandala parikrama is for them. Annually, members of the Hungarian yatra visit selected places of New Vraja-dhama over the course of several days, and as the dhama is further developed and parikrama paths established, the guided tours will become more extensive. In addition, by using the separate book of maps provided with Nava-vraja-mahima, devotees may go on parikrama at any time they want and thus relish the nectar of hearing Krsna’s pastimes and serving His dhama.  
In this way, Nava-vraja-mahima seeks to serve those devotees keen to visit Krsna’s abode, both in Hungary and in India. And for devotees who are neither residents of nor pilgrims to one dhama or the other, this work gives them the chance to visit Krsna’s holy dhama in their minds and thus bring the atmosphere of Vrndavana to wherever they reside.  
Circumambulating the dhama is a means of offering respect. It includes visiting pastimes places, remembering pastimes, bowing down, taking the dust from pastime places on one’s head, bathing in sacred waters, and performing nama-sankirtana. Many major places within the dhama — Govardhana Hill, Vrndavana town, and Varsana amongst them — have their own parikrama routes. As far as possible, these places have been or will be represented in New Vraja-dhama. There is never a dearth of transcendental diversion for the devout pilgrim!  
At the time of writing this book, the main pastime places of New Vraja-dhama have been established, whereas many parikrama paths and other secondary pastime places have been mapped out but not yet developed. These places — like the construction of a magnificent new temple for Radha-Syamasundara— remain part of future plans to develop New Vraja-dhama.  
Let me now describe the book’s structure.  
As already mentioned, this book is written in the form of my own parikrama, which is actually a compilation of multiple parikramas I made of New Vraja-dhama, some encompassing the entirety of the dhama, others only of places especially dear to me.  
In the course of describing my parikrama, there were times at which deep philosophical topics or lengthy pastimes came up that required explanations so extensive that to describe them properly would have broken the flow of the narration. These explanations became essays that are now appendices at the end of each volume.  
I request my reader not to neglect these appendices — nor the end-notes that accompany each chapter, for that matter — as readers are sometimes wont to do. They comprise roughly one third of the book’s total content and are instrumental in bringing the reader to a balanced understanding of its message. Designated stanzas in the running text direct the reader to these appendices at the proper times.  
In addition to the parikrama and appendices, the ten final chapters of Nava-vraja-mahima are dedicated to directly glorifying Radha- Syamasundara, the presiding Deities of New Vraja-dhama. In these chapters I exalt Their Lordships through the meditations that arise as I chant the Gayatri mantras and the maha-mantra and from my direct service to Them on the altar. This last section of the book therefore contains in-depth analyses of the Gaudiya Vaisnava diksa- mantras as well as the Hare Krsna maha-mantra. In this way the book has three parts: parikrama, appendices, and direct glorification of Radha-Syamasundara.  
The running text that forms the bulk of the book, comprised of the parikrama and the praises of Radha-Syama, is written in three-line prose stanzas. It is pleasant to look at and easy to read, but it was a challenge to write, edit, and lay out on the page. This challenge led us to adopt certain conventions, such as mixing Sanskrit verses with  
English translations within a single stanza, or having longer verses straddle more than one stanza. However, we feel confident that the hook’s format will enable you to relish the topic all the more.  
From the outset I wanted Nava-vraja-mahima to be well illustrated to give windows into Krsna’s pastimes and to contribute to the overall purpose of the work — to increase the reader’s attachment to the Lord. I hope this has been achieved to your satisfaction. In Sri Krsna-samhita (9.16), Bhaktivinoda Thakura writes, “By seeing pictures of Krsna or by repeatedly hearing descriptions of Krsna from persons who have seen Him, one’s greed for attaining Krsna increases unlimitedly.”  
To assist you in navigating through the unfamiliar names of pastime places and the variances in the locations of these places in New Vraja-dhama and Bhauma Vrndavana, each chapter also includes a map or maps of the area it describes.  
Altogether there are eight volumes of text. The set is complete with a ninth volume solely dedicated to maps of the various holy places of both New Vraja-dhama and Bhauma Vrndavana, along with short descriptions of each pastime place. Devotees can take this map book with them to follow the parikrama routes in both dhamas and have a reminder of Krsna’s activities there.  
Nava-vraja-mahima is meant to serve as a companion for devotees who want to take full advantage of the presence of Vrndavana in Hungary and to develop their relationship with its presiding Deities, Radha-Syamasundara. Furthermore, it is meant to encourage devotees anywhere in the world to worship their local Deities with devotion and recognise the Vaikuntha nature of those Deities’ abodes. It is my hope as the author that this work will serve these purposes in some small way and thus bring pleasure to devotees, for my own access to the dhama will be possible only by the good wishes of the Vaisnavas.  
In conclusion, I request the reader, wherever he or she may reside, to consider that in its essence this book praises the same dhama and the same Krsna that are there in their own hearts, and which are thus very near and dear to them. It is in this way that our journey around  
New Vraja-dhama through the pages of this book is synonymous with our own inner journey back to Godhead.  
The journey through Nava-vraja-mahima is a long one. The book spans over five thousand pages and took five years to write. Therein I have tried my best to portray the truths of Vrndavana as they are recorded in scriptures and narrated by perfect devotees like Srila Prabhupada. Sadly, I remain a conditioned soul and thus am prone to make mistakes. If my readers find mistakes within the pages of this book, I ask them to tolerate such faults in the way they do the pebbles or thorns that prick their feet while on parikrama of the dhama.  
Hare Krsna.  
Sivarama Swami  
New Vraja-dhama  
Gopastami, 2 November 2011

*This abode of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa is called Govinda-bhūmi in the Purāṇas, Yoga-pīṭha in the Tantras, and Cakravartī Ṭhākura calls it Kuñja rāja.*

## Chapter 15 - Yoga-pitha and Radha-kunda

Circling Nimavana, I came to its western edge. From there I offered my respectful obeisances to the heart and fountainhead of New Vraja-dhama— the divine

I have called the general area of Radha-Syamasundara’s temple the Yoga-pitha, wherein Syamasundara is also known by names like Madana-mohana, Govindaji, and Gopinatha.

The nucleus of the Yoga-pitha is Radha-Syamasundara, who have joined (yoga) the material world to the spiritual world at the place (pitha) where They appeared and stand even now.

Radha-Syamasundara are the root of the divine lotus of New Vraja-dhama. As long as we serve Them with loving devotion, that lotus will thrive; if we ever neglect Them, the lotus will wither away.

Should we overlook the care of Radha-Syama, the link with Goloka will be severed, the Yoga-pitha will disappear, New Vraja-dhama will lose its spiritual essence, and only a mundane farm will remain.But as long as we maintain strong personal sadhana, serve Srila Prabhupada’s mission, and dedicate everything to Their Lordships, the spiritual world will continue to reveal itself in New Vraja-dhama.

The twelve forests of Vrndavana, the Yamuna, the cities of the Vraja-vasis, and the unlimited pastimes Krsna enjoys in those places will remain situated on the petals of the lotus of New Vraja-dhama.

While sastra reveals that the Yoga-pitha resides in a forest setting, we may see merely a temple, but if we hear of and meditate on it with faith, we will first feel and in time perceive its spiritual form.

So that we may better understand the transcendental nature of the dhama and more fully appreciate its wonders, I will now describe this wholly sublime and mysterious Yoga-pitha.

The confidential portions of the Vedas and some of our acaryas’ books describe the transcendental form of the Yoga-pitha as it exists in Goloka and in an unmanifest form in Vrndavana here on earth.

As Sri Krsna’s foremost abode and place of pastimes, the Yoga-pitha is the residence of His most confidential companions. It is perceived directly by perfected souls and meditated upon by practising devotees.

Let us now hear about the aprakata Yoga-pitha, also called Govinda-sthali, the place of Lord Govinda, because it is His favourite abode and it is not different from His transcendental body.

The sacred Vedas call the area comprising the temple and desire tree the Yoga-pitha, or Antahpuri (the inner residence). We refer to it as simply Krsna’s playground (keli-nikunja).

The Yoga-pitha’s form is reminiscent of Krsna’s face, its fragrance of His bodily aroma, its resonance His voice, and its ambience His heart; in short, it reminds one of Govinda’s transcendental personality.

The Yoga-pitha stands as a mountainous island upon the summit of Vrndavana, rising out of the waters of the Yamuna like the back of a turtle whose shell is marked with the petals of a lotus.

These petals expand beyond the Yamuna and throughout Vraja. In total they number one thousand, each housing a prominent grove that plays host to its own variety of Krsna’s youthful pastimes.

At the very centre of that lotus is the king of desire trees. At times it appears to be wood, leaves, and flowers, at other times it appears to be valuable gems, and at still others it appears in both ways at once.

From the branches of this tree hang equally incomprehensible desire vines —golden, black, or green in colour—upon which blossom by their own will every conceivable type of flower, even those made of jewels.

The grove thus formed — like Govinda — is unfathomable even to the most purified sages. It is the emperor of all the groves and gardens of Vrndavana, and so it is also called Sri Kunja-raja.

Indeed, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes,

*govinda-bhumiti purana- gitam yad-yoga-pithakhyam apiha tantre*  
*sri radhaya sri-vidhu-yoga- dhama sri-kunja-rajam nigadama nama*

**“This abode of Sri Radha and Krsna is called Govinda-bhumi in the Puranas, and Yoga-pitha in the Tantras. In this book \[Vraja-riti- cintamani\] we call it Sri Kunja-raja.”**

A golden temple rests in the shelter of this grove, its ornately carved pillars, arches, and domes set with gems that glow with numinous splendour by day and soothing radiance at night.

That temple appears always medium in size, but it has many adjoining wings of varied dimension, each made up of a lotus-shaped courtyard with a whorl and eight petals containing a central fountain.

The temple stands upon an ornate quadrangular platform with staircases on all four sides made of the finest translucent marble, which, incredible as it may sound, feels as soft as butter to the touch.

Within the central chamber of the temple is a jewel-studded golden throne (simhasana), the most ornate, beautiful, and beguiling object in the Yoga-pitha, or anywhere else in Vrndavana.

The throne is shaped like an eight-petalled lotus in flight, with wings made from its own lustre. Its front lion-legs are raised off the ground while its hind legs carry the throne’s weight, although it is weightless.

Seated at the centre like the stamen of that lotus are Radha and Krsna; above Them is a soft cloth with the look and feel of a lion skin. This is the heart of the Yoga-pitha and the centre of all existence.

On this seat, behind the divine couple, is a cotton-filled bolster held in place by a lapis lazuli backrest. In front of and just below the seat are footrests, graced by the two most attractive pairs of lotus feet.

Radha and Krsna sit upon this throne, Their original, eternally youthful, and alluringly unassuming forms mesmerising Their friends and each other with elegance, splendour, humour, and love.

This divine couple, the Absolute Truth, source of the predominating (purusa) and predominated (prakrti) natures, immersed in the bliss of countless exchanges of spiritual love, are denoted by the syllable klim.

Around the base of Radha and Krsna’s seat is a hexagonal plinth inscribed with the six words of the Gopala-gayatri, signifying that only the followers of the gopis can enter this inner sanctum.

Two seats rest upon each of the eight petals of the throne, with one of the asta-sakhis sitting on the raised tip of each petal and her corresponding maidservant (manjari) sitting on the inner part below.

To Krsna’s immediate right sits Lalita, and beyond her Citra, Campakalata, and Tungavidya; to Radha’s left are Visakha, Ranga- devi, Sudevi, and Indulekha— these are the asta-sakhis.

And following the same order as these most confidential friends sit their most intimate maidservants (manjaris): Rupa, Rasa, Guna, Lavanga, Vilasa, Kasturi, Manjulali, and Rati respectively.

Devotees who chant the Gopala- and Kama-gayatri mantras to gain entrance into this transcendental realm must take shelter of one of these sakhis by becoming the servant of her maidservant (manjari).

Gaudiya Vaisnavas generally yearn to be counted amongst Lalita- sakhi’s group of gopis and trained by Rupa-manjari in the fine arts related to serving Radha and Krsna within the groves of Vrndavana.

Above the throne, suspended from the ceiling by a silken rope, is an exquisite umbrella with golden filigree, its sparkling diamond rim decorated with a hanging fringe of rubies and moonstone.

Even the smallest speck of dust on this throne is more valuable than all the wealth in Vaikuntha. Nevertheless, that dust has no value without its relation to Sri Radha and Her beloved Syamasundara.

Dressed in yellow clothing befitting a cowherd prince, with His unique cloud-blue complexion, Krsna rouses the hearts of Radha and Her girlfriends, who sit surrounding the divine couple.

Around Krsna’s neck hangs a long garland of sylvan flowers woven with buds of the tulasi plant; on His head rests a colourful turban bedecked with jewels, blooms, buds, and a peacock feather.

His face — more radiant than millions of moons — is made even more enchanting by rolling, restless lotus eyes, and by ears adorned with yellow flower ornaments and shark-shaped earrings.

Elegant tilaka — a round spot of sandalwood paste with a dot of kunkuma — graces Krsna’s forehead. Small curly locks of hair and diamond-like beads of perspiration decorate His brow.

Krsna raises His eyebrows playfully, glancing at His beloved as His moonlight smile flashes sparkling white teeth through bimba-red lips. Suspended by a ring, a single pearl dances beneath His nose.

Rings and bracelets ornamenting His hands—His beloved flute in the left, a delicate lotus in the right — Krsna captivates everyone around Him with the tinkling of His tiny waist bells and priceless anklets.

Krsna is completely addicted to sporting with Sri Radha; indeed, He is subjugated by Her love. On occasion He will glance at a sakhi, His entire body trembling in ecstasy as He laughs and jokes with Radha.

Seated at His left and dressed in a deep blue garment that mirrors Krsna’s complexion, golden-hued Sri Radha partly covers Her winsome face and restless eyes with the border of Her veil.

Radha accepts tambula from Lalita, demurely offering it to Krsna. Delicate bangles jingle on Her hands, and pearl necklaces move slightly on Her chest as She leans towards Her beloved.

Every part of Her enchanting transcendental body is so perfectly formed that they enrich and beautify the ornaments— rings, bangles, earrings, and necklaces — meant to decorate Her limbs.

As the youthful embodiment of bliss, She is wholly content, pleased to he at Her lover’s side. And Her devoted gopi friends — similar to Her in age, beauty, and other qualities — share in that ecstasy.

One acdrya describes the divine couple at the Yoga-pitha,

*divyad-vrndaranya-kalpa-drumadhah-srimad-ratnagara-simhasana-sthau*  
*srimad-radha-srila-govinda-devau presthalibhih sevyamanau smarami*

**“In a temple of jewels in Vrndavana, beneath a desire tree, Radha and Govinda, served by Their most confidential companions, sit upon an effulgent throne. Let us offer our humble obeisances unto Them.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Just beyond the central temple of the Yoga-pitha is a lotusshaped courtyard. On its eight petals lie the temples and groves of the eight sakhis, and beyond them, the abodes of the eight manjaris.

The temple groves of the gopis are separated from the inner domain of Radha and Krsna by an octagonal structure upon which the words of the Kama-gayatri mantra are written in sparkling gems.

Although the gopis’ residences vary in design, dimension, and colour, they simultaneously and inconceivably retain the overall symmetry of the expanding lotus petals of the Yoga-pitha.

Replete with all the things required for the gopis’ unique services to the divine couple, these groves expand and contract along with the petals upon which they rest, according to the will of Yogamaya.

Each petal of this divine lotus, regardless of which gopi resides upon it, is a pastime garden for Radha. As such, they are known as the petals (patrani) of the goddess of fortune (sri) —patrani sriyam.

Where the petals intersect or join the whorl of the Yoga-pitha, those places delineate the pathways of Vraja. And where these petals spread out into the distance, they delimit the pastures of the surabhi cows.

Successive petals expand beyond the first eight petals of the asta-sakhis and the next eight petals of the asta-manjaris, each corolla doubling in petals until there are one thousand petals in all.

From the inner courtyard, four paths of finely ground gem-dust proceed from the gates facing the four directions. Those paths lead to the southbound Yamuna, which encircles Govinda-sthali like a moat.

The petals of Govinda-sthali expand outward in concentric woodland rings, one after another as far as the Yamuna, beyond which each of Vraja’s forests appears like a single petal unto itself.

Descending from the Yoga-pitha at the peak of Govinda-sthali, these woodland rings are each comprised of one kind of tree: golden banana followed by campaka, kimsuka, naga-kesara, tamala, and bakula.

Forests abound in all varieties. There are the six forests in which the six seasons individually remain ever-present, forests of fruit trees, of blossoming flowers, and forests where the trees are tangled with vines.

The trees in these forests may appear to be of different species, but actually they are all of the wish-fulfilling sort, and even though they may seem to be firmly rooted in place, they move about at will.

Moreover, though the trees are apparently made of organic matter — wood, leaves, and flowers — they have another nature they reveal for the pleasure of Krsna: they are made of a multiplicity of gems.

A tree may display, for example, a gold trunk, opal branches, sapphire twigs, emerald leaves, ruby buds, crystal flowers, and fruit made of all manner of gems, including jewelled combinations and mixtures.

The soil of Govinda-sthali is generally gold, but it also changes its nature to match the colours of the surrounding forests; at given times and places the soil is sapphire, crystal, ruby, or emerald.

Platforms surround many of the trees in the forests of Govinda-sthali, offering the divine couple places to rest and simultaneously embellishing this peerless transcendental paradise.

These platforms may be square, hexagonal, octagonal, or circular; ornately carved from sapphire, ruby, or moonstone; set with diamonds or pearls; and stand as low as one’s knee or as high as one’s shoulder.

Radha’s and Krsna’s companions appeal to the trees when they require something to serve the divine couple, and, just as they do fruit from the trees, they receive clothes, jewellery, cosmetics, and scents.

If there aren’t enough garlands to decorate Radha and Krsna or Their gopi attendants or the groves, the divine couple’s maidservants can petition the trees for ready-made garlands of fresh, gorgeous flowers.

These marvels may be incomprehensible to conditioned souls, but in this land of love and wonder, where one can attain the topmost perfection simply by touching the soil, miracles are the rule.

For example, in at least one place on each of the Yoga-pitha’s one thousand petals, Vraja s desire trees and vines entwine to form groves whose splendour and opulence put to shame Lord Narayana's palace.

These magnificent trees select the most fitting place for their service and then join their branches together to form roofs, and with sub-branches they form many intricately shaped domes and spires.

Desire vines grow from the ground up to the beam-like branches above, then back down again from the domes to form walls, which have blossoming flowers and delicate tendrils braided into them.

These edifices are so tightly constructed that neither wind nor rain of the fiercest monsoon can enter, but at the same time they breathe to permit the slightest and most welcome breeze on hot summer nights.

So delicate and detailed are these groves that from afar they resemble intricately fashioned and ornately decorated jewellery boxes; only up close can one tell that they are actually intermingling trees and vines.

Vrnda-devi and her sylvan goddesses hang embroidered canopies from the ceilings of these groves, and furnish them with beds made soft by cotton mattresses and pillows stuffed with stemless flowers.

They also hang jewel-studded pictures that incite amorous feelings, and set up tables upon which rest boxes with pan, pitchers of nectar, goblets for drinking, scents, fans, mirrors, sindura, and collyrium.

And although the groves are no less beautiful inside than out, Vrnda- devi’s maidservants further enhance their natural ambiance by hanging sheer silk curtains, flower garlands, and festoons.

The birds and bees join the trees and vines in serving Krsna. Perched discreetly throughout the forest, they lend the sound of their coos and hums to create an atmosphere delightful to the ears and heart.

Many orchard groves lie at the base of Govinda-sthali Hill, and just beyond those fruit trees are cottages equipped with every item of service essential to the divine couple’s pastimes.

It may he a gopi-disguise for Krsna to wear and pacify Radha in Her anger, bathing clothes for His water sports, or utensils and ingredients for cooking a feast. Whatever it is, Vrnda-devi has it all on hand.

Desire trees could easily provide anything Yogamaya scripts into Krsna’s pastimes, hut the gopis take special pride in personally stocking these cottages with the most exotic amenities.

Beyond Vrnda-devi’s storehouses are two more rings of trees, the first of asoka, the second vetasa. On the other side of these forests are the sublime gardens that skirt the Yamuna’s diamond-powder beaches.

Lined by bakula trees, the four paths leading downhill from the temple meet the blackish waters of the Yamuna at four elegant, ornate ghatas, each guarded by a gopi— Vrnda in the east.

Without permission from these guards, no one — be he demigod, demon, human, or otherwise — can enter this secret domain, which is invisible to those not in love with Krsna in the mood of the gopis.

By Yogamaya’s influence, even Vraja-vasis overflowing with parental love for Krsna cannot see Govinda-sthali. And if they do see it by chance, they simply pass by, thinking it too bothersome to explore.

The banks of the Yamuna are the stage upon which Krsna and the gopis perform their renowned rasa dance. Some beaches are open and expansive, others secluded and concealed by gardens and groves. The sand on the Yamuna’s shore is naturally cooling, like powdered camphor. Kissed by moonbeams and the touch of Krsna’s soft lotus feet, that fine sparkling powder is made doubly soothing.

The blackish river water is pleasing to the touch, and its current gently massages the body. It varies in depth, reaching in some places to the knees and in others to the navel, chest, or neck.

Colourful lotuses like the red kahlara, white pundarika, blue indivara, and golden nalini dance upon the waves, scenting the water with their pollen and attracting playful honeybees.

White and black swans, cakravaka geese, and wagtail birds frolic in the drift and fill the air with their songs, air already enriched by the heady scent of musk deer cavorting at the edge of the forest.

In the most secluded part of Yamuna’s shore grows a unique flower garden. Large and round like the full moon, half of it juts out into the water while the other half is enclosed by a grove called Atimukta.

This is the rasa-mandala of the Yoga-pitha, very dear to Krsna. Atimukta’s ambience perfectly facilitates the rasa dance and helps to churn the joy of that festive pastime into rich butter-like bliss.

There the sounds of jingling ankle-hells and clapping hands intermingle with the lapping of Yamuna’s waves as they inch up the shoreline in hopes of touching the imprints left by dancing lotus feet.

Naturally blackish, in this area the water of the Yamuna has turned whitish, thus resembling the colour of the Ganga, having washed sandalwood paste from the bodies of the gopis.

O Yamuna, daughter of the sun! May thoughts of you, like the force of your swift current, wash all impurities from devotees’ hearts and grace them with love for a blackish cowherd and His golden consort.

By your devotional power, kindly transform those who desire it into eternal companions of the divine couple. Endow them with bodies fit for serving Radha and Krsna in the pastime places of Govinda-sthali.

**\* \* \* \***

Having heard a few of the limitless features of the inconceivable Yoga-pitha, let us now hear further about some of the pastime places and persons situated in and around that divine realm.

Each of the thousand petals that unfurl from the Yoga-pitha is divine, and yet the closer a petal is to the centre of the lotus, the more confidential are the pastimes that take place there.

The twelve main forests grace the eight inner petals, which include Vrndavana, Mahavana, and Kamyavana, and beyond that corolla rest hundreds of sub-forests with uncountable gardens and groves.

The first petal is hidden from Vedic scripture and difficult even for introspective saints to visualise. It unfurls to the south and is said to be the birthplace of Krsna — sacred Gokula, the very soul of Vraja.

To the southeast is the second petal, where the gopis pray to Ganesa to deliver them from the fear they might somehow lose their lover. Krsna appears there as a chubby deity of the elephant-god.

The third petal, which lies to the east, is more sacred than all holy places combined. It is there Krsna pleases Radha by digging a well with His flute-song (Venu-kupa) and filling it with the waters of love.

At the peak of the rasa dance, the divine couple sneak off alone to enjoy the happiness of each other’s company. When Radha asks Krsna for a drink of water, He creates this well by playing His flute.

The northeastern fourth petal intersects the Yamuna where the gopis worship goddess Katyayani. At that place Krsna steals the bathing gopis’ garments and demands an exorbitant fee to return them.

To the north, the fifth petal is to some savants the best of all, because there the sun god deploys his rays to serve Krsna by drying and warming the Lord after He spends many hours in Yamuna’s waves.

Brahma-kunda is also found there. On its banks a delightful asoka grove, like a thief, steals away the divine couple’s gravity and repose with the inviting fragrance of bright orange blossoms.

On this fifth petal also resides Gopisvara, whom the gopis worship. And the Vamsivata tree dances there on Yamuna’s shore because it is always enchanted by the sound of Krsna’s flute-song calling the gopis.

The sixth petal, to the northwest, is the home of two important kadamba trees: the first at Kaliya-hrada, from which Krsna jumps to challenge Kaliya, and the second at Bhadrakali-tirtha.

A hair of Sati falls at the base of this second kadamba tree. It is also a meeting place of Radha and Krsna, and some of the cowherd girls worship Katyayani here to get Krsna as their husband.

On the seventh petal, to the west, Krsna expands Himself, taking the forms of His cowherd boy friends and their calves to bewilder Brahma, who tries to test Krsna’s mystic power.

The eighth petal, called Vyoma-ghatana, lies to the southwest. It encompasses an area of Vrndavana forest wherein many pastimes occur, including the killing of the upstart Sankhacuda.

A very important place can be found on this eighth petal in a jasmine garden called Suryaspada. Also known by the name Surya-kunda, here Radha worships the sun god with a freshly blossomed red rose.

Sixteen sub-petals surround the first eight petals. The leading petal in this second corolla is named Svadha-madhava because the husband of the goddess of fortune (Madhava) considers it His home (svadha).

Upon this petal rests Krsna’s pleasure playground, sacred Govardhana Hill, the refuge of private groves and grassy pastures where the Supreme Lord enjoys playful pastimes as an amorous cowherd.

Because Govardhana Hill is so dear to Krsna, this one sub-petal equals in importance the inner core of the Yoga-pitha. In fact, there is another Yoga-pitha on Govardhana at Radha-kunda.

Like Svadha-madhava, every petal of the Yoga-pitha is named according to the specific pastimes Krsna enjoys there. The fourth sub-petal, for example, is called Mahadbhuta-rasasthala.

Krsna meets billions of gopis on this sub-petal for a great (maha) festival of dancing in which He amazes (adbhuta) everyone by expanding into as many forms as there are cowherd damsels.

But we rarely use the names of the petals to refer to the topography of Vraja; instead, we favour the names of well-known groves, forests, rivers, hills, and towns situated upon those petals.

For instance, because the stately capital of Nanda Maharaja graces that fourth sub-petal called Mahadbhuta-rasasthala, we generally refer to the area as Nandisvara or Nandagrama.

Petals are also named after cities like Varsana, Kaman, Gokula, and Vrndavana, and after pastime places where Krsna herds cows, plays ball, kills demons, or dances with the cowherd girls.

Because on the eleventh sub-petal, Bhaktanugraha-karana, Krsna favours the gopis (anugraha) by revealing to them (karana) His pastimes as Ramacandra, it is known as Kamyavana or Setubhanda.

O devotees! Please listen to a secret. In different forms, in different parts of Goloka, Krsna is eternally present so that He and His devotees can enjoy the pastimes particular to His different ages.

Madana-gopala resides on the sixteenth sub-petal (dala) of the Yoga-pitha, which is as opulent and as pleasing (vikara) as the Yoga-pitha’s filaments (kinjalka), and is thus called Kinjalkiviharadala.

This petal is guarded by stick-wielding gopas, the constant companions of Gopala. That eternal five-year-old hero of Gokula tends His father’s calves and kills the demons who threaten Vraja.

Gopala is an ocean of love, joy, and pleasure, but He also displays the traits of a dhiroddhata personality; that is, He is sometimes proud, jealous, restless, complacent, or short-tempered.

Devotees may meditate on Gopala in these moods, decorated with gold ornaments, a forest garland, and colourful turban. He sits on a gold throne within a gold temple surrounded by gopas like Subhadra.

Of the same age, these cowherd boys all have flutes, horns, garments, and forms similar to Gopala’s. They shed tears, shivering in ecstasy as they joyfully sing His names, qualities, and pastimes.

Surrounding the temple of Gopala is a beautiful garden full of blossoming flowers and a fragrant Parijata tree that attracts swarms of humming bumblebees from all directions.

Gopinatha, in contrast, resides within a cave of Govardhana Hill. His mystical flute playing entices the gopis, and His broad chest destroys by its splendour the last vestiges of those milkmaids’ self-restraint.

Ever adorned with the flowers He uses as weapons of Cupid, He is a dhira-lalita hero: carefree, expert in joking, naturally very funny, and always at the peak of His youth, nava-yauvana.

Gopinatha, who originates the rasa dance and its transcendental mellows by attracting the cowherd damsels with the sound of His flute, revels in divine sports during the three periods of the evening.

And as already mentioned, Govindaji, famous for His mind-enchanting, threefold-bending form, enjoys the pleasure of the Yoga-pitha in the company of Srimati Radharani.

He displays the character of a dhiroddhatta hero: He is naturally very grave, gentle, humble, forgiving, merciful, determined, chivalrous, highly qualified, and physically attractive.

**\* \* \* \***

Great personalities reside within or near the Yoga-pitha in their original forms or in some other form; for example, the goddesses Sri, Bhu, and Nila reside as the jati, dhatri, and tulasi plants respectively.

It is said that Savitri and Parvati live at Govinda-sthali as somavalli and haritaki vines, just as Uddhava lives as the gulma-lata at Kusuma- sarovara, and Brahma, as lowly grass on the edges of Vraja.

The great personalities who reside at the Yoga-pitha do not all perceive the Lord and His abode in the same way. Their perceptions vary according to the nature of their Krsna consciousness.

In other words, the one transcendental reality of the Yoga-pitha is simultaneously visible in various forms to various worshippers in response to the kind of perfection each worshipper covets.

Some servants conceive of the Yoga-pitha as the abode of Krsna and Radha, others as the abode of Krsna and a host of gopis, and still others as the abode of Krsna and the Vraja-vasis.

The conception of still other devotees tempers the sweetness of the Yoga-pitha with veneration for the Lord of Dvaraka, while others dilute it with the majesty of the Lord of Vaikuntha.

Thus when it is said that gopis, gopas, or associates of Narayana reside in and around the Yoga-pitha, we should understand that they reside in different dimensions of an inconceivable multi-tiered reality.

Seated at the centre of the Yoga-pitha are Radha and Krsna, surrounded immediately by Radha’s bodily expansions — Krsna’s main energies (prakrtis) — seated in two more concentric circles of eight.

Seated clockwise from Lalita in the west are Radha’s well-wisher Syamala, sweet Sri Madhumati, young Dhanya, Krsna’s beloved Visakha, beautiful Saibya, assertive Padma, and auspicious Bhadra.

Surrounding these sakhis is another circle of eight, beginning with Citravesa and followed by Vrnda, Candra, Madana-sundari, Supriya, Madhumati, Sasirekha, and Hari-priya.

These gopis, and the countless others that surround them, are inarguably prepossessing and invariably blessed with restless eyes, gorgeous dress, priceless ornaments, fresh youth, and sharp intellect.

But what makes the gopis' allure unique is their full, spontaneous, and heartfelt absorption in Krsna, which acts as a lover’s mirror to reflect Radha’s matchless beauty and sweetness back to Him.

To the southwest beneath a bakula tree is Candravali, Sri Radha’s second self, who intensifies the loving exchange between the divine couple by acting as Radharani’s arch rival.

Some distance to the right of the divine couple stand the personified Vedas in their gopi forms (sruti-kanyas). The manner in which they intently sing Krsna’s glories captures His mind as well as their own.

And on the left side of the divine couple, unsuccessfully concealing with bashful glances their desire for Govinda, are the daughters of the demigods (deva-kanyas) in their unmistakable heavenly attire.

At the top of four paths leading downhill to the Yamuna’s four ghatas, four of Krsna’s confidential cowherd boyfriends — Sridama, Vasudama, Sudama, and Kinkini — stand guard at four gates.

These boys’ relationships with Krsna are based on pure friendship. Indifferent to Krsna’s amorous exploits, they enter no further into the Yoga-pitha than the gates that they guard.

Only Krsna’s most intimate friends (priya-narma-sakhas), such as Subala and Ujjvala, enter the groves of Govinda-sthali, and then only to relay messages between Krsna and the gopis.

Just downhill from Sridama’s post and to the west, in the centre of a large garden, is an ornate golden throne set with gems such as rubies, upon which the master of all creation, joyful Vasudeva, sits at ease.

Divine ornaments enhance the Lord’s cloud-like complexion, a regal crown sparkles atop His dark curly hair, and a mace, disc, lotus, and conch lie casually in His four powerful hands.

Dressed in yellow cloth and wreathed by a forest garland that hangs to His knees, Vasudeva’s broad lotus eyes gaze compassionately at His leading wives, who crowd around Him along with their maidservants.

These dear queens, well known in Dvaraka for their chastity, beauty, and skill, are Rukmini, Satyabhama, Jambavan, Nagnajiti, Kalindi, Laksmana, Mitravinda, and Bhadra.

Towards the north end of Govinda-sthali is a magnificent park of sandalwood trees. Those trees encompass a jewelled pavilion in which Lord Balarama sits upon a throne along with His consort, Revati.

Sankarsana's form and qualities are very similar to Krsna’s, except for His crystal-white complexion, blue garments, and eyes tinged red from habitually drinking the intoxicant varuni.

On the opposite end of Govinda-sthali, beneath a samana tree to the south, resides the predominating deity of intelligence, Pradyumna, attended by a goddess adept at fulfilling His every need.

His perfectly proportioned limbs glow with the hue of blue lotuses, reminiscent of Krsna’s own limbs to such a degree that conditioned and liberated souls alike are driven to desire the limbs of Krsna alone.

To the east is the last of Lord Krsna’s quadruple expansions, Aniruddha, who sits with Usa — resembling lightning embracing a cloud — upon a lustrous throne in a majestic forest glade.The Lord’s wavy hair, arched eyebrows, and glossy dark complexion accentuate His dark eyes, intensely gazing upon the realised souls who sit at His feet and meditate with rapt attention upon His divine form.

To His left, absorbed in devotion by body, mind, and word, are Siddhas, Yaksas, Gandharvas, and Vidyadharas, and in their midst, celestial damsels like the Apsaras perform sankirtana.

To Aniruddha’s right, smouldering with love for Krsna, sit famous devotees like Prahlada, Narada, the Kumaras, Sukadeva, and Janaka, joined by the foremost servants of Lord Visnu.

Always meditatively performing loud nama-sankirtana of Lord Krsna’s holy name, these illustrious Vaisnavas are constantly decorated by symptoms of ecstasy like trembling and tears.

To ensure that only qualified persons enter the groves of the catur-vyuha, four guards, each bearing the name Visnu and each holding four divine weapons, protect the four gates that lead to these groves.

Within a ring of trees further down Govinda-sthali lie verdant, delightful gardens. Amongst them, on a western petal, is the abode of Brahma, the creator, who sits upon a lotus that dazzles like the sun.

To the north is Ananta with a thousand hoods; to the east, five-headed Siva; to the south, a second Sankarsana. These deities are all seated on their own thrones and surrounded by their own devotees.

Further down the hill, closer to the river, are assorted sacred residences of demigods like Indra, Vayu, and Yama, and the rustic hermitages of realised sages like Sandilya, Galava, and Garga.

Perfected souls who worship Krsna solely for His pleasure, with the hope of serving Him like the Vraja-vasis but who have not yet become residents of Vraja, live at the Yoga-pitha in subtle bodies.

Just as Vrndavana is the best place in Mathura-mandala, this Yoga-pitha is the best place in the forests of Vrndavana. Having come here, a person who leaves to go elsewhere is his own worst enemy.

This place, teeming with singing birds and playing deer, abounding with every variety of flowering tree and vine, rich with ponds and streams full of transcendental nectar, is Krsna’s favourite abode.

At sunrise the Yoga-pitha glows orange, and during the morning hours it shines a brilliant white. At midday it is as dazzling as the sun, and in the afternoon as green as a lotus leaf.

At sunset the Yoga-pitha turns reddish like a heap of vermilion, and beneath the full moon it appears to be a mound of cool camphor, but on the dark moon night it is mysterious like a sapphire mountain.

In the rainy season the Yoga-pitha is green like fresh grass, in autumn it glows like a ruby, and in winter it sparkles like a diamond. In spring it shines like new leaves, and in the summer it glistens like nectar.

But at all times of the day and in every season the Yoga-pitha is filled with unlimited sweetness. It is a forest-garden overgrown with endless varieties of plants and bedecked with priceless sparkling jewels.

The rustling of leaves and the whish of swaying branches — moved by breezes that carry throughout Vraja the irresistible melodies issuing forth from its mysterious peak — pervade the atmosphere.

O gentle Vaisnavas! If upon rising from sleep you call upon the Yoga-pitha’s eight names (namastaka) with affection, then Mahadeva promises that you will attract Govindaji and attain love for Krsna.

Just say,

**“Candravali-duradarsa, Radha-saubhagya-mandira, Sri Ratna-mandapa, Srngara-mandapa, Saubhagya-mandapa, Maha-madhurya-mandapa, Samrajya-mandapa, Surata-mandapa.”**

Recite the names of the Yoga-pitha as you do the eighteen-syllable Gopala mantra, and meditate upon Sri Govinda always, as Lord Brahma and his associates do on the topmost material planet.

*Vrndavane yoga-pithe kalpa-taru-vane ratna-mandapa tahe ratna- simhasane*  
*sri-govinda vasiyachena vrajendra-nandana madhurya prakdsi’ karena jagat mohana*

**“Amidst a forest of desire trees in the principal temple of Vraja, Lord Govinda sits upon a throne made of gems. Remember Him there, displaying in full His world-enchanting glory and sweetness.”**

Visualise at His left, beautiful Srimati Radharani and Her close personal friends, with whom Govinda enjoys the rasa-lila and many other confidential loving pastimes found only in Vraja.

Without doubt, Gopala’s eighteen-syllable mantra (astadasaksara) bestows upon the offenceless chanter great feelings of amorous love, love like that of the milkmaid friends and maidservants of Sri Radha.

In this mantra—klim krsnaya govindaya gopijana-vallabhaya svaha — the bija is the kama-bija, the rsi is Kamadeva, the devata is Govinda, and the sakti is Radha, the singular goddess of the Yoga-pitha.

How can any doubt then persist that devotees who meditate upon Govinda at the Yoga-pitha, as suggested by this mantra, will gradually develop affection for Him, affection like that of the gopis!

But persons attached to worldly friends, the possibility of liberation, or the abode of Narayana, should not meditate upon the smiling face of Govinda as He stands on the Yamuna’s shore.

In this regard Srila Prabhupada was very fond of ci ting a verse to warn those with lingering material attachments that it may be dangerous to see Govinda and His transcendentally beguiling form.

*Smeram bhangi-traya-paricitam saci-vistirna-drstim vamsi-nyastadhara-kisalayam ujjvalam candrakena*  
*gavindakhyam hari-tanum itah kesi-tirthopakanthe nut preksisthas tava yadi sakhe bandhu-sange ’sci rangah*

**“My dear friend, if you are indeed attached to your worldly friends, do not look at the smiling face of Lord Govinda as He stands on the bank of the Yamuna at Kesi-ghata.**

**“Casting sidelong glances, He places His flute to His lips, which seem like newly blossomed twigs. His transcendental body, bending in three places, appears very bright in the moonlight.”**

As devotees we accept what is favourable for our service to the Lord, His devotees, and our spiritual masters. Rejecting what is not favourable, we think, “Radha and Krsna are the only goal of my life.”

Confident that the divine couple will protect those who surrender to Them even once, pure devotees pray to their benefactors and well-wishers for shelter, guidance, refuge, and protection:

“Radha and Krsna! Please rescue me from the ocean of birth and death, from the troubles connected to home, friends, and family, from the fears that restrict me from becoming Your surrendered devotee.

“Today I, the abode of all offences, neglectful of my spiritual duties, and rejected by those who give shelter, place myself at Your lotus feet along with everything I possess in this life and future lives.

“O master of Radha! O beloved of Krsna! As You two are the only goal of my life, I offer to You every thought, word, and deed — my very self. I am yours. Please, therefore, be my shelter!

“O Radha and Krsna! You are like two great oceans of mercy. I beg You, therefore, to engulf this sinner with the waves of Your mercy and engage in Your service this offender who now surrenders to You.”

I have not described even the slightest fraction of the Yoga-pitha in the unmanifest realm, which can be seen in this world only by highly advanced Vaisnavas who have received the grace of Sri Radha.

Now let us hear a pastime that took place in the Yoga-pitha. By hearing such things, may we come to appreciate the laudability of the ecstatic love unique to the cowherd damsels of Vraja.

**\* \* \* \***

Krsna and Arjuna were once resting beneath a tree by the bank of the Yamuna when Arjuna, provoked by a curiosity long harboured in his heart, took hold of his dear friend’s hands andasked:

“O Krsna! If You truly accept me as a faithful and intimate friend, tell me something of Your beloved gopis that You have not disclosed to anyone else, including great souls like Sankara or Brahma."

In the silence that followed Arjuna’s request — a silence weighed down by Arjuna’s fear that he may have crossed the bounds of decorum— Krsna raised His eyebrows and gently nodded.

Arjuna took heart and continued, “Please tell me of the various kinds of gopis, their names, where they live, how they dress, what their ages are, and how You exchange loving pastimes with them.

“And tell me things I have not asked You of, things You know will enable me to understand the mysteries of the cowherd girls’ love for You, and of Your singular love for them.”

Reluctant at first, Krsna said, “What you have asked cannot be known even by men in the spiritual world — not to mention the men or women of this world — no matter how dear they are to Me.”

But when Arjuna persisted and fell at Krsna’s feet, the Lord embraced His friend and replied, What you have asked for cannot he explained in words. One must partake of it directly, in a body fit for the task.

“Worship the goddess Tripura-sundari: who guards over My eternal realm of Vraja, and propitiate her for the fulfilment of your desires. Without her blessing, even I cannot satisfy yourrequest.”

Elated, Arjuna eagerly proceeded to a temple of the goddess situated in a very beautiful grove of flower-bearing trees resounding with the chatter of parrots, cuckoos, and doves.

Dressed in red and richly ornamented, golden-complexioned Tripura-sundari sat on a lotus beside stalks of sugarcane. In her four hands she held four items — a bow, goad, noose, and a sheaf of flower-arrows.

Repeatedly prostrating himself before the deity who had now taken the form of a sixteen-year-old girl and whose left foot rested on a sri-yantra, Krsna’s friend humbly said, “I am known as Arjuna.”

Tripura-sundari was well acquainted with Arjuna’s fame as a friend of the Lord. She also knew of Arjuna’s desire to enter into the secrets of Vraja, and she had assumed the form of a young girl to teach him.

The goddess initiated Arjuna into the science known as balavidya, which demanded suitable austerities, the chanting of an appropriate mantra, and daily worship of the goddess according to scripture.

After some time Arjuna’s worship bore fruit, and Tripura-sundari again appeared before him. This time she placed Arjuna in the care of one of her female attendants and sent the two of them to Vrndavana.

But the Vrndavana Arjuna entered was the transcendental realm in which Krsna is always absorbed in a great festival of love, and the mood in which Arjuna beheld Vraja was that of a Vraja-vasi.

As he walked through Vrndavana’s forests, felt their atmosphere, and heard their sounds, Arjuna was so overwhelmed by love for Krsna, a sort of love he had never known before, that he fainted.

For a long time Arjuna was completely overcome by these newfound feelings, until the goddess’s maidservant revived him, helped him rise to his feet, and steadied him with encouraging words.

Arjuna felt convinced he was a resident of the divine realm he had just entered, but outwardly he still appeared in the guise of a warrior. Moreover, his friend Krsna, the moon of Vraja, was not to be found.

He implored Tripura-sundari’s attendant, “Is there some further penance I must undergo?” Without speaking a word, the devi led Arjuna south to a large lake that resembled a thousand-petalled lotus.

She instructed him where and how to bathe in the lake — made sacred by Krsna’s presence there during the annual celebration of the spring festival in honour of Cupid — and then she vanished.

Arjuna did as he was told and slowly immersed himself in the lake, whose waters were tinged with the pollen of lotuses and perfumed by honey from the trees flowering by the lakeside.

Thrice Arjuna fully submerged himself and then came out of the water, startled to find his previously unclothed body now fully dressed and ornamented in attire befitting a village maid.

Bending over the surface of the lake, Arjuna gazed in wonder at his reflection. It was in all ways the likeness of a beautiful young gopi whose form, dress, and demeanour were meant only to please Krsna.

The image gazing back at Arjuna, with its restless cloud-grey eyes, dancing eyebrows, and ring-studded nose, was that of a beautiful, fair-complexioned girl at the gateway of budding youth.

As Arjuna beheld his new outward appearance — dress, ornaments, and all — by Krsna’s illusory power, he gradually forgot everything he had known in his previous identity as a Yadu.

Unable to recall who she had been and unaware of who she was now, the girl — to be known as Arjuniya— stood where she was, confused and uncertain what to do, until a voice from the sky addressed her:

“Beautiful lady! Walk along the path leading east until you reach another lake. There you will meet more girls like you, your friends who will help you fulfil your heart’s desire.”

With no other option than to obey the mysterious voice, Arjuniya walked along the path, all the while feeling her amorous love for Sri Krsna steadily increase, even as she wondered who she was.

In time she arrived at a beautiful lake crowded with lotus flowers and swarming with waterfowl. The four sides of the kunda were thick with carefully manicured groves of blossoming trees and vines.

Arjuniya-gopi saw that there was no one present, and so she sat down by the waterside, dejected. As she sipped a few palmfuls of the nectarean water to quench her thirst, she heard a noise.

From the far side of the lake Arjuniya could hear the sounds of tinkling ankle bells and softly chattering voices. Soon she saw a bevy of beautiful young damsels emerge from the forest.

As the girls gathered at the top of a ghata, Arjuniya could perceive that mature amorous love was the root cause of their spiritual qualities, bodily beauty, youthful sweetness, and aristocratic manners.

Arjuniya identified with the girls’ mood of love, but she felt humbled by the greatness of their character. She simply stood there, lowered her face, and shyly scratched the ground with her toe.

But the girls could not fail to notice the solitary beauty standing on the opposite shore. They turned to each other and asked in hushed tones, “Who is she? Where did she come from?”

Driven by curiosity, they scurried around the lake and prompted the wisest among them, a gopi named Priyamuda, to question Arjuniya: “O beguiling one! Why do you sulk here alone?

“What is your name, who are your parents, and in which village were you born? It troubles us to see that in this realm of delight you clearly suffer from anxiety, bereft of friend or lover.”

Still humbled by the obvious greatness of her new-found well-wishers, Arjuniya modestly bowed before them, and in a voice and manner sweet enough to entice the mind of Cupid, she replied:

“I don’t know anything about my identity—whose daughter or whose wife I am, nor how I came to this land. I remember only that a goddess had me bathe in a lake nearby and then a voice directed me here.”

Arjuniya-gopi continued, “That voice told me I would find friends here who would help me fulfil my desire. After drinking the water of this lake, just as the voice foretold, at once I saw all of you.

“O illustrious ones whose beauty humiliates the wives of the devas! If you think me qualified, please tell me who you are, who your parents are and — most important of all — who is your lover?”

The cowherd girls of Goloka nodded knowingly to one another; they could at once understand the identity of this mysterious girl and the pastime to which Krsna was calling them.

**\* \* \* \***

Priyamuda-gopi continued to speak for her friends, “We are all the daughters of cowherds from nearby villages and our lover is the blackish moon of Vrndavana, Sri Krsna.

She then pointed out three groups of gopis amongst them: “Previously they were goddesses, they the sacred Vedas, and they were great sages. The rest of us have always been milkmaids in thisLand.

“Despite our diverse skills and varied natures, our loving disposition to the lord of Radha is our common bond. Now that Providence has sent you to us, we will introduce you to the ways of our love.”

With that, Priyamuda-gopi introduced the cowherd girls in each of the four groups, beginning with the daughters of the devas: “Here is Purnarasa, this is Rasavallari, Madayanti, and Kalavati.”

Amongst the personified Vedas she introduced beauties like Udgita, Sugita, Kalagita, and Vipanci; and amongst the sages, pure-hearted girls like Priyavrata, Ratnarekha, Saudamani, and Kanti.

Priyamuda then turned to the eternally liberated gopis, of whom she was one, and introduced Candrika, Varnavali, Malati, Kancanamala and others. Finally she said, “In time you will get to know all of us.”

Priyamuda then took Arjuniya by the hand and said, “Lotus-faced girl! Follow me back to the lake whence you came. After you bathe there I will give you a mantra that will bring success in your quest.”

Through the chanting of that secret mantra, along with the teachings and meditations that accompanied it, Priyamuda introduced Arjuniya-gopi into the worship of Sri Radha, the beloved of Krsna.

Priyamuda gave Arjuniya a grove in which to reside and visited her daily to offer further guidance and instruction on how to cultivate the moods of loving devotion unique to the friends of Sri Radha.

Then one day, in the presence of Priyamuda, Arjuniya’s austerities bore fruit: along with a few companions, Radha appeared there in the grove in which Arjuniya had been so sincerely worshipping Her.

Srimati Radharani appeared to be the source and sum total of all things sublime. She illuminated with Her bodily lustre the entire grove and everything in the ten directions beyond.

Radha’s complexion resembled a golden campaka flower, and Her limbs were perfect in every way. The indisputable paragon of womanhood, Her smile and deportment were yet kindly and simple.

She raised Her right hand in benediction and said, “You have been favoured by My friends, whose words never go in vain; therefore I will personally take you to the Cupid of Vrndavana.”

Radharani’s reassuring words resonated with the longing in Arjuniya’s heart; consequently, that gopi fell at the feet of Vrndavana’s goddess as her body erupted in symptoms of ecstasy.

After some sakhis had comforted Arjuniya and brought her back to external consciousness, they all returned, in the company of Radha, to the lake where Arjuniya had originally met the gopis.

Radharani assigned Arjuniya-gopi to one of the lakeside groves, spoke a mantra composed of Krsna’s names into her ear, and bound her to an ancient vow known as Gokulanatha.

Radha blessed Arjuniya with steady devotion to Govinda and taught her to meditate upon dark-complexioned Krsna, adorned with many ornaments, more beautiful than a million Cupids, and full of love.

She consigned Arjuniya to the care of Priyamuda, and with words consecrated by the sweetness of Her smile, said, “I will return for her after she has received the grace of her worshipable Deity.”

Radha returned to the Yoga-pitha, where gopis were dancing to the song of Krsna’s flute, and Arjuniya at once began to follow the new instructions she had received under the guidance of her gopi-guru.

Day after day eager Arjuniya rose early, bathed, collected flowers for worship, offered herself to Krsna while singing songs about Him, and then, in loving absorption, recited a mantra composed of His names.

One day Priyamuda advised Arjuniya to draw the geometric representation (yantra) of her mantra, and before a picture of Krsna, offer a lotus flower, upon the petals of which that mantra was written.

In loving devotion Arjuniya offered Krsna flowers, incense, a lamp, fruits, and perfume. With intense yearning stoking the fires of her love, she called out to Him, “O Krsna! O Krsna!”

Just at that moment in the Yoga-pitha, Govinda, whose heart is always bound by the ropes of His devotees' love, turned to Radha with raised eyebrows and said with a smile, “Quickly, bring her here.”

Radha at once dispatched a messenger, joined by Priyamuda, to where Arjuniya was flooding the lake with her tears and calling to Krsna in such a sorrowful voice that leaves were falling from the trees in pity.

The messenger raised Arjuniya to her feet, embraced her, and said, “Friend! After today you need cry no longer.” Taking Arjuniya and Priyamuda by the hand, she returned with them to Govinda-sthali.

Blissful Arjuniya’s eyes were so full of tears that she couldn’t see where she was, and her heart was pounding so loudly that she could hardly even hear what was going on around her.

Finally, Priyamuda wiped the tears from her disciple’s eyes with the edge of her own veil and whispered into her ear, “Friend! O Arjuniya! Open your eyes and see Him for whom you have pined for so long.”

At first, the only thing Arjuniya could see was Krsna enveloped by golden effulgence, the same Krsna she had been worshipping and meditating upon while on the banks of two lakes.

Although Krsna and His effulgence were shining so brilliantly that they were difficult to behold, it was Arjuniya’s overpowering love that forced her to close her eyes in a faint and fall to the ground.

Steadied by the comforting hands and soothing words of the gopis, Arjuniya gradually rose to her feet, even as ecstasy soaked her body with perspiration and made her limbs shake like windblown leaves.

But by the grace of the Yoga-pitha she finally regained control over her love-torn senses, and at long last, with divine eyes, she could see clearly — Radha and Krsna and Their remarkable realm.

Arjuniya first beheld an incredible desire tree that had a trunk and branches made of gold, leaves made of emeralds, sprouts of coral, and crystal fruit that could produce any object one desired.

Beneath the arbour stood a bejewelled temple within which a gold throne shaped like an eight-petalled lotus was served by aromatic breezes and cooled by gentle clouds of honey-sweet mist.

The flavour of the surroundings stirred passions still further aroused by the humming of intoxicated bees, the sweet cooing of doves, the plaintive call of cuckoos, and the dancing of peacocks.

Krsna’s mood of divine revelry, a collyrium-coloured effulgence emanating from His form, tinted the temple, desire tree, and the encompassing garden-courtyard with an opaque, fog-like darkness.

Fixed on the object of her arduous devotions, Arjuniya lost herself to this vision of Krsna in a way possible only for a Vraja gopi — surely unattainable and unimaginable for even great devotees like Arjuna.

Finally she saw Krsna distinctly, a dark youth with glossy black wavy hair, sporting an elaborately decorated turban topped with a peacock feather, a blue karnikara flower casually tucked over His ear.

His broad forehead, ringed with locks of hair and marked with tilaka, reigned over His buffed-mirror-like cheeks that reflected the insignia of Cupid dangling from His ears, a pair of shark-shaped earrings.

A golden pearl, on a ring piercing the skin between the nostrils of His finely shaped nose, dangled above His ruby-red lips, and a soft smile further inflamed the passion already consuming Arjuniya.

Attracting bees by its sweetness, a long garland of forest flowers graced His neck along with other necklaces fashioned from flowers and pearls, all framing His central ornament, the Kaustubha gem.

Extremely alluring with His long serpentine arms, lion-thin waist, deep lotus navel, and pinkish lotus feet, Krsna’s limbs were further embellished by ornaments fashioned by the best of artisans.

Dressed in yellow garments, radiating a loveliness superior to millions of Cupids, the lord of Radha filled the air with songs from His flute, thus magnifying the strength of His power to enchant.

Just as Arjuniya worried that Krsna — whose every limb displayed Cupid’s youthful pride — might be tired from dancing, the gopi attendants presented Him with various refreshments.

As Radha extended nicely wrapped tambula towards Krsna, Arjuniya was finally so overcome with passionate love, and thus unable to conceal her feelings, that she turned away to hide in a solitary place.

Then all-knowing Krsna rose from His seat and took Arjuniya firmly by the wrist, disappearing with her from the Yoga-pitha just as He had once disappeared with Radha from the rasa dance.

**\* \* \* \***

That great master of loving pastimes then took His beloved on a stroll through the gardens of Govinda-sthali, sometimes holding her hand, sometimes playfully draping His arm over her shoulders.

When Arjuniya complained that the grass and sprouts were hurting her feet, Krsna carried her to a flower cot and then picked a variety of flowers from which He fashioned a crown to decorate her hair.

By such gracious behaviour and romantic exchanges, Krsna plunged the gopi Arjuniya into an ocean of transcendental mellows which even His beloved wives in Dvaraka had never known.

Arjuniya’s mind and senses rose and fell with the uncountable waves of that ocean, sometimes diving beneath its surface to collect valuable pearls of ecstasy just waiting to be culled from the ocean’s floor.

Following the path of kamatmika love she had learned from Tripura- sundari, Priyamuda, and Sri Radha, and then cultivated by chanting her mantras, Arjuniya invested her entire being in Krsna’s pleasure.

Whether a few hours had passed, or an entire night of Brahma, it hardly mattered, for there was not time enough for Arjuniya to satisfy her desire to saturate Krsna’s love with hers.

In a spontaneous way unique to the eternal residents of Vrndavana — especially to the gopis — Arjuniya-gopi gave herself to Krsna without a care for what anyone in wider society might think.

Like a drunkard who is never sated by any amount of wine, Arjuniya drank without stopping from the gold chalice of paramour love, served to her by the unchallenged master of divine intimacy.

After some time, His arm resting on her shoulder, Krsna brought Arjuniya back to the Yoga-pitha, where they were met by the knowing smiles and subdued giggling of their gopi friends.

In a voice pregnant with meaning, Krsna told Priyamuda, “Friend! This girl with a sweet smile is fatigued from our excursion through the forests of Vraja. Take her to the lake for a refreshing bath.”

The two girls walked through the moonlit forest to the lake of a thousand petals, which love-inebriated Arjuniya failed to recognise as the same lake from which she had first emerged as a gopi.

Priyamuda brought Arjuniya to a ghata and helped her change into bathing clothes; then very affectionately, yet with a voice tinged faintly with sadness, she said, “Go ahead, my dear. Refresh yourself.”

Arjuniya-gopi, still thrilling with transcendental ecstasy, walked down the steps into the cool water, painted silver by moonlight, and joyfully dipped below the surface once, twice, three times.

When Arjuniya surfaced for the third time it was daylight, and she was standing chest deep in the Yamuna, facing the prince of Dvaraka, who sat comfortably on a parapet at the top of the ghata.

Before she could speak, Arjuniya caught sight of her reflection in the river’s swift current. That reflection no longer resembled a slimbodied gopi, hut rather Arjuna, the powerfully built warrior-prince.

With full recollection of what had just happened, his eyes fixed upon his dear friend Krsna, Arjuna slowly emerged from the river as a second river flowed from his eyes and into the Yamuna.

Painful separation from his gopi identity, from the secrets of Vraja, and from loving exchanges with Govinda all choked Arjuna's voice. Unable to speak, he stood before Krsna, arms hanging down, dejected.

Arjuna was unable to tolerate the burden of sorrow. He fell before Krsna and buried his head in his friend’s lap, sobbing like a child from whom all loved ones, all protection, had been taken away.

Krsna lovingly stroked Arjuna’s head and consoled him with sweet words. Swept away by the torrent of His friend’s roiling emotions, Krsna’s own tears moistened His hands as He comforted Arjuna.

Gradually both friends composed themselves and sat side by side as birds chirped overhead and waves lapped against the shore. Yet neither could speak of what they had just been through.

Arjuna looked hopefully into Krsna’s eyes and found solace from the sorrow coursing within. It was exactly as Krsna had first told him: of the things Arjuna wanted to know, no one could speak.

The loving pastimes shared between Krsna and the gopis could be known only by entering into them directly with the body, mind, and disposition of a gopi. And Arjuna had been so blessed.

Now that Arjuna was again Krsna’s fraternal companion, endowed with the perfections of a friend’s temperament, it would be futile to speak of, not to mention relive, the prema of the gopi Arjuniya.

Some things were better left unsaid. Wasn’t it with such indirect language that Krsna, at Kuruksetra, had first encouraged Arjuna to search out the Vraja-vasis’ mood?

*Sarva-dharman parityajya —*  
*Mam ekam saranam vraja*  
*aham tvam sarva-papebhyo*  
*moksayisyami ma sucah*

**“Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do notfear.”**

Krsna patted Arjuna’s hand and with an unsteady voice said, “So now you understand! Because you are so dear to Me, I have disclosed these secrets to you. But speaking of them here and there would upset Me.”

Arjuna nodded in agreement and the two friends rose from their seats, mounted their chariot, and returned to Hastinapura, where the citizens and their emperor greeted the two warriors heartily.

Arjuna’s brothers, like Bhima, immediately noticed a change in him but couldn’t discern its cause. Still, as great transcendentalists they also knew that some things are best left unsaid.

That night, and for many days and nights thereafter, Arjuna remained in seclusion, deeply immersed in chanting the mantras he had received in Vraja and remembering his life as the gopi Arjuniya.

It was only at Maharaja Yudhisthira’s explicit request that Arjuna reconnected with responsibilities to both his family and affairs of state, limiting his meditations to the wee hours of the morning.
