“Thus freed from the intoxications of false ego, my purified intelligence will enable me to easily fix my mind upon the lotus feet of that youthful couple who eternally enjoy pastimes at this place.”

In New Vraja-dhama, as in Bhauma Vrndavana, Siva-khor is more like an impression in the earth than it is a lake. It fills up with water during the rainy season and dries out during summer.

Once, in Bhauma Vrndavana, as some local children were playing near Siva-khor, a female jackal, driven by thirst, stealthily came out from the nearby forest and began drinking from the lake.

But the children quickly spotted the jackal and snuck up behind her with sticks. Blocking her escape route to the forest, they chased her down the road where there was no place to hide.

In desperation, the she-jackal ran into the shelter of a foxhole. But the children, hoping to catch and beat her, collected twigs and fallen branches and built a fire outside the hole to smoke the creature out.

Unable to escape and greatly distressed from the heat and smoke, the terrified jackal wailed long and loud, even though she doubted whether anyone would care to rescue her.

But someone who cared did hear her cries — it was soft-hearted Radha, who, along with Her friends and maidservants, was returning home from Radha-kunda to cook sweets for Krsna’s supper.

Even though Radharani had left Krsna only a few moments before, Her heart — bereft of seeing Him, of hearing His voice, of feeling His gentle, loving touch — was already breaking.

As the saying goes, “Only those who have suffered can truly understand the suffering of others." Thus, as soon as She heard the trapped jackal’s pitiful cries, Radha wanted to alleviate her misery.

Sri Radha told Her friends, "Find out who is crying so piteously and bring her to Me.” Without hesitation Lalita followed the plaintive sound to its source and found the excited children and their prey.

Lalita asked what the fire and commotion were all about. The boys explained and she reprimanded them for their cruelty, sent them home, and then scattered the fire with a stick.

The blaze extinguished, she reached inside the foxhole, grabbed the frightened jackal, and deftly pulled it out, pacifying it with sweet words and the touch of her soft, shelter-giving hand.

Lalita-devi then carried the traumatised creature back to her waiting friends, who bombarded her with questions: “Friend! What is it?” “Is it a jackal?” “What happened to the poor thing?”

As the she-jackal rested in the all-purifying embrace of Lalita-devi, spiritual intelligence supplanted her animal ignorance and she could understand herself to be Krsna’s eternal servant.

Lalita then placed that fortunate creature at Radha’s lotus feet, and the she-jackal cried, not so much from the relief of being freed from peril as from the ecstasy of being in the presence of love personified.

As Lalita told the gopis of the jackal’s previous predicament, Radharani stroked its head. By Her touch the animal at once displayed symptoms of spiritual ecstasy, trembling uncontrollably.

Sri Radha addressed the jackal, who sat up and cocked her ears. “O jiva!" Radharani said. “Because you had the good fortune to take birth in Krsna’s land, your days of suffering are now over.

“My friend Lalita embraced you and brought you into her fold. Thus I accept you as My own. From now on you will be My maidservant and daily join Me when I meet the son of Nanda by My lake. Rejoice!”

Indeed, the jackal did rejoice, as did the gopis. And just as Radha said, by the mercy of Lalita-devi and the dhama, the jackal attained the body of a Vraja gopi and became Sri Radha’s maidservant.

This pastime, although an historical event, is also allegorical. The she-jackal represents the conditioned living entity, which is feminine by nature and meant to serve the supreme male, Sri Krsna.

Just as conditioned souls seek relief from the miseries encountered in the forest of material enjoyment, the she-jackal sought to quench her thirst by drinking the waters of Siva-khor.

But material enjoyment only leads to further suffering, and so the children chased the jackal into a hole, where she felt the scorching heat of misery that conditioned souls inflict on one another.

And just as a suffering soul turns towards the Lord, who always hears the prayers of His parts and parcels, the she-jackal cried out for a saviour and was heard by Sri Radha, who is always close at hand.

Out of great compassion, Radharani sent Lalita-devi to rescue the she-jackal, just as Radha or Krsna sends the spiritual master to help the conditioned souls cross the dangerous ocean of material existence.

Such conditioned souls, forgetful of their eternal nature, do not easily surrender to Sri Guru; similarly, although Lalita had come to save the jackal, she still had to pull it forcibly from its hiding place.

But in the end, the comforting touch and teachings of the spiritual master destroy all misgivings. The goal of life, surrender to Krsna, is then self-evident, just as it was with the she-jackal.

And finally, one gets Krsna's company by the mercy of Sri Guru. The jackal likewise attained — by the grace of Lalita-devi— service to Krsna in her constitutional identity as Sri Radha’s maidservant.

**\* \* \* \***

As I stood beside Siva-khor, to my left was the greenhouse of Tulasi-devi, which represents the famous Malyahari-kunda, and where Vrndavana’s caretaker, Vrnda-devi, has her Yoga-pitha residence.

During the winter months, Gopisvara Mahadeva and his consort Yogamaya reside here with Vrnda-devi, enjoying the special atmosphere unique to a forest comprised exclusively of tulasi trees.

In the future, when Radha-Syamasundara’s temple is expanded, Tulasi-devi will have better accommodation in a new greenhouse, but the holy places associated with this site will remain where they are.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami has written a book known as “The Pearl Story,” which begins at Malyahari-kunda a day before Dipavali and takes the reader on a journey of amorous humour throughout Vraja.

Radha and the gopis usually collect flowers from Puspavana and bring them to the bank of Malyahari-kunda, where they string garlands for worshipping the sun god at Surya-kunda.

But truth be told, most of the garlands the gopis string are offered to Krsna. Only a few are used for worshipping the sun god, a fact that does not bother him at all because he also worships Krsna.

But on the day Dasa Gosvami’s story starts, the gopis were not stringing flower garlands but pearl necklaces for worshipping their cows as a part of the Dipavali and Govardhana-puja celebrations.

Through an informant—the parrot Vicaksana— news of this uncommon activity quickly found its way to Krsna. Bursting with curiosity, He left His herd at Govardhana and came to this very spot.

For some time Krsna hid behind the trees to observe the gopis as they strung one pearl necklace after another. Finally He cleared His throat to make His presence known and stepped into the clearing.

The gopis were not caught by surprise, however, as their own spies had already informed them of Krsna’s stealthy approach. They pretended to be unmoved by His presence as they continued to work.

Naturally, Krsna felt slighted by the gopis’ indifference, especially by Radha’s refusal to look in His direction. Still, He retained His composure and politely addressed the girls as He sat in Radha’s group.

Since the gopis were stringing their pearls into decorations for their cows, Krsna mildly asked, “Friends! Could you spare a few pearls so that I can also decorate My two favourite cows, Hamsi and Harini?”

But the girls were not receptive to Krsna’s proposal. Although He asked them several times, the only thing He received was ridicule from the gopis and one tiny broken pearl from Lalita-devi.

That humiliating gesture was the final straw. Krsna stood up suddenly, His face red with anger. He shook His index finger at every gopi present and said, “Just wait! You all just wait!

“You are the owners of a vast treasure-house of pearls, but you couldn’t find it in your hearts to grant Me, your prince regent, the loan of a few necklaces? All right! You just wait!

“If that’s your attitude, then don’t call Me a miser if fate somehow turns the tables on you and you end up begging Me for pearls. Don’t doubt it, your miserly ways will lead you into poverty and ruin.”

The gopis laughed at Krsna’s outburst and His aggrieved departure, but the wisest amongst them, Lalita, recognised His words as prophetic, expecting a pastime to soon enrich the mellows of Vraja.

While nursing His wounded ego on the way back to Nandagrama, Krsna hatched an ingenious plan, for which He invoked His creative potencies and solicited the co-operation of Vrndavana’s mystical soil.

In a field at the foot of Nandisvara Hill, Krsna sowed the earth with all the pearls in Nanda Maharaja’s treasury, including the special necklaces His father and mother wore every day.

In the days that followed, despite His parent’s warnings and the gopis’ ridicule, Krsna stubbornly tended His pearl field, engaging His friends in watering, weeding, and policing His garden. And then one day —

Beautiful pearls began to sprout on the golden vines that soon sagged under the weight of their enormous pearl-fruit. And Krsna joyfully harvested them right before the eyes of the incredulous gopis.

Within a few days Nanda Maharaja’s treasury was overflowing with pearls, and Krsna was decorating Himself, His friends, cows, buffaloes, and even the monkeys of Vraja with strands of costly pearls.

As Vrndavana’s soil kept sprouting this unprecedented opulence, the gopis, who had earlier begrudged Krsna a few meagre necklaces, were now scheming how they too could enrich their treasuries.

Against Lalita’s advice, Radha’s friends — and soon many other groups of gopis — collected all their families’ pearls, even priceless heirlooms, and planted them in rows, following Krsna’s example.

The gopis carefully watered their pearl-seeds with milk, but after a few days plants appeared that looked suspiciously like thorn bushes. And sure enough, instead of pearls they yielded burrs.

The gopis were devastated. The entirety of their families’ wealth had been reduced to thorns and burrs. Only out of fear of husbands and in-laws did they swallow their pride and do the unthinkable.

The unthinkable was to beg alms from Krsna. Every day, sitting at the roadside entrance to His astonishingly bountiful pearl field, Krsna made a show of counting and recounting His morning harvest.

Just as the Lord’s pastime potency had first inspired the gopis to reject Krsna’s request, it now compelled them to humbly approach Him for a donation of pearls with the hope of replacing their lost heirlooms.

To fulfil their request would have required fewer pearls than Krsna had used to ornament the monkeys of Vraja. But He wanted to spice up His loving exchanges with the gopis, and so He was reticent.

Throughout an entire day of excruciating negotiations, during which Krsna demanded impossible prices for even a single pearl, the defenceless gopis were the brunt of His jokes.

As the sun set, the gopis were no closer to realising their goal than they had been that morning, so they surrendered themselves to fate. With Radha in the centre of their group, they marched off.

Relishing His memories of the barter, arguments, and jokes He had just shared with the gopis, Krsna sat down before a large basket of His finest pearls. From amongst those treasures, He selected the very best.

Then with the help of His friends He fashioned all manner of ornaments for Radha, Lalita, Visakha, and the rest of the gopis, placing each set of gifts in its own specially labelled, ornate box.

What’s more, Krsna collected a large basket of unstrung pearls, entrusting the entire endowment to His most intimate friends, Subala and Madhumangala, who joyfully set off for Malyahari-kunda.

The gopis had failed to procure pearls from Krsna to replenish their families’ treasuries, but they felt greatly enriched nonetheless, having shared such a wonderful pastime with their beloved.

Thus the boys, upon arriving with Krsna’s gifts, found the girls surprisingly joyful: they were in the midst of exuberantly recounting the details of their day-long barter with Krsna.

The gopis graciously accepted their gifts and excitedly opened their individual boxes, immersed in the happiness of knowing that each pearl ornament was a reflection of Krsna’s love for them.

In return for the gifts, Radha sent Krsna a freshly made jasmine garland. After the boys had gone, the gopis laughed at how they had purchased untold wealth for a handful of flowers.

Lalita said, “It seemed that we could not agree with Krsna on a fair price for the pearls we wanted, but it’s clear He felt sorry for our plight. Just see! He has given us much more than we lost — ”

Visakha interrupted, “Do you think Krsna will be satisfied with a flower garland as payment for these treasures? The only item of comparable value we possess is our dear friend Sri Radha."

At this the gopis erupted in laughter. Radha covered Her face with Her veil as She hit Visakha with a lotus flower, all the while trying to conceal Her blushing cheeks and irrepressible smile.

Of course it would be just as Visakha said. After all, scripture declares that gifts should be exchanged in kind. Since Radha was a treasure chest of love’s ornaments, only She could match Krsna’s gifts of love.

That night Radha and Krsna met by the banks of the Yamuna and decorated each other with love’s most wonderful pearls, of which They both were the plants, cultivators, farmers, traders, and owners.

Ever since that time, the water of Malyahari-kunda has possessed the sweet flavour of those loving exchanges, and the surrounding garden is known as “the place of pearls” (Mukta-ksetra).

Vrndavana is an ocean filled with waves of Krsna’s nectarean fun, and Radha’s and Krsna’s quarrel over pearls is but one amongst the millions of such waves to which I offer my humble obeisances.

“Let us offer our obeisances to the prince of Vraja, who enchants the world with His pastimes, whose complexion is like a blooming blue lotus flower, and who is as lovely as millions of cupids.”

**\* \* \* \***

Dear readers, please note! When doing parikrama of the Radha-kunda area in New Vraja-dhama, all the pastime places cannot he visited at one time, as is easily done in Bhauma Vrndavana.

In Bhauma Vrndavana, the many pastime places that lie both inside and outside the parikrama path that circles Radha-kunda and Syama- kunda can easily be visited in their natural sequence.

In New Vraja-dhama, however, pilgrims must visit the pastime places outside the parikrama path first and then, by entering the temple, they can see those places that lie inside the parikrama path.

This is because Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda are inside the temple— pastime places outside the parikrama path are outside the temple, and pastime places on the banks of these two lakes are inside.

In my parikrama of New Vraja-dhama I visited all the pastime places outside and inside the temple, but for simplicity’s sake I here describe Radha-kunda parikrama mostly as it is done in Bhauma Vrndavana.

The first place on the parikrama is Radha-Kunjabihari temple and the puspa-samadhi of Gaurakisora Dasa Babaji established in 1935 by Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, a year before his departure.

Devotees who have transformed themselves into renunciation personified (saksad-vairagya-murtaye), as did Babaji Maharaja, can share the feelings of love in separation he savoured — no one else.

But truth be told, in this age it is virtually impossible to follow externally Gaurakisora Dasa Babaji’s austere way of life. The inner mood of his renunciation, however, is within reach and much needed.

That inner mood is to abandon any thing or deed that obstructs the development of pure love and, conversely, to embrace any thing or deed that promotes the development of pure love for Krsna.

Beside the Babaji’s samadhi in New Vraja-dhama is the temple of all-powerful Lord Nrsimhadeva. Devotees pray that He will free them from any and every desire, except the desire to serve Krsna.

In Lord Nrsimha’s mouth the great masters of eloquence reside, upon His chest rests the goddess of fortune, and His heart contains the divine potency of consciousness. Let us worship Him!

Following the arrival of Sudarsana cakra, Lord Nrsimha personally came to New Vraja-dhama so that Radha-Syama’s pastimes would not be disturbed by the necessity of protecting the dhama from attackers.

The advent of Laksmi-Nrsimha in New Vraja-dhama is Their own pastime, and so it deserves to be heard and remembered by devotees circumambulating the dhama. I retell it here.

A short while after Radha and Syama arrived in New Vraja-dhama, a deity of Sudarsana was donated. To protect the dhama and purify the hearts of its residents, I accepted and installed the deity.

Nrsimha’s nails are a manifestation of the Lord’s cakra, appearing specifically to kill Hiranyakasipu, and on the back of this Sudarsana deity we found a small form of a seated Nrsimha. How wonderful!

Yet I was sorry that only the pujaris were able to have darsana of Lord Nrsimha and that He was always seated with His back to His devotees. “What a shame that everyone cannot see Him,” I thought.

I am less significant than an ant. My lamentations are of no spiritual consequence. But, coincidentally, it seems that Lord Nrsimhadeva also desired to be more visible in New Vraja-dhama.

Just at that time, my beloved friend Indradyumna Swami had adopted ancient Deities of Laksmi-Nrsimhadeva whose servants could no longer worship the Lord and His divine consort.

Maharaja accepted the opportunity for Their Lordships’ worship, delighted at the new responsibility They had entrusted him with. Some time later he returned to the west with the Deities.

On his way to a nearby preaching engagement, Indradyumna Maharaja stopped over in Budapest, only to find out the following morning that his flight was postponed for two days.

With time to spare, Indradyumna Swami visited New Vraja-dhama, had darsana of Radha and Syama, met with the devotees, and returned to Budapest the same evening to fly out the following day.

But early the next morning I received a phone call from Maharaja. Excited, he said, “Last night I dreamt of Laksmi-Nrsimhadeva. They were being worshipped on an altar at the farm.

“Then, on the hill opposite the temple, enormous monsters appeared one after the other. But before they could approach, Nrsimhadeva stretched out His arms and set upon them with His long nails.

“As soon as Nrsimhadeva’s nails pierced the monsters they disappeared. The menacing threat was quickly dispatched, and New Vraja-dhama was as peaceful as it had been before.”

Maharaja paused for a moment and then said, “During the dream, and even after I woke up, I felt that Laksmi-Nrsimha were telling me They wanted to stay in New Vraja-dhama.

“And you know, this morning I can’t stop thinking that all along Their plan must have been to come to Krsna Valley. They just used me as an instrument to carry Them there.”

What could I say? If the Supreme Lord desired to relocate to New Vraja-dhama to bless us with His protection, as His humble servants we were obliged to serve Him with all our hearts.

Since that time I have reflected on these events, and my humble opinion is that protecting Krsna Valley from unwanted elements was only a pretext for Laksmi-Nrsimha’s appearance in the dhama.

Could it be that They were primarily drawn to the sweetness of New Vraja-dhama and the innocence and sincerity of the devotees who have dedicated themselves in loving service to Radha and Syama?

Merciful Lord Nrsimha and His consort, knowing how difficult it is to perfect vraja-bhakti, came to remove the monster-like impurities that obstruct devotees from reaching their goal.

O fortunate residents of New Vraja-dhama! Just behold the beauty of Laksmi-Nrsimha, roll in the dust before this great Lord, and one day your voice will become choked in the ecstasy of krsna-prema.

As long as the six enemies pollute our hearts, we will remain ineligible for loving service to Radha and Krsna, but Nrsimhadeva’s full mercy will purify us completely and make us eligible.

Then, one day, as we weep and beg at the lotus feet of Lord Nrsimha, who is fearsome to demons but pleasing to devotees, He will remove our fears and speak the following sweet words:

“Dear child!” He will say. “Happily worship Radha and Syama in New Vraja-dhama and develop attraction to the holy names. By the mercy of the acaryas and My devotees, you will transcend all obstacles.

“Serve the mission of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, live only for the basic necessities of life, and worship with a purified heart the pastimes of Radha and Krsna, which are an endless cascade of sweet nectar.”

Then the Lord will joyfully place His feet upon our heads, and by His mercy alone we will instantly display all the symptoms of ecstasy that identify one exposed to love for Radha and Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

The next place is the Purana (“old”) Radha-Krsna temple. Dasa Gosvami found the temple’s original Deities while excavating Radha-kunda and entrusted a local brahmana with Their worship.

This was therefore the first temple constructed at Radha-kunda. Unfortunately the original Deities were stolen, but replicas are now being worshipped by descendants of the original brahmana.

In the courtyard of the temple stand two entwined trees — a banyan and a nima. Elsewhere such trees would represent Laksmi and Narayana, but in Radha-kunda they are revered as Radha and Syama.

The western shore of Radha-kunda is called Jhulana-ghata because there was once a banyan tree between Tungavidya’s and Sudevi’s groves from which Radha and Krsna would enjoy swing pastimes.

At present, a humble stone frame for a swing (jhulana-sthali) stands there to commemorate the spot where the divine couple once enjoyed Their pastimes, and invisible to material eyes, still do to this very day.

The forest there is called the “happiness of the rainy season” (Varsabarsa) because whenever Radha and Krsna want to swing, Vraja provides clear skies and summer warmth, even in the rainy season.

Attached by two red ropes inset with pearls, a swing of exceptional shape, size, and qualities hangs from a horizontal branch of that enormous banyan tree at Jhulana-sthali.

It has eighteen seats — two seats for Radha and Krsna, surrounded by two whorls of eight for the sakhis and manjaris — unlike the many other two-seated swings that grace this area, like the one at Imli-tala.

As usual, Krsna eagerly mounts this swing and unwilling Radha has to be lifted up by Vrnda and others. Some gopis then push the divine couple as others stand around and sing or tell jokes.

If Radha and Krsna are seated on the swing alone, it retracts its outer seats and the gopis push it firmly. Radha then trembles slightly out of fear and holds on tightly to Her lover.

Radha’s and Krsna’s hair, sashes, and clothes loosen in the breeze, and Their sparkling earrings and garlands — as if in a contrary mood — sway in the opposite direction as the swing.

Once the tempo of the swinging picks up, restless-eyed Radha calls out for help from Her eight girlfriends, and as they climb onto the swing, it instantly unfolds its first whorl of eight seats for them.

While swinging, they render many services: Lalita and Visakha serve betel, Campakalata and Citra fan, Tungavidya and Indulekha serve nectar drinks, and Rangadevi and Sudevi apply fragrant ointments.

In addition to expanding and contracting according to the divine couple’s needs, the swing manifests another amazing quality: each seated gopi simultaneously sees Radha and Krsna facing only her.

Another wonder—caused by the swing or perhaps by Krsna — occurs when Krsna, visible to all, appears beside each gopi, including Radha, and simultaneously embraces all of them.

Then Krsna resumes a single form, and at Radha’s instigation Lalita — and the other gopis in turn — sits to Krsna’s right as He rests one arm on her shoulder and the other on Radha’s at His left.

As Krsna revels in the company of the most beautiful girls in all creation, Radha cleverly positions Lalita and Visakha on either side of Krsna and then nimbly jumps off the swing to push it by Herself.

In this way, all the cowherd girls have the chance to sit in pairs beside Krsna while the others glorify Him with songs that flow spontaneously from their love-filled hearts.

After Lalita whispers in Radha’s ear, Radha smilingly ascends the swing with sixteen gopis. She then invites any other gopi that may be waiting to ascend the swing and also sit with Her and Krsna.

As difficult as it may be to find a fitting metaphor for hundreds of gopis seated around Radha and Krsna on a swing, it is impossible to say what it looks like when Krsna expands Himself beside each gopi.

Finally, at Lalita’s signal all the gopis jump off and push the divine couple so high and fast that to Krsna’s great delight, Radha inevitably embraces Her beloved in fear.

These are but a few of the swing pastimes the divine couple enjoy at Jhulana-sthali. Such things are visible to worthy Vaisnavas who have received the gift of pure love for Radha and Krsna.

During such pastimes Radha’s maidservants are able to perform many services, like collecting fragrant flowers, spreading flower petals on the swing’s seats, and covering those flower petals with thin cloth.

While Radha and Krsna are swinging, Their maidservants throw flower petals, sing songs, and offer arati to Them. Once the divine couple get down, the gopis tidy Their hair, clothes, and ornaments.

Some gopis push the swing while others stand on either side with betel leaves in hand so that when the swing slows down they can expertly place that delicacy in the lotus mouths of Radha and Krsna.

Sometimes, when all eighteen seats of the swing are expanded, the maidservants climb aboard to serve fruits and other refreshments, and then they eat Radha’s and Krsna’s remnants.

Regarding these maidservants led by Rupa-manjari, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami writes, tambularpana-pada-mardana-payo'dandbhisaradibhi vrndaranya'mahesvarim priyataya yas tosayanti priyah —

Prana-presta-sakhi-kulad api kilasankocita-bhumikah keli-bhumisu rupa-manjari-mukhas ta dasikah samsraye: “By offering Her betel nuts, by massaging Her feet, by bringing Her water—

“By arranging for Her meetings with Lord Krsna, and by performing many other services, many gopi maidservants affectionately please Sri Radha, the great queen of Vrndavana forest.

“When the divine couple enjoy Their pastimes these maidservants are not at all shy to serve, even when the asta-sakhis are. I take shelter of these maidservants, who have Rupa-manjari as their leader."

It is said that if these manjaris cannot see Radha for a moment they feel forlorn, almost dead from sorrow. It is wonderful how they have attained this state in which they love Her more than their lives.

There are eight prominent maidservants (manjaris), including Rupa-manjari. In their sadhaka forms they appear as eminent associates of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, who are followed by all Gaudiya Vaisnavas.

Each of these eight maidservants — like Sri Radha’s eight closest friends (sakhis) —has her own grove situated around Radha-kunda, as well as her own unique form, dress, personality, and service.

So that devotees can better know these eight principal manjaris, I will now briefly describe them, beginning with Sri Rupa-manjari, whom all Vaisnavas also know as Srila Rupa Gosvami Prabhupada.

In fact, Gaudiya Vaisnavas so keenly identify themselves as followers of Rupa-manjari in her sadhaka form — Srila Rupa Gosvami — that such Vaisnavas are commonly known as “rupanuga Vaisnavas.”

In books like Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu and Ujjvala-nilamani, Rupa Gosvami has systematically set out the principles that underlie the science of devotional mellows. Thus he is known as the rasa-acarya.

Within a corner of Lalita-devi’s grove, Rupa-manjari resides in her own sub-grove called Rupollasa-kunja. In New Vraja-dhama this kunja is designated as the front left portion of the temple room.

Sri Rupa is beautiful and graceful, her complexion is the colour of gorocana, she dresses like Lalita-devi in clothes the colour of peacock feathers, and her eternal age is thirteen-and-a-half.

When the divine couple, full of laughter and mirth, try to outdo each other in a game of dice, Radha reclines on Her seat so that Rupa- manjari can serve Her by gently massaging Her feet.

At other times, when the youthful couple of Vraja — exhausted from Their pastimes, Their eyes barely open — recline and converse on a couch of flowers, Rupa cools them with a fan of blossoming vines.

Next to Rupollasa-kunja, within the grove of Visakha-devi, is very beautiful Vilasanandada-kunja, where Vilasa-manjari always stays as one of the friends and followers of Sri Rupa.

In Lord Caitanya’s pastimes Vilasa-manjari appears as Srila Jiva Gosvami to systematise the philosophical conclusions of the Gaudiya sampradaya. Sri Jiva is known, therefore, as the siddhanta-acarya.

Vilasa-manjari’s bodily hue is golden like a ketaki flower, her silken dress is black and gold like the stripes of a bumblebee, and her tender age is just four days shy of thirteen years.

Whenever bath water is needed from the Yamuna or some other source, Vilasa-manjari, along with other gopis, collects it in beautiful golden jugs inlaid with precious stones.

In the western part of Citra-devi’s grove is Rasa-manjari’s kunja (Rasanandada-kunja). ln gaura-lila she is Raghunatha Bhatta Gosvami, known as the bhagavata-acarya for reciting Srimad-Bhagavatam.

Rasa-manjari’s eternal form is that of a thirteen-year-old girl. Golden complexioned like a campaka flower, she dresses in pure white clothes like the feathers of a swan. She is very dear to Rupa-manjarl.

Early in the morning in Yavata, after other gopis bathe and dress Sri Radha, Rasa-manjari carefully smears Srimati Radharani’s body with sandalwood pulp, camphor, kunkuma, and musk.

Narottama Dasa Thakura prays to Rasa-manjari for her merciful glance so that he can meditate always on her lotus feet, a meditation that opens the gates to the divine couple’s eternal pastimes.

In the southern part of Indulekha-gopi’s grove is Ratyambuja-kunja, where mild-mannered Rati-manjari, with a complexion like lightning and clothes like the star-studded sky, resides.

Rati-manjari’s eternal age is two months past thirteen years. In Vraja she is also known as Tulasl-manjari, and in the pastimes of Caitanya Mahaprabhu she is famous as Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

Rati-manjari, the embodiment of divine attachment, is always right beside Sri Radha. She thinks, “O Devi! I am Yours! I am yours! Please know that I cannot live without You and bring me to Your feet!’’

Because Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami always lived in this intense state of love in separation from Radha and Krsna, he became indifferent to his bodily needs and thus some people call him the vairagya-acarya.

Wise persons who see Dasa Gosvami through his own words recognise him as the perfect follower of Rupa Gosvami and the acarya who taught us what bhajana means and what it takes to be a sadhaka.

According to his vows, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami daily ate no more than a leaf cup of buttermilk, offered one thousand obeisances to the Lord, and chanted at least one hundred thousand holy names.

Every day he also offered obeisances to two thousand Vaisnavas, constantly rendered service within his mind to Radha and Krsna, and for three hours spoke about the character of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

The Gosvami took three baths a day in serene Radha-kunda. And whenever he met a devotee who had just entered Vrndavana, Dasa Gosvami would embrace him and show him all respect.

In this way Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami engaged in devotional service for more than twenty-two and a half hours a day, sleeping for less than two hours, although on some days even that was not possible.

One is struck with wonder to hear the devotional practices of this truly great soul. Without a doubt, his source of inspiration was the deep attachment he felt for Rupa Gosvami, revealed by these words:

**“Now that the life of my life \[Rupa Gosvami\] is gone, the land of Vraja has become desolate, Giriraja has become like a great python, and Radha-kunda has become like the gaping jaws of a tiger.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Beyond Ratyambuja-kunja lies sagacious Guna-manjari’s beautiful grove, called Gunanandaprada-kunja, which is tucked away in the northern part of Campakalata-devi’s expansive grove.

Guna-manjari’s complexion is the colour of lightning, similar to other gopis. Three days junior to Tulasi-manjari, she likes to dress in red clothes whose hue resembles the japa flower (hibiscus).

At times Guna-manjari’s manners may seem brusque, but she is always submissive to Sri Rupa’s every desire. Ever pleasing to Krsna, in gaura-lila she is known as Sri Gopala Bhatta Gosvami.

Because Gopala Bhatta collaborated with Sanatana Gosvami in composing Hari-bhakti-vilasa and wrote his own Sat-kriya-sara-dipika, two books on Vaisnava rituals, he is called the smrti-acarya.

From Gopala Bhatta’s childhood, Sri Caitanya showed great affection to him. The Deity named Radha-ramana manifested Himself from a salagrama-sila due to Gopala Bhatta’s great devotion to Krsna.

Once, while the gopis were conversing with Krsna, Radha signalled to Her beloved with a glance. Without warning — and to everyone’s delight — Krsna jokingly kissed Guna-manjari.

Thirteen-year-old Kasturi-manjari, whose complexion is the colour of gold and who dresses in clothes the colour of white crystal, blissfully resides in a part of Rangadevi’s grove named Kasturyanandada-kunja.

In Lord Caitanya’s pastimes she appears as Krsnadasa Gosvami, the Lord’s poetic biographer and chronicler of Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes. Thus Kaviraja (“the king of poets”) was added to his name.

He resided on the bank of Syama-kunda and composed these great books in which he describes his own service to Radha’s and Krsna’s youthful pastimes. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami writes:

“\[In the morning\] Lalita sent a garland and betel leaves with Tulasi and Kasturi, saying, ‘Give this to Hari.’ \[In the evening\] Radha sent Tulasi and Kasturi with a basket full of food for Yasoda.

“After Mother Yasoda fed Krsna with the foods sent by Radha, she wanted Tulasi and Kasturi to eat, but Dhanistha replied, ‘They will not even drink water before Radhika has eaten.’”

Kaviraja Gosvami adds, “At this Mother Yasoda, pleased with the girls’ love for Radha, dotingly said, ‘Then let Tulasi and Kasturi take this rice and vegetables to Radha and Her friends.’”

In the eastern portion of Turigavidya’s crimson-coloured grove is Lavanga-manjari’s beautiful residence, Lavanga-sukhada-kunja, which enchants the eyes of the gopis who visit there.

Lavanga-manjari is well known in Vrndavana for her pleasing nature and beauty, which are enhanced by her smooth golden complexion and clothes resembling a starlit night.

Lavanga-manjari is just one day older than Rupa-manjari. But in Lord Caitanya’s pastimes she is Rupa Gosvami’s elder brother, Sanatana Gosvami, the most senior of the Six Gosvamis of Vrndavana.

Sanatana Gosvami was very humble and meek, but Caitanya Mahaprabhu considered him unequalled in the affairs of spiritual advancement, so much so that He accepted advice from the Gosvami.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructed Sanatana Gosvami to live in Vrndavana, excavate the places of Krsna’s pastimes, and write books, particularly the Brhad-bhagavatamrta and Hari-bhakti-vilasa.

Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika says that Sri Sanatana Gosvami was formerly known as Rati-manjari, or sometimes Lavanga-manjari. These two names were apparently for the same person, not different persons.

At times Lavanga-manjari assists in decorating Sri Radha, and sometimes she carries messages between Radha and Her beloved. On one occasion Sri Krsna personally dressed and ornamented Sri Radha.

He painted pictures on Radha’s face and body with vermilion, sandalwood, and musk. Then Lavanga-manjari handed Him beautiful earrings to set in Radha’s ears and fresh eyeliner for Her eyelids.

On another occasion, after Lavanga had artfully convinced Krsna to drop everything and go to where Radha was waiting, she meekly said to her mistress, “Krsna has now appeared before Your eyes.

“Attracted by hearing about the jewels of Your transcendental qualities, He has left the other gopis for You. O my queen! Please tell this maidservant what else she can do for You!”

Towards the end of the parikrama of Radha-kunda, we come to the grove of Sudevi. There, in her Lilanandaprada-kunja, resides the abode of sweetness, thirteen-and-a-half-year-old Manjulali-manjari.

She dresses in reddish clothes like Radha sometimes does, and has a complexion resembling molten gold. Also known as Lila-manjari, she serves Radha with her expert skill at dressing and ornamenting.

Manjulali-manjari always has a pleasant air about her. She appeared in gaura-lila as Lokanatha Gosvami, the spiritual master of Narottama Dasa Thakura and servant of the Deities Radha-Vinoda.

By his personal example, Sri Lokanatha taught Vaisnavas how to reside in Vrndavana — free of material encumbrances and always absorbed in thoughts of Radha and Krsna and Their gopi companions.

Those who take shelter of him will find the darkness in their hearts dispelled, the path to pure love illuminated, and the jewels of Krsna’s pastimes at Giriraja revealed by his grace, his glance, and his smile.

Just before sunrise and just after Radha and Krsna wake up and leave the groves of Vrndavana for Their homes, the manjaris crowd around to receive some remnants of the divine couple’s pastimes.

At that time Manjulali-manjari enters the kunja, collects the garlands and sandalwood pulp left by Radha and Krsna, and distributes these treasures to the gopis eagerly waiting outside.

At the centre of Radha-kunda is Ananga-manjari’s island grove, connected to the shore by an ornate bridge. Love-filled eyes can see the island, its jewel palace, and Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes there.

Dressed in blue silks, Ananga-manjari’s complexion is like a ketaki flower in springtime. She is Sri Radha’s younger sister, so one can only imagine her extraordinary beauty, qualities, and skills.

Especially dear to Lalita and Visakha, Ananga-manjari charms Sri Krsna, who charms the three worlds. Thus she is not only the maidservant of her sister hut also one of the eight exalted heroines.

While serving as a maidservant, Ananga-manjari offers Radha and Krsna sandalwood pulp scented with camphor, as Rupa-manjari places garlands of aromatic jasmine flowers around each of Their necks.

As a heroine, Ananga-manjari accepts the arrangements her sister Radha makes for her to meet Krsna on her island grove, where she mesmerises Him with her peerless mastery of Cupid’s diversions.

In the pastimes of Lord Caitanya, Ananga-manjari expands herself into two: Jahnava and Vasudha, the wives of Lord Nityananda. As the acarya for all Gaudiya Vaisnavas, Jahnava was more prominent.

Jahnava-devi once visited Vrndavana. There Jiva Gosvami humbly requested her to visit Radha-kunda in order to pacify Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, who had lost his will to stay in this world any longer.

Jahnava-devi stayed at Radha-kunda for four days along with her entourage. She met with and inspired the resident Vaisnavas, including the aged and nearly blind Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

One day, as Jahnava-mata sat on Radha-kunda’s northern shore, Krsna appeared in His threefold-bending form. He was playing His flute and looking at Jahnava-mata enchantingly.

Since that time the northern part of the lakefront and the private stairway leading to the water’s edge where Jahnava bathed has been known as Jahnava-ghata. The atmosphere there is extremely serene.

Ananga-manjari sometimes stands guard over Radha and Krsna as They are resting, and if any monkeys are nearby she signals some manjaris to shoo the obnoxious creatures away.

When a new gopi joins Krsna’s pastimes after her release from the material realm, Ananga-manjari may introduce her to the other gopis, give her a place to stay, and arrange service to the divine couple.

Let us worship Ananga-manjari, Sri Radha’s life force, whose youthful body overflows with the sweet essence of loving service and who has gained from Visakha-devi the perfections befitting a heroine.

Let us always remember the confidential service the manjaris offer to Radha and Krsna and, in their sadhaka forms, to Sri Caitanya. Let us pray for their selfless service attitude, the bedrock of pure devotion.

**\* \* \* \***

In the northwestern corner of Radha-kunda, near Tungavidya’s grove, is the Radha-kanta temple and the puspa-samadhi of Vakresvara Pandita, who is Tungavidya in Krsna’s pastimes.

To the left — past the temples of Sri Gopala, Radha-Syamasundara, and Radha-Damodara - is the temple of Radha-Madhava and the sitting place, or kunja, of Srinivasa Acarya.

Like Thakura Bhaktivinoda, Srinivasa Acarya did not live directly on the banks of Radha-kunda as did his predecessors but, considering himself their servant, stayed a respectful distance behind them.

Srinivasa immortalised the Six Gosvamis in his prayer Sad-gosvamy- astaka — a personal favourite of Srila Prabhupada — the refrain of which is vande rupa-sanatanau raghu-yugau sri-jiva-gopdlakau.

On the northern shore of Radha-kunda, known as Jahnava-ghata, is the sitting place of Lord Nityananda’s consort and the Radha- Gopinatha temple built to commemorate her darsana of Gopinatha.

Adjoining Jahnava-ghata is Dasa Gosvami-ghata, so called because the well-known samadhi of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami — the first resident of Radha-kunda — is situated there.

This samadhi is situated near the groves of Lalita, Visakha, and Rupa- manjari. It was placed there to fulfil Dasa Gosvami’s desire to live forever on the banks of Radha-kunda with his worshipable superiors.

Rati-manjari is an eternal associate of Sri Radha who lives always by the side of Her lake. But as Dasa Gosvami, the same great soul teaches us how to live there as a perfect practitioner,

*yat-padambuja—*  
*Yugma-vicyuta-rajah-seva-prabhavad aham gandharva sarasi girindra-nikate kaste ’pi nityam vasan*  
*tat-preyo-gana-palito jita-sudha radha- mukundabhidha udgayami srnomi mam punar aho*  
*Srimati sa rupo ’vatu*

**“On the strength of the service I have done to the pollen of his \[Rupa’s\] lotus feet, I am able to always reside, even in times of trouble, by the shore of Radha-kunda at the base of Govardhana Hill.**

**“Protected by his friends and associates, I chant and hear the holy names of Sri Radha and Mukunda, which defeat the sweetest nectar. I pray that Srila Rupa Gosvami may always protect me.”**

Great souls like Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami live by Radha’s lake on the strength of their unimaginable feats in devotional service. With this knowledge, we should make these devotees our very life and soul.

And if we help Rupa Gosvami and his followers fulfil Lord Caitanya’s mission, we can become qualified to live at Radha-kunda with these bodies and minds in this life and in fully spiritual forms in the next.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami opined that living at other places like Vrndavana forest, Govardhana Hill, or even the Rasa-sthali could not match even a single particle of the bliss of residing by Radha-kunda.

Even the divine couple — when absorbed as the emissaries of divine love within a flower grove or gem-studded palace of Radha-kunda — consider everything else and every other place insignificant.

For Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, Radha-kunda was a place of persistent ecstasy in separation from Radha, Syama, and Their friends—yet also sprinkled by the occasional bliss of meeting them.

At times, unable to see that sacred lake’s proprietor, Dasa Gosvami would lie upon the shore of Radha-kunda, flood the lake with his tears, and call out in a whisper, "I can’t live without You.”

At other times he would collapse on Radha-kunda’s banks in distress. Then, in order to see Sri Radha's beautiful face, he would call out Her names, names like Gandharvika, Radhika, and Varsabhanavi.

Dasa Gosvami would think of his eternal form as a gopi maidservant and yearn for a time when, in a lakeside grove filled with humming bees, Sri Radha would teach that gopi how to play the kacchapi lute.

He would be absorbed constantly in the divine couple’s pastimes at Radha-kunda. For example, he would visualise how he, as Rati- manjari, would fan Radha and Krsna as They rested beneath atree.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami considered Radha-kunda his eternal home and only residence. Thus, whether it was the fountainhead of happiness or pain — equally relishable ecstasies — there he stayed!

The very first time this beautiful lake, with its blossoming lotuses and buzzing bees, appeared before Dasa Gosvami’s eyes, an intense yearning for direct service to Srimati Radharani awoke in his heart.

By that intense yearning Dasa Gosvami came to behold Sri Radha’s pet swan, Tundikeri, playing in the lake, and witnessed the divine couple talking intimately beneath a particular kadamba tree.

Fragrant Radha-kunda — on the shores of which Radha and Her friends daily joke with the moon of Vrndavana, Lord Sri Krsna — is therefore Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s only shelter.

The banks of Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda give shelter not only to transcendentalists and spiritual aspirants but also to the goddesses of the six seasons empowered by the area’s cintamani dust.

Once, as Radha and Krsna and Their girlfriends were strolling through the gardens of Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda, Vrnda-devi and those six seasonal goddesses approached them.

Vrnda introduced the goddesses and said, “Please hear the request of these six seasons at Your lotus feet.” The goddesses then joined their palms and spoke in unison, “We are your servants.

“We have very carefully and skillfully surrendered everything to You so that Vrndavana may be exceedingly beautiful. O King and Queen, please look upon our work and thus make it worthwhile!

“Only when the master is pleased with the work of his servants is that work of any value!” Having spoken this preamble, the six seasons made a request on behalf of themselves and their subjects.

“O Radha! O Krsna! Please hear this plea we place at Your lotus feet on behalf of all the moving and non-moving creatures of Vrndavana’s pleasure-playgrounds, which are also within our jurisdiction!

“Please, allow us to behold the diverse pastimes You will enact during Your blissful meeting today. Allow us to serve You with the bounties of our individual natures and thus make our lives successful.”

We should carefully note in hearing this prayer that the all-pervading seasons residing at Radha-kunda can see and enter the divine couple’s pastimes only with the divine couple’s blessings.

Therefore, to gain entrance into the Radha-kunda of Goloka Vrndavana we must earn the grace of Radha and Krsna by serving that form of Radha-kunda now visible to the physical eyes.

Faith in the Radha-kunda we can see engenders a spirit of selfless service to that sacred lake, through which Radha and Syama bless faithful servants, like the six seasons, to see Radha-kunda as it is.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami excavated and renovated Radha-kunda for this purpose, and with the same purpose in mind we have designated a temple courtyard in New Vraja-dhama as Radha-kunda.

May Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and his beloveds, Radha and Syamasundara, accept our service and make us all qualified to one day serve the transcendental cintamani realm, Radha-kunda.

**\*\*\*\***

The shoreline of Radha-kunda between Visakha’s and Citra- devi’s groves is called Govinda-ghata. In Vraja I often pause here to recall the vision that Sanatana Gosvami once had at this place.

This pastime occurred during one of the periods when Rupa Gosvami was residing at Radha-kunda. He was visiting Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami at the time of this incident.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami's residence was on the bank of serene Syama-kunda behind Govinda-ghata near Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami’s residence, Manasa-pavana-ghata.

It was mid-morning. Birds skimmed the lakes, parrots chattered excitedly in the trees, and a family of monkeys played nearby, quenching their thirst with water from Manasa-pavana-ghata.

Rupa and Raghunatha were conversing about the pastimes of Radha and Krsna when Sanatana Gosvami arrived. The two saints greeted Sanatana respectfully and gave the venerable Vaisnava a seat.

The three saints sat beneath a bakula tree. A few Vaisnavas bathed in Syama-kunda, and the occasional bullock cart plied the surrounding roads to and from the adjacent agricultural fields.

Free from the unwanted pollutions Kali-yuga would bring in the centuries to follow, Radha-kunda was the picture of serene purity one would expect from the most sacred of all holy places.

In such an ideal spiritual atmosphere — timeless and perfectly conducive to discussing pure krsna-katha— it was only natural for the three acaryas to become oblivious to the passing of time.

At different points in their conversation these great acaryas discussed the Vedic scriptures, their own realisations, or the books that Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu had commissioned them to write.

Sanatana Gosvami, curious to bear Sri Rupa's latest composition, asked his younger brother, “Please decorate our ears with your most recent work. We are both very eager to hear you glorify the Lord.”

At his brother’s request, Rupa began to read an offering of prayers to Sri Radha that he had entitled Catu-puspanjali, but as soon as Rupa had read the first verse, Sanatana demanded, “Read that again!”

Rupa reread, “O queen as golden as fresh gorocana. O queen whose garments are a splendid blue lotus! O queen whose braid, decorated with jewels and flowers, glistens like the hood of a serpent— ”

Sanatana objected, “The phrase veni-vyalangana-phanam compares the braid of tender and charming Sri Radha to the body of a fearsome, poisonous snake. I don’t like this simile.”

Rupa Gosvami joined his palms and meekly said with a smile, “Prabhu! Whatever you say must be right. Please suggest a more fitting metaphor, and please forgive me for my impudence.”

But Sanatana Gosvami was suddenly at a loss for words. After a few moments Sanatana stood up, reassured Rupa that he was certainly beyond committing offence, and said, “I must think it over.

“Let me take my midday bath and then come back with a suggestion.” At this Sanatana walked slowly to Govinda-ghata, bowing down to offer his obeisances to Radha-kunda before entering the water.

As Sanatana rose to his feet the sound of voices drew his attention to Jhulana-sthali on the opposite side of the lake, where several girls were pushing one of their friends on a swing and singing about Krsna.

While entering the water Sanatana Gosvami casually observed the girls playing. Suddenly he noticed a black snake slithering up one of the ropes that dangled below the seat of the swing!

The snake was just about to wrap its coils around the girl on the swing, a girl whose extraordinary effulgence would have raised Sanatana’s suspicions had it not been for the imminent danger.

But the girls, absorbed in play, were unaware of the approaching peril. Meanwhile, Sanatana, still knee deep in water, excitedly called out, “Lali! Look behind you! Snake! Snake! Look out! Lali!"

The girls continued playing, apparently not hearing Sanatana’s cries, so the old saint got out of the water and ran along Jahnava-ghata, waving his arms and shouting, “Snake! Snake! Beware!”

The girls finally noticed him as he reached the corner of Radha-kunda but they just laughed at Sanatana, mocking the Gosvami’s melodramatic display. And then, in an instant, they all disappeared.

Sanatana Gosvami stopped in his tracks. Suddenly there was no swing, no snake; the girls had vanished, and only the sound of the their sweet laughter remained, echoing across the water then fading away.

After a few moments Sanatana Gosvami approached Jhulana-sthali and noticed that the banyan tree from which the swing had hung was bathed in a soft golden radiance, like that of the girl on the swing.

Sanatana’s spiritual intuition told him that the girl had been none other that Srimati Radharani Herself and that Her bevy of friends had been Her gopi companions like Lalita and Visakha.

“And the snake!” thought Sanatana. “That was no snake. It was Srimati Radharani’s braid wrapped around the rope, looking just the way Rupa described it, veni-vyalangana-phanam.”

The bliss of realising he had seen Radha and Her friends — and that the vision had been specially scripted to instruct him — overcame Sanatana Gosvami. He fell into a swoon and collapsed to the ground.

Sanatana’s earlier cries had attracted the attention of Rupa, Raghunatha, and some other devotees bathing within earshot, who all hurried to where the Gosvami now lay on the ground lost in trance.

The Vaisnavas sat around the great sage until he finally returned to external consciousness. Then they helped him to his feet, but not one of them enquired as to the cause of his ecstasy.

Devotees never speak publicly of their intimate spiritual realisations, just as chaste women never speak of intimate dealings with their husbands. Neither should devotees pry into the realisations of others.

The elderly Sanatana returned to Manasa-pavana-ghata and, his voice trembling from ecstasy, explained everything he had seen to Rupa and Raghunatha, his spiritual confidants.

Holding Rupa’s hands in his own, Sanatana Gosvami said, “Our worshipable goddess’s opinion is that your description of Her hair is exactly correct. Please forgive me for saying otherwise.”

Embarrassed by his spiritual master’s apology, Sri Rupa, along with Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, fell at Sanatana’s feet. Then the three great souls embraced, bathing one another in tears of affection.

May whoever hears this wonderful pastime or reads the prayer to the queen of Vrndavana bearing the name Catu-puspanjali (“A Handful of Prayer-flowers”) become the object of Her mercy.

**\* \* \* \***

From Govinda-ghata one can walk to the area above Manasa-pavana-ghata on the bank of Syama-kunda and offer respects to the great souls who chose to perform their service and bhajana there.

Srimati Radharani Herself is the patron of this area due to Her deep affection for Krsna’s best friend, Subala, whose beautiful grove is situated in this part of Syama-kunda.

When Krsna called upon all the holy places to enter His lake, the branch of the Ganges that flows through the lower region of the universe called Patala came out at this place in the form of a spring.

Srimati Radharani considers the holy river Ganges to be sweet honey flowing from Krsna’s lotus feet; thus She and Her girlfriends take their midday bath at this spot every day.

Before bathing, the gopis check to make sure that no one is watching and change into thin bathing clothes, leaving their fine dresses on a large pilu bush that grows luxuriantly in the centre of the ghata.

They hold hands to steady one another as they descend the stairs into the water until they are standing waist-deep. Then they dip into the water, being careful not to get their hair wet.

Saints meditate on the golden lotus face of Sri Radha, whose abundant black curly hair piled on top of Her head resembles a beehive and whose restless eyes are like two flitting hummingbirds.

As She moves about in the water, Her face appears like a roving golden lotus upon the stem of Her smooth, conch-shaped neck, which grows from the island of Her gently sloping shoulders.

Sometimes Krsna hides in the branches of a nearby tree to spy on the gopis as they bathe. And if one of them happens to see Him, He places His forefinger to His lips and silently pleads that she stay quiet.

Radha bathes in waist-deep water, and Her wet clothes cling to Her limbs. After a while She feels uncomfortable, sensing that someone is watching. Although She looks here and there, She sees no one.

Radha tells Her friends of Her discomfort, saying, “I feel like someone is looking at Me.” But the gopi in collusion with Krsna replies, “Why worry? Clearly no one is here but us girls.”

Radha’s suggestion that someone could be watching inspires wave after wave of jokes from Her friends, who all know very well who that someone must be. Inevitably, their jokes lap onto the Radha-shore.

On occasions such as these Krsna sometimes stays hidden, only to reveal Himself much later. But sometimes, as Radha is dressing after Her bath, He tosses small pebbles at Her until She discovers Him.

All glories to Sri Hari's eternal youth, the transcendental spring season in which the desire tree of amorous love blossoms with flowerlike pastimes that drip prema into the hearts of bee-like devotees.

The plants in Vraja are all fully conscious devotees serving the divine couple in their own unique ways. Thus the pilu bush that holds the gopis’ clothes while they bathe also witnesses their pastimes.

This pilu bush in particular was formerly a Vaisnava brahmana from Lord Siva’s holy city of Kasi who executed severe austerities, hoping to ask a boon from the Lord, face to face.

Pleased with this devotee’s resolve, Krsna eventually appeared to him. The brahmana requested that he be allowed to participate in Krsna’s pastimes, and the Lord fulfilled his desire.

Thereafter the brahmana became a pilu bush by the bank of Syama-kunda, from where he witnesses the many pastimes that take place in the area and serves the gopis by holding their clothes as they bathe.

The bhajana-kutira of Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura is just beside that pilu bush. It is said that while the acarya resided here he would sometimes discuss the divine couple’s pastimes with the bush.

On Cakravarti Thakura’s first visit to Radha-kunda, he stayed in the bhajana-kutira of Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami. But when the Thakura came back from Bengal to stay, he set up his own residence.

In the decades that followed the disappearance of Jiva Gosvami, the Gaudiya Vaisnava community was thrown into chaos because of frequent infighting and philosophical deviation.

It was Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, with the help of his siksa disciple Baladeva Vidyabhusana, who restored stability to the Gaudiya sampradaya by his instructions, example, and literary works.

Advanced Vaisnavas accept that Cakravarti Thakura was especially empowered by Rupa Gosvami to elucidate and expand upon Sri Rupa’s teachings and to explain things Rupa had not elaborated on.

Visvanatha Cakravarti sometimes wrote under the pen name Hari Vallabha. It is said that in Krsna’s eternal pastimes he is Sri Radha’s maidservant Vinoda-manjari, or Vinoda-vallari-manjari.

Amongst the many works Cakravartipada composed at Radha-kunda, Mantrartha-dipika typifies how inspired he was by scripture and how faithful he was to the teachings of the previous acaryas.

That book is a commentary on the Kama-gayatri mantra, for which Cakravarti Thakura did extensive research. In the process he came across a statement in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta that perplexed him.

That verse says,

*kama-gayatri-mantra-rupa, haya krsnera svarupa, sardha-cabbisa aksara tara haya*  
*se aksara 'candra' haya, krsne kari’ udaya, trijagat kaila kamamaya*

**“Krsna is identical with the Kama-gayatri hymn, which is composed of twenty-four and a half syllables that are comparable to moons that arise in Krsna and that fill the three worlds with desire.”**

Every other scripture the Thakura consulted mentioned the Kamagayatri as a mantra of twenty-five syllables. Thus Kaviraja Gosvami’s reference to twenty-four and a half syllables appeared contradictory.

For example, the Brhan-naradiya Purana says:

**“Srimati Radharani is the princess of Vrndavana-dhama, and Her beautiful, transcendental form is composed of twenty-five syllables."**

Visvanatha never entertained the idea that the Gosvami had made a mistake, or that he was ignorant of the scriptures; indeed, Kaviraja Gosvami was free from defect and possessed complete knowledge.

Throughout the day and night, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura studied this dilemma from many angles, trying to find a satisfying explanation. Unable to find one, he decided to fast until death.

Sitting on the bank of Radha-kunda he thought, “If one cannot understand the syllables of the mantra, how can one know the Lord? And if one cannot know the Lord, why should one continue to live?”

Dumbstruck and dejected, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura continued to lament until well after midnight. When he finally fell asleep Sri Radha appeared to him in dream and compassionately said:

“O Hari Vallabha! Get up! That which Krsnadasa Kaviraja has written is true. Like you, he is also My confidential maidservant. By My mercy he knows everything about My secret, innermost moods.

“Please give up your grief. This mantra is for worshipping Me, and by its syllables I can be known. But without My mercy, no one can understand the mystery of Myself or the mantra.

“The solution to your dilemma is found in the book Varnagama-bhasvadi. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami consulted that book before composing the verse that has so perplexed you.”

Sri Radha concluded with an instruction: “Now please listen! After you wake up, find that book and broadcast this evidence for the benefit of others so that they may not become confused."

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura woke up, quickly rose to his feet, and, despite feeling relieved from his anxiety, repeatedly lamented, this time over losing his vision of beautiful Sri Radha.

Then he remembered Srimati Radharani’s instructions and immediately set about carrying them out. Sitting before a solitary lamp in his cottage, he first wrote the following:

**“In my dream, Srimati Radharani was speaking of the half syllable, and She told me, ‘The letter ya (in devaya) followed by the letter vi (in vidmahe) is considered a half syllable- “This half syllable falls on Sri Krsna’s forehead, which resembles the halo of a half-moon. All the other letters of the mantra are full syllables, and so they are considered full moons.”**

The next day Cakravartipada searched for the book Varnagama- bhasvadi. He found a copy and saw that it was just as Radha had said: When ya is followed by vi, the compound is considered a half syllable.

With this revelation, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura was able to complete his book and give to the Vaisnava community a fully comprehensive commentary on the Kama-gayatri mantra.

Although Visvanatha had counted twenty-five syllables, and although every scripture he had consulted agreed with that number, Kaviraja Gosvami, the great authority, apparently disagreed.

But Cakravartipada refused to dismiss the minority opinion of his predecessor; instead, he blamed himself for not being able to reconcile the two statements and for not properly understanding Kama-gayatri.

It was Cakravarti Thakura’s great faith in the words of a self-realised acarya that prompted Sri Radha to appear in person, resolve his dilemma, and even provide the supporting scriptural evidence.

It has recently become common practice for some within Srila Prabhupada’s own Society to minimise statements or opinions he gives if they appear to contradict statements of the scriptures or previous acaryas.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura shows by his sterling example that we would do better not to jump to hasty conclusions, however obvious those conclusions may seem at first glance.

It is better for us to doubt our own intelligence. Instead we should remain patient and wait for a revelation, being resolutely determined that whatever Srila Prabhupada said or wrote must be true.

Such a revelation, coming from Krsna or some other divine source, will reveal why Srila Prabhupada said what he said and why there are sometimes contradictions amongst spiritual authorities.

Obviously by such revelation we will also come to know the answer to our original question. And until a revelation does come, we should refrain from passing judgment on our founder-acarya.

Unshakeable faith in our acaryas — based on a foundation of genuine humility—is sure to please the Lord and ensure rapid elevation to perfection, in which factual realisation resolves all contradictions.

**\* \* \* \***

To the northwest of Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s cottage is the bhajana-kutira of Gopala Bhatta Gosvami, who would visit Manasa-pavana-ghata to associate with the other Gosvamis.

When Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami began to write Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Gopala Bhatta was quick to note that it contained extensive biographical detail and glorification of the Lord’s associates.

Out of natural Vaisnava humility, Gopala Bhatta Gosvami begged Kaviraja Gosvami not to mention his name or to write about him in the text, and the author honoured this humble request.

Of this great Gosvami it is said that simply by seeing him one’s eyes would fill with tears of love for Krsna, and by hearing his sweet words one would be freed from the cycle of repeated birth and death.

He was regal in appearance, like a king amongst brahmanas, and his smile shone with compassion. The other Gosvamis of Vraja were his life air, and the Radha-ramana Deity was his very soul.

A little further south is Tin-gosvami-samadhi, the place where three (tin) Gosvamis— Raghunatha Bhatta, Raghunatha Dasa, and Krsnadasa Kaviraja--were cremated and their ashes interred.

Following the demise of Akbar, devotees in Bhauma Vrndavana were subject to persecution. Sometimes even their samadhis were desecrated. Thus Jiva Gosvami decided not to bury these saints.

Instead, he cremated them at this spot, placed a portion of their ashes in Tin-gosvami-samadhi, and had the balance of their remains individually entombed at other places in Vrndavana.

I wonder whether these great souls chose to leave this world on the same lunar calendar day due to deep attachment to one another, or because they all shared in one of Krsna’s pastimes at Radha-kunda.

Just north of—almost adjoining — Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s cottage is the residence of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. Beside that is Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami’s bhajana-kutira.

It would behove the residents of New Vraja-dhama, and devotees in general, to recall how and why Sanatana Gosvami introduced the system of living in cottages at Radha-kunda and elsewhere in Vraja.

The Six Gosvamis had renounced luxurious homes and family comforts for the privilege of living in the dhama. As Srila Prabhupada would often say, “they lived under a different tree every night.’’

To live in Vrndavana is to live as a guest in Lord Krsna’s home. One who is a guest cannot think oneself the proprietor of anything that belongs to one’s host without being discourteous.

Thus, in order to avoid any sense of ownership or attachment and to eschew the enjoying spirit, the Six Gosvamis lived without personal possessions and slept beneath the shelter-giving trees of Vraja.

But when that austere way of life proved inconvenient to Krsna, the Gosvamis constructed simple cottages in which to safely continue performing bhajana and writing books.

The residents of New Vraja-dhama should follow the Gosvamis and consider themselves privileged to live in Radha-Syamasundara’s domain, never thinking of themselves as the owners of their homes.

Rather they should accept whatever accommodations, possessions, and accoutrements they may have — be they ample or meagre — as Their Lordships’ mercy and as facilities for serving Them.

After all, we are in this world for a few moments only. Our precious time should not be spent in mundane pursuits but in perfecting our bhajana and offering selfless service to Radha and Syama.

This mood of engaging material resources in the service of Krsna without attachment to loss or gain was taught by Krsna to Arjuna and refined by Rupa Gosvami, who called it yukta-vairagya.

Twenty-first-century devotees cannot imitate the Gosvamis’ austere lives, but by applying the principle of yukta-vairagya they can surely remain faithful to the Gosvamis’ ideals.

In Vrndavana, two separate incidents precipitated the construction of cottages for the Gosvamis. The principal players were Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami, here at Manasa-pavana-ghata.

One day, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami was sitting by the hank of Syama-kunda deeply absorbed in his internal identity as Rati-manjari, blissfully serving Srimati Radharani in a variety of ways.

The earthly plane had no influence upon the eternal realm in which Dasa Gosvami had entered, and therefore he did not notice when a pair of tigers emerged from the jungle just behind him.The two jungle cats, sensing that the saint was no threat to them, came to the water’s edge without trepidation and began to drink at a distance hardly a stone’s throw away from the saint.

Dasa Gosvami continued his bhajana while the tigers drank a little, rested, and then drank again, equally relishing both the sweetness of the lake’s water and the holy names Raghunatha was chanting.

But omniscient Syamasundara, concerned for the safety of His devotee, appeared a short distance behind Raghunatha Dasa to stand guard. He leant against a tree and kept a close eye on the large cats.

Just then Sanatana Gosvami walked across the sangama, from where he could see Raghunatha Dasa and the two tigers. As he was about to call out “Tiger! Tiger!” he noticed Krsna standing there.

At the sight of his worshipable Lord, Sanatana stopped short. And the tigers, startled by Sanatana’s arrival, stood up, glanced one final time at Dasa Gosvami, and silently returned to the jungle.

Now that the tigers were gone, Krsna also disappeared. After offering obeisances and prayers to his beloved Lord, Sanatana came to Manasa-pavana-ghata and gently tried to rouse Raghunatha Dasa.

Dasa Gosvami gradually returned to external consciousness and saw his siksa-guru standing before him. At once the acarya bowed down and placed his head on Sanatana Gosvami’s lotus feet.

“My son! What are you doing here?” asked Sanatana. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami replied, “Dear sir! I was completing my daily vow of chanting Krsna’s holy names and became lost in meditation.”

Sanatana Gosvami looked lovingly at the young saint and asked, “Does your daily vow and deep meditation include enlisting Krsna in your service and separating Him from our beloved Radharani?”

The question baffled Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, who simply looked at the feet of his superior, unable to reply. When Sanatana Gosvami explained to him what had happened, Raghunatha fainted.

Thinking of the Lord’s concern for him, Raghunatha Dasa was overwhelmed at being the recipient of the kind of mercy Krsna’s associates, like the Pandavas and Draupadi, had enjoyed.

With his loving touch Sanatana Gosvami revived Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and then commanded him, “Krsna is always kind to His devotees. Thus He is always concerned for their welfare.

“He will even leave His own companions to look after His devotees. So please don’t take service from Him again; rather, take care of yourself by constructing a cottage in which to do your bhajana.”

The two Gosvamis embraced and then spent the remainder of the day discussing Krsna’s wonderful qualities and praising each other’s good fortune at having become servants of such a well-wishing master.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami took Sanatana Gosvami’s order seriously. Within a few days he requested some villagers to provide him with some type of accommodation, however modest.

But due to his natural humility, he also felt uncomfortable asking others to serve him. Therefore his request did not seem urgent to the villagers, who first tended to the harvest.

For that reason, some time passed before the kutira was built. During that interval another occasion arose in which Sanatana Gosvami saw Raghunatha Dasa cause inconvenience to the divine couple.

**\* \* \* \***

This second incident began early one morning. After bathing, Raghunatha Dasa had taken a seat by the bank of Syama-kunda to allow the rising sun to warm his body as he chanted Hare Krsna.

Dasa Gosvami absorbed his mind in the bliss of serving Srimati Radharani. As a result, he became oblivious to the passing of time and to the increasing heat and intensity of the sun’s rays.

As midday approached, Dasa Gosvami’s body became sunburned and drenched in perspiration. It would only be a matter of time before the searing heat of the sun caused serious sunstroke.

Srimati Radharani, unable to tolerate seeing Her personal attendant suffer from overexposure, stealthily appeared behind Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, just as Krsna had done before.

Standing just behind him, She held the upper portion of Her cloth above his head to shield him from the sun’s rays, thus — without the protection of Her veil — exposing Herself to the sun’s full force.

But listening to Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s recitation of Krsna’s names was like a spring breeze to Srimati Radharani. She felt refreshed, even as She perspired profusely from the heat.

As intense as Dasa Gosvami’s absorption had been before, Radha's presence now intensified that absorption many times over, so much so that the sadhu completely forgot about external reality.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami continued his sankirtana, lost in samadhi, as beautiful Radharani stood patiently behind him, feeling Her own bliss intensified in his transcendental presence.

Just imagine! That beautiful golden-limbed gopi, upon whose lotus feet millions of maidservants eternally wait, was serving Her own devotee by sheltering him from the heat of the sun.

Let us meditate upon tender-hearted Radha, smiling in the ecstasy of love, Her clothes and even the ground around Her completely soaked from Her perspiration as She exerts Herself in serving Her devotee.

Once again Sanatana Gosvami arrived on the scene, and this time he was stunned by the sight of his worshipable Deity, Sri Radha, and the thought of Her kindness in serving Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

But Sanatana would not see Radha for long. Now that a witness had arrived, Sri Radha sent a smile and a glance Sanatana’s way and then disappeared, leaving only Her footprints in the moist ground.

Sanatana Gosvami was overwhelmed with spiritual emotions. He collapsed and called out Srimati Radharani’s name. Weeping incessantly, he rolled on the ground while flailing his arms.

After some time Sanatana Gosvami composed himself and went to Raghunatha Dasa, who was still deeply absorbed in his own ecstasies, unaware that anything extraordinary had transpired.

By gently stroking Raghunatha’s back, Sanatana Gosvami brought him back to the external world and the transcendental drama in which he had been the unsuspecting lead player.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami collapsed in ecstasy at the sight of Sri Radha’s footprints. Only after a long interval was he able to collect himself and discuss the matter with Sanatana Gosvami.

This time the elder Vaisnava admonished Dasa Gosvami more forcefully. An incident like this could simply not happen again. Sanatana Gosvami looked gravely at his spiritual ward and said:

“Our lives are for serving Sri Radha and Her blissful union with Sri Krsna. Tell me, what kind of bhajana is it that not only takes service from Radha but also separates Her from Her beloved?”

Raghunatha Dasa lowered his head in shame as Sanatana continued, “If your sankirtana and smarana bring you bliss at the cost of inconveniencing Radha, Krsna, and the gopis, then what good is it?

“I told you to build a cottage so that neither Krsna nor Srimati Radharani would have to come and serve you. Now serve Them by constructing a kutira at once. Don’t delay.”

And this time Raghunatha Dasa did not delay. His friends helped him construct a cottage near Syama-kunda. When questioned by other devotees about why he was building a cottage, he would explain.

He had received an order from the most senior Vaisnava in Vraja. Following Dasa Gosvami’s lead, other renunciant Vaisnavas, who had been living in caves or under trees, also began to construct cottages.

These cottages varied in quality from unrefined thatch to burned bricks with a stone roof, but they were always simple, containing only what was needed to keep body and soul together.

About Dasa Gosvami, Sri Jiva writes:

**“Raghunatha Dasa has become world famous for being the friend of Rupa and Sanatana. He always swims in the waves of the great ocean of love for Radha and Krsna.**

**“The greatest saints say that no one in the world can compare with Rupa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami. But amazingly enough, Raghunatha Dasa has attained a position equal to theirs!”**

In his writings Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami discloses how advanced practitioners pine for Sri Radha while separated from Her and aspire to serve Her in their perfected forms as manjaris.

Amongst these books, Vilapa-kusumanjali contains Dasa Gosvami’s own aspirations as a perfected sadhaka living at Radha-kunda and yearning after Radha’s service in his eternal form as Rati-manjari.

The author’s verse-by-verse commentary on Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s work can be found in the appendix entitled “Vilapa- kusumanjali: A Bouquet of Lamentations.”

From Dasa Gosvami’s book, learned and self-controlled sadhakas can learn a great deal about the manjaris, their feelings of separation from Sri Radha, and the services they render when unired with Her.

However, those devotees whose gurus do not deem them properly qualified should not venture into topics such as these, because by doing so their spiritual advancement will be hindered, not helped.

The Krsna consciousness movement is meant to lead its members to the shores of Radha-kunda, which is filled with a liquefied form of the spontaneous love (ragatmika) that flows from the gopis' hearts.

Internally, devotees in whom attachment to the mood of a Vraja-vasi has awakened perform spontaneous devotion in practice (raganuga-bhakti), but externally behave as a regulated devotee.

Devotees in whom attachment has not yet awakened need only continue to follow the teachings and example of Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami through the chain of disciplic succession.

As regulated devotees’ attachment to Krsna gradually develops, they will see in Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami the identity, mood, and service of Rupa-manjari and Rati-manjari.

Just as no amount of extra watering can make a tree bear fruit out of season, no artificial or mechanical endeavour can awaken spontaneous devotion within a heart devoid of attachment.

The definition of spontaneous is “something that happens without premeditation or external stimulus,” thus when real attachment (raga) appears in the heart, devotion naturally flows (anuga).

Sometimes persons whose hearts are riddled with impurities foolishly imitate the moods and mannerisms of manjaris and speak openly about the manjaris’ service to Radha and Krsna in Goloka.

Because these pseudo-devotees (sahajiyas) think that the highest perfection can be purchased with the trifling currency of imitation, they live perpetually in illusion until they rectify their errant ways.

Let us therefore earnestly serve the mission of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu while praying at the lotus feet of Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and following in their footsteps.
