Krsnadasa Kaviraja has repeated over and over again that by doing so we can expect the mercy of these two acaryas. Then, and only then, will we enter the cintamani realm of spontaneous love.

**\* \* \* \***

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami came to Radha-kunda at an early age on the order of Lord Nityananda, an event the Gosvami describes at length in his magnum opus, Sri Caitanya-caritamrta.

Kaviraja Gosvami was born in the village named Jhamatapura, ten years after the birth of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Following the death of his parents, Vaisnava relatives raised him and his younger brother.

Because twenty-four-hour kirtana went on at Krsnadasa’s residence, the great devotee of Lord Nityananda, Minaketana Ramadasa, once came there to rest while visiting the village.

Absorbed in emotional love, Ramadasa sat listening to the kirtana as the people there offered him obeisances. When they did, he would occasionally slap them or climb on their shoulders in a playful mood.

From the tears flowing from his eyes, the eruptions on his body, and the trembling of his limbs, it was obvious that Ramadasa was a highly elevated transcendentalist, so everyone showed him respect.

But one brahmana who served the family Deities would not offer respect to Ramadasa. Noting this neglect, Ramadasa considered it an insult to Lord Nityananda, and in an angry voice he declared:

“Here I find the second Romaharsana-suta, who did not stand to show honour when he saw Lord Balarama.” Minaketana Ramadasa then got to his feet and danced and chanted to his heart’s content.

When Ramadasa finished kirtana and again sat down, Krsnadasa’s brother Syamananda — a staunch devotee of Lord Caitanya — argued with Ramadasa about the divinity of Lord Nityananda.

Kaviraja Gosvami at once chastised his brother. “Gaura and Nitai are like one body!” he said. “If you believe in one but not in the other, your logic is like that of accepting half a hen.”

Having seen and heard Lord Nityananda being slighted, Ramadasa was unhappy. He broke his flute and went away angry, and Krsnadasa’s brother immediately fell from devotional life.

That night Krsnadasa could not sleep. But as dawn approached, Lord Nityananda appeared to him in a dream and blessed him for his good behaviour, having chastised his brother, an offender.

Lord Nityananda was dressed like a cowherd boy: He had a glossy blackish complexion, wore many opulent ornaments, silken clothes, and a turban, and twirled a red cowherd’s stick in His hand.

His companions, also dressed like cowherd boys, were all absorbed in ecstatic love. They crowded around His lotus feet like so many bees, creating a humming sound by incessantly chanting, “Krsna! Krsna!”

Overwhelmed with transcendental ecstasy, Krsnadasa fell prostrate before Lord Nityananda, who placed His foot on Krsnadasa’s head and, smiling, spoke to him these words: “O my dear Krsnadasa!

“Do not be afraid. Go to Vrndavana, for there you will attain all things.” As Lord Nityananda spoke, He waved His hand in the direction of Vraja and then disappeared with His companions.

Roused from His dream, Krsnadasa awoke and then immediately fainted as he recalled what he had seen and heard. By the time he had regained consciousness, morning had arrived.

Krsnadasa at once embraced the order of Nityananda Mahajana and started for Vrndavana. After a long but peaceful journey, he finally arrived at his destination in great happiness.

By the mercy of Lord Nityananda, Krsnadasa Kaviraja became a disciple of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. And by that same mercy he learned the conclusions of pure devotion from Sanatana Gosvami.

By the Lord’s mercy he tasted the nectar of devotional service, and by that same mercy he attained the sidelong glance of Radha-Govinda. By divine grace he had reached the full shelter of Vrndavana-dhama.

The lesson to he learned from Kaviraja Gosvami’s personal history is that without having faith in Lord Nityananda, and without taking shelter of His lotus feet, it is impossible to approach Radha and Krsna.

Indeed, Narottama Dasa Thakura boldly declares, “If one actually wants to enter the rasa dance, Radha’s and Krsna’s dance festival, one must firmly catch hold of Lord Nityananda’s lotus feet.”

On Lord Caitanya’s order, Lord Nityananda releases a deluge of prema upon the assembly of devotees, giving equally to the worthy and the unworthy that which is difficult even for Brahma to attain.

Persons who hear of Nityananda Prabhu’s charitable disposition but still do not worship Him, and neglect to beg Him for His mercy, knowingly commit spiritual suicide. What hope is there for them?

Somehow or other we too must obtain the blessings of Lord Nityananda, which he showered upon Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami with the words, “In Vrndavana all things are possible."

The senior Vaisnavas bestowed the epithet Kaviraja (“king of poets”) upon Krsnadasa in recognition of his great literary achievements, especially Govinda-lilamrta and Sri Caitanya-caritamrta.

As an impetus for the Vaisnavas’ meditations, Srila Rupa Gosvami summarised Krsna’s daily eightfold pastimes in a short poem of eleven verses entitled Asta-kaliya-lila-smarana-mangala-stotra.

The Vaisnava community felt that these few gem-like verses should be elaborated upon, and therefore Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami requested his disciple Krsnadasa to take up that work.

Kaviraja Gosvami also acknowledged Jiva Gosvami and Raghunatha Bhatta Gosvami as instrumental in guiding him to embark upon and successfully complete that work — Govinda-lilamrta.

With the completion of Govinda-lilamrta, Kaviraja Gosvami’s literary skills and devotional achievements were fully recognised by Vrndavana’s Vaisnavas, who requested him to take up another task.

They asked him to write a biography of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Although Vrndavana Dasa Thakura had already written a biography under Lord Nityananda’s order, there was yet need of another.

The Caitanya-bhagavata of Vrndavana Dasa heavily emphasised Lord Caitanya’s pastimes in Navadvipa, thus very little detail was given of the events surrounding the Lord’s lengthy stay in Jagannatha Puri.

Dasa Gosvami had been Svarupa Damodara’s assistant in Jagannatha Puri. For years, Krsnadasa Kaviraja had listened for three hours daily to Dasa Gosvami’s eyewitness accounts of Lord Caitanya’s pastimes.

Therefore, despite his old age and infirmity, devotees felt that Kaviraja Gosvami had a sacred obligation to chronicle what he had heard from his guru, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami.

Krsnadasa accepted the undertaking. For additional references he consulted the diaries of Murari Gupta and Svarupa Damodara and interviewed other Vaisnavas who had personally met Lord Caitanya.

That Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami was able to compose a hook of such excellence while seriously impaired by old age and disease was a miracle performed by the Madana-mohana Deity.

This is confirmed by Kaviraja Gosvami himself,

*ami vrddha jaratura, likhite kanpaye kara, mane kichu smarana na haya*  
*na dekhiye nayane, na suniye sravane, tabu likhi’ — e bada vismaya*

**“I have now become too old and disturbed hy invalidity. While writing, my hands tremble. I cannot remember anything, nor can I see or hear properly. Still I write, and this is a great wonder.”**

The poetic beauty and philosophical precision with which Kaviraja Gosvami wrote has made Caitanya-caritamrta universally accepted as the foremost work on the life and teachings of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

Of Kaviraja Gosvami and his writings, Narottama Dasa Thakura has said,

**“Amongst all devotees, Krsnadasa Kaviraja is extremely expert at relishing the transcendental nectar of divine love’s mellows.**

**“When the stones hear his Caitanya-caritamrta and Govinda-lilamrta, they begin to melt in ecstasy, but in spite of this I cannot appreciate him or his writings within my heart. What misfortune!”**

From his bhajana-kutira next to Syama-kunda, Kaviraja Gosvami saw the sweetness and opulence of divine Radha-kunda and the pastimes Radha and Krsna enacted within its waters and its groves.

He recorded all these things in Govinda-lilamrta. And in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta he documented how Krsna secretly appeared in order to personally experience Radha's feelings towards Him.

Just next to Kaviraja Gosvami’s bhajana-kutira is the temple of Gaura-Gadadhara and the place of service and residence for two great saintly ladies, Ganga-mata Gosvamini and Laksmipriya-devi.

Both women were disciples of Haridasa Pandita, himself a disciple of Gadadhara Pandita. Haridasa Pandita instructed Laksmipriya to live by Radha-kunda and worship the Deities of Gaura-Gadadhara.

Ganga-devi was born into a family of royalty, but she gave up the throne to live on the banks of the Yamuna. When Haridasa gave her initiation he instructed her to join Laksmipriya at Radha-kunda.

Because of the spiritual purity of the two women and their dedication to daily chanting three hundred thousand holy names, the Vaisnavas of Radha-kunda were very favourably disposed to them.

Indeed when Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami left the world, the Govardhana-sila that he had personally received from Caitanya Mahaprabhu was given to the care of Laksmipriya-devi.

Laksmipriya worshipped the sild according to Lord Caitanya’s original instructions, and upon her demise another female saint, Krsnapriya Thakurani, served it before willing it to Cakravarti Thakura.

Along the bank of Syama-kunda stand Krsna’s close friends, the five Pandava brothers, in the form of five special trees. Today in Bhauma Vrndavana the only tree still manifested is that of Arjuna.

Like the Pandavas, many other great souls appear in Vrndavana in the bodies of trees so that they can avoid recognition and absorb themselves in bhajana without the distractions of celebrity.

While Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami was expanding Vajra-kunda into what is the present day Syama-kunda, it was decided that these trees would have to be cut down to make way for the excavation.

That night, however, Dasa Gosvami had a dream in which Maharaja Yudhisthira appeared and revealed that he and his brothers resided in the bodies of those trees and requested that they be allowed to stay.

Of course, Raghunatha Dasa at once cancelled the plan to remove the trees. Thus, due to the central location of those trees, the shape of Syama-kunda in Bhauma Vrndavana is now irregular.

**\* \* \* \***

North of Panca-pandava-ghata is the temple of Radha-Govinda — marking the divine couple’s daily meeting place — as well as the temple of the jihva-sila — the tongue of Govardhana Hill.

Radha and Krsna come together here, and so this is one of two places called the Yoga-pitha of Radha-kunda. The other place celebrated as the Yoga-pitha is the sangama, where the two lakes meet.

The Radha-Govinda Deities there are the representatives (pratibhu) of Rupa Gosvami’s original Deities, who were first installed in Their temple upon the Govinda-sthali Hill in Vrndavana.

Like most Deities around Radha-kunda, Radha and Govinda were installed after the original Deities of Vrndavana had briefly stayed there on Their way to the safety of Jaipur.

Out of fear that Aurangzeb would destroy the temples of Vrndavana, the Vaisnava leaders decided to take the main Deities to Jaipur. Only a few, such as Radha-ramana, remained there in Vrndavana.

To this day, many of Vrndavana's original Deities are in Jaipur. The Deities under Their names now worshipped in Bhauma Vrndavana were installed later as representatives of the originals.

The original Radha and Govinda Deities, for example, are worshipped at the king’s palace in Jaipur, while one set of pratibhu Deities are at Govinda-sthali in Vrndavana and a second set at Radha-kunda.

Other sets of pratibhu Deities — such as Radha-Damodara and Radha-Gopinatha— are also currently worshipped in temples at Radha-kunda or in the town of Vrndavana.

In New Vraja-dhama, all the Deities of Vrndavana town and Radha-kunda are worshipped through Radha-Syamasundara, the only Radha-Krsna Deities worshipped in an iskcon temple in Hungary.

Devotees are generally enthusiastic to worship Deities in their homes or preaching centres. They want to instal Radha and Krsna, Jagannatha-Baladeva-Subhadra, or salagrama-silas, amongst others.

Over time, however, we have seen that devotees’ initial enthusiasm to worship such Deities at home or in the temple tends not to match their ability to maintain acceptable standards of service.

As a consequence of the offences incurred by such neglect, everyone involved in the installation and responsible for the degradation of the standard — indeed everyone in the area — suffers.

For this reason the worship in iskcon’s centres in Hungary is done primarily to pictures or bas-reliefs of Radha and Syamasundara, a standard we recommend devotees follow in their homes as well.

Devotees who want to serve Deities in their homes are encouraged to worship the all-merciful Gaura and Nitai, who bestow the highest benefit with even simple worship, and without any risk of offence.

Our ardent hope is that this strategy will protect the standard of Radha’s and Syama’s worship for many years to come, which will in turn ensure the spiritual health and success of the Hungarian yatra.

The Radha-kunda of Bhauma Vrndavana is now home to pratibhu-murtis, replicas of the original Deities installed in Vrndavana town by the Gosvami followers of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

In the many temples that surround Radha's lake, devotees can worship Madana-mohana, Govindaji, Gopinatha, and other sacred forms of the Lord without ever leaving Radha-kunda.

The construction of these temples and the installation ceremonies for the replica Deities were done after the historical relocation of most of Vrndavana’s original Deities to the precincts of Jaipur.

During Lord Caitanya’s time, His followers in Vrndavana recovered the original Deities established by Vajra and constructed ornate temples for Them with the patronage of kings and merchants.

With the added renown of many famous temples, ancient Deities, and eminent devotees, Vrndavana flourished as a Gaudiya Vaisnava stronghold and one of India’s prominent religious centres.

It is said that even Emperor Akbar visited Vrndavana. Notably impressed with its saints and spiritual atmosphere, the emperor granted Jiva Gosvami permission to construct four temples.

The temple of Govindaji was one of these four. The Emperor also donated funds for constructing a library at the Radha-Damodara temple to preserve the writings of the Gosvamis.

Lord Caitanya’s desire to recover Vrndavana’s lost glory for the greater glorification of Krsna was materialising. The principal place of pilgrimage for Gaudiya-Vaisnavas had been established.

But barely a century and a half after Lord Caitanya’s visit, Aurangzeb, fearing that Hinduism was becoming a unifying force for his subjects, gave the order — destroy Vraja’s Deities and temples.

Vrndavana’s gentle devotees appealed to the kings of Rajasthan for help, and the kings complied. Thus, one night, under cover of darkness, a mysterious caravan made its way to Radha-kunda.

Without pomp, ordinary bullock carts transported the precious Deities of Vrndavana to Their new homes around Radha’s lake, joined by the Vaisnava brahmanas for whom They were life and soul.

With Vrndavana’s saints and Deities gone and its temples defaced or destroyed, pilgrims were no longer willing to risk persecution to visit there, and the land of Krsna’s youth faded into obscurity once again.

Meanwhile, the Deities were being worshipped in various temples extemporaneously built around Radha-kunda. Everyone thought that They were safe and would eventually return to Vrndavana.

But when Aurangzeb’s soldiers returned to Vrndavana and forced Gopala to vacate His hilltop temple in nearby Govardhana, devotees decided to move the Deities to Kaman, a more remote part of Vraja.

Once again a caravan of bullock carts transported the Deities and Their devotees, this time to Kaman, where They were again placed in existing, newly built, or temporary temples. Peace reigned, for a time.

As in Radha-kunda, the Deities were meant to stay in Kaman only temporarily, then return to Vrndavana when Aurangzeb softened his stance towards non-Muslims. Thirty years passed in that vain hope.

Opinions differ on how long the Deities actually stayed at Kaman, and whether They all left together or at different times to Amber, from where They were later relocated to temples in Jaipur.

When the Deities were once again ready to depart, however, Vrnda-devi , whom Rupa Gosvami had discovered in Brahma-kunda, informed her guardians that she would not leave Vraja.

Krsna may leave Vrndavana, but if Vrnda — after whom Krsna’s land is named and in whose care it is entrusted — were to leave, what hope would there be for the blessings of Vrndavana to remain?

Out of her mercy, then, she continues to reside in Govindaji’s temple at Kaman. Replicas of the exiled Deities were fashioned and then installed in temples around Kaman where They remain to this day.

After three and a half centuries, most of the Gosvamis’ original Deities continue to be worshipped in Jaipur, except for the few who have returned to Vrndavana, like Radha-Damodara.

Of all the Deities in Jaipur, Govindaji is the most popular and most revered. His temple is found in the king’s garden, where He is worshipped alongside Kasisvara Pandita's Gaura-Govinda Deity.

I often wonder why the Gosvamis' Deities did not return to Vrndavana. Historical circumstances make it clear why They left, but why have They not returned to Their original homes?

Have the Deities, like Krsna, left Vraja permanently to increase Their admirers’ attachment? Have they not returned because of offences? Or do They want to set an example for Their devotees?

Caitanya Mahaprabhu is Krsna Himself, and He clearly predicted that Krsna’s names would be chanted all over the world. Might it be that the Deities left Vraja to show how this was possible?

In Vrndavana there were already temples, Deities, and the chanting of the Lord’s holy names. Did the Gosvamis’ Deities take it upon Themselves to preach to the devotees of Jaipur?

And while devotees may vow to stay in Kaman, Radha-kunda, or Vrndavana to advance through solitary spiritual endeavours, did the Lord Himself choose to go out of Vraja for the benefit of others?

The exodus of the Gosvamis’ Deities and the self-imposed exile They observe to this day are pastimes of Their own, pastimes They enact for Their own mysterious purposes. Who can fully understand?

By His own munificence, the Lord appeared in New Vraja-dhama. With Radha by His side, He brought the sweetness and opulence of Vraja to engladden with His charms the dour souls of this land.

Let us glorify this all-merciful Lord and pray that we may humbly accept the kindness He shows. “O my dear Krsna! Ocean of mercy! You are the friend of the distressed and the source of creation!

“O beloved Lord! O merciful one! You are the master of the cowherd men and the lover of the gopis, especially Srimati Radharani. I offer my respectful obeisances unto You.”

Jaya! Jaya! Radha-Madana-mohana! Radha-Govinda! Radha-Gopinatha! Radha-Damodara! Radha-Syamasundara! Radha-ramana! Radha-Gokulananda! All glories to You! All glories to You!

*At some holy places one becomes free from all sins, at others one becomes free from the bondage of karma, at still others one attains Brahman happiness, and yet at others one attains residence in Viṣṇuloka. Let us glorify residence at Kṛṣṇa-kuṇḍa, where without any effort one attains the jewel of pure love for Kṛṣṇa. (Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura)*

## Chapter 17 - Svananda-sukhada-kunja to Radha-Gokulananda Mandira

All glories to Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda, the two love-filled eyes of Govardhana Hill! The nectarean pastimes the divine couple enjoy on the shores of these two lakes nourish the hungry ears of Vaisnavas.

All glories to Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda! By the beauty of their groves, the touch of their waters, and the recitation of their glories, these two lakes water the root of pure devotion in Vaisnavas’ hearts.

From the Radha-Govinda temple near Syama-kunda, the parikrama path first passes the temples of Radha-ramana and Mahadeva on the left before one path continues north as the parikrama path veers east.

Along this path going north we first find the samadhi of Lord Caitanya’s intimate associate, Narahari Sarakara, and a little further on to the right, the residence of Bhaktivinoda Thakura.

A resident of Srikhanda and a physician by profession, Narahari Sarakara was a pure devotee of the Lord whose body and mind were steeped in love for the divine couple and Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

During Lord Caitanya’s earthly pastimes, Narahari served the Lord in many ways, such as fanning Him with a camara, but when the Lord departed from the world, Narahari retired here to Radha-kunda.

Narahari’s book on the relationship between gurus and their disciples, Sri-krsna-bhajanamrta, was commissioned by Caitanya Mahaprabhu and to this day remains a valuable source of knowledge on the subject.

Narahari Sarakara’s disciple Locana Dasa Thakura said of his guru,

**“In the spiritual world of Vrndavana he is the great reservoir of sweetness and the dear friend of Srimati Radharani, Madhumati.”**

Further along is the bhajana-kutira of Bhaktivinoda Thakura, known as Svananda-sukhada-kunja. In this cottage Bhaktivinoda eternally resides as Kamala-manjari, his form in Krsna’s unmanifest pastimes.

Sometimes Svananda-sukhada-kunja refers to Lalita-devi’s entire grove, Lalitanandada-kunja, and sometimes it refers to just the secluded portion of Lalita’s grove that is home to Kamala-manjari.

Vrndavana is identical with Navadvipa, and so this grove appears in both places. And Thakura Bhaktivinoda constructed a house for himself within each of the earthly counterparts of both dhamas.

In his writings, Thakura Bhaktivinoda reveals certain aspects of his spiritual identity and service, thus giving practising devotees a glimpse into eternal life on the cintamani-shores of Radha-kunda.

As a resident of Radha-kunda, the Thakura is Kamala-manjari, a twelve-and-a-half-year-old gopi whose complexion is the colour of lightning and whose clothes resemble the star-lit sky.

Kamala-manjari lives in Svananda-sukhada-kunja, and so naturally she is a follower of Lalita-devi. Kamala prepares camphor for the divine couple under the direction of Rupa-manjari and her assistants.

Sometimes Kamala-manjari sits in her grove singing Krsna’s names, only to have the sound of Krsna’s murali flute enter her ear, steal her mind, and leave her madly crying in bliss.

Sometimes, during the period of midday, Rupa-manjari will call upon Kamala-manjari to engage in direct services to Radha and Krsna like fanning Them, anointing Their bodies, or massaging Their lotus feet.

At other times Kamala-manjari lives happily by Radha-kunda with other manjari followers of Sri Rupa, learning new services to the divine couple and hearing the details of Their latest pastimes.

In his writings, Bhaktivinoda Thakura also shares his deep insight into the moods of those devotees whose ambition is to reside at Radha-kunda and serve as maidservants of Srimati Radharani.

He explains that those devotees all share the intense conviction that service to Sri Radha is supreme, a conviction honoured by all transcendentalists, whatever their relationship with Krsna may be.

That conviction of Rupa-manjari’s followers is this: Persons who fail to worship Radha’s lotus feet in the gardens of Vraja can never taste the bliss of the only sublime mellow able to completely control Krsna.

The secrets of worshipping Radha are the exclusive property of Her wise and devoted companions, who surpass in grace those who have achieved perfection by following any other spiritual discipline.

The acarya of the diverse and at times unpredictable ways of amorous love is Sri Radha, whose loving exchanges with Krsna are more than worthy to be heard, discussed, and contemplated.

Fortunate devotees who have grasped hold of Srimati Radharani’s lotus feet with great care are assured of obtaining the priceless jewels of Krsna’s lotus feet, upon which perfect yogis can only meditate.

All the Vedas are actually saying that without taking shelter of Radha and Her maidservants, no one — regardless of the devotional mellow for which he or she aspires — can ever meet Krsna face to face.

To attain Krsna one should thus abandon wealth, followers, wife, sons, and friends, and giving up materialistic activities and mental speculation, absorb himself in serving Sri Radha’s lotus feet.

**\* \* \* \***

Thakura Bhaktivinoda describes Radha as residing within the transcendental land of Vraja, far beyond the Viraja River, the spiritual sky, and the countless Vaikuntha planets.

Beautiful Vraja is filled with desire trees and vines, amongst which one moving tamala tree, Sri Krsna, causes the first spring breeze of an extraordinary type of astonishment to sweep through the groves.

Entwined around that tamala tree is the beautiful golden creeper, Sri Radha, the essence of Krsna’s pleasure potency, who — by Her touch, fragrance, and flowers — enchants the enchanter of the three worlds.

Radha’s girlfriends, headed by Lalita-devi, are the leaves and flowers of that creeper. They all help to bind Krsna in an embrace so tight and so enchanting that He never even thinks to break free from it.

At the slightest touch of the Radha-creeper, the Krsna-tamala-tree blooms in bliss. And though the creeper never desires to leave the tree, if it were to do so the tree would lose its life at once.

This beloved daughter of Vrsabhanu is the diamond tiara amongst jewel-like adolescent girls. Her radiant complexion—like molten gold — elegantly complements Her blue garments and dark, curly hair.

Her forehead marked with tilaka, Her roving blue eyes outlined with collyrium, and Her limbs elegantly adorned with jewellery, Srimati Radharani appears to be sweetness personified.

When goddesses like Rati, Gauri, or Lila see the gleaming rays of excellence born from Sri Radha’s peerless mastery of hari-rasa, they abandon their pride in being universally famed for their beauty.

Similarly, goddesses of fortune like Laksmi, Saci, and Satya feel impoverished when they stand at the doorway to the treasure house of divine Providence — Sri Radha’s pinkish lotus feet.

And rival gopis, headed by Candravali, bow their heads in shame, remaining always sulky and quarrelsome because of their inability to completely control Krsna in the same way Sri Radha does.

Considering all this, what wise sadhaka would neglect to follow Bhaktivinoda Thakura’s words and refuse to worship Radha with care and enthusiasm in order to become a maidservant of Her lotus feet?

Srimati Radharani is the queen of amorous, swan-like maidens expert in relishing transcendental mellows amongst the innumerable lotuses of ecstasy that float upon the nectarean waters of love for Krsna.

Her hips bound by a red silken cloth fringed with tiny bells, Her chest decorated with a necklace of large pearls, She is so attractive that whosoever glances upon Her must lose their hearts.

And as such persons contemplate the ambrosial adolescence that mixes with the fragrant camphor of fresh youth to form the mystifying smile on Her lips, they, like Krsna, also lose their minds.

Her unique bodily lustre proclaims total fidelity to Krsna, fidelity so complete that it is a template for the sort of devotional faith aspired for by practising devotees and transcendentalists alike.

As that mischievous son of Nanda reappears on the edge of Vrndavana forest after a long day of tending cows, Radha affectionately speaks to Him through the movements of Her eyes.

Radha’s love is the life of the elder women of Vraja, especially Yasoda, just as it is for Krsna. And gopis like Lalita bask in Her affection just as golden lotuses bask in bright, warm rays of sunshine.

Radha is the well-wisher of every living entity, whether it be in Vraja or anywhere else. Her graceful limbs, artistic skills, and fully- blossomed love are all unrivalled, and yet She stays forever humble.

Radha picks forest flowers with Visakha and then calmly strings a vaijayanti garland for Her beloved Krsna, but when She hears the soft tones of a distant flute, She runs off in a frenzy to find its player.

Radha arrives at the grove where that player is and sees a black effulgence colouring the foliage. Catching a glimpse of Krsna, She shyly lowers Her smiling face and self-consciously scratches Her ear.

In the summer, fresh lotus-scented breezes cool Radha-kunda. And within the refreshing waters of that sacred lake, Radha and Her girlfriends satisfy the hero of Gokula with water sports.

In spring, the forests lining the banks of the Yamuna are especially beautiful. They satisfy the eyes with colourful foliage, the ears with melodiously chirping birds, and the nose with delightful scents.

Swarms of bumblebees fly about in search of honey, a gentle Malayan breeze caresses everything and everyone, and the full moon sends out its cooling rays, painting the forest with a fresh coat of silvery light.

At this choice moment, the pre-eminent connoisseur of love plays a lively flute-song to initiate His rasa dance. Soon, countless blissful gopis surround Him, and Radha dances alongside Him.

Krsna’s enchantress, Sri Radha, sings songs that steal away the minds of all living things in the three worlds, charm all moving and non-moving beings in Vrndavana, and excite the heart of Her beloved.

Then, suddenly, Radha disappears, as if blown away in a strong wind. Calamity instantly strikes Krsna and the rasa dance, which abruptly stops in Radha’s absence, as does a potter’s wheel without the potter.

Millions of gopis, no matter how hard they try, are unable to please Krsna. They cannot replace Radha, either in His heart or at the centre of the dancing arena; indeed, the hallisaka circle is frozen still.

Krsna raises His flute to His lips and calls out in a wordless flute-song, “Radha! Please return! Please return!” But She does not, and so He abandons all the other gopis to go out alone in search of Her.

As He wanders, weeping, through the lonely forest, Krsna calls out, “Radha! Please be kind. Come back and save My life!" But all He hears is the echo of His voice. Each step brings Him closer to despair.

But before hope runs out, Krsna finds Radha sitting in a grove, pouting but remorseful. Krsna falls at Her feet and says, “Without You there is no rasa dance. I think Vraja is lifeless without You.”

Thakura Bhaktivinoda prays,

**“At the lotus feet of Radha, who controls Krsna in this way, I beg, ‘Please! Make me Your own kept maidservant. Count me amongst Your personal entourage.’”**

**\* \* \* \***

Dear Vaisnavas! Meditate deeply upon the unfailing principles of vraja-bhakti as revealed in the loving exchanges between Radha and Krsna and understand them with the guidance of our acaryas.

One of those acaryas, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura writes, *radha-madhava-suddha-prem vicarya*: “This pure love between Radha and Madhava is worthy of discussion and contemplation.”

Any worship of Maharaja Nanda’s son that does not bring about the desire to worship Srimati Radharani is as useless and misguided as an attempt to know the sun without the sunlight.

Those who worship Madhava without His eternal consort are lacking in knowledge, but worse are those who disrespect Her. Anyone who aspires to enter Vraja must at once abandon such proud fools.

But those who consider themselves humble maidservants of Sri Radha are quickly brought by the strength of their devotion to Sri Krsna, whom yogis and jnanis strive to attain for many, many lifetimes.

Lord Brahma, Siva, Narada, the personified Vedas, and Laksmi-devi all honour and worship the dust of Radhika’s lotus feet. Uma, Rama, Satya, Saci, Candra, and Rukmini are Her expansions.

In conclusion, as Bhaktivinoda Thakura teaches, let us beg Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami to bestow upon us the wealth of those who are truly wise — eternal service to Srimati Radharani.

Such expressions of unwavering attachment to Sri Radha — which naturally include attachment to Sri Krsna — convey the mood of Radha-kunda, its residents, and the pastimes that occur there.

While residing at Radha-kunda, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura once instructed his disciples on the mood of exclusive devotion to Sri Radha, a mood he personally identified with.

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura was out walking when he came across a wealthy landowner from the district of Bharatapura performing dandavat-parikrama around Radha-kunda with his family.

The pilgrims would recite prayers with devotion as they lay down on the ground. Then they would slowly rise and again reverentially how down. In this way they circled both Radha- and Syama-kunda.

One of Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura’s disciples commented that the landowner and his family must have great respect for Srimati Radharani to circumambulate Her lake with such devotion.

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura answered,

**“No doubt they respect Radha. But their mood of respect towards Her and Her lake is different than ours. Their worshipable Deity is Krsna.**

**“And because Radha is Krsna’s favourite, they show respect to Her. But our mood is just the opposite,” he emphasised. “Our worshipable Deity is Radha. And because She wants Krsna, we serve Him.”**

This mood of devotion is the special feature of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s teachings. Gaudiya Vaisnavas thus aspire for exclusive devotion and service to Srimati Radharani.

Amongst the many liberated souls, one who has concluded that Lord Narayana is Supreme — and that the goal of life is to serve Him — is the best of all and is known by the honorific title of “Vaisnava.”

And amongst Vaisnavas dedicated solely to serving the Lord, those whose hearts have been stolen by Govinda are the best; even Lord Narayana's opulences cannot purchase their affection.

But devotees whose hearts have been attracted by the sweetness and kind disposition of Srimati Radharani, who is glorified by Narada and other sages, do not even want to serve Krsna if He is not with Her.

In fact, even more than not wanting Krsna without Radha, such devotees are prepared to leave Vraja at once if they hear that Radha has mysteriously appeared in a distant place such as Dvaraka.

I have heard of Sri Radha’s extraordinary qualities, and thus I nurture a long-cherished hope that has become like an ocean of nectar for me, a hope that gives life to my life and inspires my sadhana.

With that hope I leave New Vraja-dhama to preach elsewhere. With that hope I tolerate criticism from non-devotees and devotees alike. And with that hope I accept struggle and strife for iskcon’s success.

While so doing I gather strength from my own aspirations, which at times resemble the attempts of a dwarf reaching for the moon, and I repeat Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s inspirational words.

Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati was very fond of this verse. When in the company of confidential disciples he would sometimes quote it, and as he did so he would turn pale and show other ecstatic symptoms.

*Asa-bharair amrta-sindhu-mayaih kathancit kalo mayati-gamitah kila sampratam hi*  
*tvam cet krpam mayi vidhasyasi naiva kim me pranair vrajena ca varoru bakarinapi*

**“For me somehow the present moment is flooded by a nectar ocean of many hopes. If You do not give Your mercy, then of what use to me are this life, the land of Vraja, and Sri Krsna, the enemy of Baka?"**

**\* \* \* \***

Some distance beyond Radha-kunda is the garden called Navagrama. Sometimes called Kunjera due to its many beautiful groves, a more fitting name would be Kunjara, the place of the elephant.

The elephant I allude to is not of the species that once packed the streets of Hastinapura, but a very special sort never seen outside of Vraja. Even in Vraja, it was only seen by a select few fortunate souls.

This elephant was made of gopis who acrobatically arranged themselves into its different parts, and which Krsna mounted and drove hither and thither using Cupid’s goad.

Four gopis posed as the elephant’s four legs; one each, its tail and trunk; and many others, its torso and head. Krsna was as amazed by this marvellous creature as were the forest animals who saw it.

Climbing up into a tree, Krsna mounted the gopi-elephant and used His flute as a goad, directing the divine creature to move about the secluded garden of Navagrama according to His will.

Vaisnavas would do well to note the significance of this pastime, which broadcasts the unparalleled supremacy of Krsna, a truth always to be borne in mind while hearing about His pastimes in Vraja.

To taste the sweetness of pure love, Krsna becomes subordinate to His devotees: He bows before Radha, massages His brother’s feet, carries His father’s shoes, and performs other assorted services.

In the oceanic realm of mellows known as vraja-bhakti, such conduct by Krsna is commonplace. Therefore practising devotees may at times forget that Krsna is God, but the Vraja-vasis never do.

Underlying the raging waters of the Vraja-vasis’ spontaneous love for Krsna is the solid riverbed of their awareness of Krsna’s supreme divinity; in fact, these two are inextricably linked, one to the other.

Just as one can see the water of a flowing river but not its riverbed, devotees listening to Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes see the Vraja-vasis’ familiar dealings with Krsna, but not their reverence for Him.

What’s more, just as water without a riverbed seeps into the ground and never becomes a river, hearing of Krsna’s familiar dealings without realisation of His divinity never manifests love for Krsna.

Authentic feelings of spontaneous affection arise only in devotees who have implicit faith in Krsna’s Godhood, faith which arises only after they are able to always depend upon His protection.

The Vraja-vasis’ visible spontaneity is grounded in their inherent understanding of Krsna’s divinity. For instance, when Uddhava visited Vraja he first visited Nanda Maharaja and Mother Yasoda.

Uddhava could feel the depth of their sorrow at Krsna’s absence from Vrndavana, so he tried to pacify Krsna’s parents by reassuring them that as the Supreme Lord, Krsna was everywhere and in everything.

Hearing Uddhava’s logic, Nanda Maharaja thought, “Even though Krsna may be the Supreme Lord, we do not think of Him as an object of worship. We simply think of Krsna as our son.

“We find satisfaction by offering Him the remnants of our chewed betel. If He were not our son, our minds would not be satisfied. Before Krsna’s birth we could meditate on Narayana, our family Deity.

“But now, as soon as we meditate on Narayana, He appears directly in front of us. This is a sign of the satisfaction in our minds. Therefore acting like this in relation to our son is not a fault.”

Balarama is Krsna’s brother and sometimes, while playing like a bull, He fights with Krsna head to head. But He always knows that He is but a dancing puppet in the hands of Krsna, the supreme puppeteer.

The gopis are Krsna’s lovers, and in their intimate dealings they sometimes quarrel with Him; nonetheless, they too know that their roles as lovers are but part of a script of which He is the playwright.

To dramatise this truth — that Krsna alone is the supreme controller, and all others are servants who dance according to His will — the gopis brought this transcendental elephant to life.

Their acrobatics illustrate that both individually and collectively they are always under the control of Krsna and His flute. In all situations, whatever He asks of them they will do, unconditionally.

Shameless materialists profit by selling licentious pictures that depict the gopis as they manifest the highest form of divine surrender (atma- nivedanam), offering their bodies in Lord Krsna’s service.

These intimate scenes of absolute surrender factually appear only within the purified minds of perfected souls or to the purified eyes of Krsna’s gopi girlfriends. They will degrade anyone else.

Pure-minded practising devotees may perceive the full surrender portrayed in a picture of Kunjara-lila, but non-devotees should not even be shown such things, for their minds are full of evil thoughts.

After Kunjara is Balarama-kunda, where as mentioned in the portrait of the Yoga-pitha, Sankarsana-Balarama resides with His wife Revati upon the southern petal of Vraja in an enchanting grove.

In Bhauma Vrndavana today that grove is marked by Balarama-kunda, which, like many of the original lakes in Vraja, is dried out and thus only visible during the rainy season.

In the centre of that serene white grove — just as Syama-kunda is encompassed by several charming groves — sits refreshing Balarama- kunda, like an aquamarine gem set in a necklace of white gold.

Full of sandalwood trees, Balarama’s grove is cool even on the hottest summer days. Balarama sits on a throne made of moonstone, within a moonstone palace, eyes rolling, intoxicated from drinking varuni.

Lord Balarama’s arms, handsomely long and white, appear like silver columns. Passionate gopis, captivated by the elegance of those limbs, smear them with aguru and sandalwood.

Dressed in shimmering blue silk, Balarama’s milk-white form is pure religiosity personified, ornamented with belt, rings, and necklaces of gold inlaid with the most precious of sparkling gems.

Just as the daughters of serpent kings serve Lord Ananta at the bottom of the universe, beautiful gopis, eager for Lord Balarama’s cooling touch, smear His body with fragrant oils.

The gopis who love and serve Lord Balarama are either His eternally liberated companions or perfected sadhakas like the daughters of the king of snakes (naga-kanyas), who desired to marry Lord Ananta.

Even the Lord’s liberated associates are awarded the positions of gopis only after performing great austerities, so conditioned souls of this age cannot expect such perfection to come without great endeavour.

The truth is that in this Age of Kali only offenceless congregational chanting of Krsna’s holy names guided by the self-realised envoys of Caitanya Mahaprabhu can award vraja-bhava. Nothing else can!

To see how difficult it is to attain the Lord’s company — as a gopi— without Lord Caitanya’s mercy, let us consider the five methods of worship (pancanga) Garga Muni prescribed for the naga-kanyas.

**\* \* \* \***

One day Garga Muni left his asrama on Mount Garga and went to Vraja, planning to bathe in the Yamuna. After bathing, he sat down in a quiet grove by the riverside to meditate on Krsna and Balarama.

Gentle breezes moved the tree branches, flowering vines, and new sprouts. As bees swarmed about, maddened by the sweet scent of new blossoms, a group of girls appeared and bowed down before the Muni.

These girls were the snake king’s daughters, who had taken birth as gopis in Vraja by the blessings of Anantadeva. But their ardent desire was to enter the circle of Balarama’s intimate girlfriends.

These gopis remembered their previous births as snake princesses and asked the sage what kind of devotional service they should now perform to fulfil their long-cherished desire, lest they die of sorrow.

Garga Muni could see their great devotion. Thus he gave them the five methods of worshipping Lord Balarama: paddhati, patala, stotra, kavaca, and sahasra-nama. By these processes they became perfect.

The first limb of this worship consists of daily rites (paddhati) that include meditation on Lord Balarama, sleeping on the ground, eating only once, and drinking only twice a day.

The second limb of worship begins with perfecting a mula-mantra (patala) by chanting it more than one hundred thousand times and ends with offering fifty thousand oblations into a sacred fire.

The third limb consists of regularly reciting a prayer (stotra) to Lord Balarama. By offencelessly chanting that prayer one is freed from bodily identification and from the influence of the modes of nature.

The fourth limb consists of summoning by mantras the transcendental shield of Balarama (kavaca), which frees one from sinful reaction and protects one from obstacles and inimical persons.

The fifth limb consists of chanting the one thousand names of Lord Balarama (sahasra-nama) one thousand times, which completes the process of worship and brings one to the shore of transcendental bliss.

One who adopts this fivefold path of paddhati, patala, stotra, kavaca, and sahasra-nama surely attains material and spiritual perfection. But where is the devotee determined enough to do so without error?

For Vedic rites to be successful, the practitioner must pronounce the mantras perfectly and complete the rituals without mistake, otherwise he or she may reap results opposite to those intended.

While performing a sacrifice to kill Indra, Tvasta chanted a mantra to increase Indra's enemies, hut because he mispronounced the mantra, the sacrifice produced a demon whom Indra considered an enemy.

Similarly, Diti performed the pumsavana sacrifice with the aim of getting a son who would kill Indra. But she forgot to wash her mouth once after eating, and thus her son became a follower of Indra.

In contrast, the dying Ajamila called out his son’s name, “Narayana!" He neither intended to chant Krsna’s name, nor did he chant it purely, but simply because he uttered the holy name he was liberated.

One who chants the Lord’s name is at once freed from the reactions to unlimited sins even if he chants in jest, with something other than the Lord in mind, for musical entertainment, or even neglectfully.

If liberation can be obtained by once calling out “Narayana!" without faith, is it surprising that devotees who constantly chant the Lord's holy name with faith and attention easily attain pure devotion?

And after becoming opulent with the treasures of pure devotion, is it any wonder that even in this life devotees glimpse their spiritual forms (siddha-svarupa), which may be that of gopas or gopis!

Dear readers! Please don’t be deviated by those who recommend burdensome paddhatis, mantras, stotras, kavacas, or sahasra-namas as fast tracks to perfection. Whoever does so is ill-advised.

The appendix entitled “The Five Methods of Worshipping Lord Balarama,” adapted from Sri Garga-samhita, describes this pancanga process in detail, thus showing the obvious difficulty in following it.

The best paddhati, mantra, stotra, kavaca, and sahasra-nama is to incessantly chant the Hare Krsna maha-mantra with firm faith. That will quickly bless us with perfection like that of the naga-kanyas.

Indeed those fortunate gopis received the mercy of the Lord on a late spring night, as the rising full moon reddened the hearts of not only Balarama and His gopis but also of the whole Vrndavana forest.

That night unfurled its magic during the two-month period in which Balarama visited Vrndavana and fulfilled His desire to be reunited with the gopas, gopis, cows, and especially Nanda and Yasoda.

Delightfully gentle breezes thick with lotus pollen blew across Yamuna’s waves and then ashore, caressing the flowering vines, bushes, and trees with their cool, exhilarating touch.

The forest of Vrndavana was splendid with diverse groves and courtyards, each filled with the fragrant pollen of delicate flowers, the calls of cuckoos and peacocks, and the sweet hum of bees.

Dressed in blue garments and decorated with tinkling ankle bells, jewel necklaces, and a glittering crown, Lord Balarama, lotus eyes glinting, revelled with His winsome gopis in the rasa dance.

As the gopis and their infallible Lord enjoyed a long-awaited reunion, an intoxicating honey called varuni flowed from the hollows of the trees. Its heady aroma permeated the forest.

Lord Balarama eagerly consumed the honey-like beverage, relishing a state of transcendental tipsiness in which His lotus eyes turned red and rolled back in His head and His powerful limbs went slack.

He wandered about aimlessly like the king of elephants followed by His queens. Perspiration flowed down Lord Balarama’s moon-white face, washing away the tilaka on His forehead and cheeks.

In one forest grove or another He would sometimes sit upon a throne to rest or lean against a tree as gopis surrounded Him, raising their voices to the sky with songs of His pure glories.

For a while the Lord walked along the shore of the Yamuna, though at times He would follow a different path into the forest and enjoy the company of the gopis and the opulences of the occasion.

In this way Lord Balarama and the gopis walked south until they came to a grove within sight of the river Yamuna. There He sat down, exhausted, and thought, “I am unable to walk another step.”

He wanted to refresh Himself by bathing and enjoying water pastimes, and so He called for the Yamuna to come to where He sat. But His repeated requests were left unanswered, making Him angry.

The Lord lifted His plough and sunk it into the Yamuna’s bank, pulling the river towards Him as effortlessly as a small boy would pull the string of a toy bow with his fingers.

Lord Balarama repeatedly scratched the earth with His plough, and each time He did a new tributary was formed. It looked like the grand Yamuna would be reduced to a maze of minor rivulets.

“Come! Come!” He bellowed. Determined to transform the Yamuna into a series of trifling irrigation canals, His eyes red from both intoxication and anger, Lord Balarama rose to His feet and said:

“Even though I have called upon you, it seems that out of disrespect you have ignored Me and are determined to flow your own way. Very well, then, I will divide you into a hundred tiny streams.”

Having witnessed Balarama’s strength, Yamuna-devi, fearful and humbled, appeared to the Lord in person and fell at His lotus feet. She then attempted to pacify Him with prayers.

Later, when we pass through the southern portion of Vrndavana near Kacchapavana, we will hear those prayers of Yamuna-devi as well as more details of her pastime with Lord Balarama.

“O Lord Balarama who maintains the earth! O glorious Lord, perfect and complete, who holds a plough in Your hand. O Lord who has a thousand heads, O Lord Sankarsana, eternal obeisances to You!”

“O Balarama! You are the Lord who broke the Yamuna and dragged Hastinapura. You are the enemy of the gorilla, Dvivida. You are the king of the Yadavas and the ornament of Vraja-mandala.”

**\* \* \* \***

Further along the parikrama path is a temple of Lord Jagannatha, Lord Balarama, and Subhadra Maharani. Behind the temple in the distance is exalted Vrsabhanu-kunda.

It is said that when Maharaja Vrsabhanu and his townspeople came to observe the worship of Govardhana Hill they camped by the banks of that delightful lake and then continued on to Aniyora.

The next sacred places along the parikrama path are two kundas intimately related to Sri Radha: Lalita-kunda to the left and Mohana-kunda behind it. The bhajana-kutira of Jiva Gosvami is to the right.

The two kundas appeared when Lalita and Krsna were once sharing memories of their mutual encounters with Radha and thus increasing each other's love for the indisputable queen of their hearts.

“O Mohana!” Lalita said. “Do you remember that stormy evening when my friend ignored the threats of Her husband and the anger of Her other superiors to meet You at an appointed forest grove?”

Krsna shook His head to say that He had forgotten, but actually He remembered well. He was simply eager to hear Lalita-devi recount the details of that unforgettable encounter.

“Listen, then,” she replied, “and learn something of the eddies and whirlpools in the streams of my friend’s ecstatic love for You. That love often swells its banks due to the monsoon rains of Your neglect.

“That night Radha pushed aside the servant who blocked Her door. Blind to disgrace, She plunged into the darkness full of thundering clouds and torrential rains, calling out, ‘O Hari! O Krsna!’

“In Her eagerness to meet You, Radha tore through the jungle in which fearful owls shriek, monkeys fight with one another, and snakes slither here and there. But She was oblivious to it all.

“Finally She arrived at a beautiful cottage made from flowering vines. My eager, simple, and pure-hearted friend then cut many flowers with Her fingernails and made You a bed as white as foam.

“But Hari!” exclaimed Lalita, raising her eyebrows and showing her pinkish palms. “You did not arrive. Still, my friend kept waiting for You, Her large tear-filled eyes transfixed on the forest path.”

Krsna leaned back against the tree defensively as Lalita continued, “Her desire for You was unaffected but, severely wounded by Cupid, when You failed to arrive my dear Radha was heartbroken.

“She kept murmuring the words, ‘That sweet-talking rogue.’ Feeling that each moment was like a millennium, my bewildered friend stayed awake all night in a desire grove that knew only unrequited desires.

“Then, just as night was over and much to my relief, You appeared from out of nowhere, illuminating my tired eyes with the sight of Your blissful form and filling my heart with unbounded happiness.”

Lalita spoke as if the pastime were unfolding before her. And Krsna, though ashamed of His past negligence, experienced the sweetness of that night once again. His heart pounded with excitement.

“But as soon as I saw the telltale marks on Your body, and before my friend could react, I assailed You, saying, ‘We are very fortunate! We are privy to a competition between Your garland and Your garments.

“‘It seems that Your garland — envious of Your brilliant yellow clothes — has turned itself yellow with the help of kunkuma that not long ago was decorating the chest of some cooperative young girl.

“‘Your sleepy face and dishevelled hair both confirm that the many fingernail scratches on Your body could only have appeared as the result of performing an all night kama-yajna.”’

Lalita giggled, “Embarrassed, You tried to plead innocence while solemnly declaring Your eternal love for Radha. Syama! I knew Your excuses were as false as Your proclamation of love for Her was true.

“What else could I do but quickly chase You from our sight and allow the sun to rise on the dark night of my friend’s anguish? Thus I shouted, ‘Get out, rascal! Get out! Go away from here.’”

Krsna’s jewel necklace glinted in the rays of His beaming smile as He heard Lalita repeat her scornful words and His heart filled with boundless pleasure to recall His pastimes with His beloved.

“O Syama! As You turned away from the grove, dejected, I could not tell who amongst the three of us was the most miserable. We watched You walk away until Your peacock feather disappeared from sight.

“O friend! Your eyes constantly shoot arrows of love, Your flute-song removes the gopis’ anguish at being separated from You, and the fragrance of Your body makes the entire world mad with love for You.“The next night I brought Radharani hack to that same grove. And You were waiting there patiently in the moonlit courtyard, playing a melancholy and repentant melody on Your flute.

“When my friend saw Your shadow, remembrance of Her previous suffering transformed Her zeal to meet You into reluctance — as tamarind turns milk to curd — and She turned to leave.

“Restraining Her, I said, ‘O honest girl! Look again at Syama’s splendid smile, soothing bodily lustre, and shark-shaped earrings, which sway as He plays upon His mystical flute.

‘“This boy’s beauty and flute-playing overwhelms deer, maddens demigoddesses, and bewilders bees. Having decorated the paths of Vraja with His gentle footsteps, He has now come only to meet You.

“‘O beautiful girl! Your heart is filled with happiness. Why pretend to be indifferent? Now His glance rests upon You alone. Why give other splendidly dressed gopis a chance to be attracted by His flute?

‘“When the full moon has risen, its rays as cool as freshly fallen snow, what girl would not passionately worship her beloved, especially when he is so submissive to she who loves him?”’

Lalita smiled at Krsna, who was spellbound by her vivid account. “My words somehow melted the glacier of Radha’s unwillingness. Slowly She turned towards You and took a step in the direction of the grove.

“I said, ‘Don’t speak harshly! Don’t be angry! Place Your feet on the path towards Him and Your heart will dictate the many ways in which Your limbs should give pleasure to this forest Cupid — ’”

Lalita’s words stuck in her throat. For a few moments she was lost in reverie. She saw Radha approaching Krsna, step by step like a timid doe, as He stood expectantly like a statue in the courtyard.

Having composed herself, Lalita concluded, “May Hari — to whom I forcibly dragged Radha, averse with jealous anger, by enlightening Her with these words — bring auspiciousness to us all.”

As Lalita and Krsna spoke, their talks gradually drifted to the topic of those unfortunate souls whose sins have robbed them of all spiritual qualifications, and who are thus averse to hearing of such pastimes.

Softhearted as she is, Lalita is ever eager to make others qualified for service to Sri Radha, and so she thought of creating a lake in which even the most odious of evildoers could be relieved of all their sins.

This proposal excited Krsna, and so together they called upon eighty-four holy places to excavate and fill a lake that could wash one clean of the sinful reactions to having committed six kinds of murder.

Those six kinds of murder are the killing of a brahmana (brahma-hatya), a cow (go-hatya), a foetus (bhruna-hatya), oneself (atma- hatya), another human (hatya), and animals and insects (krmi-hatya).

Lalita’s lake overflowed and formed another lake, which she named Mohana-kunda after Krsna. After killing Aristasura, Krsna at once bathed in these two lakes to purify Himself.

Thereafter, when Radha insisted that He was contaminated by the sin of killing a bull, Krsna said, “I have already bathed in Lalita’s lake. If I have sinned, the reaction has already been washed away.”

But the gopis had neither heard of nor seen the eighty-four holy places supposedly in Lalita-kunda. As far as they were concerned, it was just a pond full of rainwater Lalita had adopted as her own.

To prove her lake had indeed been made sacred by the touch of holy waters, Lalita called upon those deities, who then appeared one by one, with joined palms and bowed heads, to identify themselves.

Radha, however, was not yet convinced that eighty-four sacred places could neutralise the sin of killing a bull, and so She insisted that Krsna bathe in every scared place in the universe or remain impure.

Those in knowledge say that the creation of Lalita-kunda was a prelude to Radha-kunda’s appearance and that by bathing in Lalita’s lake Krsna established a transcendental doctrine.

That doctrine is this: Without the blessings of Lalita-devi, no one — not even Krsna — can approach Srimati Radharani, who is under Lalita’s loving control and who never acts independently of her.

Even when Radha is eager to see Krsna, if Lalita is angry with Krsna, Radha feigns anger with Him in deference to Lalita until Her beloved friend relents and allows the divine couple to meet again.

In the pastimes of Caitanya Mahaprabhu this principle was vividly reflected by Svarupa Damodara Gosvami, who acted not only as the Lord’s secretary but also as a kind of transcendental censor.

Svarupa Damodara was an incarnation of Lalita-sakhi. As the personification of ecstatic love, he was so well-versed in devotional mellows that devotees saw him as Lord Caitanya’s second body.

If anyone wanted to recite his literary work to Caitanya Mahaprabhu he would first have to present it to Svarupa Damodara, who would correct it if necessary before the Lord would agree to hear it.

When Svarupa Damodara first arrived at Puri, Caitanya Mahaprabhu described how indispensable the Gosvami was to Him:

**“I was like a blind man, but your coming here has restored My vision.”**

In reply, Svarupa Damodara Gosvami offered an important prayer to Lord Caitanya that glorified the Lord’s mercy, mercy He freely distributes because His heart is permeated by Radha’s moods.

He said,

**“O ocean of mercy! Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu! Let there be an awakening of Your auspicious mercy, which easily drives away all kinds of material lamentation by making everything pure and blissful.**

**“Indeed, Your mercy awakens transcendental bliss and supplants all material pleasures. By Your auspicious mercy, quarrels and disagreements arising amongst different scriptures are vanquished.**

**“Your auspicious mercy pours forth transcendental mellows and causes the heart to jubilate. Your mercy, which is full of joy, always stimulates devotional service and glorifies amorous love of God.**

**“May transcendental bliss be awakened within my heart by Your causeless mercy.”**

Thus Svarupa Damodara Gosvami acknowledged that Lord Caitanya’s mood is identical to that of Srimati Radharani.

**\* \* \* \***

Adjacent to Mohana-kunda are the lakes of Radha’s seven other girlfriends. Having been filled in, they are visible only during the monsoon season and even then are indistinguishable from each other.

On the eastern side of Lalita-kunda, above a ghata that leads down to the lake, is a temple dedicated to Lalita-bihari, also known as Lalita- mohana. Unfortunately, both lake and temple are poorly maintained.

In the wall on the side of the parikrama-marga opposite Lalita-kunda is a gate leading to the compound of Jiva Gosvami’s bhajana-kutira, which overlooks Syama-kunda and Radha-kunda beyond that.

Just as Panca-pandava-ghata stretches from Madhumangala's grove to Ujjvala’s grove, Jiva Gosvami-ghata stretches along the south side of Syama-kunda from Ujjvala’s grove to the grove of Arjuna-gopa.

A short distance from the bank of Jiva Gosvami-ghata is a small cluster of bakula trees where Jiva Gosvami would stay on his visits to Radha-kunda. There his bhajana-kutira still stands today.

At the tender age of three, Sri Jiva — son of Anupama, the youngest brother of Rupa and Sanatana — met Caitanya Mahaprabhu at Ramakeli, on the Lord’s first attempted journey to Vrndavana.

This brief vision of Lord Caitanya left an indelible impression on young Jiva; the boy gave up playing with his friends in favour of studying Sanskrit and worshipping Deities of Krsna and Balarama.

In his youth Jiva took up a mendicant’s life. He first travelled to Navadvipa, where Lord Nityananda took Jiva on parikrama of the dhama made holy by the youthful pastimes of Lord Caitanya.

Jiva Gosvami wanted to go see Lord Caitanya in Jagannatha Puri, but Lord Nityananda told him that Caitanya Mahaprabhu wanted him to join his uncles, Rupa and Sanatana, in Vrndavana.

Indeed, during Jiva’s journey to Vrndavana, Caitanya Mahaprabhu appeared to him in a dream and said, “You and your uncles, Rupa and Sanatana, arc all very dear to Me. Go to Mathura!

“Together you should compose books on devotional service, dedicate yourselves to worshipping Radha and Krsna, and while living in Vraja, always remember Their many wonderful pastimes.”

On the way to Vrndavana, Jiva Gosvami met Madhusudana Vacaspati, a disciple of Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya, and spent some time studying philosophy from that learned scholar.

It is said that Sri Jiva was twenty-four years old when he arrived in Vraja to take shelter of his uncles. I will say more about his extraordinary life when I describe the Radha-Damodara temple.

It should be noted, however, that although Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami was the inspiration and driving force behind the excavation of Radha-kunda, Sri Jiva was instrumental in completing the work.

The younger Gosvami purchased the land, oversaw the excavation, and managed aspects of Radha-kunda’s construction, showing by his personal example how to serve Krsna by “doing the needful.’’

In addition, Jiva saw to it that Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami was taken care of. Dasa Gosvami was oftentimes so deeply absorbed in thoughts of Radha and Krsna that he was unable to relate to worldly affairs.

Due to Sri Jiva’s transcendental qualifications and his relationships with Rupa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami, Lord Caitanya and Lord Nityananda granted Jiva Gosvami residence in Vrndavana-dhama.

It is said, mahaprabhu tomdra gane, diyachena data bhume, sighra tumi yaho Vrndavana: “Nityananda told Sri Jiva, ‘Mahaprabhu has given a special land to your family. Immediately go to that land of Vraja.’”

Let us pray to Jiva Gosvami: “Please make the truths of love for Krsna you profess in Sat-sandarbha and the pastimes of Radha and Krsna you recount in Gopala-campu appear in our hearts.”

Near the bank of Syama-kunda I offered my respects at the samadhi of Nandini-devi. She was a maidservant to the wife of Advaita Acarya, Sita Thakurani, and a great devotee in her own right.

Returning to the parikrama path, we pass by another Radha-Govinda temple. This one was constructed two hundred years ago by the king of Manipur, who came to Radha-kunda when exiled by the British.

On the opposite side of the road is the Radha-Vinoda temple. A few steps beyond that is Gopi-kupa, from which the gopis fill their pitchers with cool drinking water before they leave for the groves.

On the pretext of being thirsty, Krsna sometimes comes here and begs the gopis for water, a request that inevitably leads to joking, argument, reconciliation, and loving exchange.

Later, when Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami renovated Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda, he had Gopi-kupa excavated so that locals need not wash their clothes in the waters of the two sacred lakes.

It is said that during the excavation the workers struck a stone that bled from its fresh “wound.” The workers informed Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, and he at once had them stop their work.

That night Krsna appeared to Dasa Gosvami in a dream and told him that the injured stone was the tongue of Govardhana Hill, and that it should be carefully taken out and duly worshipped in its own temple.

On the order of the Lord, the tongue (jihva) of Govardhana is worshipped to this day with tulasi leaves and Radha-kunda water. In New Vraja-dhama this sila is worshipped through Govardhana Lala.

While circumambulating Govardhana Hill, Madhavendra Puri rested on a path leading towards Syama-kunda. At that time Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda were only ponds in an agricultural field.

Leaving Radha-kunda, the great acarya continued his parikrama until he reached Govinda-kunda. It was there he rested and received the blessings of Gopala, who placed Himself in Madhavendra Puri’s care.

Further south on the parikrama path are temples of Gaura-Nitai with Advaita, and Radha-Krsna with the asta-sakhis — the only temple in Radha-kunda with the divine couple served by Their eight friends.

Next is Radha-Madhava temple, home to the pratibhu-murtis of Jayadeva Gosvami’s Deities and the puspa-samadhi of that great poet, who is dear to Lord Jagannatha for having composed Gita-govinda.

On the order of Lord Jagannatha, Jayadeva married a brahmani by the name of Padmavati and left Puri to reside with her in a campaka forest called Campahatta on the island of Koladvipa in Navadvipa.

It was there, five hundred years before the advent of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, that Jayadeva wrote Gita-govinda. It was also there that Lord Caitanya appeared to Jayadeva and told him to return to Puri.

Obedient to the order of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, Jayadeva Gosvami returned to Jagannatha’s abode. From there the fame of his Gita-govinda spread, first throughout Orissa, and then throughout India.

Lord Jagannatha is always feeling separation from Vrndavana and Srimati Radharani. By having Gita-govinda read to Him daily, He joyfully remembers the amorous pastimes of His youth.

Gita-govinda tells how Sri Radha once became displeased with Krsna, rejected His entreaties, and spent the day sulking silently in sorrow, until Lalita and other gopis convinced Her to show kindness to Hari.

The lyrical poetry, expert grammatical constructions, and profound devotional moods found in Gita-govinda’s twenty-four songs are unsurpassed in the rich history of Vaisnava literature.

It is also the first account of Krsna’s pastimes in which Srimati Radharani is unambiguously praised as Krsna’s favourite gopi, the source of His highest bliss, and the resting place for His full affection.

Moreover, in Gita-govinda Jayadeva revealed a facet of Krsna’s transcendental personality that had not yet been explicitly described by Vyasadeva in Srimad-Bhagavatam, or by others elsewhere.

That special trait is Krsna’s complete subservience to the will of His devotee, which Jayadeva unveils in one scene wherein Sri Krsna places Srimati Radharani’s lotus feet upon His head.

In fact, as is well known, Jayadeva Gosvami hesitated to commit this pastime to paper, and therefore in the author’s absence Lord Jagannatha personally penned the stanza for him.

The full verse Jagannatha wrote is,

*smara-garala-khandanam mama sirasi mandanam dehi pada-pallavam udaram*  
*jvalati mayi daruno madana-kadananalo haratu tad-upahita-vikaram*

**“Speaking to Srimati Radharani, who was displaying jealous anger towards Him, Krsna implored, ‘O beloved! Your tender sprout-like feet are the antidote to Cupid’s venom.**

**'“Please place them on My head as My ornament and glory. The scorching fire of Cupid’s poison is unbearable, please therefore let the touch of Your feet quell the torment of My love.’”**

Dear devotees! Please carefully take note: although Gita-govinda has achieved worldwide popularity and is readily available to one and all, it was originally intended for advanced devotees, not for everyone.

Indeed, in his introduction Jayadeva establishes the standard for who is qualified to read Gita-govinda with the words yadi hari smarane sarasam: he should be steady in meditation on Krsna’s pastimes.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu regularly discussed the verses of Gita-govinda, but He would do so only with His most advanced and confidential associates, Svarupa Damodara and Ramananda Raya.

Srila Prabhupada also made it clear that of all the songs of Gita-govinda only the invocation, known as Dasavatara-stotra, is fit to be heard and sung by his followers.

**“The songs by Jayadeva... \[are\] not approved \[to be sung\] by Prabhupada \[Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati\]. Those songs are for siddha-bhaktas, not for us, who are sadhaka-bhaktas, or ‘learning bhaktas.’”**

Jayadeva Gosvami composed Gita-govinda primarily for the pleasure of Lord Jagannatha, and the Lord was very fond of hearing it, preferring Jayadeva’s masterpiece to all other compositions.

Once the king of Puri, Purusottamadeva, insisted that his own work, Abhinava Gita-govinda, was superior to the magnum opus of Jayadeva Gosvami and should be read to Lord Jagannatha instead.

Due to the politically sensitive nature of the challenge, the brahmanas decided to let the Lord judge for Himself. So they placed both books before Jagannatha and locked the temple for the night.

The following morning the pujaris found the pages of the king's book strewn all over the floor and Gita-govinda nestled under Lord Jagannatha’s arm, close to His heart. The Lord had given His verdict!

On another occasion Lord Jagannatha had been laid down to sleep after His midday meal when a florist started singing Gita-govinda in a garden on the temple grounds within earshot of the Lord.

Jagannatha was so keen to hear this impromptu performance of His favourite work that He left the temple and hid in a bush nearby, unmindful that thorns had ripped His cloth and scratched His body.

Lord Jagannatha returned to His altar in time to give His blessings to the devotees, but His pujaris were aghast at the sight of their ragged and wounded Lord. They at once ran to tell the king.

Unable to decipher the significance of Lord Jagannatha’s dishevelled state, the king was in great anxiety until the Lord appeared to him in a dream and explained exactly what had happened.

In pastimes such as these Lord Jagannatha revealed His exclusive attachment to Gita-govinda, so Maharaja Prataparudra issued the following royal edict, a decade before Lord Caitanya arrived in Puri: “Performances of song and dance for Jagannatha and Balarama will consist solely of Gita-govinda and no other work. Performers are therefore instructed to learn the songs of Gita-govinda exclusively.

“Four musicians will accompany the dancers who enact Gita-govinda. Others may follow in chorus. Temple officials who allow any other song to be performed will be deemed enemies of Jagannatha.”’

In addition to being a great devotee of Lord Jagannatha, Jayadeva Gosvami worshipped his own Deities, named Radha-Madhava, with whom he had a very intimate relationship based on loving service.

When Jayadeva visited Vrndavana he brought Radha-Madhava and and installed Them in a temple near Kesi-ghata. From there, like other Deities in Vraja, They later left for Jaipur.

No record exists to prove Jayadeva visited Radha-kunda, but because Radha-Madhava stayed there while on Their way to Jaipur, a puspu- samadhi was established in the area to honour Jayadeva Gosvami.

In remembering the gifted poet, we cannot fail to praise his faithful wife, Padmavati. A servant and a colleague, she would dance to the verses sung by her husband and sometimes sing them herself.

These two great souls were exemplars of a faithful married couple who dedicated their lives to serving the sankirtana movement. By the Lord’s grace they surpassed the service offered by lone renunciants.

All glories to Jayadeva Gosvami, the poet nonpareil, whose talent in music, absorption in Krsna, and skill in portraying the mellow of divine love prove him to be perfectly in tune with Jayadeva-Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

On the bank of Narayana-sarovara, at the end of a small path that swerves to the left off the parikrama path, resides Bankhandi Mahadeva, who guards the western side of Radha-kunda.

Once, to surprise the gopis, Krsna playfully manifested the magnificent four-armed form of Lord Narayana at this place, similar to the form He displayed at Paitha prior to the spring rasa dance.

In the southwest corner of Syama-kunda is the grove Gandharva- sakha. After rediscovering the two divine lakes of Radha and Syama, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu rested here beneath a large tamala tree.

While on parikrama of Vrndavana, Lord Caitanya sometimes lost Himself in the ecstasy of love and at other times stopped to hear about the pastimes Krsna performed in different places.

At Arit-grama Caitanya Mahaprabhu resurfaced from His reverie and eagerly enquired from the locals, “Where is Radha-kunda?" But no one knew the answer, including Krsnadasa, His guide.

From this the Lord deduced that the two most sacred places of pilgrimage were no longer extant, so He took it upon Himself to locate Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda for the benefit of all.

A short distance from the tip of Govardhana Hill, amidst two paddy fields, Caitanya Mahaprabhu spotted two small ponds, one surrounded by kadamba trees and the other by tamala trees.

The ponds were only waist-deep at their deepest point, but while the amazed villagers looked on Lord Caitanya bathed in one pond and then the other. After bathing He offered choice prayers.

*Yatha radha priya visnos tasyah kundam priyam tatha*  
*sarva-gopisu saivaika visnor atyanta-vallabha*

**“Just as Radha is most dear to Krsna, Her lake is very dear to Him. She is the most beloved of all gopis.**

**“Because of its wonderful transcendental qualities, Radha-kunda is as dear to Krsna as Sri Radha. In that lake the all-opulent Lord performed pastimes with Sri Radha with great pleasure and bliss.**

**“Whoever bathes just once in Radha-kunda attains Srimati Radharani’s loving attraction to Sri Krsna. Who within this world can describe the glories and sweetness of Sri Radha-kunda?”**

Overwhelmed by love, Caitanya Mahaprabhu danced around the hanks of both lakes. Then He marked His body with tilaka made from the mud of Radha-kunda and collected some to take with Him.

Along with Balabhadra Bhattacarya, Lord Caitanya came to the solitude of Gandharva-sakha-kunja, sat beneath a tamala tree, and remembered the pastimes Krsna and the gopis once enjoyed there.

There at Tamala-tala, as the warm autumn breeze caressed His body, Caitanya Mahaprabhu would sometimes submerge Himself in the ecstasy of Sri Radha and sometimes remember that He was Sri Krsna.

Wavering between Radha’s and Krsna’s unmistakable moods, the Lord tasted the divine couple’s joy, beauty, and sweetness, all enhanced a hundredfold by the potency of Radha-kunda.

Finally, once again in the mood of a sadhaka, Lord Caitanya remembered Sri Krsna’s pastimes with Sri Radha, like splashing in the water, snacking on fruits and roots, or resting upon a bed of flowers.

The Lord thought of how the gopis offer Krsna betel, fan Him, and massage His feet as He quietly gazes at the delicate face of His beloved, His heart filled with happiness, His mind at complete peace.

When Krsna falls asleep, Radha and Her friends happily eat the remnants of His meal, glancing from time to time with lovelorn desire at His lotus face, just as cakora birds gaze longingly at the moon.

While the girls eat Krsna’s food and chew His tambula, they happily discuss His unmatched ability to capture their hearts with His bodily fragrance, sweet smile, and flute playing.

The murmur of the girls’ hushed voices gradually rouses Krsna, but He continues to lie still, eyes closed as if asleep, eager to feed His hungry ears with their jokes, compliments, and complaints.

Sooner or later the gopis detect signs of wakefulness on Krsna’s face. Embarrassed but also delighted to have been overheard, they look at one another with playful half-smiles and suddenly fall silent.

Tiptoeing behind His bed, one clever gopi suddenly pulls the sheet from Krsna’s body and exclaims aloud, “Sleeping soundly, were You?” Then Krsna and the gopis erupt in laughter.

While Lord Caitanya was thus absorbed in pleasant thoughts, Balabhadra Bhattacarya suggested they resume their pilgrimage. After again offering obeisances and reciting prayers, Lord Caitanya rose.

With a smiling face the Lord said to His companion, “O friend! Please meditate on Radha-kunda, which is beautified by pavilions draped in flowering vines. This lake is praised by the great splendour of Vraja.

“Its waters are filled with the beauty and sweetness of the divine couple’s amorous pastimes. It is respectfully worshipped by Giriraja, who bows down and places his peak on the ground before its banks.”

Upon visiting Tamala-tala one can intensely feel the divine presence of Caitanya Mahaprabhu and reflect upon how significant to His movement was the Lord’s personal rediscovery of Radha-kunda.

That rediscovery powerfully highlights one aspect of Sri Caitanya’s mission, reaffirming the instrumental role He plays in granting access to the esoteric truths of Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes in Vrndavana.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu travelled to countless holy places throughout India, hut the only place He requested His followers to excavate and restore to its former glory was Sri Vrndavana-dhama. Why?

Goloka Vrndavana, the divine combination of sweet Vraja and merciful Navadvipa, is the coveted goal of those who have sincerely adopted the religious process for this age — chanting Hare Krsna.
