And Bhauma Vrndavana is the place here on earth where Krsna, through His eternal pastimes, revealed the wonders of Goloka for the sole purpose of attracting wayward souls hack to their eternal home.

Yet by time’s influence the glories of Vrndavana were concealed, and that sacred place took on the outward appearance of any other North Indian village surrounded by agricultural fields and wild jungles.

Had Vrndavana not clearly distinguished itself from other places, had it not displayed some of its original splendour or shown evidence of Krsna’s glorious pastimes, its significance would have been lost.

Except to the most elevated transcendentalists, Vrndavana would have remained inaccessible. And without Vrndavana, conditioned souls would have been trapped in maya's shackles forever.

Therefore Lord Caitanya requested the Gosvamis to reclaim the places of Krsna’s pastimes and beautify Vrndavana by constructing temples, installing Deities, and building memorials.

And to corroborate the authenticity of this Vrndavana revival, the Lord also ordered His followers to write books citing the scriptural authority that underpins krsna-lila and vraja-bhakti.

A few centuries later Srila Prabhupada expanded Lord Caitanya’s mission by establishing “embassies” of Bhauma Vrndavana outside India, giving people all over the globe faith in the spiritual world.

One such embassy of that divine realm is New Vraja-dhama, where even the most materialistic visitors quickly sense its sublime significance and awaken at least an attraction to the spiritual world.

Two things were emphasised by Lord Caitanya personally rediscovering Radha-kunda: His mission to revive Vrndavana, and the unique status of Radha’s lake amongst Vraja’s pastime places.

Yet another lesson to be learned from this pastime and from the mission to reclaim Vraja is that without Lord Caitanya’s mercy, any effort to enter the divine couple’s Vrndavana pastimes will fail.

Before Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu rescued Radha-kunda from obscurity, local farmers would bring their cows to drink from these two ponds, which the villagers referred to as Kali and Gauri.

Many other people — residents of Vrndavana, learned brahmanas, and pilgrims on parikrama of Govardhana Hill — passed by these two kundas countless times without ever giving them a second thought.

The Puranas speak of Radha-kunda’s location, but until Caitanya Mahaprabhu uncovered it and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami excavated it, the world was unaware of Sri Radha’s lake.

We must conclude, therefore, that the gates of Vrndavana are open to those — and only those — who worship Lord Caitanya, who serve Lord Caitanya, and who chant Lord Caitanya’s holy names.

Otherwise, a person may possess countless pious credits and may have even taken shelter of Sri Krsna, but if he has not yet surrendered to Lord Caitanya, he remains spiritually impoverished.

In the words of Prabodhananda Sarasvati:

**“A stone, even if sprinkled with nectar, will never sprout a single blade of grass. A dog’s tail, no matter how carefully stretched out, will never become straight.**

**“A dwarf can reach out his arms as much as he likes, but he will never touch the moon. Similarly, those who follow religious rituals without the mercy of Lord Gaura will never attain ecstatic love for Krsna.”**

That same Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the golden king of dancers, who danced in ecstasy on the banks of Radha’s lake, is dancing even now on the banks of Radha-kunda in New Vraja-dhama.

After leaving Tamala-tala, Caitanya Mahaprabhu walked to Kusuma-sarovara. Overwhelmed with joy at the sight of Govardhana Hill, in the madness of divine love He embraced a stone from Giriraja.

**\* \* \* \***

Following the path towards the grove of Vidagdha, one incomes to the lakeshore called Pasa-khela-ghata along the western bank of Syama-kunda. Vallabhacarya’s followers call it Vallabha-ghata.

Pasa-khela is a complex game played with dice that requires as much skill as luck to win. Amongst Krsna’s gopi friends, Sudevi is particularly good at it. She regularly hosts games in her kunja.

Radha and Krsna play this game almost daily at Radha-kunda. Krsna, like Maharaja Yudhisthira, however, is both addicted to and not very skilled at this game; in fact, He loses more often than He wins.

Once, on the advice of Madhumangala, Krsna challenged Srimati Radharani to play pasa-khela but at Vidagdha’s grove for a change, instead of Sudevi’s kunja where They usually played.

The boys reasoned that the unique vastu configuration of Vidagdha’s kunja would favour Krsna and ensure His victory in the same way Sudevi’s grove seemed always to favour Sri Radhika and Her friends.

Of course Madhu hadn’t considered the fact that Sri Radha is the goddess of victory Herself, Jayasri. Being fully independent, She is as unaffected by vastu as She is by planetary influence (hora).

After His daily bath in Radha-kunda, Krsna made His proposal to play at Haritmanimaya-kunja, and with Campakalata’s consent the gamers assembled at their new location, each party poised for victory.

Madhu and Lalita were advisors to the players. As Radha was ready to make the first throw, Krsna piped up, “Surely a wager would make things more interesting. Why not follow the advice of professionals?”

Lalita rolled her eyes and sighed: “Pray, tell. What advice do professional gamblers give?” Krsna’s offhand reply: “Everyone knows that no stakes are better than kisses and embraces."

Radha accepted the wager with a wry smile, but as She shook the dice, She secretly sent a maidservant to call for Her Pulinda friend, Bhrngi, who after arriving waited silently in the shadows nearby.

Confident of victory, Madhu boasted that the girls would soon be put in their places, but when the dice landed obediently to Radha’s call of“Dasa! Dasa!" both Madhu and Krsna turned red in humiliation.

Sudevi mocked Madhu, “O brahmana boy! Why are you silent now? Only minutes ago you were counting how many laddus you could get by bartering the bangles you hoped to win in this game of chance.”

Quietly to Krsna, Madhumangala said, “O friend! I just remembered something very important I must attend to.” But Krsna firmly grasped His advisor by the wrist and whispered, “Don’t desert Me now!”

Radhika compassionately corrected Her companion, “Sudevi! The first wager was not for ornaments, but for kisses, and we should honour our agreement.” These words were music to Krsna’s ears.

“However,” Radha added as Krsna rose to pay His debt, “as the winner I have the option to collect My prize by proxy.” Krsna froze in an awkward position, no longer sitting but not yet upright.

With a wave of Her hand Radhika summoned Bhrngi from the shadows and had her stand before Mukunda. Radha said, “This girl is a member of the aboriginal race and is experienced in these matters.

“She can accept, on My behalf, whatever kisses and embraces You were planning to offer.” Radharani’s girlfriends held their sides and laughed as a blushing Krsna silently took His seat.

Embarrassed but undaunted, Krsna volunteered to change the stakes, wagering His flute against Radha’s necklace. But Radha again tossed a winning number before Krsna had a chance to touch the dice.

Madhu called out, head in hands, “O friend! We must still be on the wrong side of Radha’s lake.” And Lalita stood waiting to collect the flute while a chorus of gopis quipped, “Oh my! Oh my!

“Alas! The only one to whom You have been faithful is this little flute of Yours — addicted as it was to drinking nectar from Your lips — and still You could not keep it by Your side? How sad!”

Reluctant to part with His flute, with Madhu’s support Krsna called out, “Foul!” initiating a blissful argument that was interrupted by the announcement of Jatila’s arrival at Surya-kunda.

Sobered by the distasteful sound of Jatila’s name, the gopis whisked the divine couple away to Surya-kunda, where they disguised Krsna as a brahmana boy who had volunteered to help worship the sun god.

As Krsna hurried off to safety, the gopis heard Him say, “Even though I won the dice game in which kisses and My flute were wagered, My beloved still falsely claims that She is the victor.

“O Vrndavana forest! O great physician who knows the ways to please My beloved and Me! By arranging these wonderful events you have brought Me so much transcendental bliss. I thank you.”

**\* \* \* \***

Walking west one arrives at Madana-mohana-ghata, where Sanatana Gosvami, the great renunciant and scholar, would absorb himself in bhajana at his sitting place (baithaka) on the bank of Radha-kunda.

There is presently a Madana-mohana temple in this location. Worshipped here are pratibhu-murtis of the original Deities, who rested here on the way from Vrndavana town to Karoli in Rajasthan.

Sanatana’s vow was to perform Govardhana parikrama every day, so he would invariably pass by Radha-kunda. At these times he often stopped to visit Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami and other devotees.

During these daily visits, Sanatana sat here beneath a tree on the bank opposite to Manasa-pavana-ghata, meditating upon the divine couple or advising the local devotees in the ways of devotional life.

Sanatana Gosvami had many years ago renounced his post as prime minister of Gaudadesa, along with its wealth and power, to humbly serve Caitanya Mahaprabhu as an impoverished mendicant.

Although amply blessed with transcendental qualities, Sanatana never kept himself aloof from the general mass of people; rather, he was involved personally in the daily lives of the Vraja-vasis.

With all sincerity Sanatana enquired from the villagers about their harvests, cows, or children. And they in turn accepted him as a member of their clan, loving him as they would a kindly uncle.

When I am beset by the inevitable problems that come with ministering to devotees in New Vraja-dhama and elsewhere, I get strength from remembering Sanatana Gosvami’s example.

Rupa Gosvami praises Sanatana, his guru and elder brother, with these words:

*prapannah premanam prabhavati sada bhagavata-bhak paracino janmavadhi-bhava-rasad bhakti-madhurah—*  
*Gram ko ’pi sriman jayati viditah sakarataya dhurino dhiranam adhi- dharani vaiyasakir iva*

**“Eternal glories to Sakara Mallika! He is filled with transcendental love and is vastly learned in Srimad-Bhagavatam.**

**“To taste the true sweetness of devotional service, he set aside the false happiness of this world of birth and death. By his own example he is a leader of devotees in the manner of Sukadeva Gosvami!”**

Let us offer our obeisances to Sanatana Gosvami. From Sanatana’s baithaka we proceed to the corner of Syama-kunda where Kokila- gopa tends his grove and the sacred place where the two lakes meet.

Although now obscured by buildings, to the south of here was a small lake called Lagmohana-kunda, where Dasa Gosvami lived until Sanatana Gosvami convinced him to move to Radha-kunda.

Krsna killed the demon Sankhacuda here, at the end of a long battle that began in Syamavana on the night of Holi after the demon tried to abduct Srimati Radharani and the other gopis.

With Krsna and Balarama in hot pursuit, Sankhacuda soon realised that he would be caught if he kept so many gopis in tow, and so he released all the girls — all but one, that is.

With only Srimati Radharani still captive, the demon Sankhacuda continued his escape attempt. But he soon saw angry Krsna closing in on him, so he let his last victim go and ran for his life.

Krsna finally caught up with Sankhacuda at Lagmohana-kunda. Without wasting a moment, the Lord beheaded the demon and tore the brilliant Syamantaka jewel from his crown.

He then returned to Govardhana, where He found Radha beside Herself with worry for His safety. After pacifying His beloved, Krsna took Her to where Balarama was guarding the other gopis.

Overwhelmed to see Krsna return with Radha in one hand and the Syamantaka jewel in the other, Lord Balarama and the gopis surrounded Them, joyfully crying out, “Well done! Well done!”

After everyone had settled down, the cowherd girls all eyed the brilliant jewel glowing like the sun in Krsna’s raincloud-dark hand. Each of them wondered, “Will He give it to me?"

Krsna understood the minds of the gopis. He knew that to incite rivalry amongst them would simply cause another disturbance to their evening festival of colours, so He thought:

“Surely I must give this jewel to My beloved Radha. But if I give it to Her directly, the other gopis will be jealous. They will rebuke Me, and then, without doubt, a quarrel will break out amongst them."

Krsna looked at Balarama and thought, “My brother knows everything. If I give the jewel to Him, He will give it to Radha. He is everyone’s superior, and so the gopis cannot find fault with Him."

In the presence of all the gopis, Krsna offered the Syamantaka jewel to His elder brother, who graciously accepted it and tied it in the corner of His cloth, thinking, “This jewel is a host of problems.”

Lord Balarama knew that Krsna wanted Him to give the jewel to Radha, but still He was reluctant. Why? For the same reason as His younger brother — He did not want the gopis to quarrel.

First, His own group of gopis would be angry that He had not given the jewel to one of them. Then the gopis in Krsna’s group would each he jealous of Radha. “They will all berate me,” He thought.

But by dawn Balarama had worked out a solution. As soon as Madhumangala appeared at Nanda’s palace for breakfast, Balarama jovially placed the jewel in the unsuspecting brahmanas hand.

Astute Madhumangala at once understood the diplomacy behind the gift. Without hesitating he spoke up, loud enough for all to hear, “Of what use is this brilliant, inedible stone to me?"

From his seat in the centre of Nandagrama’s grand dining hall, Madhu continued, “The only one worthy of it is She whose culinary talent draws the gods from their heavenly palaces — Sri Radha!”

At that moment Radha came out of the kitchen with a tray of steaming rice. Madhu at once took the tray from Her hands and replaced it with the shining jewel, vibrating the sacred syllable, om.

As Radha looked at the jewel its effulgence grew in response to Her touch. Humbly bowing before Madhumangala, She handed the Syamantaka gem to a maidservant, and continued serving breakfast.

Madhumangala had understood why Balarama had given him the jewel. And Balarama was confident that Madhu, as Krsna’s confidential companion, would know just what to do with it.

None of the gopis would complain if Radha received the Syamantaka jewel through a third party, not to mention a brahmana. Thus Krsna achieved His purpose without upsetting anyone.

In this way the precious Syamantaka jewel became the central gem in Sri Radha’s necklace, a necklace Her maidservants also call the intimate friend of Krsna’s Kaustubha gem (kausctubha-mitram).

Dasa Gosvami writes,

*dattah pralamba-ripunadbhata-sahkhacuda-nasat pratosi-hrdayam madhumangalasya*  
*hastena yah sumukhi kaustubha-mitram etam kim te syamantaka-manim taralam karisye*

**“O beautiful-faced one \[Srimati Radharani\]! Will I make the Syamantaka jewel, which was given by Balarama to cheerful-hearted Madhumangala after the death of proud Sankhacuda—**

**“Which jolly Madhumangala with his own hand gave to You, and which since has become the intimate friend of the Kaustubha jewel, the central jewel in Your necklace?”**

Whenever Krsna embraces Radharani, the Syamantaka and Kaustubha gems also embrace. Naturally, they have a close friendship, as do any devotees who share a common service to Krsna.

The Syamantaka gem is also called Sankhacuda’s crest jewel (sankhacuda-siromani), and it is known to hang on Radhika’s chest just below a locket containing Krsna’s picture (madana).

The Syamantaka jewel is Srimati Radharani’s eternal ornament and companion. Her receiving it from Krsna through Madhumangala as the spoils of a battle with Sankhacuda is merely a pastime.

The same may be said of Kaliya’s wives’ having given the Kaustubha jewel to Krsna in exchange for sparing their husband from being trampled to death by Krsna's dancing lotus feet.

It is also understood that the Kaustubha and Syamantaka gems worn by Lord Visnu and His consort Laksmi are expansions of the original jewels in the treasuries of Krsna and His consort Radharani.

Sankhacuda's remains were scattered around the area of Lagmohana- kunda, and so crops do not grow in that area. But trees do grow at the kunda because it is a meeting place of Radha and Krsna.

**\* \* \* \***

On either side of the walkway separating Radha-kunda from Syama-kunda is Yugala-sangama-ghata. At its centre is the meeting place (sangama) where the liquid forms of Radha and Krsna embrace.

These lakes are lauded as the two most sacred places in creation. How, then, can one estimate the sanctity of the sangama where they come together, known also as “the jewelled altar,” Ratna-vedi?

Radha and Krsna perpetually mingle there in Their forms of nectar. Thus Ratna-vedi is also a Yoga-pitha— a single stem that nourishes the two lotus-lakes that blossom on either side.

Although devotees may take their baths anywhere in either lake, the recommended process is to bathe at the sangama, first in Radha- kunda, then in Syama-kunda, and then again in Radha-kunda.

Even souls unaware of the glories of Radha-kunda who cross the sangama on the walkway above Yugala-sangama-ghata gain the benefits bestowed by visiting all the holy tirthas in the universe.

To either side of Ratna-vedi are the groves of Citra-gopi and Sananda- gopa. And at its very heart is Carana-cihna, the resting place of the shimmering lotus footprints of Radha and Syamasundara.

These footprints mark the place — at the centre of a jewel-encrusted suspension bridge that spans the sangama—where Radha and Syama stand and marvel at the beauty of Their lakes, and of each other.

At this spot Krsna says to His beloved, “Radha! In many ways the beauty of Your lake reminds Me of Your own magnificence. The blooming lotus flowers are like the ever-blooming lotus of Your face.“The young fish darting here and there are like Your restless eyes, the rolling foam-topped waves like the sweetness rippling from Your smile, and those swarms of honeybees like Your swaying braid.

“The sunlight reflected on the surface of Your lake is like Your gold complexion. O Radha! In these and many other ways Your lake brings You to mind. Thus the blessed sight brings pleasure to My heart.”

Where these footprints rest today, Krsna held Radha’s hand while He spoke these lovely words. And by the effect of Radha’s touch and His own words in praise of Her, Krsna became heady with divine love.

O illustrious Vaisnavas! Just worship these impressions of Radha’s and Krsna’s lotus feet, which saintly demigods seek in vain and which Pulinda girls embrace to free themselves from lust’s torments.

In search of the young milk-fed culprit who had raided her storeroom, Mother Yasoda once followed His butter-smeared footprints to the place where He was feeding yogurt to Vraja’s monkeys.

The presence of Krsna’s footprints indicates good luck and inspires even common people to do good. In abundance in Vrndavana, those footprints spread the glory of the earth throughout the universe.

Demigods and humans are not alone in worshipping the lotus feet of Krsna; indeed, He is the Lord of all beings. Thus Vraja’s diverse creatures, especially its cows, serve His lotus feet with fixed devotion.

Even though Krsna walks before the cows along the same paths trodden by man and beast alike, His footprints remain untouched. They are never smudged or brushed away. How is that possible?

To the animals in Vrndavana, Krsna is a living treasure. Out of love for Him they preserve His lotus footprints by always carefully sidestepping them as they move about from here to there.

Krsna’s footprints are not merely good luck charms or bequests of mercy to be preserved. For great devotees like Akrura and Narada, they are a rare and treasured impetus for ecstatic love.

Simply at the sight of Krsna’s footprints, His uncle Akrura was awash in ecstasy — his bodily hairs stood on end, his eyes filled with tears, and he rolled about happily on the dusty ground.

The sight of Krsna’s footprints stimulates ecstatic love, as does hearing narrations of His uncommon pastimes, or seeing His sweetly smiling face, or hearing His enchanting flute-song.

Moreover, as the cowherd girls explained to Uddhava, the sight of Krsna's footprints decorated by divine symbols guarantees pure devotees the ability to always remain rapt in thoughts of Him.

After having received letters from their beloved in Mathura, the gopis told Krsna’s messenger, punah punah smarayanti nanda-gopa-sutam bata / sri-niketais tat-padakair vismartum naiva saknumah:

“All these remind us constantly of Nanda Maharaja’s son. Indeed, because we see Krsna’s footprints, which are marked with divine symbols, we can never forget Him.”

The marks on the soles of the divine couple’s lotus feet are unique. Pure devotees meditate on them in the same way they meditate on Radha’s and Krsna’s garments, ornaments, or limbs.

Krsna’s feet are decorated with nineteen wonderful symbols. On the left is a fish, half-moon, triangle, four water pots, a cow’s hoofprint, Cupid’s bow, two concentric circles, and a conch shell.

On His right foot are eleven marks: an octagon, four svastikas, four rose apples, a thunderbolt, a banner, an elephant goad, a lotus, a vertical line, an umbrella, a disc, and a barleycorn.

Sri Radha also has nineteen symbols on Her feet. On Her left foot is a half-moon, a creeper, a bracelet, a flower, a flag, an elephant goad, a lotus flower, a vertical line, an umbrella, a disc, and a barleycorn.

On Her right foot is a fish, spear, chariot, club, an earring, a sacrificial altar, mountain, and a conch shell. The symbols on Sri Radha’s feet, like those on Krsna’s, form attractive patterns.

These marks allow Radha and Krsna and Their companions to distinguish the divine couple’s footprints from the others on the paths of Vraja, helping the gopis to find Them, wherever They are.

Once a small band of gopis were on their way to the Yamuna when they saw the impressions of an elephant goad, flag, and thunderbolt in the sand. At once they knew that Krsna was nearby.

Another time the Vraja-vasis could tell by the presence of terrible omens that Krsna must be in danger somewhere, so they followed His footprints to the Yamuna and found Him struggling in Kaliya’s coils.

Because pure devotees like Kalidasa smear the dust of devotees’ footprints on their bodies for purification, it is no surprise that such great souls also worship Krsna’s footprints with their life’s breath.

Upon first seeing Krsna’s footprints, Akrura at once leapt from his chariot to roll on the ground amongst those footprints, blissfully and wildly calling out, “Oh! This is the dust from my master’s feet!”

And when Brahma came to realise the error of his ways after having stolen the calves and cowherd boys, he bowed down before the boyish Lord and smeared the dust of Krsna’s footprints on his crown.

Devotees familiar with the glories of Krsna’s footprints sometimes feel compassion for others who are not, and like Lalita did, they urge those souls to enthusiastically search out those lotus footprints.

Indeed, having achieved the utmost perfection of their senses by apprehending the qualities of Krsna’s footprints, devotees lament the sorry fate of those who have not yet had that chance.

On one occasion, for example, at the sight of Krsna’s effulgent glowing footprints on the ground before him, Sahadeva felt so sorry for his parents, who were not there to share his bliss, that he cried:

“O my mother Madri! Where are you now? O dear father Pandu! Where are you? I regret that you are not here at this very moment to behold the splendid footprints of Lord Krsna!”

The splendour of Krsna’s footprints is endless, but one further glory must be mentioned here: the increased potency of Krsna’s footprints when they mingle with the footprints of Sri Radha.

In Srimati Radharani’s presence, Krsna enjoys heights of pleasure He cannot attain in anyone else’s company. Those special footprints are saturated by so much bliss that anyone who touches them goes mad.

The Pulinda girls, to cite but one example, went mad in ecstasy from the touch of Krsna’s footprints because those prints were reddened by the residue of kunkuma left on Krsna’s feet from Radha’s breasts.

Indeed, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura asserts that the Pulinda girls attained the seventh stage of prema, with all its perfections, by inadvertently touching the kunkuma footprints of Sri Krsna.

Of course Srimati Radharani’s footprints are no less potent than Sri Krsna's, because — as Krsna Himself admits — the pleasure She tastes while in His company is ten million times greater than His own.

The divine couple’s footprints are so potent that just to hear of them gives one a drop of the same bliss the gopis tasted as they tracked those footprints during the night of the saradiya-rasa dance.

When Krsna disappeared from their midst, the gopis searched for Him. At first they asked the trees about Him, until in a corner of the forest they noticed a flag, lotus, barleycorn, and so forth in the earth.

The gopis recognised these symbols to be from Krsna’s lotus feet and followed them. But when they saw Srimati Radharani’s footprints intermixed with His, they could tell what had happened.

From impressions in the soil the gopis could discern where Krsna laid His arm on Radha’s shoulder, where He kissed Her, where He picked Her up, and where He gathered forest flowers to decorate Her hair.

Relentlessly following those footprints led the gopis into the heart of the forest. There Krsna had abandoned His beloved, leaving Her bewildered and crying out in agony from separation.

Some gopis were critical of Radharani due to envy, others were supportive out of friendship, but every gopis’ singular attachment for Krsna increased by seeing the divine couple’s footprints.

And when the gopis witnessed Radha’s profound expressions of love in separation, they felt ashamed of their own insignificant affections, and that further sanctified and amplified their attachment to Krsna.

All glories to the lotus footprints of Radha and Syamasundara at Carana-cihna! Set in stone, these footprints are the same ones the gopis followed on the diamond-dust floor of Vrndavana forest.

All glories to he who took complete shelter at these lotus feet and thereby became fearless in his mission to spread Krsna consciousness throughout the world. All glories to Srila Prabhupada!

All glories to those devotees who have full faith that Srila Prabhupada’s instructions and the lotus feet of Radha and Syama can empower them to express the truths of Vraja to the world.

**\* \* \* \***

Before returning to the parikrama path one should visit the Banke-bihari temple between the carana-cihna and Govinda-ghata. It is said that this was the place of bhajana of Haridasa Svami.

Of the many Deities who left Vrndavana and stopped at Radha-kunda on their journey to Jaipur, Banke-bihari remained here. When a new temple was constructed for Him, He returned to Vrndavana town.

By the parikrama path is a temple of Gaura-Nitai, who are clearly visible from the road. Every year the temple custodians hold a very popular swing festival for the pleasure of the Deities and residents.

Radha-kunda’s southern side is called Rasavedi-ghata, the place of the rasa dance. In unmanifest forms the groves of Indulekha, Rangadevi, and Campakalata respectively decorate its two corners and centre.

On the other side of the parikrama path, a little distance from the Gaura-Nitai temple, is the Imli-tala, an ancient tamarind tree related to one of Rupa Gosvami’s wonderful pastimes.

No written record exists of Rupa Gosvami having a cottage at Radha-kunda in which to perform bhajana or write, but it is common knowledge that he visited this holy place many times.

Indeed, pastime places associated with Rupa Gosvami, such as Govinda-ghata and Imli-tala, testify to his having spent time at Radha-kunda in the company of its well-known residents.

Vaisnava oral tradition records that Sri Rupa once came to Imli-tala and, inspired by its majesty, sat there to chant Hare Krsna and gaze upon Radha-kunda as the afternoon sunshine danced upon its waves.

After some time Rupa Gosvami glanced at the tamarind tree and saw something he had not seen there before: a beautiful bejewelled swing with two lotus-shaped seats facing each other.

As the Gosvami wondered how he could have overlooked such a prominent and beautiful thing, he heard voices, familiar voices that heralded the appearance of Radha, Krsna, and Their gopi friends.

Speechless, Rupa felt intoxicated by what he first heard then saw. The divine couple’s beauty defied description, and the influence of Their youthful playfulness put to shame the effect of immortal elixir.

Soon enough, Krsna climbed onto the swing, pointed to the seat opposite Him, and said, “Dearest! Come make this lovely seat even lovelier with Your presence. Let Us enjoy the wind in Our faces.”

Radha shook Her head and firmly replied, “Whenever We swing together You frighten Me by making the swing go too high. You can swing alone, and all of us will watch You from here.”

Not one to be easily put off, Krsna insisted that Radha join Him. He gave Her many assurances that Their swinging would be very calm and restrained, but still Srimati Radharani refused.

Krsna continued pleading with Radha. The other gopis even came to His side and assured Her that they would take great care to push the swing in a way that would be completely safe and satisfying to Her.

Radha should have known from previous encounters that She still had cause for concern, but She yielded to the voice of the majority and accepted Krsna’s helping hand, finally taking Her seat.

As promised, the gopis pushed the swing gently, and the divine couple enjoyed the pleasing atmosphere of Radha-kunda and the cooling effect of swaying back and forth in the warm afternoon air.

Some girls sang of Krsna’s heroic deeds, others showered flower petals, and yet others sprayed perfumed water from an elegant crystal atomiser to scent the air and refresh the swinging lovers.

But just as Srimati Radharani was beginning to relax, naughty Krsna began to lean and kick in a way that made the swing go higher and higher until it was finally out of the gopis’ control.

As They began to swing above the heads of Her girlfriends, Radharani nervously asked Krsna to slow down, but He just laughed and raised His eyebrows at Her tauntingly.

“Here we go again!” She thought with dismay. As Krsna made the swing go higher and higher, and She became more and more worried, Radha pleaded with Him, “Please don’t go so high. Please let Me off.”

From the ground the gopis also protested, reminding Krsna of His promise, but He just grinned at them. Meanwhile, the swing had reached the tree’s canopy, scattering leaves to the ground.

As soon as the rope went slack at the top of the swing’s arc, Radha’s concern transformed into fear, and then finally erupted into panic when She saw that They were about to wrap right around the branch.

But Krsna was relentless. At that point, seeing no other shelter than the very cause of Her fear, Radha threw Herself at Krsna and wrapped Her arms around His neck, shrieking, “Stop! Please stop!”

Actually, Krsna was willing to stop under the circumstances, but by jumping from one end of the swing to the other, Radha gave it enough momentum to make a full circle over the branch.

For a moment Syamasundara tasted a unique exhilaration: the combination of seeing Radha-kunda upside down, feeling Radha’s desperate embrace, and hearing Her shrieks in His ear.

In the meantime, the cowherd girls watched in disbelief as Radha and Krsna flew around the branch like black and yellow firebrands and then came to a full stop in their midst.

At that point, Rupa Gosvami, who was also watching this scene, fainted, overcome by ecstasy. Sadly, by the time he had regained consciousness, Radha, Krsna, and the gopis had disappeared.

But in the shadows of twilight, Sri Rupa saw the bejewelled swing still hanging from the branch. The branch itself was completely twisted by the force of Radha’s and Krsna’s wild swinging.

The Gosvami at once credited the tamarind tree for his good fortune and offered it his prostrated obeisances, loudly chanting Krsna’s names, and left to share his experience with others.

Each time I remember this pastime I think of the old acacia tree that marks the place of the Imli-tala in New Vraja-dhama, and whose branches offer so many services to Radha-Syama and Their devotees.

This acacia was the only tree upon the hill before temple construction began, as if it had grown there as a marker to let us know that Radha and Syama should be worshipped at this place.

Sadly that tree gave way to old age and was replaced by a white-beam tree that now serves as a reminder of the intimate relationship between Rupa Gosvami and the divine couple.

**\* \* \* \***

By following the parikrama path one comes to the Radha-Gopinatha temple and the sitting place of Lord Nityananda — the only shelter for fallen souls. Here all Vaisnavas offer humble obeisances.

Dear devotees! With palms joined I say to you: “No one can approach Radha and Krsna without the mercy of Lord Nityananda, so let us all take shelter at His lotus feet without delay.”

Perpetually intoxicated by the varuni wine that seeps from the desire tree of devotional service, Lord Nityananda liberally distributes that tree’s precious fruits to one and all without discrimination.

Lord Nityananda’s servants are as compassionate as He, and so intelligent devotees pray to both master and servants, rakha ranga caranera pasa: “Always keep me in the corner of your lotus feet.”

Nityananda is very handsome. He dresses in blue clothes, wears golden jewellery, and sports a fancy turban on His head. He is always inebriated by love for Gaura and by Balarama’s boyish love for Krsna.

Appearing in the village of Ekacakra thirteen years before Lord Caitanya’s advent, Nityananda stayed at His birthplace until the age of twelve, playfully enacting Krsna’s pastimes with His friends.

Then He left home as the servant of a sannyasi on a pilgrim’s tour of Bharata-varsa. Very soon He set out alone to see the many holy places Lord Balarama visited in the year that lead up to the Kuruksetra War.

One spring day on pilgrimage, Lord Nityananda entered Mathura and bathed at Visrama-ghata before going on parikrama of Govardhana Hill, where He gave mercy to a pure devotee of Lord Balarama.

Lord Nityananda then toured the twelve forests of Vrndavana. Upon His arrival at Gokula, the Lord found the palace of Nanda Maharaja, the mere sight of which made Nityananda shed profuse tears.

The Lord offered obeisances to Madana-gopala and then left Vraja for Hastinapura, the Pandavas’ royal capital. From there He travelled to many other destinations, including Kuruksetra.

On His way the Lord met Madhavendra Puri, in whom the seed of devotional service in ecstatic love had first sprouted, and to whom Nityananda said, “My pilgrimage has at last borne fruit today.”

In reply, Madhavendra Puri said to Lord Nityananda, “I have never before seen such ecstatic love as Yours, but wherever such love of God is found, that is my favourite holy place.”

Lord Nityananda remained with Madhavendra Puri and his associates for several days and then continued on His way, travelling through Jagannatha Puri and returning to Mathura once again.

Lord Nityananda knew well that Caitanya Mahaprabhu had appeared in Navadvipa, but Nityananda waited in Vrndavana until Lord Caitanya had revealed His divinity and earnestly begun His mission.

Lord Nityananda had been travelling for twenty years. But at the advent of Lord Caitanya’s sankirtana movement, He rushed to Navadvipa for an emotional reunion with His Lord.

Lord Nityananda could have begun to distribute Krsna consciousness Himself at any time, but like all devotees who wait patiently and respectfully for the order of their superiors, He restrained Himself.

This is a perfect example of how Vaisnavas are always careful not to transgress the codes of etiquette in the name of saving conditioned souls. To whimsically accept the role of guru causes chaos.

While He waited there in Vraja, Lord Nityananda would sometimes visit pastime places and at other times stay in Vrndavana forest absorbed in thoughts of Krsna, unaware if it was day or night.

Nityananda Prabhu made no effort to care for His transcendental body: if on occasion someone offered Him milk, then He would drink it, but if no one offered anything, He would simply fast.

The locals were bewildered by the way Lord Nityananda behaved; a grown man, He sported in the waters of the Yamuna like a boy and played with the village children as if He were one of them.

Nor could they understand the Lord’s way of showing His ecstasy; at times He would cry for hours on end, laughing like a madman, or run off into the forest, calling out, “Kanhaiya, where are You?”

The spiritually astute, however, could perceive that Nityananda Prabhu was no ordinary devotee of the Lord. Some even speculated that He was an incarnation of Lord Balarama.

But many were unable to accept Lord Nityananda’s unorthodox behaviour or His lack of sadhana. Judging Him by the measure of their own meagre spiritual accomplishments, they criticised the Lord.

Those who fault Nityananda in any way — be they devotees of Krsna or followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu — cannot attain pure devotional service. They must suffer for their offences instead.

As Balarama, Lord Krsna’s second self, Nityananda is the Supreme Absolute Truth, the predominating Deity of the sandhini energy, the sustainer of the spiritual world, and the source of pure goodness.

Lord Caitanya says,

**“Whoever worships Lord Nityananda with faith and devotion also worships Me, but one who has even the slightest envy towards Nityananda I will not accept even if he is a devotee."**

Taking Lord Caitanya’s words to heart, again I say, “No one can approach Radha and Krsna without the mercy of Nityananda Prabhu, so let us all take shelter at His lotus feet without delay.”

It is unclear exactly when Lord Nityananda visited Radha-kunda, which as a devotee of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu He was welcome to do but as Balarama in krsna-lila He had to avoid.

Other than on formal occasions, like the meals at Nandagrama, Lord Balarama avoids meeting Srimati Radharani, knowing His presence would create an awkward situation if His brother were with Radha.

Therefore Lord Balarama would never go to Radha-kunda or Syama-kunda, the most likely places for Him to find His younger brother in an intimate exchange with Srimati Radharani.

As a devotee, however, through the transcendental process of remembrance, Nityananda Prahhu can enter any pastime, even those pastimes He would have otherwise avoided as Lord Balarama.

**\* \* \* \***

The parikrama of Radha-kunda ends in the lake’s southeastern corner at Kundesvara Mahadeva, the primary guardian of Radha-kunda and the divine gatekeeper from whom one must beg permission to enter.

To the guardian of Radha-kunda I prayed, “O Kundesvara Mahadeva! You protect Radha’s lake from egotists and fools by covering it with a layer of matter, preventing them from seeing the real Radha-kunda.

“Please, Mahadeva! Do not deceive me as well with your illusory powers, rather give me the eyes with which to behold, without limit, Radha’s celestial lake in its true form of sweetness and opulence.”

Some distance away from Radha-kunda and further along the parikrama path to Govardhana is Radha-Gokulananda temple and the bhajana-kutira of Their foremost servant, Lokanatha Gosvami.

At this same spot Lokanatha Gosvami took refuge from prying eyes and the summer sun in an underground cave (gupha), where he absorbed himself in solitary worship of the divine couple.

Further along the road, on the outskirts of the town, is Mayura-kunda, where Krsna took the form of a peacock to shun the Apsaras, proclaiming the transcendental glories of the rasa dance.

Along the parikrama path in the general area encircling both the Yoga-pitha and Radha-kunda are many different spots favoured by Krsna and the gopis as arenas for their rasa dances.

Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda appeared on the night of Bahulastami. Radha, Krsna, and the gopis thus celebrate Bahulastami with a festival of dancing that roams about this entire area.

Wherever the rasa dance moves, the celestial features of Radha’s lake—ghatas, groves, and gardens — fully manifest themselves, like night-blooming lotuses respond to the rays of the moon.

It is helpful to examine the rasa dance’s basic structure in order to reflect upon the prominent role it plays in Lord Krsna’s pastimes for fulfilling His desires for loving exchange.

The acaryas give elaborate accounts of the rasa-lila, but define it in short and general terms. Srila Sridhara Svami, for example, says that it is a type of dance involving many women.

Srila Sanatana Gosvami elaborates on this definition by adding that the women dance in a circle holding hands, and that a single male dancer embraces them around their necks.

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura cites a source that says:

**“When a male dancer performs, surrounded by a circle of many female dancers moving about, it is called a hallisaka.**

**“When a hallisaka dance is accompanied by a variety of refined tunes, dance steps, and gestures it is called a rasa dance. Since a rasa dance does not exist even in heaven, how could it exist on earth?”**

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura elaborates on the spirit of the rasa dance’s typical amorous exchanges by saying that it includes romantic elements like touching, singing, kissing, and embracing.

Finally, Srila Prabhupada adds to all these points, emphasising what he sees as essential:

**“When a theatrical actor dances among many dancing girls, the group dance is called a rasa dance.”**

Information about the rasa dances of Krsna and the gopis is obtained through two sources: realised souls like Sukadeva Gosvami and observers like the wives of the demigods who watch from overhead.

Through these two sources both qualified and unqualified persons come to hear about the rasa-lila, and according to their mindset they judge the dancing to be either sublime or mundane.

At the height of one particular dancing festival the cowherd girls were unable to stay composed; their clothes and hair became dishevelled, and their garlands and ornaments were in disarray.

From flower-airplanes hovering above the scene, the demigods and their wives watched secretly. Just by seeing Krsna’s exchanges with the gopis, those heavenly ladies were overcome by lust.

Their husbands, however, were not able to see the gopis’ bodies or to witness the gopis’ intimate dealings with Krsna; Yogamaya obscured the demigods’ vision so that they could not see the full spectacle.

The devas returned to their homes disappointed. Indra in particular felt insulted from being unable to see the rasa dance and disturbed by the obvious attraction his wife Saci had shown for Krsna.

His mind polluted by such unfavourable thoughts, Indra, like an ordinary materialist, concluded that Krsna was just a lusty cowherd taking advantage of ignorant young milkmaids.

Indra falsely assumed that the milkmaids’ desire for Krsna was the product of lust, just like his wife’s, and that Krsna’s desire for the gopis was also mundane and based on physical attraction.

He could not comprehend that the gopis’ attraction to Krsna was a display of their exalted spiritual perfection, nor that Krsna was attracted to the gopis because of their pure spiritual love for Him.

Hoping to expose Krsna as a libertine, Indra ordered many Apsaras — heavenly dancing girls whose beauty was irresistible to ordinary men of this world — to go to Vrndavana and entice Krsna.

So, one day, as Krsna was passing by this area of Radha-kunda, Indra’s courtesans appeared in a garden to the left of the road and tried to accost Krsna with the sight of their shapely bodies and bright faces.

Although these girls were famous for having disturbed the mystic trance of many a great yogi, their sensual movements and alluring words had not the slightest effect on Krsna’s mind or senses.

Krsna showed complete indifference to the Apsaras’ feminine wiles. Indeed, to teach Indra and his entourage that He is attracted only by pure devotion, Krsna transformed Himself into a peacock.

Krsna’s transformation left the beautiful women of heaven amazed beyond words; with eyes wide and mouths agape they watched as Krsna fanned out His tail feathers and proudly strutted away.

When the Apsaras returned to heaven and reported everything to Indra, the king of heaven could understand Krsna’s message clearly. Indra was ashamed for having once again tried to test his master.

This pastime reminds us of Krsna’s words to Arjuna on the battlefield of Kuruksetra,

*avajananti mam mudha manusim tanum asritam*  
*param bhavam ajdnanto mama bhuta-mahesvaram*

**“Fools deride Me when I descend in the human form \[manusim tanum\]. They do not know My transcendental nature \[param bhavam\] as the Supreme Lord of all that be.”**

The garden where Krsna became a peacock is called Mayura-kunda. Devotees pray at this place to be freed from any misconceptions they may have about Krsna’s character and pastimes.

**\* \* \* \***

Dear readers! This completes my description of the parikrama of Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda as it is presently performed by Gaudiya Vaisnavas in Bhauma Vrndavana.

Devotees touring New Vraja-dhama will, with the help of the maps accompanying this book and the signposts in Radha-Syamasundara’s temple, find the pastime places mentioned in these chapters.

But before I complete this parikrama with a prayer I shall mention a few more pastime places in New Vraja-dhama that are in the vicinity of the temple and are thus included in Radha-kunda parikrama there.

When entering or leaving the main entrance of Radha-Syamasundara’s temple, the tip of the Yoga-pitha’s western petal, I remember and pray to Lord Brahma, who happily dwells here.

My ardent prayer to the creator is this: May I catch hold of Radha’s and Syama’s lotus feet with the same intensity of zeal as you did the Lord’s; and may I attain the three perfections you did.

What are those perfections? That whatever you say never proves to be false; that the progress of your mind is never deterred; and that material attachment never degrades your senses, even temporarily.

Vaisnavas do not worship demigods for material gain, but they always seek the blessings of exalted devotees for the betterment of their service to Lord Krsna, even if those devotees happen to be demigods.

On His tour of South India, Caitanya Mahaprabhu would offer His obeisances at temples of Lord Siva. The gopis worshipped Katyayani, Gauri, and Surya with the hope of becoming dear to Krsna.

To the right of the entrance is a garden that represents the forest known as Anjanavana (or Anjanaka). In this grove Sri Krsna, humbled by the devotion of His dearmost gopi, sweetly served Her.

On most days Srimati Radharani’s maidservants and friends carefully dress and ornament Her, but on rare occasions She adorns Herself, thinking that Krsna will be even more pleased, and rightly so.

On one such occasion, in a grove by Her sacred kunda, Radha was preparing to see Krsna. She donned a dark blue sari, put on priceless jewels, braided Her hair, and applied cosmetics to Her face.

Maidservants stood by, carefully watching Radha’s every move. They were eager to learn the arts of adornment directly from their mistress, so that later they could dress Sri Radha as She had done Herself.

Just as Srimati Radharani had applied anjana to Her left eye, the sound of Krsna’s flute-song disturbed the tranquil atmosphere, accosting Radha’s consciousness with thoughts She could not ignore.

At one moment Radha was decorating Herself with fixed attention, and at the next She had dropped the collyrium brush from Her hand as She abruptly rose to leave, exclaiming, “Krsna! Krsna is calling!”

It was obvious to the gopis that Krsna’s flute had made off with Radha’s mind. As much as they tried, they could not persuade Her to finish putting on Her makeup — Radha was oblivious to all but Krsna.

Without a care for Her friends or for Her appearance, Radha ran from the grove and along the bank of Her lake, following the flute’s song like a mad person running after the thoughts of a volatile mind.

Let us meditate upon that enchanting cowherd girl. She runs wildly through the trees as forest creatures watch in startled silence and Her gopi friends, alarmed yet amused, run along behind.

Following the path laid out by the flute-song’s winding melody, Sri Radha came to Anjanaka and a woodland courtyard. There sat handsome Krsna upon a throne of flowers, flute to His lips.

Radhika's sudden breathless entrance startled Sri Krsna, who at once rose and offered Her His seat. The cowherd prince graciously waited to speak until His princess had caught Her breath.

Just as Krsna was about to speak to Srimati Radharani, Her maidservants arrived, as breathless as their mistress, and with looks of loving concern decorating their flushed but pretty faces.

Of His beloved Radha, Krsna asked, “O breathless beauty! Why are You so winded? Was a demon chasing You? Perhaps You are late to serve the sun god. Pray, tell. What is the matter?”

Still somewhat out of breath Sri Radha said, “I heard You call, so I came as fast as I possibly could!” The single-minded resolve with which Radha had responded to His flute-call touched Krsna deeply.

As He gazed at Radharani’s beautiful face, rosy from exertion and adorned with diamond drops of perspiration, Krsna noticed that only Her left eye was decorated with collyrium.

Speaking to Her and the gopis, Krsna asked, “Why does My beloved have anjana on only one eye?” The gopis told Krsna how Radha had been preparing to come and meet Him. They concluded: “When Srimati Radharani heard the distant call of Your flute, She instantly dropped the collyrium brush and, with only one eye decorated, rushed out to find Your lotus feet.”

Krsna took a deep breath, hoping to contain the effects the joy and gratitude He felt for Radha and Her selfless display of love could precipitate, lest His tears blur His vision of Her face.

A gopi, of her own accord, then approached Krsna with a tray that held collyrium and a brush. She knelt beside her Lord, offering Him the chance to decorate Radharani’s unanointed eye.

Krsna sat down beside Sri Radha, and with great care and expertise applied anjana to Her right eye, feeling profound satisfaction from personally serving the embodiment of divine service.

When He was done, Krsna placed His hands on Radha’s shoulders, carefully examined His work, and said, “That is not anjana on Your eye. It’s the very essence of My being.” Radha looked down shyly.

Because Krsna personally applied anjana to Radha’s eyes within this forest grove, it is known as Anjanaka. By praying to the dust in this place, one’s eyes may also be anointed with the salve of love.

Not far away, on the tip of this northern petal of the Yoga-pitha, sits Lord Ananta, a plenary portion of Lord Nityananda, who with His thousand mouths constantly recites the glories of Sri Krsna.

The Lord is called Ananta, or “unlimited,” because He gives shelter to numberless souls. Possessed of a thousand hoods, boundless strength, and an enormous body, He always holds a club and plough.

Those hoods, decorated with brightly shining jewels, are the resting place of unlimited universes, whose weight He feels to be no more significant than the weight of mustard seeds. Such is His strength!

As an incarnation of the Lord in the form of His own devotee, Anantadeva recites Srimad-Bhagavatam to brahmana sages headed by the four Kumaras, all the while holding the universes on His hoods.

Because Sri Krsna’s pastimes are without end, Ananta never completes His recitation. As He chants, His heads and necks sway gracefully back and forth under the intoxicating power of krsna-lila.

Why are Lord Ananta’s mouths a storehouse of Krsna’s gem-like glories in the form of Srimad-Bhagavatam? One can find the answer in the saying “valuable jewels are kept in a most appropriate place.”

This area of Radha-kunda is, therefore, a most appropriate place in which to hear Srimad-Bhagavatam from the Lord’s own lips and in the august assembly of Sanat-kumara and his brahmana brothers.

Because Anantadeva serves Krsna by expanding on Krsna’s glories, devotees pray to the thousand-headed Lord for inspiration to deliver the message of Srimad-Bhagavatam and distribute it in written form.

How can one gain the strength for such an undertaking in this age of sin? That strength will also come from He of unlimited power, which is yet another reason the Lord is called Ananta.

But there is a secret behind the source of Ananta’s power, knowing which devotees may mould their conduct and thus acquire the prerequisite strength to disseminate the Lord’s names and glories.

That secret is that Anantadeva, the original bhagavata-acarya, expands into another form, Ananta Sesa, to render ten varieties of intimate service to Sri Krsna. He is consequently inspired.

The ten forms into which Ananta Sesa expands to render personal service to the Lord are: Sri Krsna’s friend, brother, fan, bed, conveyance, residence, umbrella, garments, ornaments, and seat.

By this example devotees can see that Krsna consciousness — as a train moves on two tracks — moves forward on the two tracks of serving Srimad-Bhagavatam and worshipping the Deity of the Lord.

Devotees who follow both tracks in full awareness of Sri Krsna will feel Ananta’s strength empowering them to preach the Lord’s glories, and in due course to defeat all the impediments of conditioned life.

The last place which is on the eastern petal of the Yoga-pitha is Patala, sometimes called Patalavana, a beautiful garden filled with pink roses where Radha and the gopis come to collect flowers and make garlands.

While chattering sweetly about Krsna’s exploits, gopis busy themselves under Radha’s guidance in a shady grove at the centre of the garden by stringing garlands to offer to the Lord.

Coincidentally, this is also where in New Vraja-dhama, on festivals like Janmastami and Radhastami, devotees come together to make all kinds of garlands and floral arrangements for Their Lordships.

**\* \* \* \***

Having commented on but a drop of Radha-kunda’s glories, I offer my obeisances to that gem, the central jewel in the crown of Govardhana Hill, the kunda very dear to the queen who rules over Krsna’s heart.

I pray that I may always reside in a cottage within view of Sri Radha’s lake, eat the produce grown from the soil of Krsna Valley, drink the milk from Syama’s cows, and chant the names of Radha and Syama.

O beautiful lake! Our acaryas and scriptures declare that you are as dear to Krsna as Radha Herself; indeed, they say that you are the liquefied form of Vrsabhanu’s daughter’s love for the Lord.

You are more sacred than the sum total of all holy places. Within the hearts of persons who think of you, glorify you, or offencelessly bathe in your water, a love arises like the love the gopis have for Krsna.

In this world such love takes the shape of selfless service to the divine couple, which like a fire bums away all traces of lust in the heart and assures the devotee of seeing Radha and Krsna.

In the next life such love transports one to where Krsna is present in the material world, awards one a spiritual body, and cultivates itself until it is the mature love required to see Krsna’s pastimes forever.

Ignorant and envious persons claim that Sri Radha is not mentioned in the pages of scripture. They say that Her role as Krsna’s primary consort is a recent concoction, but these allegations are false.

The truly wise know Radha to he the ultimate treasure the Vedas concealed from those without the prerequisite faith. Thus Her position as Krsna’s own potency remains undisturbed.

By citing statements from both sruti and smrti, the appendix entitled “How Sri Radha Is Revealed Through the Vedic Literature” confirms that Srimati Radharani embodies Krsna’s primordial potency.

Despite the sad truth that I am riddled with bad habits, I have followed my heart in attempting to glorify Radha and Krsna. By so doing I have tried to serve those who seek the quintessence of all.

It is said that those who are thoroughly honest accept literary works filled with descriptions of the glorious names, forms, and pastimes of the Lord, even though those works may be imperfectly composed.

I therefore humbly request that You, Radha and Syama, overlook the many defects in this composition, and instead accept that which is at its heart — my strong desire to sing and make known Your praises.

If You are at least the slightest bit pleased by my efforts, then please, in this lifetime allow me to continue living and serving near You, and in the next life also, allow me to serve You and witness Your pastimes.

Every morning — year in, year out—the devotees of New Vraja- dhama and I pray to Tulasi-devi for this blessing, mora ei abhilasa, vilasa kunje dio vasa nayana heribo sada yugala-rupa-rasi.

I now turn to You and offer that very same prayer and self-same aspiration, knowing You will hear me and hoping that on the strength of my prayers to Tulasi You will show me Your mercy.

“O dear, dear Radha and Krsna! My desire is that You will also grant me a residence in the pleasure groves of Sri Vrndavana-dhama. Thus within my vision I will always behold Your beautiful pastimes.”

## Appendix 25

**Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali - (“A Bouquet of Lamentations”) by Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami**

(This appendix follows from the description of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami's life and works while residing on the banks of Radha-kunda as described in chapter sixteen. The English translations of the verses are adapted from the translations of Kusakratha Dasa and Advaita Dasa. The commentary is my own.)

**Introduction**

At the stage of perfection, love of God fully reveals one’s spiritual identity (siddha-deha), including one’s eternal name, form, and service in the spiritual world. A perfected devotee in the mood of maternal love, for example, serves Krsna in the manner of Krsna’s mother, Yasoda, through the medium and under the guidance of other senior ladies of Vraja, like Rohini-devi.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami is an eternal associate of the Lord in two forms. In the first form he eternally serves Lord Caitanya as a practising devotee (sadhaka) under the supervision of Svarupa Damodara, Sanatana Gosvami, and Rupa Gosvami. In the second form he eternally serves Sri Krsna as Srimati Radharani’s gopi maidservant, known both as Rati-manjari and Tulasl-manjari.

In Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, as a perfected practitioner who has fully realised his spiritual identity, yearns to be reinstated as Rati-manjari in eternal service to the divine couple in Goloka Vrndavana.

At times, Sri Radha personally appears before Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, and at other times Dasa Gosvami is so absorbed in thoughts of serving Sri Radha that he feels as though She is with him. But neither sort of brief revelation can compare to living with Radha and Krsna on Goloka Vrndavana in the spiritual sky, because whenever Dasa Gosvami again loses his sought-after contact with Sri Radha, the pains of maintaining a material body and the weight of his preaching responsibilities remind Dasa Gosvami he is still in this world. At these times he laments.

After a long life of success in pushing on Lord Caitanya's mission, Dasa Gosvami’s hankering to be Rati-manjari, who is perpetually serving Sri Radha, became so strong that it may well have been the cause for his departure from this world. No longer able to tolerate the infinite pain of separation, he turned to his only shelter, Sri Radha, and deeply lamented. These lamentations, the fragrantly blossoming flowers of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s spiritual ecstasies, grew into verses that were then bound together in a bouquet called Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali and offered at the lotus feet of Srimati Radharani.

By studying these verses, practising devotees will understand the moods of service in separation and how those moods can be properly cultivated and expressed. However, the levels of realisation exhibited by Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami cannot be imitated; in fact, those who attempt to artificially imitate exalted souls endanger their own spiritual lives. Still, devotees should be aware that such advanced states of service in separation exist because that awareness can lead one to follow the regulated process of devotional service with rigour, attention, and care. One whose heart is purified by this sort of serious sadhana can easily cross over any obstacle that might otherwise block the development of spontaneous feelings for the Lord, which arise naturally as one progresses in devotional life.

In agreement with his teachings, Srila Prabhupada encouraged us to think of ourselves as servants of Krsna and gave us the motto “Back home, hack to Godhead!” Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali describes one kind of service to Krsna — service of the gopis, specifically the manjari-gopis, the maidservants of Srimati Radharani — and in so doing paints a vivid picture of what going back to Godhead is actually like.

Yes, devotees may aspire for such services in Goloka Vrndavana, provided that they are properly qualified. Those qualifications are the desire to aspire for such services and the purity of heart not to he sensually aroused when hearing of Krsna’s loving exchanges with the gopis. Of the qualifications for spontaneous devotion, Srila Prabhupada writes:

**“We must always remember, however, that such eagerness to follow in the footsteps of the denizens of Vraja (Vrndavana) is not possible unless one is freed from material contamination. In following the regulative principles of devotional service, there is a stage called anartha-nivrtti, which means the disappearance of all material contamination. Sometimes someone is found imitating such devotional love, but factually he is not freed from anarthas, or unwanted habits. It has been seen that a so-called devotee proclaims himself a follower of Nanda, Yasoda or the gopis, while at the same time his abominable attraction to mundane sex life is visible. Such a manifestation of divine love is mere imitation and has no value. When one is actually spontaneously attracted to the loving principles of the gopis, there will be found no trace of any mundane contamination in his character.**

**“Therefore, in the beginning, everyone should strictly follow the regulative principles of devotional service, according to the injunctions of the scriptures and the spiritual master. Only after the stage of liberation from material contamination can one actually aspire to follow in the footsteps of the devotees in Vrndavana.”**

In short, Srila Prabhupada summarises those qualifications as the “special \[and\] natural" attraction to services that arises in a devotee’s purified heart.

Devotees who feel that they are not qualified to actively aspire for vraja-bhakti may still read Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali to better understand the nature of loving service in Vraja. As already mentioned, sadhakas must at least know such a reality exists.

But if reading the verses and the accompanying commentaries found in this appendix triggers critical thoughts concerning Krsna’s propriety, or stirs up sensual thoughts or feelings connected to mundane sexuality, then devotees should leave this appendix aside until their Krsna consciousness further matures. The ability to accurately gauge one’s own spiritual development, and the courage to be honest with oneself regarding the same, are important consequences of having completed the stage of anartha-nivrtti. The desire to hear about topics such as those described in Sri Vilapa-kasumanjali comes with faith and purity of heart, neither of which can be induced artificially. When a devotee has attained that sort of faith and purity it will be self-evident to him or her. Then the hearing of Krsna’s pastimes with the gopis will be properly appreciated and fully effective. This same conclusion is given at the end of Krsna’s rasa-lila pastime:

*vikriditam vraja-vadhubhir idam ca visnoh*  
*sraddhanvito ’nusrnuyad atha varnayed yah*  
*bhaktim param bhagavati pratilabhya kamam*  
*hrd-rogam asv apahinoty acirena dhirah*

**“Anyone who faithfully hears or describes the Lord’s playful affairs with the young gopis of Vrndavana will attain the Lord’s pure devotional service. Thus he will quickly become sober and conquer lust, the disease of the heart.”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami injects the mood of his aspirations into every verse of this work with phrases like “will I,” “when will I,” and “may I.” In this way the acarya (who had no doubt already achieved full access to the object of his meditations) places his “hopes” within the reach of conditioned souls.

Had he said,

**“O auspicious girl! When I took the sweets You \[Radha\] cooked to the queen of Vraja \[Yasoda\], she placed her forehead to mine as if she were my mother and enquired about Your well-being, knowing me to be Yours!” (verse 47)**

then the mood of the verse would be inaccessible to practitioners. There are two reasons why this must be so. First, it would not have been a statement of aspiration but attainment, something a mere practitioner cannot share. And second, it would have expressed the sentiments of meeting rather than separation.

Instead, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami composed the verse as follows:

**“O auspicious girl! When will I take the sweets You cooked to the queen of Vraja who will place her forehead to mine as if she were my mother and enquire about Your well-being, knowing me to be Yours!” (verse 47)**

In this way, devotees who are merely inclined, as well as devotees who are thoroughly qualified, can follow the lead of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami in cultivating the moods of vraja-bhakti as exhibited by the gopis. Rupa Gosvami outlines this process of cultivation:

*seva sadhaka-rupena siddha-rupena catra hi*  
*tad-bhava-lipsuna karya vraja-lokanusaratah*

**“In the transcendental realm of Vraja \[Vraja-dhama\] one should serve the Supreme Lord, Sri Krsna, with a feeling similar to that of His associates, and one should place himself under the direct guidance of a particular associate of Krsna and should follow in his footsteps. This method is applicable both in the stage of sadhana \[spiritual practices executed while in the stage of bondage\] and in the stage of Sadhya \[God realisation\], when one is a siddha-purusa, or a spiritually perfect soul.”**

For devotees who share the devotional feelings of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, hearing, remembering, and repeating the verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali is synonymous with following in the footsteps of the acarya.

Before continuing, one final note is required. Many of thecommentaries to the following verses include conversations between Rati-manjari and Srimati Radharani. It is my intention that these conversations further elucidate the moods and the philosophical truths contained within the verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, much in the same way that Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains the verses of the Bhagavad-gita by presenting what he calls “parallel conversations” between Arjuna and Krsna. Thus, when in the commentary to text fifty-three we find, “Radha replies to her maidservant with a smile, ‘Why do you say that Rati?’” the intended meaning is rather, “Radha may have replied to her maidservant with a smile, ‘Why do you say that Rati?’” For ease of reading, however, qualifying words and phrases — such as “may have replied” and the like — are not always included in the conversations. At those times they are implicit.

**Verse 1**

*tvam rupa-manjari sakhi prathita pure ’smin*  
*pumsah parasya vadanam na hi pasyasiti*  
*bimbadhare ksatam anagata-bhartrkaya*  
*yat te vyadhayi kim u tac chuka-pungavena*

**“O friend, Rupa-manjari! In this town of Vraja you are well known for being so chaste that you would never even look at another man. It is therefore surprising to see a mark on the bimba fruit of your lips, a mark that suggests someone has bitten them, although your husband is away from home. Was this mark made by the best of parrots?”**

Commentary: The author speaks this and the following two verses from the position of his eternal spiritual identity as Rati-manjari . Then the next three verses, beginning with verse four, are spoken from the position of the practising devotee Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. And all the remaining verses, from verse seven through verse one hundred and four, are again in the voice of Rati, the maidservant of Sri Radha.

Because Dasa Gosvami is absorbed in his spiritual identity as a maidservant of Radha, he here addresses his spiritual master, Rupa Gosvami, as the gopi Rupa-manjari. This verse discloses just how pure is the manjaris’ love for Sri Radha. One of the defining characteristics of a manjari is that she never desires direct physical contact with Krsna. Her only interest is to see that her mistress, Sri Radha, comes in contact with Sri Krsna, and thus she does her best to prepare Radha for such meetings. The marks of loving pastimes Rati sees upon the lips of Rupa-manjari automatically appeared there at the same time they appeared on the lips of Sri Radha. This incident is testimony to the fact that the servants of Krsna’s servants indirectly attain the same ecstatic benefits directly attained by His servants themselves.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu identified Himself—as do His followers — as a servant of the servant of Krsna’s servant (dasa-dasanudasah). By translating this phrase as “the servant one hundred times removed,” Srila Prabhupada established the superiority of this indirect connection to Krsna over a direct one. Indeed, he even discouraged the attempt to become Krsna’s direct servant, saying that such a goal was “not possible.”

Worldly experience tells us that the further away one is from a source of pleasure, such as Krsna, the less one is able to enjoy it. The transcendental reality, however, is just the opposite, as confirmed by this verse. Without physically touching Krsna, Rupa-manjari displays the same love marks that appear on Radha’s lips and enjoys the same amorous pleasure that Radha enjoys. A physical, bodily connection is not required for one to be connected to Krsna. Rather, service to those who do have physical contact with Krsna is the true connection, a connection that does not decrease in potency with any amount of distance from its source. That connection retains the same potency regardless of how many intermediaries exist between servant and master. This concept is expressed well by the axiom “things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.”

At the time Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami composed Sri Vilapa- kusumanjali his mentors, Rupa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami,had already left this world. Dasa Gosvami’s feelings of separation from Radha’s and Krsna’s eternal pastimes were thus amplified by his feelings of separation from Lord Caitanya’s foremost associates.

To understand Sri Vilapa-kusumanjahli's importance in the canon of Gaudiya Vaisnava literature, as well as its bearing on the systematic cultivation of devotional service, one need look no further than the books of Rupa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami, not to mention the remainder of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s own literary output.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu ordered Sanatana Gosvami to write about regulated devotional service and its relationship to spontaneous devotion, and to describe Krsna’s manifest and unmanifest pastimes in Gokula. Sanatana Gosvami fulfilled this direct order by writing Sri Hari-bhakti-vilasa and Sri Brhad-bhagavatamrta. To Rupa Gosvami, Lord Caitanya assigned the task of writing books on the science of mellows (rasa), the foremost of which is Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu.

Although Sanatana Gosvami taught the general principles of pure devotional service, and Rupa Gosvami taught the intricacies of transcendental mellows, the detailed process by which an aspiring devotee can enter into the mellows of pure devotional service in Vraja was not fully explained. That task was given to Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, who had assimilated the science as Svarupa Damodara taught it to him. In Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami also summarises the teachings of his guru, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, in the conversation between Ramananda Raya and Caitanya Mahaprabhu. He writes,

**“I have tried to preach the pastimes of Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s meeting with Ramananda Raya in accordance with the notebooks of Sri Svarupa Damodara.”**

Having been given the task to provide a detailed description of the process by which one enters into spontaneous devotional service, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami composed several books to accomplish his mission. Amongst them, Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali describes direct service to Radha and Krsna in the spiritual world; Vraja-vilasa-stava, the mentality with which to properly appreciate the liberated associates of the Lord; Visakhanandabhidha-stotra, along with other poems, the divine couple’s eightfold daily pastimes; and Sva-niyama-dasaka, the vows taken by those on the platform of ecstatic devotion through which Krsna’s pastimes are revealed. Finally, since practising devotees cannot meditate with rapt attention on Radha’s and Krsna’s lila without controlled minds, Dasa Gosvami composed Manah-siksa, his famous instructions to the mind, as the prerequisite for reading his other works.

In this way the works of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami are of inestimable value to serious practitioners of bhakti. And out of all of them, Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali is most essential. Devotees who want to use it as a guide for spiritual cultivation should first assimilate Manah-siksa and then align themselves with the vows found in Sva-niyama-dasaka.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s contribution to Gaudiya Vaisnavism is not only literary, but practical as well; indeed, his entire life serves as an example of how to put these teachings into practice. Thus he is a true acarya in every sense of the word. Devotees intent on entering into the teachings of Dasa Gosvami emulate his strict devotional practices, according to their capacity. And for those who think they can engage in spontaneous devotional service without observing regulative principles and Vaisnava conduct, they should take heed — not a trace of such hypocrisy could he found in the personal example of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. Krsnadasa Kaviraja declares as much in this verse:

*ananta guna raghunathera ke karibe lekha?*  
*raghunathera niyanui—yena pasanera rekha*

**“Who could list the unlimited transcendental attributes of Raghunatha dasa? His strict regulative principles were exactly like lines on a stone.”**

During a conversation in Calcutta in 1930, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura cited this first verse of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali. When he first began to explain the verse, ecstatic symptoms like crying, trembling, and horripilation were visible on his body. Finally the effects of ecstasy were so intense that the acarya fell from his chair, and disciples had to help him into another room. Not only Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura but also his disciples were stunned and motionless due to the bliss of ecstasy. After some time both guru and disciples returned to external consciousness, having been transported to the realm of ecstasy in which Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami shares.

**Verse 2**

*sthala-kamalini yuktam garvita kanane 'smin*  
*pranayasi vara-hasyam puspa-guccha-cchalena*  
*api nikhila-latas tah saurabhaktah sa muncan*  
*mrgayati tava margam krsna-bhrngo yad adya*

**“O land-lotus! You have every right to be smiling proudly through Your petals. After all, the black Krsna-bee has left all the other fragrant flower vines and is now searching for the pathway to You.”**

Commentary: This second verse glorifies Radha’s supremacy over all other gopis of Vraja. Every gopi is anointed with pure love for Krsna, but Radha’s love, by which She thinks, “Krsna is mine,” is by far superior and makes Krsna forget all others in favour of Her. Aware of Her own exalted position, Radha smiles with transcendental pride.

Lotuses generally grow in bodies of water, but those that grow on land are called sthala-kamalini. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami gives Sri Radhika this name to imply that the Radha-lotus is distant from the Krsna-river, confirming that Krsna is apart from Radha because He is looking for Her.

Krsna sometimes appears to act like a lusty prince chasing after village girls. Of course, non-devotees or neophyte devotees may interpret His behaviour in that way. Advanced devotees, however, know that Krsna’s pastimes with the gopis are displays of the most precious exchanges of love, called prema. Because Krsna sometimes appears to be deceitful, naughty, or crooked, He also seems to be lusty. But factually He is not. The proof of this statement lies in the fact that Krsna shows no interest in the unlimited number of lusty girls in this mundane world. He is interested only in the devotion of His liberated companions. The external aspects of mundane lust and divine love may appear similar, but the motives underlying those exchanges are worlds apart.

*kama, prema — donhakara vibhinna laksana*  
*lauha ara hema yaiche svarupe vilaksana*  
*atmendriya-priti-vancha— tare bali ‘kama’*  
*krsnendriya-priti-iccha dhare ‘prema’ nama*

**“Lust and love have different characteristics, just as iron and gold have different natures. The desire to gratify one’s own senses is kama \[lust\], bur the desire to please the senses of Lord Krsna is prema \[love\].”**

Thus sastra accepts Krsna’s attraction to the gopis, and the gopis’ attraction to Krsna, as fully spiritual. Their loving exchanges are pastimes of prema. Firm faith in the transcendental nature of Krsna’s pastimes with the gopis is the absolute, indispensable prerequisite for appreciating them, not to mention entering into them.

The gopis of Vraja appreciate Krsna’s love according to their individual qualifications, and He is attracted to them proportionately. In this way there are varieties of relationships between Krsna and the gopis. Of all the gopis, however, Krsna is most attracted to Srimati Radharani because, of all His beloveds, She is the most qualified. Indeed, Krsna considers Radha’s love to be like Mount Meru when compared to the love of the other gopis, which appears like so many mustard seeds in proportion.

This raises a question: If Krsna feels in this way about the love of gopis other than Radha, then why does He reciprocate their affection at all? The answer is that He feels obliged to them because they are His pure devotees. This can be seen in Krsna’s statement, *ye yatha mam prapadyante tams tathaiva bhajamy aham*: “As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly.” However, while Krsna is giving pleasure to one gopi—as Radha waits for Him elsewhere — He is always thinking of Radharani and feeling unhappy for standing Her up.

Knowing this, Gaudiya Vaisnavas in the mood of amorous love want to become Radha’s maidservants, not Her competitors.
