This is the fullest concept of pure devotion, as perfected by the gopis of Vraja. Caitanya Mahaprabhu therefore said, *ramya kacid upasana vraja-vadhu-vargena ya kalpita*: “There is no better mode of worship than that which was conceived by the damsels of Vrndavana.”

**Verse 22**

*paniyam-cina-vasiraih sasi-mukhi sanakai ramya-mrdt-anga-yastair*  
*yatnad utsarya modad disi disi vicalan-netra-minancalayah*  
*sronau raktam-dukulam-tad aparam atulam-caru-nilam-siro ‘grat*  
*sarvangesu pramodat pulakita-vapusa kim-maya te prayojyam*

**“O moon-faced one! When will I slowly and carefully dry the water from Your beautiful, delicate limbs with a silken towel? And as the two fish of Your eyes happily and restlessly swim from one direction to another, when — the hairs on my body standing up in bliss — will I be allowed to cover Your hips with a matchless red silk cloth, and all Your limbs, from Your head down, with a beautiful blue sari?”**

Commentary: Srimati Radharani is sometimes called “moonfaced,” and sometimes “one whose beautiful lotus face defeats the moon.”

To call Radha “moon-faced” is to say that Her stunning facial features are as soothing as the rays of the full moon. The sight of Radharani's face pacifies Krsna’s heart, satisfying Him in every way.

Even though the full moon is universally celebrated, there are marks upon its surface. Does Radha’s face have any marks? Yes, it does. But as we hear about the nature of these marks, we will see that they serve only to enhance Her charm.

Sometimes Krsna cannot resist the sight of Radha’s restless eyes, and so He kisses them. The black ointment from Her eyelids sticks to Krsna’s lips, and the sight makes Radharani break out in joyful smiles.

When Krsna sees the nectar radiating from Radha’s happy face, He is immediately forced to kiss Her once again. The black ointment from Radha’s eyes is thus transferred from Krsna’s lips to Hers. When Krsna now sees Sri Radha’s face adorned by these small black marks — evidence of His unrestrained affection — He is dumbfounded by their natural grace, even though they were not placed there by design. Krsna can only stare at Radha’s moonlike face, transfixed, and murmur, “Oh My! Oh My!"

Just as he did in verse twenty-one, here Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami compares Sri Radha’s face to a golden lotus that defeats the moon. Radha’s beloved Krsnacandra is compared to the moon for many reasons: because, like Radha, His face is also like the moon, because He appears in the dynasty of the moon, because different parts of His body are compared to twenty-four and a half moons, and because one of His eyes is the moon. The lotus blooms in the daytime, whereas the moon appears at night, so the two can never see each other. How then can the lotus defeat the moon? Actually, the Krsna-moon cannot last a moment without seeing the golden lotus of Radha’s face. Regardless of whether it is day or night, He appears wherever She does. Therefore, because the movements of this moon depend upon the appearance of the golden lotus, not on planetary laws, the Krsna-moon is controlled by the golden lotus, Sri Radha.

The red petticoat Rati places around the waist of her mistress signifies Radha’s passionate attachment to Krsna. On top of that petticoat she wraps a silk sari the same colour as Krsna. As this garment envelops Srimati Radharani, She feels Krsna’s embrace, and like an imperilled boat suddenly sinking into the ocean, Her mind submerges itself in thoughts of Her lover. Rati silently looks on, reading Radha’s thoughts by examining the expressions on Her face.

Sri Radha dresses in blue cloth to remind Her of Krsna, and Krsna dresses in gold silk to remind Him of Radha. Actually, neither one of Them need be reminded of the other, for They are always absorbed in thoughts of each other, even while They sleep. Thus Their choice of clothing is, more precisely, a declaration of Their love.

One of Radha’s names is Krsna-mayi, which means “one whose within and without are Krsna.” In this way She sees Krsna wherever She casts Her glance. Because Srimati Radharani sees Krsna everywhere and in everything, She is the very emblem of Krsna consciousness.

**Verse 23**

*praksalya pada-kamalam tad-anukramena*  
*gosthendra-sunu-dayite tava kesa-pasam*  
*ha narmada-grathita-sundara-suksma-malyair*  
*venim karisyati kada pranayair jano ‘yam*

**“O beloved of the son of Vraja’s king! When will this person, after washing Your lotus feet, lovingly braid Your hair with many delicate garlands artistically fashioned by the florist girl, Narmada?”**

Commentary: Rati-manjari gazes at Radharani, who sits silently immersed in samadhi. Rati does not want to disturb her princess, but Radha must be on time to cook Krsna’s breakfast. Therefore Rati softly calls Sri Radha by a beautiful name, “O beloved of the son of Vraja’s king!” In this way, the words the maidservant uses are harmonious with the thoughts of her mistress, and the sound of Rati’s voice retrieves Radha from Her reverie.

Radha then opens Her eyes wide, as if to say, “Oh, Rati! It’s you!” Rati takes Radharani’s extended hand, leads Her to the dressing room, and offers Her a seat on an oval-shaped bench bedecked with jewels. Then Rati washes Sri Radha’s feet once more before preparing to dry and braid Her hair.

Some saints say that Radha’s constant meditation upon Her beloved has caused Her thoughts to take on Krsna’s blackish lustre and sprour-Iike vines. Sprinkled by the profuse nectar of Her love for Krsna, those vines have grown long and thin, appearing as Sri Radha’s hair.

Others say that Sri Radha’s eyes and mind have both absorbed the fine blackish hue of Krsna’s body, a translucent sheen that was then transferred to Her incomparably soft and luxurious hair. Indeed, Sri Radha’s lovely braid and the locks that circle Her forehead like honeybees proclaim themselves to be the radiant beauty of Her face in the form of hair.

Likening Radha’s hair to a celestial camara or to peacock feathers could never do it justice; in fact, comparing Her braid to the sacred junction of the Ganga, Yamuna, and Sarasvati rivers does not even hit the mark. It is accurate, however, to say that Radha’s hair is like a dense jungle where the mad elephant of Krsna’s heart roams unrestrained, or to say that it is like a net cast by Cupid, the hunter, to trap the two restless deer of Krsna's eyes.

After drying and combing this inconceivable, indescribable substance known as Radha’s hair, Rati sits on a stool behind Sri Radha and plaits that hair into a long thick braid, interwoven with delicate jasmine-flower garlands. Rati has watched Krsna braid His beloved’s hair before, so she uses His technique, even mimicking His hand movements, to increase the pleasure of her princess.

**Verse 24**

*subhaga-mrgamadenakhanda-subhramsu-vat te*  
*tilakam iha lalate devi modad vidhaya*  
*masrna-ghusrna-carcam arpayitva ca gatre*  
*stana-yugam api gandhais citritam kim karisye*

**“O Goddess! When will I happily mark Your forehead with musk tilaka as splendid as the full moon, anoint Your limbs with glistening kunkuma, and decorate Your breasts with delightful pictures in fragrant colours?”**

Commentary: Srimati Radharani’s daily bathing, dressing, and adornment are, like the worship of Her Deity form, standardised and systematic. The complete procedure is comprised of sixteen adornments and twelve ornaments that Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami offers to Sri Radha one by one.

In summary, the sixteen adornments of Sri Radha are a pleasant bath, earrings, blue garments, a belt, a necklace, betel nuts, Her plaited braids, the tilaka on Her forehead, the mascara around Her eyes, a nose ring set with a pearl, sandal paste to anoint Her limbs, flowers for decorating Her hair, a musk dot on Her chin, a play lotus in Her hand, red lacquer (alta) on the soles of Her feet, and colourful designs and pictures drawn on Her cheeks.

The twelve ornaments are rings, bracelets, armlets, toe rings, ankle bells, golden earrings, a pearl necklace, a locket for Her neck, a belt around Her hips, a flower choker, a golden salaka hairpin, and a tiara atop Her head.

But does Srimati Radharani require all this beautification? Not at all!

Her beauty is so naturally stunning that neither exquisite garments nor priceless ornaments can enhance it in any way. But because daily ablution and beautification are parts of Vedic culture, Radharani accepts these things, and thereby gives Her girlfriends the chance to serve Her. By Radha’s gracious acceptance of whatever services and items the gopis offer, those fortunate girls become truly useful and even more attractive themselves.

Sri Radha’s transcendental form is an unequalled festival of splendour to which no worldly object can compare. Yet the saints feel compelled to describe Her glories and in so doing attempt to compare Her beauty to the most beautiful of worldly forms.

Her face is like a blossoming golden lotus around which curly locks of hair hover just like bumblebees seeking the nectar of Her breath. Her gracefully billowing hair is like the river Yamuna’s flowing waves in which that lotus blossoms. Her full breasts, slender waist, and graceful shoulders steal the pride of the most beautiful of Vraja’s hills and vales by surpassing their alluring contours. And the effulgence of Her fingernails baffles the sun and moon by its brilliance.

To glorify the unprecedented beauty of Sri Radha—beauty which gives pleasure and happiness to Sri Krsna, the source of all pleasure and happiness — Dasa Gosvami continues to divulge the details of his early morning service to his mistress.

**Verse 25**

*sindura-rekha simante devi ratna-salakaya*  
*maya ya kalpita kim te salakam sobhayisyati*

**“O beauty of my heart! When will I draw a line of red sindura with a jewelled Salaka to decorate the part in Your hair?”**

Commentary: In the Vedic culture, married women decorate the part in their hair with red sindura. With a golden stick inlaid with jewels, Rati reddens Radha’s part in one neat stroke, reminding Her, “You are married but have accepted Vraja’s prince as Your lover. Seeing this bold red line, everyone will think You are a chaste housewife. They will never guess Your infidelity."

Amorous love (madhurya-bhava) is of two kinds: wedded and unwedded. Krsna enjoys wedded love in Dvaraka with His queens and unwedded love in Vraja with the gopis. The queens of Dvaraka cannot taste the love for Krsna the gopis taste in Vraja, because to taste it one must follow the path of spontaneous devotion and cherish Krsna as a paramour.

The rules of moral conduct condemn unwedded love, but when Krsna is the hero in such escapades, then the most elevated moralists, the transcendentalists, praise Him. As the Supreme Absolute Truth, the Supreme Lord of all souls, Krsna is the friend, wife, and husband of every living entity. To say, therefore, that He consorts with someone else’s wife is a contradiction by definition. It is only a figure of speech referring to the role He takes within His self-invented dramas.

Every living entity belongs to Krsna, but by the influence of Yogamaya, He forgets His own divinity and thinks Himself a cowherd prince. Fervently in love with Radha, the wife of another man, Krsna can satisfy His yearning for Her only by breaking through the barrier of Vraja’s social customs and meeting Her in secret rendezvous.

The exciting nature of parakiya-rasa makes the love between the hero and the heroine so fresh, passionate, and exhilarating that svakiya-rasa seems dry and staid by comparison. It is said that in parakiya-rasa there are two kinds of heroines: the unmarried girl and the wife of another. Rati-manjari now reminds Radharani that She is the wife of another.

**Verse 26**

*hanta devi tilakasya samastad*  
*bindavo 'runa-su-gandhi-rasena*  
*krsna-madaka-mahausadhi-mukhya*  
*dhira-hascam iha kim para-kalpyah*

**“O Devi! With a steady hand, when will I paint fragrant red dots around Your tilaka and thus create the most powerful aphrodisiac to madden Krsna?”**

Commentary: An aphrodisiac is something that stimulates sexual desire, but this verse does not use the word in that sense. Krsna has no mundane sexual desires. In fact, as the source of everything, He is fully satisfied in and of Himself. Thus, He is stimulated by love and love alone. But when, out of love, devotees want to offer Him their bodies, He accepts the loving sentiments they selflessly offer in a mood of service by reciprocating with those devotees in a way that resembles the amorous dealings of conditioned souls. The resemblance is, however, entirely external.

Krsna is called Madana-mohana, “the enchanter of Cupid.” And Radharani is called Madana-mohana-mohini, “the enchanter of the enchanter of Cupid.” He who can make Cupid forget his wife, his kingdom of spring, and his work of arousing sexual desire in conditioned souls, must logically be beyond all those things. That is Krsna: the original, divine attractor, who by His love and qualities coaxes Cupid away from sexual dalliance. Krsna is therefore known as “the transcendental Cupid” (aprakrta navina madana). And the fullest feature of the attractive potency Krsna exerts on Cupid manifests itself in the form of Srimati Radharani, a potency so powerful that it attracts and bewilders even Krsna.

Srila Prabhupada nicely summarises this phenomenon:

**“It appears that Radharani is the queen of Vrndavana and that Krsna is simply Her decoration. Krsna is known as Madana-mohana, ‘the enchanter of Cupid,’ but Srimati Radharani is the enchanter of Krsna. Consequently Srimati Radharani is called Madana-mohana-mohini, ‘the enchanter of the enchanter of Cupid.’”**

The red dots Rati-manjari paints around Radharani’s tilaka are, like everything else about Sri Radha, features of the Lord’s pleasuregiving potency (hladini-sakti). In short, everything about Srimati Radharani increases Krsna’s pleasure. Moreover, when that pleasure reaches some inexplicable height, it is said to drive Him mad. The red dots are therefore referred to as a transcendental aphrodisiac.

**Verse 27**

*gosthendra-putra-mada-citta-karindra-raja-*  
*bandhaya puspa-dhanusah kila bandha-rajjoh*  
*kim karnayos tava varoru varavatamsa-*  
*yugmena bhusanam aham sukhita karisye*

**“O girl with enticing thighs! When will I happily decorate Your ears with arresting earrings, two ropes used by the god of love to bind that mad elephant, the heart of the son of Vraja’s king?”**

Commentary: Whether it is Radha’s tilaka, earrings, or Her other items of adornment, Rati-manjari applies them only to increase the pleasure of Sri Radha’s lover. She knows that Radha’s only purpose in life, the very substance of Her being, is to please Krsna. And as a maidservant, Rati’s only purpose is to serve the purpose of her mistress.

The movements of Srimati Radharani's thighs and earrings are synchronised during the rasa dance. When She moves Her thighs to the left, Her earrings swing to the right, and when She moves Her thighs to the right, Her earrings swing to the left. Meanwhile, Krsna watches in amazement and calls out, “Sadhu! Sadhu!” At these times, every part of Radha’s body is in motion, including Her eyes, hands, and feet. But for now, Krsna’s eyes and heart are apparently bound to Her thighs and earrings.

Rati refers to Krsna as the son of Vraja’s king (gosthendra-patra). Because His father manages the concerns of the kingdom, Krsna can afford to be a carefree prince who, although dutifully herding His father’s cows, can enjoy Himself at will. In Goloka Vrndavana, Krsna is eternally a youth just nearing sixteen years of age. He is too young to rule and too young to be married. Only in Dvaraka does He accept the burden of royalty and family life, while in Vraja He runs free like the maddened king of elephants (mada-karindra-raja). Unfettered by royal obligations, He can enjoy Himself in the company of the gopas and the gopis, free to fully realise His desires.

It is well known that Krsna walks with the peerless gait of an elephant, moving slowly, swaying from side to side, unmindful of anything in His path. And when He is intoxicated by amorous desire, He does not notice whether He walks on or off the path, over hills, across valleys, into rivers, or through forests. Indeed, He does not see who is ahead of Him or behind Him. In fact, He is even unaware of Himself. At times like these, goaded by His handler, Cupid, Krsna is a maddened king of elephants, whose haunts are the groves by the Yamuna and the caves of Govardhana Hill.

Who can control a runaway bull elephant? Only Srimati Radharani! But She need not tie Krsna to a stake in order to bring Him under Her control. She mesmerises Him with Her love and Her allure, controlling His heart and thereby rendering Him docile.

Even as a child barely able to walk, Krsna displayed His uncontrollable nature. When He broke pots of yogurt and ted their contents to the monkeys, Mother Yasoda’s only recourse was to tie her naughty son to a mortar. But still Krsna was able to drag the mortar and uproot two large arjuna trees. Therefore Krsna is called Yasoda-Damodara. And later, in His youth, when Krsna exhibited His wild side before Srimati Radharani, She would stop Him in His tracks with nothing but a glance, making Him immobile, as if tied around the waist with invisible ropes. In this case, Krsna is called Radha-Damodara. From this we can understand that even when Krsna’s mother cannot completely control Him, Radha can. Prabodhananda Sarasvati Thakura encourages us, for our own salvation, to come under Radha’s control in the same way:

*yayonmilat-keli-vilasita-kataksaika-kalaya*  
*krto bandi vrndavipina-kalabhendro mada-kalah*  
*jadi-bhutah krida-mrga iva yad-ajna-lava-krte*  
*krti nah sa radha sithilayatu sadharana-gatim*

**“May Sri Radha, who with a single glistening playful sidelong glance captures the wild elephant of the Vrndavana jungle, ties Him up, and makes Him Her helpless pet, slacken the bonds that tie us to this world of birth and death.”**

Just how complete is Radha’s control over Krsna? Govinda Dasa describes the extent of Her control: Once Radha became angry with Krsna for showing affection to another gopi. She decided She would never calk to or see Him ever again. Radha’s friends, however, were sad to see Her and Krsna suffering apart. Thus they selected one girl to pacify Radha’s anger.

The envoy sat before the tearful, stubborn Radha and said, “Manini! Do You know how Krsna burns in flames of love for You? Although He is like Kamadeva’s wild elephant, He now sits in theforest, thinks of You, and weeps. Unable to scale the high wall of Your proud and jealous anger, He stays awake both day and night.

“O angry gopi, what fruit will You taste from this conduct? You know Krsna very well. His body is glorious like a dark monsoon cloud, and You are like a glistening flash of lightning at His side. He wears bracelets of new flower buds. He is anointed with sandalwood paste. He is adorned with lotuses. But without You His body, burned by the flames of His misery, simply rolls about on the ground in agony.

“You have tested Him enough! Can’t You see how dearly He loves You? At this very moment, He is worshipping Kamadeva with offerings of campaka flowers. Listen to me! Release the ropes of anger that bind this young elephant king and give Him the shelter of Your lotus feet."

**Verse 28**

*ya te kanculir atra sundari maya vaksojayor arpita*  
*syamacchadana-kamyaya kila na sa tathyeti vijnayatam*  
*kintu svamini krsna eva sahasd tat tam avapya svayam*  
*pranebhyo ’py adhikara svakam nidhi-yugam sangopayaty eva hi*

**“O beautiful girl! When will I carefully place this garment over Your breasts to cover them from Krsna’s gaze, even though He has not understood my intention. Tightly embracing You, He Himself has become the garment covering those two treasures dearer to Him than His own life.”**

Commentary: Rati yearns to dress Sri Radha and while doing so remind her mistress of Krsna. That is an important aspect of her service. Otherwise, feelings of separation will bring Radha to despair and spoil a pleasant morning. Rati offers a blue choli to Radha, chatting all the while. She explains to Radha that because Krsna is in all things blue, He Himself is the garment. “I wanted to cover Your breasts with this choli, but Krsna has personally assumed its formand covered them by embracing You. What can I do? Better I offer You the next ornament.”

After bathing Radharani, Rati pats Radha’s hair dry with a towel and then dries it further with smoke from burning aguru wood. Then, with a soft delicate cloth, Rati pats Radhika’s face, dries Her lovely graceful limbs, and offers Her fresh new clothes that have been artistically sewn by a seamstress.

Both Sri Krsna and Srimati Radharani are born of royalty. Therefore They wear new clothes daily. Every morning at Their dressing time, Their servants receive newly sewn clothes made from the finest available silk. A Nandagrama tailor named Raucika is in charge of sewing new clothes for Krsna.

What happens to the clothes worn by the divine couple? They give them to Their associates as gifts, often in recognition for services especially well done. In this way, Radha’s maidservants often dress in clothes they have received from their mistress, as Krsna’s attendants sometimes dress in clothes received from Him. When Sri Radha gives a skirt to a manjari, that girl very proudly wears the gift before her friends, who immediately recognise her as the fortunate object of special mercy.

Uddhava arrived in Vrndavana wearing clothes given to him by Krsna, forcing the gopis to exclaim, “He’s wearing Krsna’s clothes and ornaments!” They eagerly crowded around Uddhava, knowing that he must have been very dear to their beloved.

In Dvaraka Uddhava explained to Krsna that accepting remnants from the Lord is a regulative principle, granting one the power to easily conquer maya. Thakura Bhaktivinoda adds that the practice of accepting the Lord’s remnants is also characteristic of those who have attained love (rati). Whatever Krsna leaves behind His servants accept as the Lord’s mercy. Uddhava says:

*tvayopabhukta-srag-gandha-vaso-’lankara-carcitah*  
*ucchista-bhojino dasas tava mayam jayema hi*

**“Simply by decorating ourselves with the garlands, fragrant oils, clothes, and ornaments that You have already enjoyed, and by eating the remnants of Your meals, we, Your servants, will indeed conquer Your illusory energy.”**

Anything Radha or Krsna accepts acquires Her or His transcendental qualities. Such items impart those same divine qualities to the fortunate souls who in turn accept them, in due proportion to the recipients’ devotional advancement. For example, devotees in the mode of goodness who receive Krsna’s prasada are freed from maya’s clutches, and for the Lord’s eternal companions, ecstatic love is stimulated.

After Krsna eats His evening meal in Nandagrama, Mother Yasoda gives some of His remnants to Rati-manjari, who carries those morsels back to Yavata and serves them to Radha along with Her supper. The quantity of remnants Rati brings from Nandagrama is very small, yet there seems to he no end to the rice and vegetables served to Radharani and Her girlfriends. Already glorious because they were left by Sri Hari after having been sweetened by His lips and touched by His hands, those remnants, coveted the world over, attain an even higher pinnacle of perfection simply being touched by Radha’s glance.

The tiniest spark of boundless bliss Sri Radha relishes while tasting Krsna’s remnants can be likened to the happiness of a swan tasting lotus stems left over by her husband, of a hungry doe tasting fresh sprouts, of intoxicated bees tasting honey, or of cakora birds tasting nectar from the moon.

After washing their mouths, Radha and Her girlfriends relish the remnants of Krsna’s betel leaves and lay down on their beds to rest while the manjaris offer them a variety of services. Rati-manjari and Rupa-manjari send a messenger to Vrnda with some of the remnants of Radha’s rice and vegetables, and then the other maidservants blissfully sit down to eat what’s left of Radha’s meal. In a jolly mood the girls sometimes serve their mistress’s prasada to one another and sometimes playfully quarrel over it. After eating, they wash their mouths and share Sri Radha’s half-chewed betel leaves. In this way their evening meal comes to a joyous end.

Early the next morning, as Radha and Krsna sadly leave Vrndavana forest to return home, some sakhis and manjaris stay behind to retrieve Radha’s and Krsna’s broken flower garlands, the nectarean remnants of Their food, and various leftover ornaments from the kunja. Then the gopis excitedly divide these items amongst themselves.

**Verse 29**

*nana-mani-prakara-gumphita-caru-pustya*  
*mukta-srajas tava su-vaksasi hema-gauri*  
*sranty-abhrtalasa-mukunda-su-tulikayam*  
*kim kalpayisyatitaram tava dasikeyam*

**“O golden girl! When will this maidservant place a necklace of pearls interlaced with gems upon Your chest, which will later serve as a soft pillow for Mukunda’s head when He is sleepy and fatigued?”**

Commentary: The sunlight coming through the window forms a golden rectangle on the marble floor and fills the room with sparkling rays. But the thought of being embraced by Krsna has awakened Radha’s prema, which now surges forth from Her every limb with a golden splendour of its own, making the sunshine appear like shadow. Therefore Rati calls out to Radha, “O golden girl!”

Rati-manjari has joined Radha in Her dressing room. No one else is present. Only the early morning noises of Yavata village outside the window, the distant intermittent ching-ching of jingling bangles, and a quiet rubbing sound punctuate the stillness. The rubbing comes from a room in the middle of King Vrsabhanu’s moon-tower, where maidservants are cleaning Radha’s furniture, grinding sandalwood, making garlands, and preparing pan. Srimati Radharani smiles gratefully at the thought of Her maidservants’ labours. She deeply appreciates even the most apparently insignificant service.

Radha’s pearl necklace is called Hari-mohana because it enchants Krsna. When She walks, dances, or swings from side to side the necklace follows, adding to the elegance of Her rhythmic movements.

Krsna is enchanted! In the presence of Her elders, even when Krsna is right before Her, Radha cannot look directly at Him, but must shyly hang Her head and peer at His reflection, captured in the large pearls on Her necklace. Radha is enchanted!

At Radha’s and Krsna’s meetings at Terh-kadamba or Surya-kunda, when it comes time for the two lovers to part, Hari-mohana renders an invaluable service to Sri Radha. As She turns to leave, Radha pulls on Her necklace and breaks it, spilling the pearls all over the ground. “Oh! My necklace!” She exclaims. At once Radha gets down on Her hands and knees and begins to collect the fallen pearls one by one, every so often glancing at Krsna, who is watching Her every move. With help from Hari-mohana, Radha is able to steal a few more life-infusing glimpses of Her beloved Krsna.

The manjaris restrung Hari-mohana. Rati now places it over Sri Radha’s head and sets it neatly upon Her chest, all the while chatting with her mistress: “Great saints call Krsna Mukunda because He gives (da) them liberation (mukti). But we gopis like to think of Him as Mukunda because He always frees You from the bonds of shyness and timidity.” Rati looks down at the pearl necklace, sees the reflection of Radharani’s soft smile, and concludes, “Of course He is also called Mukunda because whenever He sees You, His wide smile reveals His kunda-flower teeth.”

**Verse 30**

*mani-caya-khacitabhir nila-cudavalibhir*  
*hari-dayita-kalavid-dvandvam indivaniksi*  
*api bata tava divyair angulir anguliyaih*  
*kvacid api kila kale bhusayisyami kim nu*

**“O girl with eyes like a blue lotus! Will the time ever come when I adorn Your fingers with glittering rings and Your two graceful hands, which are so dear to Hari and so expert in all the arts, with blue bangles studded with jewels?”**

Commentary: In the previous verse, Rati-manjari called Krsna Mukunda because He liberates Radha’s limbs from the bonds of Her garments and loosens Her hair from its tightly braided state. Here Rati extends that theme by calling Krsna Hari as she pours nectar into Sri Radha’s thirsty ears.

Hari removes all obstacles to meeting Srimati Radharani, and once the two have met, He removes every remaining obstacle that prevents Him from relishing Her abundant sweetness. But sometimes, when She suspects that He has been unfaithful, Hari has His work cut out for Him.

Pained at heart in these times of apparent infidelity, Srimati Radharani vows to never set eyes upon Him again. But Krsna refuses to leave the grove. He stands nearby in His threefold-bending form until Radha can no longer resist stealing a furtive glance at Him from the corner of Her eye. And although She also tells Her friends that She will never speak to Him again, the sunlight of Krsna’s effulgent form quickly melts Her icy resolve and She angrily calls out to Him, “Why are You still standing there! Go to Your new love.” Finally, despite Her firm decision not to touch Krsna anymore, when He refuses to leave She takes Him by the hand and begins to lead Him away, at which point Her determination dissolves completely, like a carefully sculpted sandcastle washed away by high tide. This is the Hari who steals Radharani’s heart.

Radha’s blue bangles, like Her blue sari, remind Her of Krsna. So much so that they inspire in Her a state in which She sees Krsna whenever any dark-coloured item crosses Her line of sight. Radha therefore favours the black deer, the dark tamala tree, the blackish water of the Yamuna River, the dark monsoon cloud, the newly-blossomed blue lotus, and the darkening sky of the waning moon. And because Her eyes, which are always full of Krsna, have assumed Krsna’s bluish colour, Rati calls Radha Indivaraksi, “girl with eyes like the blue lotus.”

In the manner of Her other ornaments, the blue bangles play a part in bringing Krsna under Radha’s sway. When Radha enters Nandagrama at the place where Krsna sits by the main gate with

His friends, She covers Her face with Her veil and moves Her hands in such a way that Her bangles jingle insistently, a sound that is enchanting to Krsna’s mind.

Radha’s bangles play a particularly important role in games of dice with Krsna, helping Her to win hands down, so to speak. As She sits and plays dice with Krsna, Her bangles shake each time She rolls the dice. She notices that Krsna becomes distracted from the game by the mystical sound of Her bracelets, so She shakes the dice much longer than would otherwise be necessary. The result? Krsna loses — first His concentration, then the game.

On Radha’s left hand Rati places rings on every finger, but on Her right, only on the ring and little finger. Her signet ring is called Vipaksamardini, the destroyer of rivals. This ring also destroys the pride of rivals because it contains Sri Radha’s name, which boldly declares that She is the best worshipper of Krsna. The victory this ring signifies is only complete and absolute, however, when She exchanges it with Krsna’s signet ring. When competitors like Candravali see Vipaksamardini on Krsna’s little finger, they turn away in shame, and when they hear that His Ratnamukhi is on Her finger, their humiliation doubles.

**Verse 31**

*padambhoje manimaya-tula-koti-yugmena yatnad*  
*abhyarcyaitad-dala-kulam api prestha-padangutiyaih*  
*kanci-damna kati-tatam idam prema-pitham su-netre*  
*kamsaraier atulam acirad arcayisyami kim te*

**“O beautiful-eyed girl! Will I soon carefully worship Your two lotus feet with jewelled anklets, the petals of Your lotus feet with toe rings, and Your hips, the sacred pilgrimage place of Krsna, with a splendid sash fixed with tiny bells?”**

Commentary: Radha becomes lost in thoughts of Krsna by hearing Rati-manjari talk about Him, and as Rati continues, Radha starts to feel that Krsna is present in the dressing room. Startled, Srimati Radharani opens Her eyes as if to ask, “Is Krsna here?” Seeing Radha’s beautiful eyes so full of love and yearning, Rati calls out to Her, “O beautiful-eyed girl.”

Krsna is not physically present in the way Radha would like Him to he, but by Her intense desire He is present in the pastimes Rati narrates, in the blueness of Radha’s ornaments, by the repetition of His names, and in the picture on Her wall. Radha’s blue eyes travel to Visakha’s sketch of Krsna’s face hanging in the dressing room. Intoxicated by love Sri Radha thinks, “He’s watching Me!” She then lowers Her eyes in shame and pulls the upper portion of Her garment around Her shoulders.

Meanwhile Rati kneels before the seat and places Radha’s right foot in her lap. First she fastens a jewelled anklet in place and then slips rings on each of Radha’s toes, repeating the process with Her other foot. But as Rati holds onto Radha’s dainty lotus foot, reluctant to put it down, she says, “Your feet resemble pink lotuses, and Your toes, the petals of those flowers. But I have never seen lotuses with marks resembling a moon, elephant, or flag. Therefore I have put these ankle bells on Your feet so that everyone, Krsna included, can hear them coming and offer them due respect.”

Devotees, even Krsna, desire the unprecedented good fortune these ankle bells enjoy, for they live always upon Radha’s lotus feet and glorify Her with their sankirtana. Narottama Dasa Thakura sings, “Entering Vraja, I will become ankle bells on the feet of a gopi and cause a sweet tinkling sound.”

Amongst Srimati Radharani’s ornaments, Her ankle bells are most prominent. For any gopi, nose rings and ankle bells are indispensable. Where would they be without them? Only while Radha is leaving Her husband’s home at night does She silence Her anklets, tying a cloth over them tightly so that they will not expose Her as She tiptoes through the house, out the door, and into the darkness. But once She approaches the meeting place, Radharani frees Her ankle hells from bondage. After all, Krsna is nearby, waiting. And in the darkness, the first sign of Sri Radha’s approach will be the rana, rana of Her anklets. As He waits, Krsna paces back and forth before the kunja, His ears straining to hear the tinkling sound that will herald the beginning of a night of bliss.

Some of Radha’s toe rings also have hells on them, creating a jingling response to Her anklets. Radha’s toe rings, anklets, sash of bells, and bangles are the talented players in a quartet that provides accompaniment to a virtuosic concerto in which the soloist is Krsna’s flute. Srimati Radharani sees Krsna pleased at hearing these jingling sounds and Her eyes beam in happiness. This is another reason Rati calls Her Sunetra, “beautiful-eyed girl.”

**Verse 32**

*lalitatara-mrnali-kalpa-bahu-dvayam te*  
*mnrajayi-mati-hamsi-dhairya-vidhvamsa-daksam*  
*mani-kula-racitabhyam angadabhyam purastat*  
*pramada-bhara-vinamra kalpayisyami kim va*

**“Will I humbly and blissfully place jewel-studded armlets on Your two graceful lotus-stem arms, which are expert at destroying the patience of Murajayi’s swan-like intelligence.”**

Commentary: To praise the power of Srimati Radharani’s love, Rati calls Krsna Murajayi, “the killer of Mura.”

Once Krsna went to Pragyotisa-pura and killed the five-headed demon Mura, who was the embodiment of ugliness. One of Krsna’s names, therefore, is Murajayi (or Murari), in recognition of the great intelligence it took to overcome that formidable foe. Yet Krsna’s unfathomable intelligence, like the swan habituated to coiling its neck around lotus stems, is always absorbed in finding ways for Krsna to wrap Himself in Sri Radha’s beautiful arms. Indeed Krsna, whose intellect could not be foiled by clever Mura, loses all patience and self-control when He sees Radharani’s arms swaying in the rasa dance or playing with a ball in sport.

What is it about Sri Radha’s beauty that attracts Sri Krsna so? Didn’t Krsna Himself say that He is not enchanted by mere beauty?

The answer is that Radha’s beauty is not the result of good karma; in fact, it is in no way material. Her beauty, like the beauty of all gopis, is a spiritual transformation of Her love for Krsna. But because Radha’s love for Krsna is the greatest, Her beauty must be the greatest too; therefore, She is the most beautiful of all of Vraja’s milkmaids. It is love — manifest in the form of alluring beauty—that attracts and controls Krsna. He says, “The love of Radhika is My teacher, and I am Her dancing pupil. Her prema makes Me dance various novel dances.”

Radha’s armlets are also able to attract Krsna and keep Him under control (santaiasrava-kesava), having taken on this quality belonging to Sri Radha. Therefore, although Krsna is as indifferent to jewelled ornaments as He is to any worldly opulence, when Radha wears such ornaments, He is as drawn to them as He is to Her. The same may be said for all things belonging to or worn by Srimati Radharani.

This same principle is implied by the famous words spoken by Lord Siva to his wife, goddess Durga:

*aradhananam sarvesam visnor aradhanam param*  
*tasmad parataram devi tadiyanam samarcanam*

**“My dear devi, although the Vedas recommend worship of demigods, the worship of Lord Visnu is topmost. However, above the worship of Lord Visnu is the rendering of service to Vaisnavas, who are related to Lord Visnu.”**

**Verse 33**

*rasotsave ya iha gokulacandra-bahu-*  
*sparsena saubhaga-bharam nitaram avapa*  
*graiveyakena kim u tam tava kantha-desam*  
*sampujayisyati punah subhage jano ‘yam*

**“O fortunate girl! Will this person some day worship Your neck, which attained all good fortune when touched by the arm of the moon of Gokula during the rasa dance festival, with a graiveya necklace?”**

Commentary: In his recitation of Srimad-Bhagavatam, Sukadeva Gosvami withholds the names of the gopis involved in the rasa dance on the full moon night of Karttika. He merely hints at Radha’s name and refers to Her friends only as “one gopi” or “another gopi."In their commentaries, the acaryas reveal the identities of these other gopis, but they do not mention the manjaris present. In this verse, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami mentions the rasa dance, making it clear that Rati was there. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura elsewhere clearly describe the manjaris’ participation and services in the rasa dance, supporting the possibility that Rati was indeed there.

Rati calls Srimati Radharani “fortunate girl” (Saubhaga), because She, along with the other gopis, gained the fortune of being embraced by Krsna during the rasa dance, a favour neither the goddess of fortune nor Lord Visnu’s other consorts in the spiritual world enjoy. And if Laksmi never knows such a favour, then how can the beauties of heaven or earth even imagine such a thing happening tothem?

Amongst the gopis, who are all truly fortunate, Srimati Radharani is the most fortunate because She is the cynosure of the nisa dance, the centre of Krsna’s attentions. Krsna dances with the other gopis and shows them love, but that love pales in comparison to the love He shows Radha. In fact, the other gopis participate in the rasa dance simply to help increase the joy of Krsna’s pastimes with Radharani. They are instrumental in embellishing the divine couple’s mutual enjoyment, but without Srimati Radharani the gopis are incapable of giving Krsna pleasure on their own, no matter how hard they try. For this reason Sri Radha is called Rasesvari, “the queen of the rasa dance.” The proof of Radha’s pre-eminence is that Krsna left the other gopis during the rasa dance and went alone with Her into the heart of Vrndavana forest, where He was able to realise the essence of His desires.

Thinking of Radharani’s exceptional fortune, Rati says, “You danced alone with Krsna at the centre of the rasa dance, where He placed His arm upon Your shoulder and touched Your neck. Until Krsna again worships Your neck with His arm, I will worship it with this graiveya necklace. It is the best I have, so please accept it.”

During the rasa dance, the gopis sometimes place another special necklace on Sri Radha's neck — Krsna’s gunja berry necklace. And when Krsna is especially pleased with one of Radha’s extraordinary dance performances, He personally removes His treasured gunja-mala and places it on Radhika’s heaving chest.

**Verse 34**

*dattah pralamba-ripunodbhata-sankhacuda-*  
*nasat pratosi-hrdayam madhumangalasya*  
*hastena yah sumukhi kaustubha-mitram etam*  
*kim te syamantaka-manim taralam karisye*

**“O beautiful-faced one! After Krsna killed proud Sankhacuda, He took the Syamantaka jewel from the demon’s head and gave it to Balarama, the enemy of Pralambasura, who with a happy heart gave it to Madhumangala, who in turn with his own hand gave the jewel to You. When will I hang this Syamantaka jewel, which has become the friend of the Kaustubha jewel, in a locket around Your neck?”**

Commentary: By speaking this verse, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami indicates that the obstacles to serving Sri Radha — as represented by the two demons mentioned, Sankhacuda and Pralambasura — are cleared away by Krsna and Balarama.

In the guise of a cowherd boy, Pralambasura tried to carry Lord Balarama away, but Balarama killed him instead. Pralambasura represents the covered form of Buddhist philosophy — Mayavada— which has its source in Kamsa, who represents atheism, while Lord Balarama is the reservoir of all living entities. In other words, atheism disguises itself as Mayavada philosophy in order to carry the living entities away from God. But by Lord Baladeva's grace, this conspiracy to steal living entities away from a blissful life in Vraja and condemn them to an atheistic mentality and a life of sense gratification leading to spiritual suicide is thoroughly destroyed.

Sankhacuda, who was killed by Krsna, represents the desire for gaining fame and sense gratification through devotional service. This kind of motivated devotion is cleared away by Krsna’s grace. Thus freed from all bad qualities represented by the demons that entered Vraja, devotees are given the opportunity to cultivate the kind of devotion that further qualifies them to serve Srimati Radharani.

Once, in a forest of Govardhana Hill on the night of Holi, Krsna and Balarama were enjoying the beauty of the spring season together with their respective gopis by singing songs and wandering through the groves. At the height of their merriment, a demon friend of Kamsa named Sankhacuda kidnapped the gopis, but was quickly caught and killed by Krsna. The demon was wearing a very costly gem called the Syamantaka, which Krsna took from his turban, intending to give it to Radharani. Upon returning to the assembly of gopis, however, Krsna realised that if He were to give the jewel to Radha, the other gopis would become jealous and blame Him, starting a quarrel that would certainly bring their happy festival to an end.

“I will give the gem to My older brother,” thought Krsna. In front of the astonished gopis, Krsna placed the Syamantaka jewel in Balarama’s hand, confident that His brother would ascertain His unspoken desire. Krsna was also sure that, as the senior person present, the actions of His brother would be considered beyond reproach. Dauji graciously accepted the gift, but the next day He handed it to Madhumangala, explaining its origin and its intended destination. Cheerful, Madhu then presented the Syamantaka to Radharani, along with his demand: “You must give me its weight in laddus, daily.” In this way Krsna’s gift made its circuitous route into Radha’s treasury.

That same Syamantaka jewel now sits on a tray before Rati, who says to Radharani, “This Syamantaka gem came from the faraway kingdom of Kuvera, but it has quickly become the best friend of the Kaustubha jewel on Krsna’s chest. Isn’t that wonderful?”

As Rati speaks, she is standing behind Radha, looking at Her face in the mirror as she hangs the gem on Radha’s neck by tying the ends of the silken thread from which it hangs. When Rati sees Radha’s face light up at the mention of a friendship between the two jewels she again calls her mistress Sumukhi (“beautiful-faced one”).

Radha teases Her maidservant, “Rati! Why do you think My diamond has become friends with the Kaustubha gem?”

Rati comes around the chair to face Sri Radha and answers with a smile, “These two gems spend so much time together, embracing each other, they must be friends.” Obviously Rati is implying that when Radha and Krsna embrace, the two gems upon Their necks embrace as well, and therefore have become the best of friends. Radha’s face flushes slightly as She retorts, "O Rati. You are so naughty!”

**Verse 35**

*pranta-dvaye parivirajita-guccha-yugma-*  
*vibhrajitena nava-kancana-dorakena*  
*ksinam krudhaty atha krsodari ced itiva*  
*badhnami bhos tava kadabhibhayena madhyam*

**“O slender girl! Your waist is so thin! It looks as if it could break. When will I carefully bind it with a new golden cord splendid with flower-cluster tassels at each end?”**

Commentary: Of course, Radha’s waist will never break, but compared to Her full breasts and shapely hips it looks quite fragile. It is said that Radharani’s exquisitely beautiful waist is slender enough to be encircled by a single hand. Rati-manjari will therefore feel reassured by tying a golden silk rope around it.

The girls of Vraja arc all very slender and therefore, like Sri Radha, they are often referred to as Krsodari. The slenderest gopis, called su-krsodari, are the maidservants, because at twelve to thirteen years of age they are the youngest. Slightly older, Radha and Her sakhis are in their fourteenth year, so they are more physically developed but still quite slender. Candravali and her friends, however, are one year older still, and because their breasts, waists, and hips are fuller, their beauty, though dazzling, is rarely called slender.

Because the manjaris have dedicated their very selves to Radha, their features reflect the beauty of Her transcendental form. In fact, their perpetual love for Sri Radha acts upon their physical features in various ways: it radiates spiritual splendour through their charming, slender limbs; moulds their flower-bud breasts and youthful hips; and tightens their flat, narrow waists.

Covered in fresh silk cloth and an embroidered bodice, each man- jari fixes a pearl to her nose with a golden ring, decorates her chest with necklaces, and places glittering rings upon her fingers and toes. Her cheeks shine with light reflected off the jewels dangling from her earrings, her hips are tied with a sash affixed with bells, and the motion of her lovely feet causes her ankle bells to jingle. As these gopis go about their services, their thick black braids interlaced with flowers move along their backs like snakes, and the splendid lotuses at the ends of those braids make perpetual offerings to the divine footsteps of those girls.

By calling Radha “slender girl,” a term also used by other gopis, Rati-manjari invokes memories of Krsna, like the time the Vraja- vasis stood beneath Govardhana Hill as He held it above His head.

Some young gopis had begun to worry that Krsna’s unobstructed view of Radharani was distracting Him from the task at hand, and thus one excitable girl called out to Radha, “Please go far away from the path of Krsna’s eyes. O slender girl! Don’t let Govardhana Hill fall from Krsna’s hands as a result of His constantly gazing at You." When Krsna heard that slender Radha was advised to leave His field of vision, He sighed in disappointment, and for that reason Giriraja tottered on Hishand.

There is another meaning to Radha being called “slender girl,” a meaning not intended by Rati. Despondent at being separated from Krsna, Radha displays symptoms of ecstasy that are sometimes disturbing. For example, at times She loses weight so suddenly and drastically that Her bangles fall off Her arms. Caitanya Mahaprabhu would also display such symptoms, sometimes to the extent that His body would appear as though no more than skin and bones.

Once Subala spoke to Krsna about Srimati Radharani's extreme condition. Subala said, “As soon as Radhika saw You, She felt great pain at heart. Bereft of patience, She rolled on the ground in ecstasy, bathing Her body in Her tears while She wailed out loud. To ease Radha’s distress a girlfriend said, 'O girl who has become so slender. The darkness of night is approaching. Soon You will meet Mukunda, but should He see You in such an emaciated state?’ At this Radha took heart, composed Herself, and covered Her face with Her veil.”

**Verse 36**

*kanaka-gunitam uccair mauktikam mat-karat te*  
*tila-kusuma-vijetri nasika sa su-vrttam*  
*madhumathana-mahali-ksobhakam hema-gauri*  
*prakatatara-maranda-prayam adasyate kim*

**“O golden one! When will Your nose, which defeats the sesame flower, receive from my hand a beautiful golden pearl that agitates the great bumblebee of Sri Krsna with its nectar?”**

Commentary: As the morning wears on, every moment brings Radha closer to Her rendezvous with Krsna. The suspense increases Her ecstasy, which shows in Her golden complexion, now twice as brilliant as usual. Therefore, in this and other verses, Rati calls Her Hemagauri and Svarnagauri, both epithets for “golden girl."

Krsna is often referred to as a bumblebee because He is always seeking nectar. But the nectar He is after is neither that of flowers nor immortality. He is after the nectar of divine love, of which He is the fountainhead.

But in trying to taste that love, Krsna encounters an obstacle: love can only be relished when it is exchanged between two persons, a lover and a beloved. As long as Krsna’s love remains withinHimself, He is unable to enjoy it; therefore, He transforms His love into Srimati Radharani, the repository of all good qualities and the crest jewel amongst His innumerable consorts.

Love, with its ontological purpose to give pleasure to Sri Krsna, is invested in His internal energy (hladini-sakti), which is personified in Srimati Radharani, but it is the taste of loving exchange, known as ecstatic emotion (bhava), that makes love pleasurable. Therefore it is said that emotion is the essence of love. Moreover, the depth of love determines the intensity of its accompanying emotions, the most profound of which is called mahabhava. Because Sri Radha is said to be the embodiment of mahabhava, it is in Her, and in Her only, that Krsna’s full love and full emotion are invested.

Just as Krsna is the source of all incarnations, Radha is the source of all the consorts of Krsna’s incarnations. To assist in Krsna’s pastimes, She expands into the goddesses of fortune and the queens of Dvaraka, and in so doing makes Him taste the wide variety of emotions in ecstatic love, which is also Her purpose in expanding into the countless gopis of Vrndavana.

The Vraja gopis express an unlimited variety of loving sentiments towards Sri Krsna, all of which compose but a fraction of Radha’s full, complete, and total love for Nanda’s son. And although it sometimes appears from Krsna’s pastimes that these gopis are Radha’s competitors and that Krsna is attracted to them, the truth is that only Sri Radha can fully satisfy Krsna’s senses. The service of these gopis is therefore to help Krsna taste the nectar of the rasa dance and the other pastimes He enjoys in the company of Srimati Radharani. This conclusion is corroborated in scripture:

*devi krsna-mayi prokta radhika para-devata*  
*sarva-laksmi-mayi sarva-kantih sammohini para*

**“The transcendental goddess Srimati Radharani is the direct counterpart of Lord Sri Krsna. She is the central figure for all the goddesses of fortune. She possesses all the attractiveness to attract the all-attractive Personality of Godhead. She is the primeval internal potency of the Lord.”**

Rati-manjari is in full knowledge of all these truths regarding Radha’s identity and potencies. She knows that the princess of Varsana is like a golden lotus of loving flavours irresistible to the Krsna-bee. He may collect nectar from another gopi-flower, but the taste of that nectar can never compare to the sweetness of the Radha-lotus. Therefore He always comes flying back to Her.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami says that Krsna will be drawn to the pearl on Radha’s nose ring. Why? Because whatever touches Radha — the unlimited reservoir of mahabhava— takes on Her qualities; thus the pearl is transformed into the same spiritual substance She embodies. Krsna then sees the pearl as a drop of sweet nectar and cannot help but be attracted to it.

The quest for ultimate happiness, then, depends on contact with Srimati Radharani — She is indispensable not only to Krsna’s quest but also to the quest of every living entity. The Vedanta-sutra establishes at the outset that living entities are, by nature, pleasure-seeking (ananda-mayo ’bhydsat). Yet seekers of pleasure, even if they come to understand the divinity of Sri Krsna, will remain far distant from the ultimate pleasure for which they yearn as long as they isolate themselves from service to Sri Radha.

*radha-dasyam apasya yah prayatate govinda-sangasaya*  
*so ’yam purna-sudha-ruceh paricayam rakam vina kanksati*  
*kim ca syama-rati-pravaha-lahari-bljam na ye tam vidus*  
*te prapyapi mahamrtambudhim aho bindum param prapnuyuh*

**“Persons who yearn for Lord Krsna’s company without service to Radha are like persons seeking moonlight without the moon. They do not understand that Radha is the fountain from which the nectar waves of love for Krsna surge forth, and so they can attain no more than a single drop of that great ocean of nectar.”**

**Verse 37**

*angadena tava vama-doh-sthale*  
*svama-gauri nava-ratna-malikam*  
*patta-guccha-parisobhitam imam*  
*ajnaya parinayami te kada*

**“O golden beauty! When, by Your order, will I tie an amulet of nine gems strung upon a tasselled silk chord on Your left arm?”**

Commentary: It is said that when Radha’s bliss expands, Her bodily complexion can tinge the entire Vrndavana forest with a golden hue. Rati-manjari, noticing how Radha’s glow now colours Her dressing chamber, says, “Not only are You magnificent because of Your affection for Krsna, but Your love for Him is painting the world golden.”

Sri Radha asks, “Rati! What will You decorate Me with now?” And Her maidservant replies, “Whatever You request, I will do.” Radha looks through Her jewels and selects a talisman of nine gems (nava-ratna) strung on a silken chord. This talisman protects its wearer from the malefic affects of various planetary forces, and from such dangers as demons, snakes, and disease. But Radha does not wear it for Her own sake. She wears it for Krsna’s protection. She wears it to bring Him auspiciousness. She wears it for the fulfilment of His desires. In fact, all that Radha ever thinks is, “May Krsna be happy.”

Radharani extends Her left arm, and Rati-manjari ties on the talisman called Hari Rangada just as she has seen Visakha-devi do. Radha’s soft, supple arm enchants Rati with its elegance, and as she knots the black silk chord she tries to think of something comparable to such a thing of beauty.

Are Radha’s arms like lightning flashes? No, lightning is hard, whereas Radha’s arms are soft. Are they like Cupid’s staff? No, Cupid has only one staff, but Radha has two arms. Are they like graceful golden lotus stems? The gopis often make that comparison, but no, Radha’s right and left arms and their combined beauty more closely match the humour, love, and artfulness of Lalita and Visakha respectively. After all, those two chief gopis are Radha’s aides-de- camp in Her eternal mission to bring happiness to Sri Krsna.

Rati-manjari sits back and marvels at the amulet on Radha’s arm. She whispers, “Svarnagauri! Do You know what?”

Radha replies, “What?"

Rati continues, “From what little I know about telling the future,

I can see that today this amulet will bring You good fortune.”

Curious, Radha sits up and leans forward. “Tell Me what you see.” Rati carries on, “Today as You walk along a forest path, out of the darkness and without warning, dark-complexioned Krsna will step out from behind a tree, grab You by the blossoming vine of this very arm, and then tug on Your silk garments.”

A shiver of bliss runs through Sri Radha’s body as She listens to Rati, making the fine hairs on Her left arm stand up in ecstasy. “Wait!” Rati continues. “I can see even greater fortune for this arm later in the day, when, alongside Your smiling and laughing friends, You will wander through Vrndavana forest with Your left arm resting on Krsna’s shoulder.”

Srimati Radharani closes Her eyes to meditate on the scene, and in a slow and deliberate way says, “O Rati! You are an expert fortune-teller.”

**Verse 38**

*karnayor upari cakra-salake*  
*cancalaksi nihite mayaka te*  
*ksobhakam nikhila-gopa-vadhunam*  
*cakravad bhramayatam mura-satrum*

**“O girl with restless eyes! When will I place above Your ears hoop-shaped earrings that make Krsna, who agitates all the gopis, aimlessly wander in a circle?”**

Commentary: Radha sees Krsna wherever She looks, whether it be at His picture, Her dark sari, or the bluish clouds floating by outside. Her eyes therefore appear always restless, and for this She is called Cancalaksi. To have restless eyes is a symptom of ecstatic love. Wandering eyes, mild smiling, and enchanting singing are the three special features of adolescence found in Radha and Krsna. Rati thinks, "This girl’s exceptionally stunning bodily features have become the refuge of Cupid, and as their new proprietor he has made playthings of Her eyes; that is why they are so restless.”

Yet, despite Radha’s unparalleled ability to control Sri Krsna, profound humility makes Her anxious and uncertain. “Rati!” She exclaims. “Do you think He will call for Me today?”

Now the maidservant offers confidential service by giving encouragement to her mistress. “Will He call for You?” Rati asks with disbelief. “When Krsna sets eyes on You, He will beg to have Your audience. But don’t dare go to Him first! He will come to You. And when He does — ” Rati raises an earring in front of Radha’s face by way of demonstration, “ — Krsna will be mesmerised, like a snake charmer’s serpentine companion. Bewildered by Your beauty, He will walk around aimlessly in circles. In this helpless condition, just pierce Him with an arrow of a glance and He will be Your slave.”

By nature, Radharani wants to he submissive to Her beloved. However, the laws of Vraja dictate that playing hard-to-get is a superior strategy for cultivating divine love and extracting the greatest bliss from amorous exchanges. Rupa Gosvami likens these dealings to the movements of a snake, *aher iva gatih premnah svabhava-kutila bhavet*: “The progress of loving affairs between a young boy and a young girl is like the movement of a snake.”

Rati-manjari advises Radha along the same lines that Lalita-devi did when both Rupa-manjari and Rati were once present. Lalita’s words are sometimes harsh, but her only desire is to see the divine couple happily united. As Radha’s guru in the arts of love, Lalita often instructs her disciple in ways that initially appear painful, but ultimately elicit bliss. This principle is called sreyas: voluntarily accepting some present inconvenience for a greater future good. Rupa Gosvami records an edict of this type once spoken by Lalita to Srimati Radharani:

*dhurte vrajendra-tanaye tanu susthu vamyam*  
*ma daksina bhava kalankini laghavaya*  
*radhe giram srnu hitam iti siksayantim*  
*devim gunaih su-lalitam lalitam namami*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances to charming and virtuous Lalita-devi, who gives the following instruction. ‘Radha! Please hear these beneficial words: Be contrary with the rogue who is the prince of Vraja. O unchaste girl! For Your own good, do not become gentle and submissive.”’**

**Verse 39**

*kada te mrgasavaksi cibuke mrganabhina*  
*bindum ullasayisyami mukundamoda-mandire*

**“O fawn-eyed one! When will I place a dot of musk upon Your chin, the temple of Mukunda’s happiness?”**

Commentary: According to the science of physiognomy, Radha’s round, smooth, soft, symmetrical, and perfectly proportionate chin is a sign of good fortune. How could it be otherwise? After all, isn’t She the supreme goddess of fortune? Yet in Krsna’s human-like pastimes, considerations such as physiognomy are important because they give Radha confidence that She will indeed meet with Krsna.

Sri Radha’s chin is not a mere physical feature: it is the temple of Mukunda. Earlier, Rati-manjari told Radha that the Krsna-bumblebee would come to taste nectar from the pearl on Her nose. Indeed, to worship Her with its blackness, that bee will now appear in the form of a musk dot on Radha’s chin.

Rati sits before Radha on a stool. With the thumb and forefinger of her left hand she holds Radha’s chin steady, and with the other fingers she holds a gold container of musk, while in her right hand she takes up a delicate brush. Srimati Radharani at once smells the musk in the container and says excitedly, “I can smell Krsna’s fragrance. He must be nearby." Looking here and there for Krsna, Radha moves Her head about, thus making Rati’s service impossible.

“Krsna has not yet come,” Rati says to pacify her mistress. But the thought of Krsna’s absence makes Radha at once despondent like a captured doe. Her heart aches. Luckily Rati-manjari knows how to cheer Her up. “Fawn-eyed girl!” she says. “Be patient and Mukunda will soon fly to Your chin, His place of worship.”

Radha is finally still for a moment or two, allowing Rati to paint a drop of musk on Her chin. “There! The bumblebee has arrived.” Radha closes Her eyes and inhales deeply, again smelling the musk. It is like the fragrance of Krsna’s body — a blue lotus smeared with musk. It is a fragrance that pervades the universe and blinds young women with desire.

Rati chatters, “When you meet Krsna in person, He will become envious of this musk drop and will insist on tasting the nectar of Your chin by kissing it. That I can guarantee.”

As Rati-manjari is speaking, a memory appears in Radha’s mind.It is midday at Radha-kunda and Krsna has lost His flute. Regardless of where He may have actually mislaid it, the most exciting place to look for it is on the gopis’ persons. Krsna’s cousin Kundalata plays detective, looking for obscure clues to pass on to the owner of the flute. Convinced that she has solved the crime, Kundalata tells Krsna, “That black krsna-rasa with which You fill Your flute and colour the world blue can be seen on Radha’s chin. She must have stolen the flute. Obviously this dark blue drop stained Her face while She was playing it. Quickly, collect the evidence with Your lips and then retrieve Your flute! After punishing the thief, You may reward the detective!”

“It seems that in Vraja no one’s property is safe from these crafty gopis,” Krsna proclaims indignantly. “They are not satisfied to simply steal your heart, they pilfer your belongings too. First I will remove the mark My flute has left on Radha’s chin, and then I will take the flute back from Her, lock Her up in a forest prison, and give Her fitting punishment!”

Krsna then quickly kisses Radha's chin, but Lalita at once steps between the divine couple and pushes Him away, saying, “Have You no respect for the demigods or the principles of purity? Radha has not yet performed Her surya-puja, and You insist on contaminating Her with Your sordid touch! Go away!”

Krsna feigns innocence as He speaks over Lalita’s shoulder to Radha, “Dearest! There is no fault on My part. That black dot on Your chin originally came from Me. It was My friend, and it has now returned to take shelter behind the fortress of My teeth.”

**Verse 40**

*dasanams te kada rakta-rekhabhir bhusayamy aham*  
*devi mukta-phalaniha padmaraga-gunair iva*

**“O Goddess! When will I decorate Your teeth with red lines, making them look like pearls inset with lines of ruby?”**

Commentary: In this verse, and throughout Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami calls Srimati Radharani “Devi,” a name he uses to refer to Her more often than any other.

The direct meaning of “Devi" is “resplendent and most beautiful.” Rati-manjari uses the name to address Radha in order to glorify Her glowing golden complexion and Her ethereal loveliness. These two characteristics give Sri Radha such heavenly appeal that one is obliged to think, “She cannot be human. She must be a goddess.” As Srila Prabhupada said, “Devi means goddess.” That is another meaning of the word.

“Devi” has two additional, more exclusive meanings: “the lovely abode of Krsna’s worship" and “the lovely abode of Krsna’s love sports." The two are related as cause and effect respectively.

The cause is Radha’s and Krsna’s worship of the mutual love that unites Them — the supreme power and the supreme powerful. The effect is the love sports of an adolescent couple, in which Radha fulfils the amorous desires of Krsna, thus giving Him unlimited pleasure. In other words, Krsna’s worship of divine love upon the altar of love, Radha, is disguised as love-sports by which He fulfils all His desires through Radha.

Thus, just as the name “Radhika” means that Her worship \[aradhana\] consists of fulfilling Krsna’s desires, the name “Devi” means that His worship is to submit to Sri Radha’s will.

Since no one is as qualified as Radha to give pleasure to Krsna, these two meanings of “Devi" exclude others from using that name. When any other damsel is called by this name, it should be understood to actually mean devi-dasi— all other damsels are but servants of Radha.

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami defines Devi as an appellation of Sri Radha in this way: “‘Devi’ means 'resplendent and most beautiful.’ Or else it means ‘the lovely abode of the worship and love-sports of Lord Krsna.’” Thus, strictly speaking, the title or name Devi applies to Srimati Radharani. However, because other gopis are resplendent, beautiful, and the abode of Krsna’s sports, they are also addressed as devi, like Lalita-devi and Visakha-devi. But because every gopi serves Radha in Her service to Krsna, and is thus Radha’s servant, or dasi, when they are called devi the implicit meaning is that they are devi-dasi, or the servant of the original Devi, Radha.

Even today, in some parts of India women maintain the tradition of painting vertical red lines on their teeth. Rati-manjari now paints these red lines on Radha’s front teeth. It is yet another adornment that will give pleasure to Krsna, and thus Radha patiently clenches Her teeth and parts Her lips so that Rati can perform her service. Every ornament and adornment acts to stimulate both Krsna’s and Radha’s pleasure equally. How do these ruby-red lines give pleasure to Radha? Because Krsna says, “Amongst jewels I am the ruby.” Remembering this, Radha thinks, “Krsna resides on My teeth."

**Verse 41**

*utkhadirena nava-candra-virajitena*  
*ragena te vara-sudhadhara-bmiba-yugme*  
*gangeya-gatri mayaka pariranjite ‘smin*  
*damsam vidhasyati hathat kim u krsna-kirah*

**“O golden girl! May I colour Your wonderful, nectarean lips that are red like bimba fruit with lipstick of red khadira mixed with camphor, even though the Krsna parrot may appear at any moment and forcibly bite them?”**

Commentary: Just after replacing the ruby-red paint she used on Radha’s teeth, Rati picks up lipstick made by mixing khadira with camphor from where it waits on a gold tray. The tray is full of sparkling containers, each one filled with some special item for adorning Sri Radha. But these items do not really beautify Radharani. Actually, it is the other way around. By accepting the service of these items Radha lends Her beauty to them and thereby validates the skills of their makers.

As Rati smears her middle finger with lipstick, preparing to apply it to her mistress, Radha teases, “You said My lips are naturally red like bimba fruit. Why bother applying lipstick?”

Rati leans back to look Radha in the eyes and answers, “A certain black parrot is very fond of bimba fruit. By applying this lipstick, You are making that fruit more inviting.”

After a moment’s pause Rati lowers Her voice and continues, “When Krsna sees this lipstick, He will take the hint and come to kiss You. Listen, beautiful one! You may push Him away and say, ‘No! No!’ I have seen You do so many times before. But this lipstick will proclaim the desire hidden in Your heart, ‘Yes! Yes!’ Then Your true purpose will be fulfilled.”

Rati-manjari smears the lipstick on Radha’s lips, removing the excess with a soft cotton cloth. Now that she has put Radha’s mind on the path to another Krsna-inspired reverie, Rati continues, “The medicinal properties of bimba are well known. But Your bimba-lips have a side effect that entices this black parrot to bite them over and over again.”

Her fine bodily hairs bristling with excitement, Her limbs radiating golden effulgence, Radha asks, “What is that effect?”

Rati-manjari replies, “O girl with golden limbs! Don’t try to trick me. You know very well that Your lips are imbued with a special kind of addictive honey called syama-rasa. After just one taste of this honey Krsna begs for You to fulfil His lusty desires with more of the same, thus bringing Him completely under Your control. Can it be at all surprising that He is so adamant about His demands that He often leaves evidence of His eagerness upon Your lips?”

There is so much more Rati could say about Sri Radha’s lips: how they are bandhuka flowers whose honey the Krsna-bee constantly drinks; how Krsna forcefully extracts from them the betel nuts Radha has chewed; and how Radha bites them in anger when Krsna brags to Her friends about His romantic adventures with Her. But Rati has a few things left to do to prepare Radharani, and Rati’s main absorption is her service.

**Verse 42**

*yat-pranta-desa-lava-lesa-vighurnitena*  
*baddhah ksanad bhavati krsna-karindra uccaih*  
*tat-khanjarita-jayi-netra-yugam kadayam*  
*sampujayisyati janas tava kajjalena*

**“When, with black eyeliner, will this person worship Your eyes, which defeat the capricious wagtail birds, and which, with the slightest movement at their corners, can in an instant tightly bind the regal elephant known as Krsna?”**

Commentary: The time has come to serve the most prominent feature of Sri Radha’s face: Her beguiling eyes. “Perhaps they are the most prominent feature of Her entire body,” thinks Rati-marijari. “Only by the mercy of Vraja and my gopi friends like Rupa have I approached this pinnacle of personal service to Radharani.”

With a bashful glance Rati requests Radha’s consent to go on with her service, which Radha grants with Her own silent look. But Rati cannot keep quiet, bubbling over as she is with exuberance for her beloved Radha. “I wonder whether Your eyes have become blue-grey by always looking at Krsna. Or perhaps He has become that colour by being always gazed upon by You. All the gopis know that when Krsna leaves for the forest in the morning, Your sidelong glance competes with His garments for the right to clothe Him.”

With a slight toss of Her head and a smile Radha asks, “How do you know all these things, Rati?”

Without a second’s hesitation, Rati replies, “Devi! Your grace makes all things possible. Now Your eyes are moving like a blue lotus in a gentle breeze, hut when another breeze blows by a certain kadamba tree, carrying the sound of flute-song, then Your eyes dart wildly about as if to invade the territory of Your ears and somehow hear that sublime musical vibration.”

As Radha listens to Rati talk about Krsna, Her eyelids close in reverie, but that cannot stop Rati from delievering her ecstatic monologue. “These eyes of Yours are very tricky. Sometimes they behave like cakoras, sometimes like does’ eyes, sometimes like saphari fish, and sometimes like wagtail birds."

Her eyes still closed, Radha asks, “What do you think causes My eyes to behave in these various ways?”

Rati answers, “Your eyes are never influenced by anything but love for Syama. But many different features of that love are reflected in the various actions of Your eyes.

“When You use them as vessels through which to nourish the desire creeper of Your love, Your eyes act like cakora birds that subsist upon the moonbeams of Krsna’s smile and nothing else. Your eyes act like the innocent, bashful eyes of a doe when You shy away from Krsna’s bold advances, thereby denying His adamant requests for a festival of embraces. Thus unrequited, His desire increases a hundredfold. And Your eyes become restless saphari fish during those rare times You are able to gaze upon Krsna without impediment. Then Your eyes dart here and there in the lake of Your lover’s beauty without becoming tired, always greedy to explore another limb.” Srimati Radharani slowly opens Her eyes quite wide and softly asks, “And when are My eyes like wagtail birds?"

“It is my opinion,” Rati replies, “that Your eyes generally express themselves through the movements common to grey or blue wagtails. Listen as I explain the mannerisms of these birds and You will know why Your eyes are often compared to them.

“Wagtails get their name from their habit of almost constantly wagging their long, graceful tails. Certainly, the constant movement of Your eyes, accentuated as it is by their large size, resembles the wagtail bird. It is said that wagtails move their tails to flush out prey, to signal submissiveness to their mate, and to ward off other birds. Aren't the movements of Your eyes meant to attract Krsna, indicate Your submission to Him, and to ward off Your competitors? When Krsna cannot be found in the path of Your vision, Your eyes move like wagtails in search of Him. And when He stands before You, bashfulness and contrariness force You to look away. But when Krsna leaves for the forest, the birds of Your eyes, transfixed by His movements, yearn to leave Your body and fly after Him.”

Rati stands, raises Radha’s face and requests Her to close Her eyes so that she may paint them with kajjala. As Rati-manjari performs this service, she continues to speak, “This kajjala has the same dark hue as the splendour of Syama’s body. It will also serve as a garment to cover Your eyes. And what’s more, the soothing sheen of this ointment will immunise You against feelings of separation from Krsna. In fact, based on the law ‘like attracts like,’ the kajjala will quickly attract that dark person to Your eyes.”

Rati turns Sri Radha’s face to one side and then the other in order to inspect her handiwork. “There, it’s done," she says, and Radha opens Her eyes, blinking to adjust them to the light. Looking directly into Radha’s lotus-blue gaze, Rati has to steady herself to keep from fainting. She thinks, “What are these beautiful, hypnotic things I call Her eyes?”

For a moment Radha gazes silently at Her maidservant, and as She does so Rati understands the power of Srimati Radharani’s glance. Simply being blessed by the touch of Radha’s vision one may attain the opulences of demigods or the perfect knowledge of mystics. That glance grants detachment from the desire for liberation and bestows pure devotional service unto Krsna; in fact, it bestows devotional service unto even Radha Herself.

Within her mind, Rati bows before Radha’s feet, and then she says out loud, “When Maha-visnu glances over Rama-devi, the conditioning by which jivas become attached to this creation is aroused. But when You glance at someone, You dissolve their attachment to possessions, home, and family and make them attached to You.” Radha raises Her eyebrows, “O Rati!” She exclaims. “You have become so philosophical.”

“How can I avoid these truths?” Rati replies. “Every kind of transcendental glory and opulence is manifested from Your sidelong glance. Even the creator could not describe them all.”

Acutely aware that her primary duty is to remind Radha of Krsna, Rati continues, “When Your transcendental glance is enhanced with cunning and good fortune in the form of this mascara, You can rest assured that Your purposes with Krsna will be well served. When

Krsna just remembers — not to mention sees — Your glance, His heart will skip a beat.

“Once, when You aimed the enchanting arrow of a sidelong glance at Krsna, He was so bewildered that He placed His flute alongside a bouquet of flowers at Your lotus feet. Although the cowherd boys had been unable to pilfer Krsna’s flute, even while He slept, by no more than a careless glance, You made off with it before His very eyes.”

“Tell me more," sighs Radha happily, as She floats away upon the currents of Her amorous pastimes with Krsna.

“This mascara will declare Your glories to the other girls of Vraja like a great fanfare,” Rati continues. “Tonight You will meet with the master of Vraja’s groves, and after assorted pastimes in which He will no doubt kiss Your eyes, tomorrow morning He will return to Nandagrama with spots of kajjala on His lips." Rati holds Radha’s hands and exclaims, “O gorgeous one! Imagine Krsna’s lips when they have thus eclipsed a bandhuka flower covered by black bees. Imagine the expression on Candravali’s face!” But Radha does not require any prompting from Rati-manjari. Within Her mind’s eye, Radha was already busy picturing Krsna’s lips beautified by the kajjala from Her eyes.

It is now time for another important adornment: the lacquering of Radha’s soles. As Rati busies herself with mixing the lacquer, she stops and says to Sri Radha, “If You want to see kajjala upon Krsna’s lips, be sure that before You leave this house tonight it is re-applied to both Your eyes, not just one. Last time, You were in such a hurry to meet Him that I could only put kajjala on one eye. And when Krsna saw the sweetness of Your face, He kissed the eye without the ointment. If that becomes His habit, I may be bereft of service!"

**Verse 43**

*yasyanka-ranjita-siras tava-mana-bhange*  
*gosthendra-sunur adhikam susamam upaiti*  
*laksa-rasah sa ca kada padayor adhas te*  
*nyasto mayapy atitaram chavim apsyatiha*

**“When will I decorate Your feet with the nectarean lac that once made Krsna’s head very handsome with its red marks as He tried to soothe Your jealous anger by placing Your lotus feet upon His head?”**

Commentary: As if to answer Rati-manjari’s last statement (“I may be bereft of service!”), Radha sticks Her feet out and places them in Her maidservant’s lap. Rati sits on a low stool before Radha, her gaze transfixed on the priceless treasures in her hands. With her palms, Rati dusts Radha’s soles and begins to apply the red laksa with a brush. Radha would never be so forward in requesting such a service from Lalita or the other sakhis, whom She regards as equals. Such intimacy is the singular privilege of the manjaris.

As Rati expertly applies the lacquer, she marvels at the limitless splendour, delicate softness, and sweet fragrance of Sri Radha’s lotus feet. Radha’s feet are radiant from a combination of their golden effulgence, the moonlight emanating from their toenails, and the sparkling of their ornaments. “These are not ordinary feet," Rati, thinks. “Laksmi and the other demigoddesses cannot even hope to worship Sri Radha’s lotus feet.”
