Aware that tears are blurring Radha’s vision, Rupa-manjari will walk in front of Her, making sure Radha doesn’t walk off the path or into a bush by the roadside. Lalita and Visakha, noting the manjaris’ concern, will take up posts on either side of Radha to complete Her security detail.

One may ask why a princess would go to so much trouble to cook for Krsna when there are hundreds of others who can take up the task. In Krsna’s pastimes, whether the Vraja-vasis play the roles of parents, superiors, or even of royalty, they all have one thing in common — they are His servants.

Nanda Maharaja shared with Uddhava the Vraja-vasis’ eternal feelings of servitude:

*manaso vrttayo nah syuh krsna padambujasrayah*  
*vaco ’bhidhayinir namnam kayas tat-prahvanadisu*

**“May our mental functions always take shelter of Krsna’s lotus feet, may our words always chant His names, and may our bodies always bow down to Him and serve Him.”**

There may be so many cooks who can prepare Krsna’s breakfast, hut serving Him is so blissful that princess Radha happily walks barefoot over any distance just for the privilege to serve. Rendered in any of the various stages of practice or perfection, this is the secret of devotional service: devotees never feel they have enough of it, just as they never feel they have enough of Krsna’s mercy or love.

Once Krsna invited Narada to select whatever benediction he desired. Narada replied, “Sri Krsnacandra, please grant that no one will ever feel he has enough of Your mercy, Your devotional service, or pure love for You, the reservoir of ecstasy.”

Krsna looked perplexed by Narada’s request and answered, ko namayam varo matah: “What kind of benediction is this?” To Krsna, it seemed paradoxical that Narada would ask for something that was already an established fact. Although pure devotees are of different grades of excellence—with Srimati Radharani and the gopis standing supreme — none of them ever think that they have had “enough” of serving Krsna. To the contrary, the more they serve Krsna, the more they want to serve Him; the more they love Him, the more they want to show their love for Him. Therefore, Krsna replied to Narada:

*svabhavo mat-krpa-bhakti-premnam vyakto ‘yam eva yat*

**“My mercy, My devotional service, and ecstatic love for Me all have this nature \[that no one ever feels he has had enough\]. That should be simply obvious.”**

Indeed, the pleasure one feels from serving Krsna is greater than the pleasure Krsna feels from being served. For this reason Krsna is sometimes found serving His servant, like when He becomes Arjuna’s chariot driver. This is also one of the reasons Krsna appears as His own devotee in the form of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

The same can be said of loving Krsna: A devotee tastes greater bliss from loving Krsna than he tastes from being loved by Krsna. This phenomenon is most notable in the exchanges of love between Radha and Krsna.

*nija-premasvade mora haya ye ahlada*  
*taha ha'te kati-guna radha-premasvada*

**“Whatever pleasure I get from tasting My love for Srimati Radharani, She tastes ten million times more than Me by Her love.”**

Rati-manjari is fully absorbed in seeing to Radha’s welfare and in fulfilling Her needs. Practising devotees who share that mood, who absorb themselves in serving Sri Radha’s or Lord Caitanya’s mission to make the world conscious of Krsna, are freed from material suffering. The insatiable nature of pure devotional service and the pleasure it brings ensure that such preachers and servants of the sankirtana movement become oblivious to the trivial problems so common to the material world. In Srila Prabhupada’s own words, “What is the difficulty?”

**Verses 60-61**

*hamvarair iha gavam api ballavanam*  
*kolahalair vividha-vandi-kalavatam taih*  
*samrajate priyataya vraja-raja-sunor*  
*govardhanad api gurur vraja-vanditad yah*

*praptam nija-pranayini-prakaraih paritam*  
*nandisvaram vraja-mahendra-mahalayam tam*  
*dure niriksya mudita tvaritam dhanistha*  
*tvam anayisyati kada pranayair mamagre*

**“When You arrive at Nandisvara, the king of Vraja’s great abode, which is filled with the lowing of cows, the shouts of cowherds, and the songs of bards, which is dearer to Krsna than even Govardhana Hill, and which shines with love, will I see Dhanistha — after watching You coming from afar — affectionately guide You in front of me into the great palace?”**

Commentary: Why would Nandisvara Hill be dearer to Krsna than Govardhana? From one point of view, that of philosophical truth, it is common knowledge that Nandisvara Hill is Lord Siva and that Govardhana Hill is Krsna Himself. Since Krsna loves devotees, such as Lord Siva, more than He loves Himself, it can be said that Nanda Maharaja’s capital is dearer to the Lord than even His favourite playground. But from the point of view of service rendered in Krsna’s pastimes, the verdict of Srimati Radharani offers a different conclusion: Govardhana is Krsna’s best servant (hari-dasa-varyo).

As the gopis approach Nandagrama, Kundalata tells Sri Radha, “The thirst of Your cataka eyes will soon be quenched.” At this, Radha trembles, stops dead in Her tracks, and then momentarily loses control of Herself But Kundalata revives her ecstatic mistress with these words: “Now I can see Your unmatched chastity. Without even seeing Krsna — indeed, simply by thinking of Him — You are overcome by transcendental emotion.”

As they arrive at Nandagrama, Radharani catches a glimpse of Krsna sitting on a crystal dais in the courtyard just inside the main gate. He has finished milking the cows and playing with His friends and has now strategically positioned Himself to catch sight of Radha and Her entourage. The lustre of Krsna’s cloth and the hue of His body spread waves of rapture in all directions, and His restless eyes beam rays of splendour wherever He looks. He rests His left arm on Subala’s shoulder, while with His right hand He twirls a blue lotus — and with it, Sri Radha’s mind.

Radha asks Lalita, “Is there no other way to enter the palace?” Lalita nudges Radha forward and replies, “Krsna will be waiting for You at every entrance, won’t He? Go ahead. Don’t be afraid.” Bolstered by the support of Her friends behind Her, Radha proceeds through the gate and exchanges glances with Krsna. That one glance from Krsna completely bewilders the gopis, and in their bewildered state the entire retinue stands motionless until Kundalata quite literally pushes them forward in the direction of the palace. As the gopis pass Krsna, they swiftly cover their heads and faces with their veils. But, secretly, they each take one last greedy look at Him through their thin veils.

Under the watch of Krsna’s yearning eyes, the gopis move gracefully— like a flock of swans plying on peaceful waters — as they climb the stairs leading to the mountain-top palace. Meanwhile, Dhanistha, Mother Yasoda’s maidservant, is standing on the parapet above the palace entrance eagerly waiting for Srimati Radharani.

On this particular morning Radha is late. Anxious, Yasoda occasionally comes out of the kitchen to scan the horizon, hoping to see Kirtida’s daughter and Her friends, and then again goes back to supervise the preparations for breakfast. Finally Radha and Her friends come into view. While waving to the girls below, Dhanistha excitedly calls to Yasoda through the doorway behind her, “She’s coming. Radha is here!” Dhanistha is there to greet Radha as She reaches the palace door, and as they embrace, Dhanistha says, “Devi! I was in such distress, what with You nowhere to be seen. Quickly, come inside! The queen of Vraja has been asking for You.”

As Dhanistha leads Her by the hand, Sri Radha turns to look for Rati, who is just behind Her, and says softly, “Stay nearby.” Rati smiles as if to respond, “Don't worry. Where else would I be?”

The capital of Nanda Maharaja is a bustling market-place, trading briskly in the commodity love. The lowing cows, gossiping ladies, bartering merchants, shouting cowherds, and singing minstrels all have one thing in common: each of them, in his or her own way, is constantly glorifying Krsna in love.

Even though their only means of livelihood is the protection of cows, the residents of Nandagrama are more opulent than the demigods in heaven. The luxury and comfort of their homes puts Indra’s court to shame; in fact, even the cow barns are more impressive than Brahma’s own residence. The walls of the city, the homes of the cowherds, and the palace of their king are all constructed solely from priceless gems and metals: diamond, ruby, sapphire, gold, emerald, silver, pearls, and many others.

Because of the Vraja-vasis’ unconditional loving surrender to Krsna, the goddess of fortune has blessed them with unlimited wealth. But despite the fact that Nandagrama is the envy of the universe, the Vraja-vasis are not even aware of their own opulence, for they are always distracted by the priceless treasure of seeing Krsna and chanting His names and pastimes.

**Verse 62**

*praksalya pada-kamale kusale pravista*  
*naiva vrajesa-mahisi-prabhrtir gurus taih*  
*ha kurvati rasavatim rasa-bhak kada tvam*  
*sammajayisyatitaram sukha-sagare mam*

**“Auspicious girl! O talented cook! When, after I wash Your lotus feet, will You plunge me into an ocean of bliss as You enter the main kitchen, bow before the queen of Vraja and Her associates, and prepare an ambrosial feast for Krsna?”**

Commentary: Radharani looks to see if Rati-manjari is nearby. She is, of course. Just before entering the kitchen, Radha sits as Rati quickly washes Vraja’s camphor-cool dust from Her lotus feet. Because Radha may be feeling unqualified to serve Krsna, as she dries Radha’s feet with a soft towel, Rati speaks words of encouragement to her mistress. “O Kusala! By Your auspicious presence Mother Yasoda will gain hope that her Krsna, who is a poor eater, will get His appetite back.”

Radha says softly, “Do you think Krsna will like My cooking?” Rati replies, “How will He be able to resist Your cooking? Especially because the taste will be mixed with Your devotion! Don’t worry.” Why would Srimati Radharani, Krsna’s most exalted and intimate devotee, feel unqualified? She naturally feels that way because love and humility are intimately and inseparably linked — the greater the love, the greater the humility. Narada Muni tells Gopa-kumara:

*paripakena dainyasya premajasram vitanyate*  
*parasparam tayor ittham karya-karanateksyate*

**“When humility (dainya) fully matures, love unfolds without limit. And so we see humility and love acting in a relationship in which each is both cause and effect."**

Moreover, the wise have defined humility as the state in which one thinks oneself exceptionally inadequate and fallen, even when endowed with all excellences.  Therefore, Radha’s supreme, unrivalled love demands that She feel the greatest inadequacy. For example, She once said to Visakha: “My friend! Unlike I — who am totally unqualified—you are expert and eloquent. For this reason I request You to speak with Krsna and make Him pleased withMe.”

As Radharani enters the kitchen it lights up with Her golden splendour. Thus Yasoda can’t help but notice Radha the moment She arrives. Mother Yasoda joyfully calls out Radha’s name while the young gopis offer their respects to each of the elder ladies. Yasoda-devi pulls Radharani to her bosom, embraces Her, smells Her head, and kisses Her closed eyes while simultaneously laughing and crying out loud, “O my dear! O Goddess of beauty and sweetness! Once again You are sanctifying my house with Your presence.” After asking about Radha’s welfare, Mother Yasoda greets every other gopi and then takes them all into a small room to fuss over them and feed them sweets.

The drawing room in which the young gopis sit has been set aside especially for them. It adjoins the kitchen on one side, Krsna's apartments on another, the storeroom on a third, and on the fourth it leads to a forest garden where the divine couple sometimes meet. As the girls nibble on sweets, Yasoda instructs them: “Children! It is well known throughout Vraja that you are all expert cooks. Despite my son’s weak appetite, your excellent dishes will induce Him to eat heartily. As your hearts command, please make sweets, yogurt dishes, salty preparations, and items fried in ghee.”

The cooking soon begins. Dressed in a blue sari, Rohini directs every girl to her own fireplace and provides her with the ingredients she will need to cook her specialty: Lalita, a sweet yogurt drink; Visakha, sherbet; Tungavidya, cheeses; and Rangadevi, cakes. Rati assists Radha, who along with Rohini will cook the main dishes: vegetables, pastries, rice, and Krsna’s favourite drink, called granthi-puli. Tending to fires, lifting pots, pouring ingredients, and preparing chaunces, Radha moves around the kitchen like a field marshal inbattle. And like the field marshal’s assistant, Rati-manjari is always right beside Her.

As She stirs the preparations, Radha’s hair scatters, Her breasts shake, and Her garments loosen. Such a sight cannot go unnoticed. From Krsna’s quarters, through a small lattice window, Hari and Madhu watch.

For quite some time Krsna gazes through the latticework, His bumblebee eyes following Radha’s every move. He is mesmerised! Aside from Radha’s charming elegance, Krsna is drawn to the intense devotion that absorbs Her consciousness and with which She perfects each and every dish. Radha cooks with the same full-hearted enthusiasm and dedication with which She dances or sings.

Because it’s time for Krsna’s worship of the family Deity, Madhu-mangala clears His throat, which attracts not only Krsna’s attention but Radha’s as well. The divine couple’s eyes meet for a moment, but then Rohini says something and Radha is forced to resume Her service.

While moving amongst two dozen preparations — stirring, spicing, and so on — Radha and Rati engage in conversation.

Rati talks softly as she helps Radha, “Rasavati! I know the secret of Your cooking.”

While stirring two pots, Radha casually says, “Then you are a clever girl.”

Rati continues, “Whatever I know is only by Your grace.”

Radha asks, “And what do you know?”

Again Rati replies, “I know that it is not by Durvasa’s blessings that You are so empowered. You are self-sufficient. You hardly require a yogi’s blessings.”

Radha raises Her eyebrows, “And?”

Rati continues, “Your expertise is not in mixing ingredients together over a fire, but in seasoning these dishes with the different tastes of paramour love.”

Radha stops moving about and slowly stirs a soup as She looks deeply into Rati’s eyes, “Who has told you all of this?”

With a graceful shrug of her shoulder, Rati says, “The same person who is in Your heart and mine.”

Nodding Her head, Radha again busies Herself, “What else did that person say?”

Rati quips, “That person told me that You are Rasavati because You combine the original rasa into the foods You cook. Krsna mainly tastes that rasa and not the ingredients from which the dishes are made. It is that rasa which nourishes and sustains Him. In a different way, You serve Krsna the same tastes in the kitchen of Nandagrama as You do in the groves of Vraja. In short, the special feature of Your cooking is the love You mix into every dish."

Radha comments, “Yasoda and Rohini also cook with love.” Shaking her head slightly, Rati replies, “Of course they do. But the taste of Your love includes the taste of theirs, and more — ” Radha cuts her off, “Shh! Don’t say such things here. Concentrate on your service!”

Although Radharani does not want Mother Yasoda to hear that her cooking and love are inferior to Radha’s, Rati’s statement is not untrue. According to the spiritual science of mellows, the ingredients of parental love are included in amorous love but surpassed by the additional feature of intimacy. The taste of amorous love is therefore Krsna’s favourite; it is the only taste that completely nourishes His divine existential yearnings. The opinion of Vaisnava acaryas is that this truth is the last word of all scriptures and is contained in the aphorism, raso vai sah rasam hy evayam labdhvanandi bhavati: “When one understands the Personality of God, the reservoir of pleasure, Krsna, one actually becomes transcendentally blissful.”

Rati-manjari’s statement implies that Srimati Radharani is the source of the amorous rasa, and as such is the only source of pleasure for Krsna, a statement confirmed by Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami:

*ka krsnasya pranaya-jani-bhuh srimati radhikaika*  
*kasya preyasy anupama-guna radhikaika na canya*  
*jaihmyam kese drsi taralata nisthuratvam kuce 'sya*  
*vancha-purtyai prabhavati hare radhikaika na canya*

**“If one asks about the origin of love of Krsna, the answer is that the origin is in Srimati Radharani alone. Who is the dearmost friend of Krsna? The answer again is Srimati Radharani alone. No one else. Srimati Radharani’s hair is very curly, Her two eyes are always moving to and fro, and Her breasts are firm. Since all transcendental qualities are manifested in Srimati Radharani, She alone is able to fulfil all the desires of Krsna. No one else.”**

**Verse 63**

*madhavaya nata-vaktram adrta*  
*bhojya-peya-rasa-sancayam kramat*  
*tanvati tvam iha rohini-kare*  
*devi phulla-vadanam kadeksyase*

**“O Goddess! When will I see You lower Your blushing face and steal an affectionate glance at Madhava as You place His food and drink in the hands of Rohini-devi?”**

Commentary: The cooking is complete. Rohini-devi is pleased to show every preparation to Mother Yasoda, who asks with astonishment, “How have all these dishes become so beautiful and aromatic?” Rohini replies, “These culinary masterpieces have been created by the elegant hands of Sri Radha.”

Krsna’s mother praises Radharani profusely, and while the servants call Krsna and Balarama to the table, Radha straightens Her dress and dons Her ornaments.

The dining hall is decorated to create a festive atmosphere conducive to eating, and when Krsna and Balarama enter along with Their friends, the gaiety at once begins in earnest. The boys joke and laugh good-naturedly. They are eager to see what is on the menu, and they pat their stomachs to show how hungry they are. Because Radha was responsible for the cooking She hands the dishes to Mother Rohini one by one in the order in which they should be eaten. Meanwhile, Rohini directs the sakhis in serving the boys, and Mother Yasoda walks around encouraging everyone to eat heartily, calling for second helpings when needed, and keeping a special eye on Krsna.

Bhaktivinoda Thakura names some of the foods served to Krsna. The meal begins with sukta, various kinds of spinach, fried things, and a salad made of the green leaves of the jute plant. Then come pumpkins, baskets of fruit, small square cakes made of lentils and cooked-down milk, thick yogurt, squash cooked in milk, and vegetable preparations made from flowers of the banana tree. These preparations are followed by capatis, square patties of fried mung and urad dahl, and rice topped with ghee. Next come sweets made with milk, sugar, and sesame, rice flour cakes, thick cooked-down milk, cakes floating in milk, and sweet rice. Then there is another type of sweet rice that tastes just like nectar because it is mixed with camphor, bananas, and cheese. Then come twelve kinds of sour preparations made with tamarind, limes, lemons, oranges, and pomegranates. There are also puris made with white flour and sugar, puris filled with cream, laddus, and dahl patties boiled in sugared rice. Along with all of these dishes, rice, curried vegetables, sweets, and pastries are constantly on offer. Eating these ambrosial foods makes Krsna and His friends very happy.

In such an open assembly Radharani keeps Her head covered and Her face down. But every time She comes out of the kitchen with a new dish, She steals a brief glance at Krsna, as He does at Her.

Every preparation looks like a work of art and tastes like celestial nectar. The hoys eat with enthusiasm, and Krsna, knowing how hard Radha worked to please Him, eats with uncommon gusto, occasionally saying, “this is delicious” or “give Me more.”

With every bite Krsna takes, Yasoda’s maternal needs are met and Radha’s amorous sentiments are aroused, while every bite the boys take nourishes their unique, individual devotional mellows. In fact, in Radha’s cooking Krsna tastes the amorous mellow, Balarama the parental mellow, and the others the mellow of friendship. From this it is evident that the amorous mellow of Vraja is completely different from material sexual enjoyment, which is dependent upon physical contact. Therefore it is said:

*priti-visayanande tad-asrayananda*  
*tanha nahi nija-sukha-vanchara sambandha*

**“The happiness of the abode of love is in the happiness of the object of that love. This is not a relationship of desire for personal gratification.”**

In other words, Krsna enjoys loving mellows with Radha as much by tasting Her cooking, dancing with Her, or seeing Her exhibit ecstatic transformations, as He does by intimately exchanging with Her in secluded forest groves. This fact is further corroborated by Krsna’s appearance in Kali-yuga as Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. In that incarnation the Lord appears along with His gopi associates to taste the happiness of amorous love, but most of the gopis appear in male forms and explore the endless tastes of divine love with Lord Caitanya, a strict sannyasi, solely through the medium of nama-sankirtana.

For materialists, such transcendental loving exchanges are beyond conception. But then all things transcendental remain beyond the purview of those whose consciousness has not been spiritually awakened. To persons such as this, Lord Caitanya is surely inconceivable, being the combined form of Radha and Krsna in which the divine couple unite to taste Their mutual love.

*radha krsna-pranaya-vikrtir hladini saktir asmad*  
*ekatmanav api bhuvi pura deha-bhedarii gatau tau*  
*caitanyakhyam prakatam adhuna tad-dvayam caikyam aptam*  
*radha-bhava-dyuti-suvalitam naumi krsna-svarupam*

**“The loving affairs of Sri Radha and Krsna are transcendental manifestations of the Lord’s internal pleasure-giving potency. Although Radha and Krsna are one in Their identity, They separated Themselves eternally. Now these two transcendental identities have again united, in the form of Sri Krsna Caitanya. I bow down to Him, who has manifested Himself with the sentiment and complexion of Srimati Radharani although He is Krsna Himself.”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami is praying to Radha:

**“Like the cakora bird that lives on moonlight, I live by drinking the nectar radiating from Your moon-like face. That nectar tastes especially wonderful when Your stolen glance meets Krsna’s in the dining hall at Nandagrama. When will You give me the opportunity to savour it?”**

**Verse 64**

*bhojane guru-sabhasu kathancin*  
*madhavena nata-drsti-madotkam*  
*viksyamanam iha te mukha-padmam*  
*modayisyasi kada madhure mam*

**“O sweet girl! When will I be filled with happiness upon seeing Madhava glance at Your eager lotus face with its lowered eyes as He dines with His superiors?”**

Commentary: Paramour love is distinguished by its forbidden nature. The fact that something is forbidden makes it all the more exciting; indeed, children will sometimes do something their parents have forbidden because it gives a special thrill. So it is with amorous love!

In the Vedic culture boys and girls can be intimate with one another only when they are married. This rule is strictly upheld. Because Srimati Radharani is already married, She is not supposed to talk to or to look at any young man besides Her husband, and young men are expected to similarly restrain themselves in their dealings with Her.

In the previous verses Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami has described how, in spite of tradition and the risks involved in transgressing it, Radha glances furtively at Krsna whenever the opportunity presents itself. If someone were to notice, especially the elder gopas or gopis, there would be a scandal. Now it is Krsna who is secretly looking at Radha, and although others do not notice, Rati does. She shadows Radharani so closely that nothing can escape Her attention.

Rati says, “Madhura! You look especially sweet when You steal glances at Krsna.”

Radha replies, “Oh, you saw?”

Rati replies, “I watch everything You do. How could I not see?” Concerned, Radha says, “I hope that no one else saw.”

In verse sixty-three and sixty-four, Rati encourages Radha by referring to Krsna as Madhava. Now she explains, “Ignorant people may take exception to You looking at Madhava, but those who are enlightened know that since You are the goddess of fortune (ma), there can be no harm in You looking at Your own husband (dhava)" Radha smiles to hear this explanation.

Rati continues, “But do You know what else? When You notice that Krsna is looking at You, the irrepressible smile in the corners of Your lips and eyes makes Your face most sweet.”

Whenever She acknowledges these glances from Krsna, Radha’s face displays such sweetness that it disorients Krsna, who is unable to openly express His love. As a result, Krsna loses the will to eat. Even as Rohini repeatedly tries to serve Him, and even as His refusal to eat causes Mother Yasoda anguish, Krsna just picks at His food.

Yasoda exclaims to Rohini, “Mother, look! Although this whimsical, emaciated boy is clearly hungry, still He will not eat."

Both mothers repeatedly beg and cajole their darling boy to take more food, but Krsna refuses, “Mother! I have already eaten so much! I cannot eat any more.”

Finally Yasoda-devi places a tray of laddus in Sri Radha’s hands, ushers Her into the dining hall, and announces, “This lovely girl laboured all morning to prepare these delicacies.” Radha is now standing right in front of Krsna as Mother Yasoda pleads, “Will You add grief to Her labours by refusing to eat?”

Radha looks down at the tray in Her hand, occasionally glancing up at Krsna’s alluring face. He looks at Her, then at His mother, and then back at Radha. Yasoda says, “Radha, please serve Him with Your own hands.” Slowly Radharani places the sweets on Krsna’s plate. And to Yasoda’s delight, He eats them.

Rati continues, “When You personally served Krsna those confections, Your face was like a lotus exuding sweet fragrance under the sun rays of Madhava’s glance. Madhura! That sweetness is the transcendental mellow of paramour love.”

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami hopes that one day he may be able to directly taste that sweetness in the dining hall of Nandagrama.

**Verse 65**

*ayi vipinam atantam saurabheyi-kulanam*  
*vraja-nrpati-kumaram raksane diksitam tam*  
*vikala-mati-jananya lalyamanam kada tvam*  
*smita-madhura-kapolam viksyase viksyamana*

**“When will I see You exchange glances with the prince of Vraja, His cheeks sweet with a smile as He wanders in the forest fulfilling His vow to protect the surabhi cows after having lovingly freed Himself from the embrace of His grief-stricken mother?”**

Commentary: Once the boys have fully satisfied their hunger, they are impatient to go to the forest. Taking permission from their elders, they leave the table, wash their mouths and hands, and then take rest in Balarama’s room in great bliss. A servant brings Krsna a fresh pan leaf, and then He too lays down on a spacious bed in His own room as servants fan Him with peacock-feather fans. Meanwhile, Yasoda has Radha and Her friends eat food into which Dhanistha has secretly mixed Krsna’s remnants.

In the ocean of Krsna’s pastimes, the wave of His festive morning meal has finally crashed upon the shore of Nandagrama. With the sound of His buffalo horn, that wave recedes, and finally the fish-like Vraja-vasis are left floundering in the sands of separation.

As Krsna strolls down the streets of Nandagrama in the company of His friends, He repeatedly blows His Mandraghosa buffalo horn to inform the Vraja-vasis and the cows that it is time for Him to go to the forest. At the barns the boys open the pens, and the cows automatically form rows, filling the directions with their happy mooing. The lowing of the cows and the bellowing of the bulls mingles with the music of the gopas’ flutes, horns, and panpipes, and although the combined sound is quite melodious, it proclaims Krsna’s imminent departure and therefore strikes the Vraja-vasis’ hearts like the foreboding sound of thunder.

In fact, Krsna’s kith and kin are plunged into a certain wondrous condition during the time that Krsna is gone from Nandagrama, a condition unseen, unheard of, and unimaginable by anyone in this world. Gopa-kumara explains this state of affairs:

*niscetum nasakam kim te paramananda-nirvrtah*  
*kim va duhkha-bhara-grasta janah sarve dvijottama*  
*gopikanam ca yad-gitam sruyate rodananvitam*  
*tat-tosasya suco vantya-kasthayeti na buddhyate*

**“O best of brahmanas, I couldn’t discern whether the people there were all enjoying the highest bliss or suffering in the grip of terrible misery. I heard the gopis’ songs, coupled with their crying, but were they songs of the greatest contentment or the greatest sorrow? I couldn’t tell.”**

In this state of consciousness, the citizens of Nandagrama mechanically go about their duties as if possessed by a supernatural force. Only in the late afternoon, when Krsna returns from the forest, do they regain the same mood they had enjoyed in the morning. It is as if the Vraja-vasis are caught in the throes of some lethal poison during the day and are then administered the antidote of heavenly nectar in the evening. But the most amazing thing is that the effect of the two — poison and nectar — is almost identical.

An unearthly remedy initiates the daily transformation from poison to nectar: the murmur of Krsna’s enchanting flute. Emerging from a distant cloud of dust that moves towards Nandagrama, Krsna’s flute-song, in concert with the lowing of the cows, is unlike anything heard in the material world. Not only does it overwhelm the Vraja-vasis , it causes honey to flow from the trees, tears to fall from every eye, milk to pour from the elderly gopis' breasts, and the waters of the Yamuna to stand still. And when the call rings out from the watchtower, “He is coming! Krsna is coming!” the Vraja-vasis feel life return to their bodies. And so it shall remain until the following morning, when with Krsna’s departure the essence of their lives leaves their bodies once again.

It is morning now. Krsna and Balarama stand in the pastures outside the cow pens as the gopas energetically sing and dance, glorifying the two brothers and otherwise exhibiting their talents. Then, after performing the rituals prescribed for an outing and accepting blessings from the brahmanas, Krsna blows His buffalo horn and the caravan of boys and cows moves forward. Mother Yasoda and the elder ladies follow behind. Unable to tolerate being separated from Krsna and dragged by the ropes of love, Sri Radha walks behind Her elders with Lalita’s arm around Her waist for reassurance. Rati is just behind Her.

To describe Yasoda’s behaviour as the loving concern of a protective mother, while appropriate, would not do it justice. But to describe her behaviour to be like the symptoms of one forcibly and abruptly separated from the source of an addiction might come closer to the truth. When Yasoda sees Krsna perspire, she runs to wipe His face. When He again turns to leave, she puts some pan in His mouth. When for the third time He turns to go, she makes Him eat some sweets. Every time Krsna starts for the forest, Yasoda reluctantly turns back towards her home but, unable to bear even the thought of separation, she finds yet another excuse to run after her son and dote on Him. The fourth time she adjusts His clothes and straightens His hair, and the fifth, Yasoda calls the other boys to her side and plaintively says:

“Balarama! Make sure that you boys don’t wander too far away, never roam where there are thorns, and always walk in front of Your younger brother. Sridama! You are very brave, so you guard Krsna from behind. Amsu should stay on Krsna’s right and Subala on His left."

Finally she turns to her son and says, “Child! While taking care of the cows in the distant forests or caves of Govardhana Hill, if You see a dangerous animal, then immediately meditate on the ancient Supreme Person, Lord Narayana. He will protect You.” At this, Krsna has great difficulty preventing a smile from curling up His bimba-fruit lips. Thus the sage Sri Sarvananda says, “May that suppressed smile protect all the worlds.”

Krsna is full of love for His mother, but her extreme displays of affection make Him feel embarrassed before His friends, hindering His playful pastimes with them. And so He bows down, touches His mother’s feet, holds up His dust-covered palm, and sweetly says:

“Dear Mother! The potency of this dust can protect Me from any demon or danger.” As He smears it over His body, He continues, “And even if this universe were to vanish, I would continue to exist by your loving grace.” Embracing her and speaking logical arguments, Krsna finally convinces Yasoda to stop following Him. Tears in her eyes, milk dripping from her breasts, Yasoda stands upon a small hill and watches her son depart.

By this time Radha is immersed in an ocean of sorrow. Yet, due to shyness, She is unable to speak. She can merely wipe the tears that flood Her eyes. At the edge of the forest Krsna turns back. His eyes meet Radha’s eyes as if to ask Her, “Will You meet Me at Your lake?”

To which Her eyes reply, “Yes.” Rati-manjari witnesses this exchange and understands that Krsna’s sweet smile at that moment of apparent sorrow is due to His happiness at the promise of meeting Sri Radha. In that joyous mood He bounds into the forest and is lost from view.

But Radha is still crying, and so Rati enquires, “Princess! Why are You weeping?”

Radha looks at Her maidservant and replies, “I fear that as Krsna walks in the forest His soft lotus feet will be pricked by thorns and stones.”

Rati lovingly pats Radha’s hands, “Don’t worry. There are neither thorns nor stones in Vraja’s forests. And if by chance there were, the animals would sweep them away with their tails before Krsna could step on them. Come, let us return to Nandagrama and then to Your home.”

The gopis echoed this selfless loving concern of Sri Radha when Krsna left them on the night of the rasa dance:

*yat te sujata-caranamburuham stanesu*  
*bhitah sanaih priya dadhimahi karkasesu*  
*tenatavim atasi tad vyathate na kim svit*  
*kurpadibhir bhramau dhir bhavad-ayusam nah*

**“O dearly beloved! Your lotus feet are so soft that we place them gently on our breasts, fearing that Your feet will be hurt. Our life rests only in You. Our minds, therefore, are filled with anxiety that Your tender feet might be wounded by pebbles as You roam about on the forest path.”**

**Verse 66**

*gosthesayatha kutukac chapathadi-purvam*  
*su-snigdhaya sumukhi matr-parardhato 'pi*  
*ha hri-mati priya-ganaih saha bhojyamanam*  
*kim tvam niriksya hrdaye mudam adya lapsye*

**“O shy one! O fair-faced girl! When will my heart feel great joy as I watch the queen of Vraja, more affectionate than billions of mothers, take eager vows to make You sit down with Your friends and eat in her home?”**

Commentary: Nanda Maharaja, like his queen, is distraught. He cannot help but fuss over his departing son. Again and again he embraces Krsna, smells His head, and sheds tears of grief; then he does the same to Balarama. As the affection of Krsna’s friends pulls Krsna into the forest, He is finally able to convince His father to resume his kingly duties. After the cows and hoys pass from view, Nanda consoles his wife and the gopis, and then leads them hack to Nandagrama. As they return home, the gopis sing of Krsna’s pastimes, remaining thus absorbed in thoughts of Him.

The daytime pastimes of the Vraja-vasis are unlimited, and therefore even Anantadeva cannot describe them fully. However, even if he could, it is doubtful that he would, since it is not fitting to speak of something so pathetic. Sanatana Gosvami gives the following warning about such an attempt:

*tat-tad-viseso nirvacyo ’nanta-saktyapi naparah*  
*maharti-janake tasmin ko va dhiman pravartate*

**“Even a person with unlimited power could not describe those dealings in further detail. But why would someone intelligent try? It would only create abysmal distress.”**

Sometimes before Krsna’s departure and sometimes after it, Yasoda personally feeds Radha and Her friends. “Radhika worked so hard,” Yasoda thinks, “She must eat before She returns home.” Yasoda-devi holds Radha’s slender arm and forcibly seats the jewellike gopi on her lap, telling the other girls, who struggle to hide their amusement, to sit on the other chairs around the table. Meanwhile, Rohini and her assistants bring plates of food from the kitchen.

Mother Yasoda holds Radharani to her breast just as she holds Krsna. At first Radha bashfully hides Her face, but Yasoda says, “O my daughter! Why are You so timid before me when I am just like Your mother.”

Raising Radharani’s chin with her forefinger and looking into Her eyes, Yasoda says, “Actually, because I love You as much as I love my son, it is I who am Your mother, not Kirtida. Like a cakora that lives by seeing the moon, I live only because Your face appears before me every morning. Otherwise I would die. Be kind to me! Give up Your bashfulness and comfort me by eating in my presence.”

Yasoda looks at Lalita and the other gopis and adds, “O girls! You too are like my daughters! Do not be shy in front me. Eat happily here. Laugh and joke as you would in your own homes.” With her own hands, the queen of Vraja lovingly feeds Radha, making maidservants like Rati and Dhanistha float on waves of bliss.

Rati-manjari says, “O shy one! (Hrimati) You are so bashful in the presence of Krsna’s mother, but ultimately You cannot resist her stirring maternal love.”

“How can I?” Radha replies. “That would be like expecting ice not to melt over an open flame.”

Rati continues, "I have seen Your stunning face so many times before. But when Yasoda decorates Your lips and chin with morsels of the food she personally places in Your mouth, the sight of Your face gives new meaning to the name Sumukhi.”

**Verse 67**

*alinganena sirasah paricumbanena*  
*snehavalokana-bharena ca khanjanaksi*  
*gosthesaya nava-vadhum iva lalyamanam*  
*tvam preksya kim hrdi mahotsavam atanisye*

**“O girl with eyes as restless as khanjana birds! When will my heart celebrate a great festival of bliss as I watch the queen of Vraja fondle You, embrace You, kiss Your head, and lovingly stare at You as if You were her new daughter-in-law?”**

Commentary: At those times that Mother Yasoda addresses Radha as “daughter,” she actually means “daughter-in-law.” A mother loses her own daughter to the house of her in-laws, whereas a mother- in-law can enjoy the company of her husband’s wife throughout her life. Before Radha’s marriage to Ahhimanyu, Yasoda-devi wanted Radha to marry Krsna. But divine fate did not fulfil her desire, and Yasoda constantly laments the injustice. She thinks, “Who else but Radha is qualified to be my son’s wife?” In fact, Kirtida is equally sorry that she was unable to give her daughter away to Yasoda’s son.

As friends in childhood, Kirtida and Yasoda would play with dolls and pretend that the dolls were married, as girls often do. At such times the two young girls would say that when they grew up Kirtida's daughter would marry Yasoda’s son. And sure enough, when Radha was approaching puberty, Yasoda sent her friend Kirtida a proposal, which Kirtida joyfully accepted.

But that is as far as the matter went. The divine couple’s eternal relationship in Vraja is one of extramarital, not marital, love. To preserve this unchangeable truth, Paurnamasi (Yogamaya) arranged a series of events that led to Radha’s marriage to Abhimanyu.

When Yasoda informed Paurnamasi of her plans for Krsna and Radha, the guru of the Vraja-vasis insisted that it was not an astrologically auspicious time for the two youths to marry and urged Yasoda to wait. Paurnamasi then went to Kirtida and informed her that Radha’s beauty and virtues were like the hidden fragrance of musk, broadcasting themselves throughout the land. As a result, Paurnamasi told her, King Kamsa was already making plans to marry Radharani.

Terrified at the prospect of her daughter falling into the hands of a demon like Kamsa, Kirtida sent Radha along with grandmother Mukhara into hiding at Satoha-grama. Paurnamasi then prevailed upon the king and queen of Varsana that Radha should marry Abhimanyu, the son of Mukhara’s friend Jatila. Paurnamasi explained that Kamsa was so inimical towards Krsna that if Radha were to marry Him She would be put into harm’s way. Abhimanyu, on the other hand, was in good standing with Kamsa. If Radha were to marry Abhimanyu, not only would Kamsa abandon his plan to marry Radha, but he would also have one fewer reason to be envious of Krsna. Paurnamasi’s arguments convinced King Vrsabhanu. Thus, even though a more unsuitable groom could not have been found, Abhimanyu accepted the hand of Radha in Satoha-grama.

Soon after the wedding, Radha moved with Her new husband to Yavata, and in no time at all She had accepted Krsna as Her paramour. Despite the risks and difficulties involved, from that time on She maintained Her illicit connection with Yasoda’s son.

Nevertheless, Mother Yasoda perpetually laments the loss of a perfect daughter-in-law. As the gopis prepare to return to Yavata, Yasoda offers them gifts. To Radha she makes a special presentation, one typically made to a new daughter-in-law — betel, sandal-paste, vermilion, new garments, and ornaments. Seeing moon-like Radha surrounded by Her star-like friends, Yasoda fantasises that Radha is a new bride entering her home. Finally, Yasoda embraces Radha, kisses Her head, and says, “Let a thunderbolt fall on the creator’s head for depriving me of a daughter such as You. There is no girl in Vraja as fitting for my son.”

Still in Yasoda’s embrace, Radha glances naughtily at Her friends, who cover their faces to keep from laughing. Dasa Gosvami says, “Khanjanaksi! As Yasoda embraces You, Your eyes dart humorously around Your girlfriends as if they were restless wagtails. If Yasoda only knew that the creator did fulfil Her desire, albeit in a way she did not expect. Nonetheless, You are her son’s only love.”

In composing Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami meditates on Srimati Radharani, and in so doing first eases the pain of being separated from Her, then dispels it, and finally transforms that pain into bliss. The process of this transformation is a transcendental wonder.

Some persons may question the necessity of willingly subjecting oneself to suffering, whatever its outcome. They may object, “If remembering a loved one causes suffering, then it is better to forget.” But Krsna has a reply to such misgivings:

*kathancana smaranam eva tesam*  
*avehi taj-jivana-danam eva*  
*tesam yato vismaranam kadacit*  
*pranadhikanam maranac ca nindyam*

**“Please understand: when somehow made mindful of those one loves, one is given back one’s life. Forgetting those more dear than one’s own breath is more painful than dying.”**

Before making this statement, Krsna had explained to Narada that when one is separated from loved ones, pure love makes him suffer as if tossed into fire, the scorching flames of which inflict pain that intensifies unto undying grief. But, just when death seems a welcome relief from such misery, that same separation transforms into an abundance of pleasure beyond description or comprehension by all but the best of Vaisnavas expert in relishing mellows.

One marvel of this pain of separation is that after satisfying the heart, it enables the afflicted to enjoy a greater pleasure when again meeting Krsna face to face. And another, even more intriguing wonder, is that one may want to feel that pain of separation again. If unable to do so, one may even feel distress. Krsna concludes that the pain apparently suffered by pure devotees in separation is actually pleasure; indeed, it is the greatest ecstasy. Otherwise, why would they want to feel that separation again? Thus, when the words of great devotees — as they appear in books like Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali — remind devotees of Radha and Krsna, great service is done. In this regard, the gopis say, *bhuvi grnanti ye bhuri-da janah*: “Those who spread the message of Godhead are most munificent.”

In other words, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami sings the verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali to invoke feelings of separation, and when feeling such separation, he sings the same verses to ease the pain that separation brings. But ultimately, by remembering Radha’s pastimes with Krsna, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami feels he has regained his life. And although he can never really forget Sri Radha, when he remembers Her through the agency of loving devotion in separation, Dasa Gosvami again feels happy and fortunate.

Practising devotees who understand the principles of love in separation can gradually develop these emotions within themselves by carefully studying the verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali and being sensitive to the moods of its author.

**Verse 68**

*ha rupa-manjari sakhi pranayena devim*  
*tvad-bahu-datta-bhuja-vallarim ayataksim*  
*pascad aham kalita-kama-taranga-rangam*  
*nesyami kim hari-vibhusita-keli-kunjam*

**“My dear Rupa-manjari! May I follow behind our wide-eyed queen when She becomes a dancing arena for waves of amorous passion and as you, wrapping your vine-like arm in Hers, lovingly guide Her to the grove that Hari has personally decorated?”**

Commentary: Somehow the gopis manage to return Srimati Radharani to Yavata, a journey made all the more challenging by their mistress’s varied symptoms of ecstasy in separation. When She faints, the gopis have to carry Her. When She raves like a madwoman, they have to hide Her from public view. And when She starts to run, they have to run after Her. As the girls draw nearer to Yavata, Kundalata is able to revive Radharani from a swoon by telling Her that they are about to meet Krsna. And finally, they arrive at the home of Radha’s husband, where Jatila is busy making cow-dung patties in the courtyard.

Jatila rejoices at Radha’s safe return and at the gifts sent by Yasoda. After thanking Kundalata for keeping her promise, Jatila requests Radha to collect milk, ghee, yogurt, and other ingredients to worship the sun god at Surya-kunda. This time Jatila puts Radha into Lalita’s care: “You are an outspoken, chaste woman. Never let Radha out of your sight. And by all means, keep Her away from that libertine, Krsna.”

The gopis become heady with bliss at Jatila’s order to visit Surya- kunda. Kundalata and Lalita reply, “O mother! Rest assured, we will protect Radha just as eyelids protect the eyes.”

The gopis erupt with glee once in the privacy of Radha’s quarters. What a turn of events! The manjaris at once set about to refresh Radha and help Her gather together the ingredients for worship.

But where will they meet Krsna? No one knows yet. Lalita calls Rati-manjari over and gives her a basket containing pan and a garland, both made by Radharani. She says, “O Rati! Bring these gifts to Krsna and ask Him where Radha should meet Him."

Rati takes the basket and gives Radha a look that says, “Don’t worry. I’ll find Him.” Then, with the determination of a soldier following orders, she hurries off to Vrndavana forest.

Meanwhile, Krsna has spent the morning hours herding cows and playing with His friends. As the cows and gopas rest at Gvalavana, Krsna wanders off to Kusuma-sarovara in search of Radha. By divine arrangement — which is to say, by His will — Krsna meets Rati- manjari there. Krsna is pleased to see Rati because He knows that wherever she is Radharani is never far away. After receiving the gifts sent by Lalita, Krsna eagerly enquires, “O friend, Rati! Is your mistress, Radha, well?”

Confident that teasing Krsna will increase His eagerness for Radha’s company, Rati decides to mislead Him with false information. “She is fine!" Rati curtly replies.

Krsna smells the garland Radha made for Him and asks, “But where is She?”

“She’s at home," Rati nonchalantly replies.

Krsna looks downcast. With Rati standing there in front of Him, He expected Radha to be hiding nearby. “Won’t She come out to the forest?”

Rati shakes her head, “Because She was out all morning cooking for You, Her elders would not allow it!”

Krsna sighs deeply and enquires, “What is She doing?”

“Well,” Rati answers, “before I left She was trying to churn water into yogurt!”

Krsna’s eyes fill with tears and He asks, “What happened then?”

Rati looks Him straight in the eye and shakes her head: “Jatila scolded Radha terribly, then escorted Her inside the house and locked Her in Her room.”

Krsna turns to Vrnda, who happens to be standing nearby. “Couldn’t Vrnda go to Jatila and bring Radha here on the pretext of picking flowers?"

Despite feeling sorry for Krsna’s obvious distress, Rati-manjari carries on with her ruse, “O Hari! Now that Jatila thinks Radha is daydreaming about You, Vrnda will not be able to deceive the old woman.”

His heart crushed, Krsna slumps down upon a golden seat. “Alas! Radha is always hard to attain, but it appears She is lost to Me today.”

Now Rati feels that her teasing has gone far enough. Clearing her throat, she says, “O joy of Vraja! Don’t be sad. Fate is smiling upon You. I was only joking to increase Your desire for the priceless treasure Jatila has herself just sent to worship the sun god.”

At this happy news Krsna’s determination to see Radha is revived. Rather than get even with Rati for having teased Him, Krsna takes a gunja garland from His neck and gives it to her as a reward. Krsna then takes two campaka flowers from His ears, puts them in Rati’s hand, and says, “Give these to Radha! Tell your mistress that Her servant waits for Her in the grove called Kandarpa-keli-sukhada on the bank of Radha-kunda!”

Her mission accomplished, Rati hurries off to Yavata to inform Radharani of the meeting place. Playfully baiting Krsna is hardly out of place for one in Rati’s position. In fact, increasing the divine couple’s attachment to each other is one of the sixteen aspects of a manjari’s service (tayor asakti-karita).

Making Radha seem unattainable increases both Krsna’s desire to be with Her and His appreciation for Her company when They finally come together. The manjaris' pure, spontaneous love empowers them to take such liberties with Krsna, but only out of service. Just think! The residents of Vaikuntha would hardly dream of teasing Lord Narayana in any way at all.

In trance, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami meditates on how, in his form as Rati-manjari, he returns to Yavata to inform Radha of the proposed meeting place. But after handing Her the two campaka flowers, his trance breaks. He finds himself, an elderly Gosvami, in his cottage by the banks of Radha-kunda. Gone is Yavata, gone are the gopis, and worst of all, gone is Srimati Radharani. He laments only as great devotees can. Such a devotee, frustrated in his pursuit of the goal of Krsna consciousness, turns to his guru for help.

*tasmad gurum prapadyetam*  
*jijnasuh sreya uttamam*

**“Therefore any person who seriously desires real happiness must seek a bona fide spiritual master and take shelter of him by initiation.”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami thus calls out to Rupa-manjari and, through the medium of loving devotion, he hears a soft melodious voice reply, "Rati! Do not cry. I have come.”

Again in divine trance as Rati-manjari, Dasa Gosvami sees brilliantly effulgent Sri Rupa-manjari standing there before him. Having lost sight of Radharani, Rati asks, “Goddess! How long must I be separated from my service to Sri Radha?”

Rupa-manjari enquires, “Sweet girl. What service do you want?” Sitting at Rupa-manjari’s feet, Rati softly weeps, “After Radha receives Krsna’s message through me, Radha will cross over all obstacles posed by Her relatives. She will then depart for Radha- kunda with you by Her side. I would like to accompany you.”

Smiling, Rupa says, “It will be midday and the sandy paths of Vraja will be very hot.”

Rati dismisses such an insignificant obstacle with a shake of her head. “Devi! Nothing burns me more than separation from Sri Radha."

“What will you do if you come?” Rupa asks, “What is it about this particular meeting that attracts you so?”

Joining her palms, Rati is ready with her reply. “Although Radha will be wide-eyed with eagerness to see Krsna, that same eagerness will obstruct Her movements with the thorns of passionate ecstasy. You will then have to hold Her vine-like arms to steady Her. Therefore you will need me to carry the paraphernalia for worshipping the sun god, not to mention whatever may be needed for worshipping Krsna."

Rupa-manjari nods her head in approval as Rati continues, “I know how eager Krsna is to meet Radha. As soon as I left Him, He went to the grove to decorate it personally.

“O Rupa-manjari! There are many groves in Vrndavana tended by many goddesses under Vrnda-devi’s care. Each of these groves surpasses in sweetness, beauty, and opulence the aggregate of all gardens and forests in Vaikuntha. We gopis are regular visitors, residents, and servants of these kunjas. But how rare is it, even for us, to see a grove personally decorated by Krsna’s hands? Surely, that is the special feature of this meeting.

“I yearn to see the kunja floor that Krsna swept, the garlands He strung, the doorway He decorated, and the flower-bed He made. But more than that, I crave to see Radharani’s reaction when She first sees Krsna’s handiwork. It will be wonderful to hear Her words of praise and to watch Krsna’s humble response. No doubt His offering of menial service will awaken in Radha an especially submissive loving mood, and the exchange that follows will be incomparably sweet.” With pleading eyes and joined palms Rati looks into Rupa-manjari’s grey eyes and begs, “Please! May I come?”

Suddenly, by Rupa-manjari’s touch, Rati finds herself on that very path to Radha-kunda. Rupa-manjari is holding Radha’s arm as wideeyed Radha looks down the path and asks, “Rupa! Is it still far away?”

**Verse 69**

*sakam tvaya sakhi nikunja-grhe sarasyah*  
*svasyas tate kusuma-bhavita-bhusanena*  
*srngaritam vidadhati priyam isvari sa*  
*ha ha bhavisyati mad-iksana-gocarah kim*

**“O friend! When will I see you and our mistress, together decorating Her dearest one with flower ornaments in a forest cottage by the shore of Her lake?”**

Commentary: It is just as Rati-manjari had predicted! The elaborately decorated grove — made beautiful both by Krsna’s painstaking efforts and by Krsna’s presence as the central ornament — is decorated further still by the many sweet exchanges between the divine couple that take place upon Radha’s arrival. Radharani expresses Her deep appreciation for Krsna’s labour and craftsmanship, and He is moved by Her eagerness and determination to be with Him.

Krsna says, “Devi! You came barefoot along paths made scorching hot by the midday sun. Are Your feet not sore?”

Looking indifferently at Her feet, Radha replies, “By fixing Your form in My mind, the soothing rays of Your moon-like face kept Me cool along the way. It was like walking on smooth marble.”

But Krsna isn’t completely satisfied with Her answer. “Let’s have a look,” Krsna says as He sits Radha on a daybed, kneels before Her, and takes Her feet in His lap. He feels Her soles to see if they are bruised, and then wipes the dust from them with His upper cloth.

Rupa and Rati watch, ready to assist. They fan the divine couple and massage Their lotus feet when They become tired. Rati-manjari notes that Sri Radha is taking a dominant role in Her dealings with Krsna, and so she calls her mistress Isvari, meaning that Radha is the monarch and controller of the grove — and of Krsna.

Krsna is the supreme controller, Paramesvara, but that supreme controller is controlled by Srimati Radharani. Many powerful demons like Madhu and Hiranyakasipu failed to conquer Krsna by physical strength, but Radha easily subdues Him with the essence of spiritual strength: pure unconditional love.

Sometimes the gopis gossip that Sri Radha knows a magic potion or a mystic mantra by which She controlsKrsna. But the truth is that Her ability to always keep Krsna submissive to Her, indeed to keep Him under Her control (santatasrava-kesava), is an aspect of Her very nature. It is one of Her twenty-five essential qualities. Jiva Gosvami comments that this special quality of Sri Radha is indirectly described in the following famous verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam:

*anayaradhito nunam bhagavan harir isvarah*  
*yan no vihaya govindah prito yam anayad rahah*

**“Certainly this particular gopi has perfectly worshipped the allpowerful Personality of Godhead, Govinda, since He was so pleased with Her that He abandoned the rest of us and brought Her to a secluded place.”**

Rati-manjari addresses Radha as Isvari also because her mistress has taken the dominant role in the divine couple’s acts of transcendental enjoyment (viparita-vilasa). Radha sees that Krsna’s appearance has become dishevelled, and so She wants to tidy Him up — not in His regular attire, but in a floral costume.

Sri Radha tells Rupa-manjari, “Bring a basket and follow Me."

The two girls leave Krsna by the side of Radha-kunda in order to collect assorted aromatic flowers in a nearby garden. Upon returning, they string the flowers into anklets, bracelets, earrings, garlands, and a crown — everything needed to make Krsna look like vernal Cupid himself. When the decorations are complete, Radharani dresses Krsna according to Her liking. Just as Krsna sits submissively while His mother dresses Him, He does likewise for Sri Radha.

Rati is spellbound by Srimati Radharani’s expertise in dressing Krsna. She watches closely as Radha leans over Krsna and ties a garland around His neck, intoxicating Him with the excitement of Her nearness. Rati whispers to Rupa-manjari, “Our mistress is dressing Krsna not only with floral ornaments (bhusanena srngaritam) but also with loving mellows (srngara-rasa)

**Verse 70**

*srutva vicaksana-mukhad vraja-raja-sunoh*  
*sastabhisara-samayam subhage ’tra hrsta*  
*suksmambaraih kusuma-samskrta-karna-pura-*  
*haradibhis ca bhavatim kim alankarisye*

**“Auspicious girl! When will I be able to joyfully decorate You with elegant garments, floral earrings, and sparkling necklaces, after You have heard from the parrot Vicaksana that Krsna has already left for His noontime rendezvous with You?”**

Commentary: The previous pastime is finished. This verse refers to another day. After having seen Radha dress Krsna, the desire awakens in Rati to dress Radharani, and she wants to do so at midday in order to prepare Radha for Her noontime tryst with Krsna. The verse does not mention the time of the meeting, but it does say that the parrot Vicaksana is the messenger. Since parrots don’t fly at night, the meeting must be during the daytime.

The word abhisara means “motion (sara) towards (abhi)"; in one word, it means “meeting.” In this instance, Srimati Radharani is an abhisarika heroine, a girl who meets Her lover at a rendezvous, one of the eight kinds of heroines described by Srila Rupa Gosvami.

The heroine who goes to meet Krsna at night wearing white clothing when the moon is bright is called jyotsndbhisarika, and if she goes dressed in black when the moon is dark, she is called tamo-’bhisarika. Although happy at heart, such a gopi is so shy that she seems to hide behind her very own body. She goes silently, nicely decorated, her head carefully covered, accompanied by a single trusted friend. Although such meetings normally take place at night, Jiva Gosvami confirms that they also take place during the day. Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami heralds such a daytime meeting in this verse.

Obsessed with the thought of serving Krsna, Sri Radha wants to immediately follow the parrot Vicaksana into the forest. Rati must lovingly, but firmly, hold onto Radha’s arm to restrain Her from leaving.

“O auspicious girl (Saubhaga)! You must be properly dressed and ornamented before You go.” Radharani is eager to go, but Rati explains, “If You do not let me dress You properly, then how will You bring auspiciousness to Krsna?”

As soon as Radha hears that there could be a question of misfortune for Krsna, She sits down in Her dressing room, although still humming with impatience. “All right,” She says, “but hurry.”

Rati reassures her mistress, “It won’t be but a moment.” Then she expertly dresses Radha in a new sari, decorates Her with glistening ornaments, and fits the floral earrings she had earlier prepared.

Radha fidgets through the whole procedure, frequently saying, “Hurry! Krsna’s waiting.”

To calm Her, Rati goes on chatting, “Do You want to go out dressed in haste, like You did that time — forgetful of the world — You put the necklace meant to decorate Your chest in Your braid, the lotus for Your braid on Your chest, smeared eyeliner on Your limbs, and the musk for Your limbs on Your eyelids? What a sight Youwere!”

But Radha isn’t interested in talk. She stands up and declares, “I’m going.”

Rati smiles sweetly, “Good! I’m finished. You look perfect.”

But suddenly, humility stops Radha in Her tracks. She comes back to Her maidservant and asks, “Are you sure He actually wants to meet Me, and not someone else?"

Rati grasps her mistress firmly by the shoulders and pushes Her towards the door, saying, “Don’t think twice! Krsna is waiting for You, and for You alone. You know that we call him Radhabhisara-sarvasvah (“one for whom meeting Radha is everything”). O beautiful one! I don’t understand why, while He sits alone in the grove, waiting to hear the jingling of Your ankle bells, You insist on dawdling here.”

In this way Rati gives Sri Radha’s strength. The two girls walk unnoticed through the house like shadows, leaving by the front door to follow Vicaksana flying overhead. A Vaisnava poet describes Radha’s first steps along the forest path.

*dvi-traih keli-saroruham tri-caturair dhammilla-malli-srajam*  
*kanthan mauktika-malika tad anu ca tyaktva padaih pancasaih*  
*krsna-prema-vighurnitantarataya durabhisaratura*  
*tanv-angi nirupayam adhvani param sroni-bharam nindati*

**“After two or three steps, She thinks Her toy lotus flower a burden and sets it down by the road. After three or four steps, She sets down the garland of jasmine flowers decorating Her braids. After five steps, She removes the pearl necklace from Her neck. Then slender Radha, unhappy that the meeting is so far away, Her heart trembling with love for Krsna, rebukes Her hips for being so heavy. But She cannot abandon them, and so She is forced to carry them.”**

**Verse 71**

*nana-puspaih kvanita-madhupair devi sambhavitabhir*  
*malabhis tad-ghusma-vilasat-kama-citralibhis ca*  
*rajad-dvare sapadi madananandadabhikhya-gehe*  
*malli-jalaih sasi-mukhi kada talpam akalpayami*

**“O moonfaced Goddess! When will that day come when I prepare a bed of flowers for You in the bee-filled cottage named Madananandada-kunja, beautified with splendid gates, vermilion pictures, and a network of flower-strands?”**

Commentary: Meditation is said to be of two types: fixed on one specific scene or pastime (mantropasana) or passing through a sequence of consecutive pastimes (svarasiki). For example, devotees who fix their minds on an image of Sri Krsna, such as the one described in the following mantra of Lord Brahma, are engaged in mantropasana.

*venum kvanantam aravinda-dalayataksam*  
*barhavatamsam asitambuda-sundarangam*  
*kandarpa-koti-kaminiya-visesa-sobham*  
*govindam adi-purusam tam aham bhajami*

**“I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, who plays on His transcendental flute. His eyes are like lotus flowers, He is decorated with peacock plumes, and His bodily colour resembles a fresh black cloud although His bodily features are more beautiful than millions ofcupids.”**

And devotees who meditate on each of Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes in their proper sequence, as described in books like Govinda-lilamrta , are engaged in svarasiki meditation. Although practising devotees can follow either process, Jiva Gosvami explains that mantropasana generally refers to meditation by effort. Such effort gradually matures into direct perception in the manner of svarasiki. Krsna then appears within devotees’ hearts by revelation and personally manifests His pastimes.

All of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s meditations are of the svarasiki category, meaning that they are direct perceptions of Krsna’s pastimes manifested from his spontaneous attraction to the divine couple. Rupa Gosvami describes this effortless attraction and the devotion that naturally follows from it:

*iste svarasiki ragah paramavistata bhavet*  
*tan-mayi ya bhaved bhaktih satra ragatmikodita*

**“When one becomes attached to the Supreme Personality of Godhead, his natural inclination to love is fully absorbed in thoughts of the Lord. That is called transcendental attachment, and devotional service according to that attachment is called ragatmika, or spontaneous devotional service.”**

The meditations of Dasa Gosvami should not be confused with those of practising devotees who are still aspiring to develop attachment like that of the Vraja-vasis. The difference between the two is that Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s attachment is complete and perfect, whereas the attachment of sadhakas is generally partial and materially tainted.

The verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali that are out of sequence should not be mistaken for the mantropasana of practitioners — they are fully on the svarasiki platform. Like their sequential counterparts, the individual meditations of Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami are also outpourings of spontaneous love. Their non-chronological appearance may be attributed to the independent nature of ragatmika-bhakti.

Rati-manjari’s desires have expanded to include service in the groves of Radha-kunda. She is now meditating on Visakha-devi’s grove, called Madananandada-kunja or Visakhanandada-kunja, which is on the northeastern bank of Radha-kunda.

This grove is comprised of campaka trees with flowers of different colours — red, green, yellow, and blue — and similarly hued birds and bees. The madhavi vines that hang from these trees create a palace-like atmosphere with four grand entrances and a sixteen- petalled jewel lotus at its centre.

While the divine couple stroll in the gardens and glorify each other’s qualities, at times singing songs, Rati makes a thick mattress and pillows by stuffing soft cotton cases with fresh jasmine flowers. The bed is smooth and aromatic. “A suitable place for Them to rest,” she thinks.

Satisfied with Radha’s and Krsna’s resting place, Rati then quickly checks the grove to make sure everything is just right. Everywhere are pictures painted in vermilion, produced by Citra, Visakha, Manjumukhi, and others — pictures of animals and of Krsna’s pastimes like His falling in love, the rasa dance, and His killing of demons. The pictures of Krsna increase Radharani’s desire for Him, and the pictures of Radha, His longing for Her. Vermilion is the colour of divine passion, and so the pictures in the grove are painted with this substance to arouse such amorous feelings.

Just as pictures excite and nurture Radha’s and Krsna’s mutual feelings of love, they can also be an impetus for the spiritual emotions of practising devotees. Srila Prabhupada wanted that his books contain many pictures, which he called “windows to the spiritual world.” Thakura Bhaktivinoda writes:

*srutva krsna-gunam tatra darsakaddhi punah punah*  
*citritam rupam anviksya varddhate lalasa bhrsam*

**“By seeing pictures of Krsna or by repeatedly hearing descriptions of Krsna from persons who have seen Him, one’s greed for attaining Krsna increases unlimitedly.”**

Rati is now confident that everything is as it should be. She leans against the doorway to the kunja and watches Radha and Krsna as They sit beneath a campaka tree, immersed in humorous conversation. The entire grove is illuminated by the emerald-green glow of Their combined auras. The whole lake resounds with echoes of Their youthful laughter, which resemble the sound of peacocks crying during a thunderstorm.

In her mind, Rati addresses Sri Radha, “O Radhika! You are my Sasi-mukhi, my spotless full moon. Until Krsna’s message lured You into the forest, You were waning. Having overcome all obstacles by His grace, You now shine here in Your fullness, even though social convention dictates that You have no business here.

“Your appearance in this grove is like the appearance of the full moon on Janmastami. Krsna was horn on the eighth day of the waning moon, but to welcome Him into this world, by His grace, that waning moon became full, although astronomical calculation dictates such a thing to be impossible. All glories to You and Your beloved!”

**Verse 72**

*sri-rupa-manjari-kararata-pada-padma-*  
*gosthendra-nandana-bhujarpita-mastakayah*  
*ha modatah kanaka-gauri padaravinda-*  
*samvahanani sanakais tava kim karisye*

**“O golden girl! When will I be able to gently and happily massage Your lotus feet while Sri Rupa-manjarl massages the lotus feet of Vraja’s prince, upon whose arm You have placed Your head?”**

Commentary: Accompanied by Rupa-manjari, Radha and Krsna enter the kunja where Rati hangs flower garlands around Their necks, anoints Their limbs with cooling sandalwood paste, and gives Them betel nuts to chew. She requests Them to lie down on the bed she has painstakingly made, and then she sits at Their feet. Rupa-manjari. sits beside Rati. Both girls have the same thought in mind: “I will massage Sri Radha’s lotus feet.”

*kunje prasuna-kula-kalpita-keli-talpe*  
*samvistayor madhura-narma-vilasa-bhajoh*  
*loka-traydbharanayos caranambujani*  
*samvahayisyati kada yuvayor jano ‘yam*

**“When, as You two ornaments of the three worlds recline on a pastime bed of flowers and exchange sweet joking words, will this person massage Your lotus feet?”**

Rupa and Rati brush shoulders and exchange glances: who will massage Radha’s feet and who will massage Syama’s? Krsna is a prince accustomed to being served hand and foot, but now He offers His arm to Radha as a pillow. As She lies on Her side and rests Her head on His arm, Radha extends Her feet into Rati’s lap. The friendly squabble is resolved and the girls happily worship whichever pair of lotus feet divine Providence has bestowed upon them.

The two manjaris undo their braids, and while listening to Radha and Krsna conversing, they massage the divine couple’s feet using their soft black hair. What do Radha and Krsna talk about?

Krsna says, “Beloved! Are You comfortable?”

Belligerent Radha answers, “No!”

Krsna enquires, “My beautiful love! What offence have I committed?”

Knitting Her brow, Radha says, “I cannot even begin to list Your misdeeds.”

With a hapless glance, Krsna responds, “Then what can I say?”

Radha wags Her forefinger at Him, “Am I expected to just forgive all Your sins?”

“Yes!” Krsna smiles. Then, as He tries to pull Radha towards Him, She says, “After You leave I shall sleep comfortably.”

As a last resort, Krsna sits up to massage Her feet, “Let me serve You.”

But She pushes Him away, “You’re not very good at that.”

He then holds Her hands and says, “Since I am Your servant, You can teach Me.”

Radha playfully pushes Him away, “You’ve lost Your mind!"

But Krsna again takes Her hand: “I didn’t lose it, You stole it. Now tell Me where You’re hiding it, so I can know where to search it out and take it back.”

Radha is so happy to be with Krsna! Her happiness is visible in the brilliance of Her complexion. Rati thinks, “Because of Your fair complexion You are called Gauri, but that fairness is not white, it’s golden. Therefore You are Kanaka Gauri.”

Just as devotees pray to Rupa Gosvami and Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, they may also pray to Rupa-manjari and Rati-manjari:

“I will constantly serve the lotus feet of Sri Rupa-manjari. Her lotus feet are my only mantra and my medicinal herb. O Sri Rati- manjari! O divine goddess! Please he merciful to me. Please give the shelter of your lotus feet!”

**Verse 73**

*govardhanadri-nikate mukutena narma-*  
*lila-vidagdha-sirasam madhusudanena*  
*dana-cchalena bhavatim avarudhyamanam*  
*draksyami kim bhru-kuti-darpita-netra-yugmam*

**“On the day the crest jewel of clever pranksters, Madhusudana, stops You on the pretext of collecting a toll near Govardhana Hill, will I be there to see Your knitted eyebrows and Your eyes as they burn with pride?”**

Commentary: Krsna enjoys two kinds of pastimes: regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika). The regular pastimes take place every day at the exact same time, events such as Radha’s cooking breakfast for Krsna or Krsna’s taking the cows out to pasture. Occasional pastimes may take place only once, like the killing of demons, or they may be seasonal, like the Holi festival. Krsna’s toll pastime at Dana-ghati near Govardhana is one such occasional pastime.

Rati-manjari is like Srimati Radharani’s shadow. She is inseparable from her mistress. However, her proximity to Radha is for service only, not for her own enjoyment. As a gopi, Rati maintains the same austere conduct as a sannyasi would in Lord Caitanya's pastimes. For example, in the evening she delivers sweets to Nandagrama, and when Yasoda wants to feed her, Dhanistha tells Yasoda, “Not to mention eating, Rati will not even think of drinking water unless Radha has already eaten.”

On the day of a sacrifice conducted by the brahmanas at Govinda-kunda, Radha and Her friends gather at Her lake and walk in a colourful convoy along Govardhana Hill, anticipating that they will meet Krsna along the way. Rati asks Radha, “May I also go with You?”

Radha welcomes Rati with a smile but asks, “Why do You want to come?”

And Rati replies, “I’ve heard from reliable sources thar a tollbooth has been set up just past Manasa-ganga. They say that the local customs official is especially corrupt and quite aggressive. I should be there to guard You.”

And so Rati —all of thirteen years and with a rather frail build — goes along as Sri Radha’s bodyguard. Eventually they approach a tollbooth that glows with a cloud-black sheen it has borrowed from the colourfully dressed tax collector, Krsna. With His eyes arrogantly flashing and His eyebrows knitted mischievously, Krsna stops the gopis as if He had suddenly lowered a barricade. Then, with the utmost impudence, He demands a duty on the milk products they are carrying. When Radha refuses His request a witty quarrel ensues in which Krsna displays the last word in bawdy humour, for which Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami calls Him mukuta-narma-lila-vidagdha- sirasa (“the crest jewel of clever pranksters”).

*nityam garvini vanya-vartmani misat sangopya gavyadikam*  
*vikrinasi sathe tvam atra patita bhagyena haste 'dya me*  
*tvam baddhvoru-manoja-raja-purato nesyamy avasyam tatha*  
*pritya yacchati mahyam eva sa yatha tarunya-ratnani vah*

**“\[Krsna told Radha:\] Proud thief! I know that You regularly travel in these forest pathways, carefully hiding these milk products and lucratively selling them on the black market. By good fortune You have now fallen into My hands. I will now arrest You, bind You with ropes, and take You before King Kamadeva. He will certainly be pleased to reward Me by giving Me the precious jewel of Your youth.”**

Krsna’s words may strike one as arrogant, crude, and derisive, but to Radha and the gopis they arc like sweet honey oozing from a beehive. And so Rati addresses Him as Madhusudana, the lord of sweetness.

Although Krsna and His friends repeatedly and forcefully demand outrageous taxes from the gopis, Radha challenges the validity of their assessments with Her glittering cakora eyes, defiant eyebrows, and a flood of angry, crooked words. And although Rati doesn’t stand out as a formidable bodyguard, her presence at Dana-ghati is of inestimable benefit not only to Srimati Radharani, but to all devotees.

Upon Rupa Gosvami’s request, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami would later recount in his Dana-keli-cintamani everything he saw and heard that morning as Rati-manjari. Vaisnavas devoted to the pastimes of Radha and Krsna treasure that book as they would a cintamani gem.

*radha-madhavayor dana-keli-cintamanim girau*  
*labdham andhena viksantam srimad-rupa-ganah priyah*

**“A blind person found this cintamani jewel of Radha’s and Madhava’s dana-keli pastimes that transpired at the base of Govardhana Hill. That blind man prays that the dear followers of Srila Rupa Gosvami become pleased by gazing at this jewel.”**

**Verse 74**

*tava tanu-vara-gandhasangi-vatena candra-*  
*vali-kara-krta-malli-keli-talpac cchalena*  
*madhura-mukhi mukundam kunda-tire milantam*  
*madhupam iva kadaham viksya darpam karisye*

**“O sweet-faced girl! On the day that a kindly breeze carries Your peerless bodily fragrance to a pastime bed decorated by Candravali’s own hands, will I see Mukunda find a clever excuse to fly like a black bee to the shore of Your lake where You wait for Him?”**

Commentary: A meeting was scheduled at Radha-kunda. Srimati Radharani arrived on time, but Krsna has still not come. Rupa and Rati are there to witness how fate throws Radharani into the role of the cheated heroine (vipralabdha). No matter how hard they try to cheer Her up, Radha’s unhappiness increases with every passing minute. Wringing Her hands, Radha paces in and out of the grove, berating Krsna with abusive language one moment and praising His kindness the next. At last Her eyes become two fountains of tears. Suffering intolerable pain, She faints.

Frantic, Rupa and Rati revive Radha, who is heartbroken to find that Krsna is still not there. Radha wanders along the lakeshore until She sits down on a solitary seat, dejected, and aimlessly throws pebbles into the water. In a brooding melody (gauri-raga) She sings a melancholy song, similar to this song She once sang on the bank of the river Yamuna:

*komala-kusumavali-krta-cayanam*  
*apasaraya rati-lila-sayanam*

**“Take away this soft bed of flowers meant for transcendental amorous pastimes!”**

*sri-harinadya ne lebhe sam aye*  
*hanta janam sakhi saranam kam aye*

**“Today I have not attained the happiness of Hari’s company! O friend! Of whom can I take shelter now?”**

*vidhrta-manohara-gandha-vilasam*  
*ksipa yamuna-tata-bhuvi pata-vasam*

**“Scatter this charming aromatic powder meant to inspire romance on Yamuna’s shore!”**

*labdham avehi nisantim ayamam*  
*munca sanatana-sangati-kamam*

**“O mind! Be peaceful now! Give up this desire for the company of the Eternal Person!”**

The sound of Radha's plaintive voice and the content of Her despondent song are both intolerable to Rupa and Rati, and so they make a plan: Rupa should stay behind while Rati goes out in search of Krsna. He must be somewhere in Vraja, and Rupa suspects that somewhere to be Gauri-tirtha.

But the manjaris are not the only ones to hear Radha’s plaintive appeal. Vayu, Krsna’s great devotee, is everywhere, and he decides to answer Radha’s plea for help. While Rati is running along the parikrama path by Govardhana, a breeze carries the fragrance of Radha’s body to Gauri-tirtha, where Candravali is happily pampering Krsna.
