One of Srimati Radharani’s names is Gandharvika because Her bodily fragrance (gandha) perfumes all of Vraja.When He catches wind of it, Krsna is startled by the fragrance of Radha’s body, like a person forcibly awoken from a dream, and He suddenly remembers where He is supposed to be. In fact, the very fragrance makes Govinda mad with love, which is why Radha is also called Gandhonmadita-govinda.

Thinking quickly, Krsna tells Candravali, “Devi! I forgot that at midday I was supposed to give cows in charity to the brahmanas. I must return home at once.”

Naive and submissive, Candravali accepts her fate and says, “Do Your duty, but please come back as soon as You can.”

Krsna rises to His feet, tidies Himself, and hurries off to Radha-kunda. He is like a bee abandoning one blossom to follow the scent of a superior blossom instead. Somewhere along the parikrama path He literally runs into Rati.

From her angry gaze and trembling lips Krsna can tell that He has His work cut out for Him. He thinks, “If I don’t first win over Rati-manjari, then Radha will never talk to Me.” Beneath a banyan tree Krsna humbly and honestly explains why He is late.

He tells Rati that He was on His way to Radha-kunda as agreed, but was waylaid by Padma, who made Him feel guilty for neglecting Candravali’s invitation for a momentary visit. Krsna could not refuse, and so He went to visit Candra’s grove near the shrine of Durga-devi. “But somehow I lost track of time and a few minutes became an hour,” He concludes.

Rati wags her finger in Krsna’ face, “It’s that ‘somehow’ that makes me so angry. That ‘somehow’ turned into excruciating torture for Radharani, who is just now making Her lake overflow with tears.”

Krsna is visibly disturbed to hear this. With no other alternative He surrenders to Rati without reservation. She is won over by the stream of litanies He employs to beg for her forgiveness and convince her to intercede on His behalf. Rati then leads Krsna back to Radha- kunda, where she explains everything to Rupa and begs her permission to take Krsna into the grove where Radha waits. Rupa agrees.

Taking Krsna by the wrist, Rati enters the grove. Radha is sitting on the edge of the bed. Her beautiful face is stained with mascara, Her eyes are red from crying, and Her tears have muddied the ground. Krsna waits timidly behind Rati, who says, “O Madhura-mukhi, my sweet-faced girl! Just as Lord Visnu never rejects a surrendered soul, please do not reject this wayward cowherd.”

Srimati Radharani’s heart has been softened by Krsna’s absence.

She doesn’t want to quarrel; She just wants to he with Krsna. For the first time in what seems like ages Her face lights up and shows sweetness instead of sorrow. Still unsure of Himself, Krsna smiles sheepishly and shows His kunda-flower teeth, for which Rati calls him Mukunda. Now speechless with joy, Radha simply nods Her head gently and pats the seat beside Her. Rati whispers in Krsna’s ear, “Sit down!”

*na muncec charana-yatam api dustam dayamayah*  
*ato gandharvike ha ha muncainam naiva tadrsam*

**“O Gandharvika! Just as Lord Visnu never rejects a surrendered soul, please don’t reject me.”**

**Verse 75**

*samastad unmatta-bhramara-kula-jhankara-nikarair*  
*lasat-padma-stomair api vihaga-ravair api param*  
*sakhi-vrndaih sviyaih sarasi madhure prana-patina*  
*kada draksyamas te sasi-mukhi navam keli-nivaham*

**“O moon-faced girl! When will we behold You and Your friends enact ever fresh water sports with the Lord of Your heart in Your own sweet lake, which is filled with the humming of bees, the cooing of birds, and a host of blooming lotuses?”**

Commentary: In this verse Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami uses the plural pronoun “we” to indicate that he is not alone in his eagerness to see Radha’s and Krsna’s water games in Radha-kunda; other manjaris are also eager to see them. Caitanya Mahaprabhu once emerged from ecstatic trance and described to His companions how He, along with some gopis, had watched Krsna’s water pastimes with Radharani:

*tire rahi' dekhi ami sakhi-gana-sange*  
*eka-sakhi sakhi-gane dekhaya sei range*

**“I saw this pastime as I stood on the bank of the Yamuna in the company of the gopis. One gopi was showing some other gopis the pastimes of Radha and Krsna in the water.”**

After Their meeting and reconciliation, Radha and Krsna exchange many gifts of love. When They become weary, Krsna suggests that They refresh themselves, in the company of the gopis, with a swim. Krsna, Radha, and the sakhis change into simple bathing clothes and enter the nectarean waters of Radha-kunda as the manjaris stand on the shore as spectators and supporters of their mistress: if Radha is leading in a game, they cheer Her on, but if Krsna has the upper hand, they keep silent.

As the inventor of all frolicsome diversions, Krsna has unlimited games He likes to play with the gopis in which He alone is one competing team and all the gopis comprise the other. Their favourite game is splashing, in which both sides see who can out-splash the other. The winner is awarded the stake of a wager by the loser, which is generally a kiss. In this way, whatever the outcome of the game, everyone is a winner.

There are also different games of hide-and-seek, where the contestants sometimes hide amongst the lotuses and sometimes underwater.

A third game is called “escape.” The gopis form a circle around Radha and Krsna and join hands beneath the water to form a net. Krsna must somehow escape by swimming underwater without being caught. Radha begins the game by saying, “All right! My friends will tighten the net of their arms while You try to escape.” Krsna smiles boastfully and then ducks underwater. The gopis, their hands well beneath the surface of the water, move towards the centre of the circle from where Radha cheers them on. But when the net is drawn, they find that Krsna has disappeared.

“Where is He?” asks Radha.

The gopis kick their feet in the little space left between them and Radha, but there’s no Krsna to be found. “He must have escaped!” says Visakha.

Radharani frowns at Her friends, “Now the question is, who let Him escape?”

The girls look at Radha blankly and swear that Krsna could not have gotten past them. But where is He? Everyone looks around, but Krsna is nowhere in sight. As the minutes pass, Radha’s concern turns into panic. “What if He drowned?” She thinks. The girls begin to chatter wildly amongst themselves. Then, suddenly, Krsna shoots out of the water right in front of Radha and scares the life out of Her.

Laughing at the gopis, Krsna calls out, “Escape! Escape!”

Radha says, annoyed, “How did You escape the net and get back again, unnoticed?”

With a philosophical air, Krsna replies, “It was easy. I am as much inside everything as I am outside. I simply made Myself one with the water and flowed out between your fingers. In the same way I flowed back in again.”

Now it is the gopis' turn to laugh. “That’s crazy,” Radha replies. “You must have had too much sun. You need to cool off.” And with that She begins to splash Krsna vigorously. At once all the other girls bombard Him with splashes from all sides, filling His ears, eyes,and nose with water. Helpless but blissful, Krsna calls out, “I give up! I give up!”

As Rati-manjari watches the water fight, it appears to her that Krsna is like a cloud that occasionally covers the moon of Radha’s face with kisses, and thus splashes the cataka-like gopis’ eyes with blissful showers. The gopis splash Him with water, but Sri Radha showers Him with rasa. Thus, because the moon is the source of rasa, Rati calls her beloved mistress Sasi-mukhi.

**Verse 76**

*sarovara-lasat-tate madhupa-gunji-kunjantare*  
*sphutat-kusuma-sankule vividha-puspa-sanghair muda*  
*arista-jayina kada tava varoru bhusa-vidhir*  
*vidhasyata iha priyam mama sukhabdhim atanvata*

**“O girl with beautiful thighs! When will the ocean of my bliss overflow to see the subduer of Aristasura decorate You with flowers in a grove that abounds with blossoming flowers and humming bees on Your lake’s charming shore?”**

Commentary: In Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s description of Radha’s and Krsna’s water pastimes, the Lord describes Himself as standing amidst the gopis on the shore.

Lord Caitanya describes how Krsna, after His water sports, takes the gopis onto the shore. There the maidservants who were watching now massage the divine couple and Their friends with scented oil and amalaki paste, which they then wash off with another bath. After dressing in fresh clothes, Krsna and His entourage go to a jewelled palace where Vrnda has them decorated with flowers, garlands, and other floral ornaments.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu then describes a picnic with Krsna and the gopis and concludes His narration with Radha and Krsna taking rest in a grove while Their friends and maidservants rest in other groves nearby. He says, dekhi' amara sukhi haila mana: “When I saw this, My mind was very happy.”

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami expresses his aspiration with words similar to Lord Caitanya’s, *mama sukhabdhim atanvata*: “When will the ocean of my bliss increase to see...” However, by using the word iha (“here”) Dasa Gosvami indicates that while aspiring to serve as Rati-manjari, he is also aware that he is at Radha-kunda in Bhauma Vrndavana in his sadhaka form as an elderly sannyasi. He is not fully absorbed in his internal identity.

In this connection, Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami describes three levels of consciousness exemplified in the behaviour of Caitanya Mahaprabhu:

*kabhu bhave magna, kabhu ardha-bahya-sphurti*  
*kabhu bahya-sphurti— tina rite prabhu-sthiti*

**“The Lord would maintain Himself in three states of consciousness: sometimes He merged totally in ecstatic emotion, sometimes He was in partial external consciousness, and sometimes He was in full external consciousness.”**

In partial external consciousness Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami is eager to see Krsna serve Srimati Radharani. Of the unlimited facets of the Absolute Truth, the one in which supreme rasa personified serves supreme love personified is the one favoured and worshipped by Gaudiya Vaisnavas. Krsna, who has subdued the powerful demon Arista, is Himself subdued by the love of slender-limbed Radharani.

Earlier, Rupa and Radha decorated Krsna. Now, on the plea of having been defeated in the water, Krsna asks if He can decorate Radharani. The grove is heavy with the aroma of blossoming flowers. So dense is the fragrance that it appears like a fine mist that attracts and maddens the bumblebees, the natural messengers of Cupid. Radharani sits upon a golden dais and directs Krsna to serve Her, a mood known as svadhina-bhartrka — a heroine who controls her lover.

Radha says, “Draw nice pictures on My breasts and cheeks, decorate My hips with a sash, twine a garland of flowers in My braid, and decorate My hands and feet with bracelets made from lotus petals.”

Krsna has received His orders and He carries them out obediently and with great pleasure. All the while, Krsna and Rati send messages to each other through their glances.

Casting a look at Rati, Krsna seems to say, ‘‘Rati! Radha is now treating Me like a maidservant and I can serve Her just like you."

In return, Rati’s glance says, “Indeed, You are very fortunate.”

Krsna’s eyes enquire, “How am I doing?"

Rati’s eyes respond, “I’ll tell You later."

Absorbed in service, Krsna takes flowers, garlands, and ornaments from the hands of Radha’s transcendental ladies-in-waiting. He happily paints incomparably beautiful designs and pictures on the upper portion of Radharani’s breasts. The blue lotus flowers He places on both Her ears are so fragrant that they make the bees go mad. And lastly, He threads an equally delicate lotus flower into Her braid.

Rati carefully watches Krsna. She wants to learn the technique He uses for every service, no matter how small or large, because she knows that Radha prefers Krsna’s artistry first and foremost.

In obedience to Sri Radha’s order, Krsna ties a sash around Her hips. She has to stand so that Krsna can tie the floral cloth around Her, and when She does She is face to face with Her beloved. By tying the sash, Krsna unintentionally touches Radha’s thighs. This intimate encounter powerfully enchants Krsna, who momentarily reels from the force of Radha’s overwhelming radiance.

Rati giggles and thinks, “O Varoru! O beautiful-thighed one! Is it Your delicate thighs, or is it perhaps Your flawless face that has paralysed Krsna? I think it must be a potent combination of the two.”

Once some gopis were discussing the wonder of Radha’s capacity for dominating Krsna. One gopi said, “Even though in Their pastimes Radha is like a campaka vine subordinate to the Krsna tamala tree, we also know that because of Her great passion and domineering spirit, Radharani makes Krsna into Her subordinate. In short, She controls Krsna with Her love.”

**Verse 77**

*sphita-svantam-kayacit sa-rabhasam acirenarpyamanair darodyan-*  
*nana-pusporu-gunjaphala-nikara-lasat-keki-pincha-prapancaih*  
*sotkampam-racyamanah krta-ruci-harinotphullam angam-vahantyah*  
*svaminyah kesa-pasah kim u mama nayananandam uccair vidhata*

**“When will the joy of my eyes increase upon seeing a maiden hastily bring blooming flowers, large gunja beads, and peacock feathers that Hari braids into Radha’s hair, as His body shivers and Her limbs blossom in Their mutual ecstasy?”**

Commentary: The intimate contact between Krsna and Radha described in the previous verse gives rise to amorous enjoyment between the divine couple, following which Radharani orders Krsna to braid Her hair. Because Rati-manjari is watching Krsna, hoping to learn His techniques, Krsna sends another maidservant to bring the flowers, gunja beads, and peacock feathers He needs. As Krsna goes about His service, Rati notices something wonderful, something even more wonderful than Krsna’s artistry. She notices that Radha’s and Krsna’s absorption in amorous love has caused Them to become transcendentally confused and to each identify Him or Herself with the other. This state of affairs, called prema-vilasa-vivarta, may result in, amongst other things, Krsna wearing Radha’s clothing or vice versa. Usually, Krsna’s hair is decorated with peacock feathers and gunja beads, not Radha’s, so in this verse it appears that Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami is chronicling an incidence of prema-vilasa-vivarta.

In the private talks between Ramananda Raya and Caitanya Mahaprabhu, Ramananda hesitates to introduce a description of this particular state of spiritual affairs because it is a very confidential topic. Yet, because the Lord says, age kaha ara: “Please go forward and say more,” Ramananda sings a song of his own composition, which quotes Srimati Radharani:

*pahilehi raga nayana-bhange bhela*  
*anudina badhala, avadhi na gela*  
*na so ramana, na hama ramam*  
*dunhu-mana manobhava pesala jani’*

**“Alas, before We met there was an initial attachment between Us brought about by an exchange of glances. In this way attachment evolved. That attachment has gradually grown, and there is no limit to it. Now that attachment has become a natural sequence between Ourselves. It is not that it is due to Krsna, the enjoyer, nor is it due to Me, for I am the enjoyed. It is not like that. This attachment was made possible by mutual meeting. This mutual exchange of attraction is known as manobhava, or Cupid. Krsna’s mind and My mind have merged together.”**

Ramananda Raya describes a stage in the development of love, manobhava, in which the minds of lover and beloved merge together. This is not an existential oneness as the Mayavadis would have it, but an emotional oneness that facilitates the interchange of identities, also known as pranaya, between Radha and Krsna. It is this state of affairs that defines Caitanya Mahaprabhu. It allows Him — who is Krsna — to fully lose Himself in Radha's mood. Svarupa Damodara Gosvami describes this state in the following famous verse, upon which Jagadananda Pandita later composed the book Prema Vivarta as a treatise:

*radha krsna-pranaya-vikrtir hladini saktir asmad*  
*ekatmanav api bhuvi pura deha-bhedam gatau tau*  
*caitanyakhyam prakaiam adhuna tad-dvayam caikyam aptam*  
*radha-bhava-dyuti-suvalitam naumi krsna-svarupam*

**“The loving affairs of Sri Radha and Krsna are transcendental manifestations of the Lord’s internal pleasure-giving potency. Although Radha and Krsna are one in Their identity, They separated Themselves eternally. Now these two transcendental identities have again united, in the form of Sri Krsna Caitanya. I bow down to Him, who has manifested Himself with the sentiment and complexion of Srimati Radharani although He is Krsna Himself.”**

What Ramananda Raya calls the “merging of minds” and Svarupa Damodara Gosvami calls “manifesting a sentiment” is also described by Rupa Gosvami as the “melding of hearts”:

*radhaya bhavatas ca citta-jatura svedair vilapya kramad*  
*yunjann adri-nikunja-kunjara-pate nirdhuta-bheda-bhramam*  
*citraya svayam anvaranjayad iha brahmanda-harmyodare*  
*bhuyobhir nava-raga-hingula-bharaih srngara-karuh krti*

**“O my Lord, You live in the forest of Govardhana Hill, and, like the king of elephants, You are expert in the art of amorous love. O master of the universe, Your heart and Srimati Radharani's heart are just like shellac and are now melted in Your spiritual perspiration. Therefore one can no longer distinguish between You and Srimati Radharani. Now You have mixed Your newly invoked affection, which is like vermilion, with Your melted hearts, and for the benefit of the whole world You have painted both Your hearts red within this great palace of the universe.”**

The primary symptoms of prema-vilasa-vivarta are rebelliousness and confusion, both consequences of how one under the influence of such a loving mood perceives his or her circumstances.

For example, when Radha is with Krsna, She feels separated from Him, and when separated from Him, She sees Him before Her. Moreover, for Radha all sensual encounters appear reversed: being at home feels like being in the forest and being in the forest like being at home, a moment lasts as long as a millennium and a millennium as long as a moment, sorrow feels like happiness and happiness like sorrow, wakefulness is like sleep and sleep is like being awake, and finally, cold feels hot and hot feels cold. But the most wonderful thing is that She feels that She is Krsna, and He feels that He is Radha.

Rati is enthralled by this exchange of identities between Radha and Krsna; thus, she does not want to leave the kunja. It is also for this reason that the service of bringing ingredients for decorating Radha’s hair is given to another happy maidservant.

Thinking Himself to be Radha, Krsna decorates Radha’s hair with flowers and peacock feathers just as the gopis or gopas usually decorate Him. In Krsna’s boundless pleasure His entire body trembles; in Radha’s limitless bliss, Her entire body blossoms with goosebumps. Rati’s ecstasy knows no bounds, but she anticipates that when the divine couple’s loving intoxication recedes, They will resume Their original identities.

It was the same with Caitanya Mahaprabhu. When in trance watching Radha’s and Krsna’s water sports, He was exceedingly happy, but when His associates brought Him back to external consciousness, He said:

*hena-kale more dhari, maha-kolahala kari',*  
*tumi-saba ihan land aila*  
*kanha yamuna, vrndavana, kanha krsna, gopi-gana,*  
*sei sukha bhanga karaila!”*

**“Suddenly, all of you created a great tumult and picked Me up and brought Me back here. Where now is the river Yamuna? Where is Vrndavana? Where are Krsna and the gopis? You have broken My happy dream!”**

Similarly, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s trance is abruptly broken, his bliss is gone, and he is again in his cottage by Radha-kunda. In the way that Caitanya Mahaprabhu looked at His associates with sorrowful eyes, Dasa Gosvami looks at the walls of his cottage and repeats the Lord’s words, “Why have you brought me here?”

**Verse 78**

*madhavam madana-keli-vibhrame*  
*mattaya sarasijena bhavatya*  
*taditam sumukhi viksya kintt iyam*  
*gudha-hasya-vadana bhavisyati*

**“Sweet-faced girl! When will I gently laugh upon seeing You proudly strike Madhava with a lotus flower in the excitement of Your amorous pastimes?”**

Commentary: Every aspect of devotional service has its prescribed process. By gauging one’s ability to follow the process, one can gauge one’s overall perfection. A mistake in following the process is called vibhrama. Caitanya Mahaprabhu rejected Junior Haridasa lor a slight transgression in the rules of sannyasa, and Balarama killed Romaharsana Suta for failing to properly show honour to the Lord. Now, during the divine couple’s amorous pastimes, Krsna also makes a mistake and Srimati Radharani corrects Him by striking Him with a lotus, just as a teacher disciplines a student. She has every right to do so because She is His prema-guru, Krsna having surrendered to Her as Her prema-sisya.

*radhikara prema — guru, ami — sisya nala*  
*sada ama nana nrtye nacaya udbhata*

**“The love of Radhika is My teacher, and I am Her dancing pupil. Her prema makes Me dance various novel dances.”**

Of course, in the realm of pure devotion, not to mention the realm of loving devotion, there is no such thing as a mistake. The strength of ecstatic emotion (bhava) nullifies the negative effect of a technical error in service. For example, in ecstasy Vidura offered Krsna the peel of the banana instead of the fruit itself, hut Krsna accepted and ate the peel nonetheless. Because of Vidura’s love for Krsna, such a mistake was completely overlooked by the Lord.

However, as part of the variety of the spiritual dimension, Yogamaya induces the Vraja-vasis, and even Krsna Himself, to make apparent mistakes. Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura calls these contrivances of Yogamaya “seeming mistakes” (vibhrama-vilasa). For example, after Krsna pulled down the two arjuna trees with the mortar and brought all of Gokula running to His aid, Nanda Maharaja scolded His wife for putting Krsna into such danger. “How could you do such a thing?” he angrily demanded.

At times of intimacy between Radha and Krsna the manjaris may leave the grove, but from outside they watch what goes on through the open spaces between the creepers. By watching and serving Radha’s amorous pastimes with Krsna, the manjaris — although qualified to be heroines themselves hut preferring not to he—nurture their own divine lust (kama), which lies at the very core of their eternal spiritual identities. This cultivation of the manjaris’ amorous spirit is made possible by their exclusive dependence upon Radha’s mercy:

*sprsati yadi mukundo radhikam tat sakhinam*  
*bhavati vapusi kampa sveda romanca vaspam*  
*adhara madhu mudasyas cet pibatyesa yatnad*  
*bhavati bata tad asam mattata citram etat*

**“How amazing! When Mukunda touches Radhika, Her girlfriends all start shivering, crying, and perspiring from joy. And when He drinks the nectar of Her lips, they all go mad.”**

Through the latticework of the grove Rati sees that Krsna no longer knows what He is doing, so bewildered is He by loving ecstasy. At this Rati giggles, and Krsna, hearing Rati’s tittering, regains His senses. In her mind, Rati tells Radha, “Sumukhi! Your face is especially sweet when You are disciplining Krsna. But You know, even though He is the husband of the goddess of fortune, it appears that His wife has failed to properly train Him in these finer arts. Thus it is proper that You do so in her stead.”

**Verse 79**

*su-lalita-nija-baht-dslista-gosthendra-sunoh*  
*su-valgutatara-baht-aslesa-divyan-natamsa*  
*madhura-madana-ganam tanvati tena sardham*  
*subhaga-mukhi mudam me ha kada dasyasi tvam*

**“O fortunate girl! May I watch with great joy as You and the prince of Vraja sing sweet love songs, His long arm resting on Your shoulder, and Your vine-like arm wrapped around His waist?”**

Commentary: The divine couple have left the grove to walk freely through the gardens and forests surrounding Radha-kunda. Arm in arm, They feel great joy at each other’s touch, and Their complexions colour the surroundings — golden to one side and cloud-blue to the other. Even the animals and birds are tinged with these hues. Radha and Krsna enjoy the seasonal forests — each one perpetually displaying a single season, from spring through winter — marvelling in the bounty and opulence of Their transcendental realm. Sometimes Rati walks ahead of Them and throws flower petals in Their path, sometimes she walks behind and fans Them.

As they walk, Radha and Krsna sing sweet-sounding love songs. Sometimes Radha sings to Krsna, sometimes He sings to Her, sometimes They sing together. Radha’s and Krsna’s soul-stirring voices and lyrics rouse the birds, animals, and even the trees to join in the prema-sankirtana. In this way the entire forest resounds with the sound vibration of the divine couple’s names, qualities, and forms. All that is missing is the music of the flute. Krsna is too absorbed to play it, but it doesn’t want to be left out and so it plays itself, thus completing the transcendental concert.

Completely under the dominion of Radha’s love, Krsna sings songs such this one:

*pekhalum braja-naba-nari tarunima saisaba bujha-i na pana*  
*hrdaya-nayana-gati-rite so kiye ana nahe paratite*  
*aichana hera-ite gon hatha sane paithala mana maha mori*  
*tabahim kusuma-sara bhora chutala banba putala hiya mora*

**“I have carefully watched the girls of Vraja, but I cannot tell whether they are grown women or still young girls.**

**“I watch their gestures, eyes, and hearts, but I cannot decide. “One day an exceptionally beautiful, fair young gopi forcefully attacked My heart.**

**“She shot a flower-arrow of Cupid at Me, and now My heart is gravely wounded \[like the sun falling in love with the moon\].”**

Hearing Krsna’s words, Radha blushes with happiness, and then, overcoming all reservation, She sings in response:

*mani nao manika nao ancale bandhile rao*  
*phula nao ye kene karibese*  
*nari na karita vidhi tuya hena gunanidhi*  
*laiya phiritama dese dese*  
*aguru candana haitama tuya ange makha raitama*  
*ghamiya paditama ranga paya*  
*ki mora manera sadha vamana haye canda hata*  
*vidhi ki sadha purabe amara*

**“O My beloved! You are neither a sapphire, nor a diamond that I can keep tied in the end of My veil. You are not a flower with which**

**I could decorate My hair. If I were not a woman, I would flee with You, the ocean of divine qualities, to another country.**

**“If I were aguru or sandalwood, then I could be smeared over Your limbs, and when You perspired I would fall at Your reddish lotus feet. What desires I have! I am like a dwarf that wants to touch the moon. Will the creator ever give Me what I longfor?”**

Humbled by Sri Radha’s song of surrender, Krsna stops and looks into Her eyes, searching His heart for a way to best express what He feels. There are so many words, but He finds that none of them will do. Then He begins to sing the premier anthem of love, and when Radha hears it She joins Him by singing responsively.

*hare krsna hare krsna krsna krsna hare hare*  
*hare rama hare rama rama rama hare hare*

For both Radha and Krsna, this short song composed only of Their names says everything They want to say. When Krsna sings it, the meaning is,

**“O Radha! My uncommon features steal everyone’s mind, but Your unfathomable sweetness captures My very self. Eager for wonderful pastimes, the echo of Your love brought Me to the bank of Your lake. And upon arriving here I discovered a treasure-mine of bliss by enjoying You and being enjoyed by You. O Goddess! You, and You alone, put an end to My miseries and give Me true happiness.”**

Srimati Radharani responds with the same words, but when sung by Her, they mean:

**“O Hari! Just hearing Your name and recalling Your unique sweetness enthrals My mind. Today, the fragrance of Your body drew Me from My home into this forest. And when I arrived, You, the transcendental Cupid, whisked Me away into a grove in which You revealed Yourself to be the embodiment of love itself. O Hari! In the activities of love, You are like a lion by the boldness You display.”**

*antanyaga-su-ratna-mandape*  
*sviya-kundam anu varsabhanavi*  
*syamalena saha-gana-kautukam*  
*kurvati sphuratu me sakhi-vrta*

**“May King Vrsabhanu’s daughter appear before Me as She sings wonderful duets with dark-complexioned Krsna in the company of Her gopi friends within a beautiful jewel pavilion by the shore of Radha-kunda.”**

**Verse 80**

*jitva pasaka-khelayam acchidya muralim hareh*  
*ksiptam mayi tvaya devi gopayisyami tam kada*

**“O Queen! After You defeat Krsna in a game of dice and snatch away the wagered flute, will You toss it to me so I can hide it somewhere?”**

Commentary: To a materialist, Krsna’s eternal, eight fold daily pastimes might seem boring because of their constant repetition. Such a viewpoint is, however, blind to spiritual truths; the laws of nature in the spiritual realm are different than they are in this material world. In the spiritual world there is no influence of mundane time: there is no past, present, or future. Everything there exists in the eternal present. And thus Krsna and His pastimes remain always fresh. In this regard, the Lord Himself says:

*amara madhurya nitya nava nava haya*  
*sva-sva-prema-anurupa bhakte asvadaya*

**“My sweetness is always newer and newer. Devotees taste it according to their own respective love.”**

This attribute of being “always newer and newer” is not limited to Krsna’s sweetness, but is inherent in all things related to Him, such as His beauty, love, service, pastimes, entourage, abode — and on and on.

Moreover, the ever present nature of spiritual time ensures that every pastime — no matter how many times it is repeated — appears to those participating as if it has never occurredbefore. Thus every pastime is brimming with the kind of newness and excitement expected of a unique event. Lord Brahma explains, *nimesardhakhyo va vrajati na hi yatrapi samayah*: “...and transcendental time, ever present, without past or future, eternally exists, not subject to passing away even for the space of half a moment...”

Krsna’s transcendental pastimes are called nitya-nava-navayamana, which means that “one can go on chanting and hearing about \[them\]...and never feel tired but remain fresh and eager to hear more and more.” This is due to the spiritual or internal pleasuregiving potency of Krsna.

Just as that pleasure potency gives bliss to Krsna in His pastimes, it also gives devotees bliss in devotional service, of which chanting and hearing are the foundational activities. The ever fresh nature of Krsna’s names, as well as the ever-increasing bliss derived from serving those names (by chanting, hearing, and remembering them), is wonderfully expressed in the following verse by Rupa Gosvami:

*tunde tandavini ratim vitanute tundavali-labdhaye*  
*karna-kroda-kadambini ghatayate karnarbudebhyah sprham*  
*cetah-prangana-sangini vijayate sarvendriyanam krtim*  
*no jane janita kiyadbhir amnaih krsneti varna-dvayi*

**“I do not know how much nectar the two syllables ‘Krs-na’ have produced. When the holy name of Krsna is chanted, it appears to dance within the mouth. We then desire many, many mouths. When that name enters the holes of the ears, we desire many millions of ears. And when the holy name dances in the courtyard of the heart, it conquers the activities of the mind, and therefore all the senses become inert.”**

In the presence of Radharani — the full embodiment of Krsna’s pleasure potency — Krsna’s excitement makes it impossible for Him to resist the gopis’ proposal to play dice. Generally Krsna wins the games requiring physical strength, such as splashing, swinging, and drinking honey-wine. But can He win at a game that requires moresubtle skill and intelligence? Radha and Her friends consult Lalita on the matter and conclude that He cannot; thus they confidently challenge Him to a game of dice.

Beneath a tree at the edge of a grove and surrounded by beautiful fair-faced gopis, Krsna blends into the sapphire platform on which He sits. In fact, He almost seems invisible. Opposite Krsna is Radha, and beside Her are Lalita and other prominent gopis, their minds burning with love and the exhilarating prospect of defeating Krsna. Rati-manjari sits midway between her mistress and her master.

Srimati Radharani starts to shake the dice, but Krsna stops Her and suggests, “Let’s make the game interesting by agreeing upon a wager. For the first throw I bet my Kaustubha gem against Your pearl necklace, and for the second, My flute against Your Lalita.”

Lalita is speechless with indignation, but Radharani replies, “The second wager is not even. You are comparing a stick to a jewelled wand.” After some discussion on the mystical nature of the flute the second wager is accepted, as are successive wagers for successive throws.Against good advice, magnanimous Radha allows Krsna to go first, and He throws a winning number. Admitting defeat, Radha offers Him Her necklace and then takes up the dice with determination. Lalita whispers encouraging words in her friend’s ear, and Radha shakes the dice. Krsna keeps His lotus eyes fixed on Radha’s hands to make sure She doesn’t cheat, but the flashing of Her rings and the jingling of Her bracelets mesmerise Him and He loses His concentration. Radha throws a winning number!

“Not fair!” calls Krsna. “I couldn’t see Your hands.”

“That’s not My fault,” Radha replies. “I won fairly. Now hand over Your flute as We agreed.”

But Krsna continues to call foul and holds the flute tightly to His chest, refusing to part with it. The gopis, the parrots, and even the monkeys, all chide Krsna, creating an overwhelming din, but Hari holds His ground.

“Give Me the flute!” demands Radha.

“I will not!” Krsna firmly replies.

Suddenly, Radha throws Herself at Krsna with full force and the electrifying touch of Her body stuns Him. Reeling in ecstasy, Krsna loosens His grip on the flute, enabling Radha to slide it out of His hands. As Krsna swoons, Radha secretly tosses the flute to Rati, along with a glance that says, “Quick! Hide it!”

It only takes moments for Krsna to recover from His ecstatic stupor and grab hold of Radha’s arm. Realising He has been robbed, Krsna complains, “First You cheat at dice, and now You steal My flute.” Radha’s body shivers with waves of bliss at Krsna’s touch, but She feigns indifference, pulls Her arm out of His grasp, and turns to leave.

Krsna yells out, “Thief! I won’t let You get away without returning My flute.”

As Krsna starts to follow Radha, Lalita blocks His path and assails Him, “Scoundrel! You are not only a sore loser, but a libeller as well. If You want the flute, ask Rati for it.”

As Rati hears her name she turns to leave, at the same time discreetly passing off the flute to Rupa-manjari. But Krsna grabs onto Rati’s dress, making her tremble in both ecstasy and fear. Covering her face with her small hands, Rati cries out excitedly, “O merciful one! Let me go. I don’t have Your flute!” But through an opening between her fingers she shoots a glance at Rupa, revealing to Krsna that Rupa has the flute.

In this way, Rati inaugurates a chain reaction in which the gopis pass the flute from one to the other before Krsna can find it on them, thus giving bliss to both the accuser and the accused.

While all this is going on, Rati walks up to Radha and asks, “Why don’t You just return the flute?”

Radha replies with a smile, “I want to keep it for a little while.”

“What for?” Rati asks.

Raising Her beautiful eyebrows, Radha says, “I want to ask the flute to bless Me.”

Rati is amazed. What blessing will Sri Radha ask from a dried-up bamboo stick? In time, while Krsna is busy quarrelling with the other girls, the flute comes around to Radha, who then retires to a grove alone. Of course, Rati follows Her unnoticed and from a short distance eavesdrops as Radha prays:

*acchidram astu hrdayam paripurnam astu*  
*maukharyam astu mitam astu gurutvam astu*  
*krsna-priye sakhi disamsi sad-asisas te*  
*yad vasare murali me karunam karoti*

**“O flute, dear to Krsna! If you grant Me your mercy I will give you many benedictions in return. I will bless you, saying, ‘May you become faultless. May your heart overflow with the nectar of Krsna’s lips. May you become very eloquent. May you become charmingly slender. May you become the object of Krsna's worship.’”**

*sunyatvam hrdaye sa-laghavam idam suskatvam angesu me*  
*maukharyam vraja-natha-nama-kathane dattam bhavatya nijam*  
*tat kim no murali prayacchasi punar govinda-vaktrasavam*  
*yam pitva bhuvanam vase vidadhati nirlajjam udgayasi*

**“O flute! You have blessed Me with the emptiness in your heart, your lightness, the dryness of your body, and your eloquence in constantly chanting the holy name of Vraja’s Lord. Why don’t you now give to Me the nectar of Govinda’s lips, nectar you drink continually and then turn into a song that shamelessly enchants and enslaves the entire world.”**

**Verse 81**

*ayi sumukhi kadaham malati-keli-talpe*  
*madhura-madhura-gosthim bibhratmi vallabhena*  
*manasija-sukhade ’smin mandire smera-gandam*  
*sa-pulaka-tanu-vesa tvam kada vijayami*

**“O beautiful one! Will the time come when the hairs of my body stand up in ecstasy as I fan You in a temple that gives bliss to Cupid, where You lay on a pastime-bed of jasmine flowers, sweetly conversing with Your beloved, Your cheeks blossoming with a smile?”**

Commentary: Rupa Gosvami has instructed devotees attracted to the devotional moods of Vraja to always think of Krsna within themselves and to follow in the footsteps of a Vraja-vasi of their choice. Those aspiring for the service mood of the gopis first follow a manjari. By the grace of that maidservant, they will be able to serve one of the sakhis, and by the grace of that sakhi, they will attain the audience and service of Srimati Radharani.

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami here shows us this process by accepting Rupa-manjari’s guidance and thus, in turn, becoming a servant of Lalita-devi and, finally, Srimati Radharani.

Now, as Rati-manjari, he finds himself fanning Radha and Krsna as They recline in a grove and converse in Cupid’s language. The portrait Dasa Gosvami paints with this verse echoes another verse in Rupa Gosvami’s Utkalika-vallari:

*kadaham sevisye vratati-camari-camara-marud-*  
*vinodena krida-kusuma-sayane nyasta-vapusau*  
*daronmilan-netrau srama-jala-kana-klidya-dalakau*  
*bruvanat anyonyam vraja-nava-yuvanat iha yuvam*

**“O youthful couple of Vraja! When will I serve You by making a breeze with a fan of vines as You recline and converse on a pastime - bed of flowers, Your eyes slightly open and Your flower-petal bodies sprinkled with perspiration?”**

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami again refers to Radharani as Sumukha Sri Radha is always beautiful. But when She is basking in Krsna’s love She is especially stunning. Krsna anoints Radha’s body with His love- laced words, and She in turn anoints Him with Her coquettish replies. In this verbal exchange — as in Their sensual exchanges— Radha and Krsna are completely devoid of desire for personal enjoyment. Their only motives are to give each other happiness. And if either of Them should express a need for loving exchange, They do so only because satisfying that so-called need will give a greater pleasure to the other.

But what is this sweet conversation between Radha and Krsna? Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura has written a book, Surata-kathamrta, which gives an account of these talks and elucidates the aforementioned verse by Rupa Gosvami. What follows is an abridged version of Krsna’s and Radha's talks, which sometimes appear disjointed due to the intoxicated condition of the speakers as They engage in Their amorous sports.Krsna: O My beloved! I consider You to be My teacher, but although learned in the science of amorous love, You still refuse to teach Me. Why is that?

Radha: I know how expert You are at weaving spells to uproot the chastity of pious girls, but why are You showing off in this way?

Krsna: Please do not think Me irreligious. I am simply repeating the moral codes of Cupid’s kingdom, as outlined by Vatsyayana Muni, following which one attains happiness and auspiciousness.

Radha: Even though the chaste young fawns of Vraja have heard that You are like a lion residing in the caves of Govardhana Hill, they still approach You. Perhaps You cannot be blamed for pouncing on them.

Krsna: I find it strange that You call Me the supreme monarch of Vraja but never treat Me as if I am. Is it because of Your pride in worshipping the demigod Surya?

Radha: And what demigod do You secretly worship that You have become so expert at these playful amorous jokes?

Krsna: Every day I go to a small cottage in a secluded grove and worship a peerlessly attractive, nectar-like deity.

Radha: By that worship You have become as handsome as Your deity and very successful at polluting the pious girls of Vraja. All this has certainly made Your head swell.

Krsna: My dear friend! Why is it that when I uncover Your exquisitely beautiful limbs they shrink from Me and dive into the ocean of bashfulness? Let Me rescue them from that ocean and bring them onto the dry land of My glance.

Radha: I am simply a young girl unable to break free from the strong rope of Your arms. O crest jewel of debauchees! Your eyes are about to cast Me into the ocean of shame.

Krsna: This is Your righteousness. Vatsyayana-lantra clearly states that modesty is the primary virtue of a pious girl.

Radha: I think Your eyes are so saintly that they can teach religion even to Arundhati. And although a million beauties of Vraja have given You their hearts, You are yet unsatisfied.

Krsna: None of those girls could enter My heart and extinguish the blazing flames of desire. You are the only one able to rescue Me from this distress.

Radha: Why don’t You intone the names of the beautiful damsels of Indraloka on Your flute? They will instantly rush here to please You.

Krsna: They won’t come! Although crowned with flowers from the Nandanandana gardens, the women of Indraloka are ashamed to appear beside Your lotus toenails. They know they cannot compare to You.

Radha: I am just an amorous female shark swimming in the ocean of Your youthful handsomeness. How will I ever find the shore of that ocean? Let Us stop these talks and enjoy amorous pastimes without interruption.

Krsna: I was just thinking the same. Just see, by engaging Our minds in the service of Cupid, the best of the demigods, Our minds have become one.

Radha: Do not deceive Me, My Lord! I know that You and that great Cupid are one, and now You have charmed both My body and mind to merge into Your own existence.

As the divine couple continue Their conversation, They finally succumb to fatigue on the flower-bed made more fragrant by the ointment of Their mutual love. Rati-manjari’s body erupts in goose- bumps as she watches Radha and Krsna resting in each other’s arms. As They sleep, she continues to gently fan Them.

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments on Radha’s and Krsna’s amorous talks:

**“By the mercy of Radha and Krsna, one who attentively reads these verses may directly perceive Their pastimes as if his eyes were placed against the window of Their grove.”**

**Verse 82**

*ayatodyat-kamala-vadane hanta lilabhisarad*  
*gaty-atopaih srama-vilulitam devi padabja-yugmam*  
*snehat samvahayitum api hri-punja-murte ’py alajjam*  
*nama-graham nija-janam imam ha kada notsyasi tvam*

**“O lotus-faced Goddess! By walking quickly to a rendezvous, surely Your feet will become fatigued. Will You affectionately call me by name, even though You are shyness personified, so that I may know You have accepted me as belonging to You?”**

Commentary: Pure devotional service is a reciprocal relationship between the worshipper and the worshipped. It begins when the worshipper realises, “I am Krsna’s eternal servant” and culminates when the worshipped accepts the servant as His own. Krsna Himself refers to this stage of mature intimacy when He says, “You are in Me.”

*samo 'ham sarva-bhutesu na me dvesyo 'sti na priyah*  
*ye bhajanti tu mam bhaktya mayi te tesu capy aham*

**“I envy no one, nor am I partial to anyone. I am equal to all. But whoever renders service unto Me in devotion is a friend, is in Me, and I am also a friend to him.”**

And so it is for Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami. After he repeatedly petitions Srimati Radharani to accept him as Her servant, Radha finally says, “Rati! You are mine!”

This exchange takes place as Srimati Radharani is on Her way to meet Krsna. It is night. Radha has just left home and Krsna is waiting in some far away grove. Innumerable obstacles lay between Them. Radha thinks:

“How will I reach Krsna? There are so many obstacles in My way. My sister-in-law envies Me, My husband is bitter, and My mother- in-law is crooked. The enemy party, like Padma, is very strong. And Krsna is out there somewhere in the fields, surrounded by His cows and cowherd boyfriends all day long!”

But Radha’s determination to serve Krsna is unflagging. With Her friends’ help She deceives Her in-laws, slips out of Her husband’s house, and plunges into the darkness of the forest. The moon is waning but just about to rise above the horizon. To go unnoticed Radha is dressed in dark blue and Her bracelets are covered by the edge of Her sari. When She asks a friend which path to take, Her friend warns, “Reckless girl! Don’t talk. Your glittering teeth light up thedarkness.”

In that darkness, however, the gopis choose the wrong path and add further excitement to their journey. “What kind of path is this?" asks one sakhi. “It twists and turns like the coils of an angry snake. Why on earth did we come this way?”

But Radha is not deterred. If the path is longer, She walks faster. Radha will let nothing obstruct Her service to Krsna: not the moon, nor snakes, nor even Her own physical limitations. That is the nature of pure loving devotion.

Love even makes Radha reckless in Her pursuit of Krsna’s service. When a gopi whispers, “The sky is getting brighter,” Radha shoots an angry glance at Candra and forbids him to rise any higher in the sky. When a king cobra slithers across the path She, who fearfully trembles at the mere image of a serpent, covers the shining jewel on the cobra’s hood with one hand and silences its hissing mouth with the other.

Rati follows right behind Srimati Radharani and calls out, “O Ayatodyat-kamala-vadanti! O You whose face is like a blooming lotus!” because she sees that Radha’s eyes, ears, and nose are open like nightblooming lotus flowers, alert to everything except Her own needs.

Radha stops. Rati says, “You can’t keep up this pace. I can tell it’s causing You to limp.” Until now Radharani did not notice the pain in Her feet. The agony of separation from Krsna overshadows any physical discomfort. Ignoring Her pain, Radha again starts walking, but Rati won’t allow it. “If Your feet are bothering You,” she says, “how will You dance for Syama?”

This line of reasoning has immediate effect. Radharani’s eyes are wild with desire, but She calms Herself and sits down on the trunk of a fallen tree. Looking at Her maidservant, Radha abandons the natural reticence by which She has earned the name Hri-patta-vastra-guptarigi, “She whose body is concealed by a silken garment of bashfulness.”

Beckoning slightly with Her right hand, Radha says, “Rati, come here.” Rati runs and kneels before Her. Radha continues, “You are right! I have to be fit for Krsna. Please, massage My feet a little to alleviate the pain and soothe My fatigue.”

At this, Rati feels as if the whole world is smiling, as if all her anxieties have vanished, as if she has suddenly reached the summit of her life’s journey. Radharani would never call Lalita by her name, and She would never ask Visakha to massage Her feet. She would never show Her friends such intimacy or ask them for any kind of personal service.

Rati takes Radha’s feet in her lap and expertly massages them with nimble hands. She has had much practice. Unable to control her ecstasy, Rati’s blissful tears wash the dust from Radha’s lotus feet.

Soon Rati feels Radha’s hand on her head and hears Sri Radha’s gentle voice, “Rati! That’s enough. Let’s go.” They both stand, and Radha leads the way. Then She turns Her head and says with a smile, “Come, My Rati!”

These words make Rati feel as though someone has poured nectar into her ears. Her head echoes with the phrase, “My Rati.” Her heart beats loud enough to wake all of Vraja. When she finally arrives with Radharani at the spot where Krsna is waiting, her feet will not be sore because they no longer touch the ground.

**Verse 83**

*ha naptri radhe tava surya-bhakteh*  
*kalah samutpanna itah kutto 'si*  
*itiva rosan mukhara lapanti*  
*sudheva kim mam sukhayisyatiha*

**‘“O granddaughter, Radha! It’s time for You to worship the sun god! Where are You?’ When will these angry words of Mukhara- devi sound like nectar to me and make me happy?”**

Commentary: Throughout the night, Rati floats on clouds of bliss. Even as the other sakhis and manjaris are resting she continues to fan Radha and Krsna while They sleep. Weariness is far from Rati-manjari.

Returning to Yavata, Rati quickly enters her home, where her own assistants help bathe, dress, and ornament her. As the sound of ladies churning milk greets the sunrise, Rati sings the names of the divine couple on her hasty journey to Radha’s house. Everywhere in the village, brahmanas recite the Vedas and cows call to their calves. In the surrounding forest, birds chatter and sing, reminding the Vraja-vasis that it’s time to rise and attend to their morning duties.

Rati and Mukhara arrive at Radha’s front gate at the same time. Rati offers her respects to the old lady and leads her into the house, where Jatila is already waiting. Because it is Sunday, Jatila asks Mukhara to send Radha off to Surya-kunda, thinking that the purpose of her daughter-in-law’s weekly worship of the sun god is to increase Abhimanyu’s span of life and wealth of cows. As Jatila speaks, manjaris arrive one by one and stand around listening to the conversation, eager to serve Sri Radha.

Jatila’s order puts the girls into ecstasy because they know that today no obstacles will prevent Radha from meeting Krsna. Finally, the gopis follow Mukhara to Radha’s apartments on the second floor. Unable to contain herself, even as she is still ascending the stairs, that jewel-box of parental affection, Mukhara, calls out, “Radha! My daughter! Where are You?”

Somehow, from deep sleep Radha hears Her grandmother’s voice and dreamily replies, “O holy mother, I am here!” Then She falls hack to sleep.

Mukhara opens the bedroom door and mutters, “How amazing! Morning has broken and my granddaughter still slumbers.” After entering the room, the old lady sits on the bed and caresses Radha’s face and limbs, saying, “O my girl! Get up now. It’s Sunday, and You must prepare to worship the sun god.”

Meanwhile, Visakha, who is sleeping on the daybed in Radha’s room, gets up and wearily calls to her mistress, “Dearest friend! It’s time to get up.”

Radha hears Mukhara and Visakha and tries to rouse Herself again and again like a swan from a lake, but She repeatedly falls back to sleep, exhausted from the pastimes of the night before. Rati sees Radha’s plight and comes to the foot of the bed, where she serves her friend’s lotus feet. Upon repeated requests from Mukhara and Visakha, Radha manages to sit up in bed, just as sunlight comes streaming through the window.

Radha sits up, and Mukhara is shocked to see her granddaughter wearing Krsna’s upper cloth. “Vis'akha!” she says anxiously. “Last evening Krsna wore this cloth that now covers Your friend. What is this! How can this happen to a chaste housewife?”

If Visakha was struggling to wake up before, she is no longer. In a dismissive tone she says, “O lady! Your eyes are not what they used to be, are they?”

Visakha points to the sunshine streaming through the open window and says, rather matter-of-factly, “Look! The rays of the sun paint my friend’s blue cloth yellow."

While Mukhara stands up and walks to the window to investigate, Rati-manjari quickly removes Krsna’s golden cloth and replaces it with Radha’s blue one. The old lady looks hack and sees that the cloth is indeed blue. Visakha lovingly chides her, “Bewildered old lady! Why are you giving anxiety to pure-hearted girls?”

Mukhara clears her throat and says, “Anyway, it was an innocent mistake. Now I must go to Nandagrama and see Krsna." And with that she walks out the door and down the stairs, passing Lalita and other sleep-weary sakhis on their way up to Radha’s room.

Once again Radha blesses Rati with a grateful glance that says, “How can I repay you?” Ever resourceful, Rati looks back as if to say, “The bliss of serving You is my payment. Say no more.”

*brahmanandaika-vadah katucana bhagavad-vandanananda-mattah*  
*kecid govinda-sakhyad anupama-paramanandam anye svadante*  
*sri-radha-kinkarinam u akhila-sukha-camatkara-saraika-sima*  
*tat-padambhoja-rajan-nakha-mani-vilasaj-jyotir eka-cchatapi*

**“Some persons talk only of the happiness of impersonal Brahman. Others are wild with the bliss of offering prayers to the Supreme Person. Still others taste the peerless bliss of Krsna’s friendship. But Sri Radha’s maidservants taste the highest, most wonderful bliss, the bliss found in a single particle of the splendour of the glistening toenails of Her lotus feet.”**

**Verse 84**

*devi bhasita-piyusam smitakarpura vasitam*  
*srotrabhyam nayanabhyam te kim nu sevisyate maya*

**“O Goddess! When will I serve Your nectarean words with my ears and Your camphor-scented smile with my eyes?”**

Commentary: To qualify oneself to see Krsna, one must first hear about Him; such hearing (sravanam) is service to the Lord rendered by the ears. The initial result of hearing is to remove all inauspicious things from the heart (hrdy antah stho hy abhadrani), and to the degree the heart is purified, attachment to hearing about Krsna proportionately develops. As we continue to hear krsna-katha we become indifferent to the pleasures of heaven and the relief that comes from liberation, until finally we become qualified to enter the spiritual kingdom. There, in the spiritual world, hearing about Krsna with love mitigates the misery of being separated from Him. The following verse describes the last phases of this development:

*sa sraddadhanasya vivardhamana*  
*viraktim anyatra karoti pumsah*  
*hareh padanusmrti-nirvrtasya*  
*samasta-duhkhapyayam asu dhatte*

**“For one who is anxious to engage constantly in hearing such topics, krsna-katha gradually increases his indifference towards all other things. Such constant remembrance of the lotus feet of Lord Krsna by the devotee who has achieved transcendental bliss vanquishes all his miseries without delay.”**

As soon as Krsna and Balarama could walk They began to play with other cowherd boys, which naturally awakened the bliss of the elderly gopis. Krsna’s childish restlessness captivated these ladies, who would speak of the two boys again and again in order to constantly relive Their pastimes. And so it is with all Vraja-vasis; talks of Krsna are the elixir that sustains them in His absence because such talks are not different from Sri Krsna Himself.

And not only in Krsna’s absence but also while His pastimes are occuring, the conversations that take place appear to be rivers of nectar flowing from His lips — or the lips of His companions — in the form of words.

After Mukhara leaves, while Sri Radha is sitting on Her jewelled divan joking with Her friends, in comes beautiful Syamala-sakhi. She is a group leader like Radha, but unlike Candravali, one very favourable to Srimati Radharani.

Radharani offers Syamala a seat and says, “Syamala! I was just thinking of you before you arrived. Perhaps this means that the tree of My desires will bear fruit and I will also see Krsna today.”

Syamala replies, “If the tree of Your desires has not yet borne fruit, it surely will. But I think You regularly eat this fruit and simply forget due to its overpowering taste.”

Shaking Her head, Radha says, “Friend, perhaps You misunderstand Me. Just as lightning illuminates the night but upon disappearing creates a darkness twice as dense, after having seen Krsna once, His subsequent disappearance doubles the misery of His absence.” Syamala understands the meaning of Srimati Radharani’s profound words, but she would rather hear directly of Radha’s pastimes with Krsna. “Radha,” she presses, “be frank with me. The Ganges-stream of stories about Your nocturnal pastimes with Krsna is my daily morning bath. I cannot begin any activity unless You shower me with it.” After taking a deep breath which seems to draw Her friends in closer, Radha says, “Last night a fresh, blue lustre began to shower Me within a grove, after which it took Me to see innumerable Cupids dancing on a stage. I offered the activities of My senses as an entrance fee for watching the performance, hut what wonderful things happened after that, I cannot remember.”

Laughing sweetly, Syamala says, “You are the producer and stage manager of this host of dancing Cupids. How can You forget Your own production?”

Radharani just shrugs Her shoulders and continues, “I passed through so many more things than what I just described, but by some magic I cannot remember them. Perhaps it was all a dream — a trick of the mind and nothing more.”

“No!” replies Syamala. “It was neither a dream, nor magic, nor Your imagination. But You drank so much nectar from that performance of a thousand Cupids that it is hardly surprising to see You unable to remember anything in Your post-intoxicated state!”

As Radha speaks, Her eyes become envious of Her ears for being able to see Krsna through the descriptions of His glories, and thus those dazzling blue-grey orbs begin to flood with tears of sorrow. Radha takes Syamala’s hands and says, “I took birth in Gokula, but I could never relish Krsna’s sweetness. And even when I heard about that sweetness, My restless mind could not retain a drop of it.” Syamala places her hand on top of Radha’s, turns to Lalita, and says, “I have to go home now. Please offer this lotus-like girl to the thirsty honeybee in the abode of Vraja’s king.”

After Syamala leaves, Radharani’s friends also depart to bathe. Radha is then alone in the room with Rati. To Rati it appears that Radha is about to be swallowed by the python of separation from Krsna, and thus she chants mystic mantras for dispersing serpents. “Devi!” she begins.

Radha looks up with sorrowful eyes, and Rati says, “Did You forget what Your superiors said?”

Radha returns a blank stare as Rati goes on, “They told You to go to Surya-kunda for puja.”

A light stirs in Radha’s eyes as Rati continues, “And I have heard that a new brahmana from Mathura will be there to conduct the worship and chant the mantras.”

Suddenly the light in Radha’s eyes glows brighter. Her eyes open wide and a smile comes to Her lips. Rati concludes, “You should hurry and bathe so that You will be in a purified state acceptable to the brdhmana priest.”

Sri Radha is now grinning ear-to-ear. She tells Rati, “Quick. You must help Me.”

As Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami remembers these pastimes, he prays to Srimati Radharani,

**“O Devi! When will I hear Your sweet talks with Syamala-sakhi and see the camphor-scented smile on Your lips? At that time my ears and eyes will have fulfilled the plan of the creator.”**

**Verse 85**

*kusuma-cayana-khelam kurvati tvam parita*  
*rasa-kutila-sakhibhih prana-nathena sardham*  
*kapata-kalaha-kelya kvapi rosena bhinna*  
*mama mudam ati-velam dhasyase su-vrate kim*

**“O steadfast girl! When will I be filled with happiness to see You in a mock quarrel with the Lord of Your heart as You and Your crooked girlfriends pick flowers?”**

Commentary: In his book entitled Sri Radha-krsnojjvala-kusuma-keli, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami describes how one day, hearing that Sri Radha and Her friends are in Vrndavana forest picking their favourite (lowers, leaves, shoots, and fruits, Krsna approaches the girls and arrogantly quarrels with them in these words:

Krsna says, “My dear thieves! How could you have become so intoxicated by youthful pride that you would destroy My priceless forest?”

Visakha replies with a smile, “It’s You who should give up Your pride and go back to Nandisvara before harsh Lalita shames You.”

With dramatic flare, Krsna says, “As your guru, have I not taught you the path of non-violence? Why, then, do you want to kill these innocent flowers?”

When the gopis hear these words they become simultaneously angry and ashamed, but their enthusiasm for the quarrel is not diminished.

From amongst them, Lalita answers, “This forest is not Yours! Indeed, many people collect fruits and flowers here. Why must You harass us?”

Hearing this logic, Krsna proudly declares, “Do you mean to say that you are deaf to the Vedic injunctions? They openly declare that this forest bears My name and therefore belongs to Me."

At this Sri Radha shoots Krsna a crooked glance and says, “My dear liar! If this forest is Yours and is named after You, then why does everyone call it Vrndavana, after our dear friend Vrnda-devi?”

“Because Vrnda-devi is My chaste wife,” Krsna retorts, “and everyone knows there is no difference between husband and wife. Therefore, when the people say that this forest bears the name Vrnda, the word ‘Vrnda’ refers to us both.”

Blissful but incredulous at what She has just heard, Radha turns to Vrnda and whispers, “Tell me it’s not true.” Vrnda vigorously shakes her head to reject Krsna’s claim, and thus Radha vows, “Then we must defeat this king of liars.”

Vrnda-devi is spurred on by Radha’s call to arms and the gopis’ crooked glances. Red with feigned anger, she replies, “O eunuch of Padma! O laughing-stock of Vraja! If You want to be the king of a forest, then worship Candrāvalī, the goddess of Sakhī-sthalī. Satisfy her and she will grant You a grove of jujube trees as Your kingdom.”

As the gopīs’ laughter echoes all around her, Vṛndā begins her arguments in favour of Rādhā’s sovereignty over Vṛndāvana by comparing her princess’s bodily beauty to the opulence of the forest.

“The reflection of Rādhā’s face is more beautiful than a host of lotus flowers, Her eyes more charming than a restless deer’s. Her raised nose is sweeter than the beak of a baby parrot. Her glistening lips more delightful than the splendid bandhūka flower.”

As Vṛndā compares her forest to her friend’s every limb, the gopīs visibly gloat over their collective success and, internally, Kṛṣṇa revels in the description.

“Because of the obvious similarities between Rādhā’s form and this forest,” Vṛndā says in summation, “and because Her pastimes take place here, it is clear that the land of Vraja belongs to Her.”

At this, flames of desire ignite in Rādhā’s heart, Viśākhā embraces Rādhā in affection, and Kṛṣṇa, feigning anger, replies with an arrogant laugh:

“Rādhā’s beauty is similar to My Vṛndāvana forest not because it belongs to Her, but because She has stolen its splendour and made it wilt. If it were otherwise, if She were not a thief, then why would She be here plucking tiny flowers to enhance Her beauty?”

And rebuking Vṛndā, Kṛṣṇa adds, “By claiming Rādhā’s beauty to be reflected in My forest, you seem to give the impression that She should be Mine. But She is chaste and faithful to Her husband, so unless he comes and personally hands Her to Me, I will not accept Her.”

The playful waves of Kṛṣṇa’s crooked words rock the solid boat of Rādhā’s heart, seeing which, the gopīs smile. Then, one by one, Her dearmost friends take up Kṛṣṇa’s verbal challenge.

Lalitā ridicules Kṛṣṇa, telling Him that He already has too many mistresses. Not to be rebuffed, Kṛṣṇa replies that the issue at hand is the theft of flowers, a crime for which He, as King Cupid’s proxy, should collect a fine in the form of the gopīs’ jewellery. When, however, Kṛṣṇa increases the fine to include the gopīs’ bodices, Tuṅgavidyā threatens to break His flute.

Perhaps the most infuriating of Kṛṣṇa’s accusations is that, as a “compulsive thief,” Rādhā is bad association for the gopīs, who should turn Her over to Him so that He can rehabilitate Her.

Finally, with knitted eyebrows, Rādhā says, “Don’t make a fool of Yourself before these sophisticated girls. Return to Your village and play the buffoon with Your comedian friends.”

Followed by the gopīs, Her anklets tinkling, Rādhā turns to leave, but Kṛṣṇa suddenly assails Her, taking as many liberties as He can before the other gopīs beat Him back.  
Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī concludes his book with the following verse:

*idaṁ rādhā-kṛṣṇojjvala-kusuma-keli-kali-madhu*  
*priyālī-narmāli-parimala-yutaṁ yasya bhajanāt*  
*mamāndhasyāpy etad-vacana-madhupenālpa-gatinā*  
*manāg ghrātaṁ tan me gatir atula-rūpāṅghrija-rajaḥ*

**The dust of Rūpa Gosvāmī’s lotus feet, the goal of my life, has enabled this blind old man, who is like a tiny bee, to taste some of the honey dripping from the flower-like quarrel between Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā, and Her dear friends, a quarrel further enhanced by the pollen of many clever jokes.”**

Rati-mañjarī addresses Rādhā as Suvratā because, despite Her apparently disparaging comments to Kṛṣṇa, She is dedicated to making Him happy. She says, “Suvrata! If I am able to see this pastime and to hear You tease Your beloved, then my mind will certainly be joyful. Although externally You show anger, I know that within Yourself You are enjoying the many fruits of ecstasy.”

**Verse 86**

*nana-vidhaih prthula-kaku-bharair asahyaih*  
*samprarthitah priyataya bata madhavena*  
*tvan-mana-bhanga-vidhaye sa-daye jano ‘yam*  
*vyagrah patisyati kada lalita-padante*

**“O merciful girl! When will this person anxiously fall at Lalita’s feet, pleading that she soothe Your intolerable pique with Madhava, who piteously petitions me in so many sweet ways?”**

Commentary: Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami here describes a unique situation. Srimati Radharani persists in Her jealous anger (maria) against Krsna, not by Her own volition, but on the order of Lalita-devi.

Rupa Gosvami defines mana — sometimes called pride, anger, or jealous anger — as a stage of love in which the lover displays contrariness and rudeness to the beloved. Mana acts as an obstacle to the divine couple’s desires, preventing Them from seeing and embracing each other. But, at the same time, this mana acts as salt does to water — as an additive that keeps love ever fresh. Mana is therefore an integral aspect of Sri Radha’s disposition. It appears in Her behaviour as jealous anger. Describing mana in esoteric terms, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami calls it the arrangement of Her hair and the silk garment that covers Her body.

There are two kinds of mana: that which has a cause, and that which has no cause.

*aher iva gatih premnah svabhava-kutila bhavet*  
*ato hetor ahetos ca yunor mana udancati*

**“The progress of loving affairs between a young boy and a young girl is like the movement of a snake. On account of this, two types of anger arise between a young boy and girl — anger with cause and anger without cause.”**

If Krsna is late for a meeting with Radha because He is elsewhere giving His attention to another gopi, Radha’s subsequent anger is with cause. Such clearly occasioned anger is something Krsna can readily address. If, however, Radha becomes angry without cause due to the winding course of youthful love, Krsna will have much more difficulty in pacifying Her.

In the pastimes in which Radha apparently learns how to control Krsna, Radha’s friends coach and encourage Her in the art of mana. Rupa-manjari’s logic is that Krsna will not be attracted to passive saintliness because “a cheater does not consider honesty a virtue.” So Radha repeatedly practises knitting Her eyebrows, staring without blinking, remaining silent with a sarcastic smile, and — most importantly of all — not losing Her composure. In this way, Radha practises exhibiting anger at Krsna. But, in the end, She concludes with a shrug, “My final success still remains in the hands of fate.”

Other gopis are more aggressive, boldly declaring that only proud and jealous girls are glorious, whereas the submissive remain ever wretched. This thought makes Radha feel as though a lance has pierced Her heart, and She trembles like a leaf. To an aggressive gopi of this ilk, Radha once protested, “If you again and again insist that I should remain angry with Krsna, then draw Me a picture of Him. I will stay in My room, plug My ears, gaze at that picture, and happily pass the night.”

But the most forceful of Radha’s advisors in these matters is Lalita-devi, who in a letter once even apologised to Krsna for her “wickedness” in persistently training simple-hearted Radha in the art of jealous anger. Lalita’s nature is harsher and more volatile than Radha’s; thus Lalita is quicker to show anger and slower to forgive. Even though Radha may be inclined to abandon Her mana, if Lalita is not in agreement, Radha will continue to feign jealous anger out of fear of Her friend. Thus Radha is called Lalita-bhiti-kampini, “one who trembles in fear of Lalita."

*vrnda-prasadhitottunga- kudungananga-vesmani*  
*krsna-khandita-manatval lalita-bhiti-kampini*

**“When He failed to show up at the rendezvous in the forest cottage carefully decorated by Vrnda, Radha, trembling out of fear of Lalita, did not dare to give up Her jealous anger, although Her heart was inclined to do so.’’**

Truth be told, without the mystique of jealous anger, Krsna can neither be attracted nor controlled. Therefore He is called *Lalitavsya-dhi-radha-manabhasa-vasi-krtah*, “one who is controlled by the shadow of unsubmissive Radha’s jealous anger.”

Of course, Krsna is expert at all things. As such, He is surely expert at subverting Radha’s mana. Simply by sweetly smiling at Her, exciting Her ears with His voice, or showing Her the splendour of His face, Radha’s icy disposition melts away. And if Sri Radha’s pique is resistant to these temptations, then a mystical song from His flute often succeeds where Krsna fails.

But it’s not always as easy as that. Sometimes Radha’s mana is resolute. Sometimes She joyfully feeds the snake of Her jealous anger with the milk of stubbornness. At such times, Krsna despairs. Emaciated, He rolls on the ground as His alarmed friends helplessly stand by and watch. Such a sight causes both moving and non-moving creatures to waste away. It even silences Krsna’s flute.

When Radha is in such a state, however, Krsna wins Her over by placing Her foot on His head and begging Her forgiveness with a litany of impassioned pleas. Such humility gradually melts Radha’s heart and forces Her to look at Krsna with tear-filled eyes, a sure sign the reconciliation has begun.

When Krsna can’t win Radha over on His own, His only recourse is to beg Her maidservants or friends to intercede on His behalf. On various occasions, Krsna turns to Rupa-manjari to soothe Sri Radha’s anger. And after Rupa speaks to her mistress about Krsna’s good qualities and the depth of His love for Her, Radha’s heart melts and She welcomes Hari once again.

However, if Lalita-devi dictates the conditions of Radha’s anger, things become more complex. In these cases, Krsna has to pacify Lalita as well as Radha. And, as already mentioned, until Lalita relinquishes her anger, Radha must keep Krsna at arm’s length, whether She has personally forgiven Him or not.

Krsna sometimes approaches Rati-manjari in a secluded place to beg her to untie the knot of Radha’s jealous anger. But when Lalita finds out what Rati is up to, she immediately drives Rati out of Radha’s grove and rebukes her severely. In short, the intercession fails.

With a more experienced gopi, however, intercession can be successful. At other times Krsna appeals to Visakha-devi, describing His utter misery at being rejected by Srimati Radharani. Astute Visakha knows well the dynamics of these situations and is often able to sweet-talk Lalita into breaking Sri Radha's jealous anger.

In this verse of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, it once again appears that Krsna has cheated Radharani. He provides many excuses for not arriving until the morning after the scheduled meeting, but Radha wants no part of it. She’s fed up with His lies. Lalita reinforces Radha’s stance and warns, “Don’t You dare speak to Him again.”

But before long, Radha regrets having ever sent Krsna away. She sighs, laments, and wrings Her hands in grief. She thinks, “I should have accepted Madhava’s story at face value. Now My heart is shattered. He repeatedly bowed before Me, but I kicked Him away. Now where is My virtuous Syama?”

Rati shares Radha’s grief and leaves Her in the care of other manjaris, hoping they will find a solution. Meanwhile, not far away she finds Krsna, who appeals to her with joined palms and tearful eyes. This is the beauty of Vraja: everywhere else, great devotees and saints worship Krsna with joined palms, but in Vrndavana, Krsna prays with joined palms for the mercy of Radha’s maidservants.

Unable to tolerate the sorrow of the divine couple, Rati-manjari cautiously enters Lalita’s grove and at once falls at her feet. Smiling, Lalita-devi asks, “What is it, sweetheart?”

Rati sobs through her tears and says, “Devi! Radha and Krsna are so eager to meet each other. But until you lift the ban you placed upon Her, Radha will burn in the fire of misery, unable to see Syama.” Lalita-devi’s only desire is to see Radha and Krsna happy. Now that Their love has been sweetened and refreshed by jealous anger, Their happiness at meeting will be all the greater. Placing her hand on Rati’s head, Lalita says, “Tell your mistress that I request Her to be merciful to Her lover.”

Elated, Rati runs back to Radha’s grove and relays Lalita’s message. Radha feels as if Her ears are being showered with nectar. She looks gratefully at Rati and asks, “Where is He?”

Grinning from ear to ear, Rati waves her forefinger gently, “Just stay here and I’ll get Him for You.”

**Verse 87**

*pritya mangala-gita-nrtya-vilasad-vinadi-vadyotsavaih*  
*suddhanam-payasam-ghatair bahu-vidhaih samvasitanam-bhrsam*  
*vrndaranya-mahadhipatya-vidhaye yah paurnamasya svayam*  
*dhire samvihitah sa kim-tava mahotseko maya draksyate*

**“O wise and solemn one! I long to see You being bathed with many pitchers of pure, scented water, while others dance, sing auspicious songs, and play instruments like the vina, in the wonderful ceremony of love that Paurnamasi orchestrates to coronate You as the queen of Vrndavana!”**

Commentary: Srimati Radharani’s coronation ceremony was initially described in the Padma Purana, and the acaryas repeatedly refer to the event in their writings. In his Radhastakam, Rupa Gosvami says, *atula-mahasi vrndaranya-rajye 'bhisiktam*: “I worship Sri Radhika, who is the crowned queen of the incomparably glorious kingdom of Vrndavana forest.”And Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami writes:

*sardham manasa-juhnavi-mukha-nadi-vargaih sa-rangotkaraih*  
*savitry-adi-suri-kulais ca nitaram akasa-vanya vidheh*  
*vrndaranya-varenya-rajya-visaye sri-paurnamasi muda*  
*radham yatra siseca sincatu sukham sonmatta-radha-sthali*

**“Ordered by Brahma as a voice from the sky, and accompanied by Savitri-devi and other delighted demigoddesses, Paurnamasi-devi crowned Srimati Radharani queen of the beautiful forest of Vrndavana by jubilantly sprinkling the waters of the Manasa-ganga and other sacred rivers upon Her head. When will the sacred place known as Unmatta-radha-sthali (the place where Radha was overcome with bliss) sprinkle some transcendental happiness on me?”**

Finally, under Rupa Gosvami’s order, Sri Jiva wrote a book entitled Madhava-mahotsava, which elaborately recounts the entire pastime, especially the bathing ceremony. By reading this work one can understand how Radha received the beautiful name Vrndavanesvari (“the ruler of Vrndavana”).

Rati voices her eagerness to witness this occasional pastime by addressing Radharani as Dhira (“wise and solemn one"). In other words, the formal setting of the coronation, as well as the royal court, brings out in Radha the deep wisdom and the grave decorum expected of a monarch.

Curious to hear about Rati’s desire, Radha asks, “Rati! What interests you so about this coronation pastime?”

Smiling, Rati replies, “Everything connected to You is of interest to me. But I am especially eager to see the nine baths offered to You from different pots made of coral, ruby, pearl, and other precious elements.” Radha replies, “You regularly see Me bathing. What is so special about this particular bath?”

Raising her eyebrows, Rati says, “This bath is different because Krsna is present throughout, shyly stealing glances at You as He suppresses His loving ecstasies.”

“Oh, I see,” replies Radha. “You find those exchanges amusing?” Rati answers, “O wise and solemn one! Please consider how the entire event is arranged just for the pleasure of You and Krsna. I am not the only one amused to see how You are both so shy in the presence of others that You hardly dare to glance at each other.”

“I know!” Radha replies. “Our friends take no small amount of pleasure in teasing Us about how reserved We were in the presence of others.”

Rati bubbles over, “I am especially eager to take part when Your maidservants bathe You. We want it to be special."

Radha enquires, “Tell me, what’s so special about you and the other manjaris bathing Me?”

As if divulging a state secret, Rati whispers, “Our bathing You from a blue sapphire pot proclaims Your supremacy over Laksmi by confirming our supremacy over her maidservants.”

Visibly impressed, Radharani enquires, “How will you accomplish such a feat when Laksmi-devi is in Vaikuntha?”

Rati answers excitedly, “Unseen by others, You will mount the chariot of our hearts and, with the charioteer of Your beauty, ride to Vaikuntha, where together we will conquer, with rasa, Laksmi and Narayana and Their servants.”

Radha enquires further, “Will anyone else know of our conquest over Vaikuntha?”

“No one!” replies Rati emphatically. “No one but Krsna of course. He will glorify You with a honey-thick melody from His flute, and that will cause Your love for Him to expand and Your bodily complexion to glow. And when it does, that radiance will silhouette Your form, even through Your thick bathing clothes. The hair on Krsna's body will then stand on end, and tears will shoot from His eyes. That I want to see!"

Radha continues by asking, “And how do you hope to benefit by seeing My abhiseka?"

Rati replies, “The main benefit I receive will be to see You glorified. But with that, automatically my devotion to You will increase, along with my bliss.”

*karnau mangala-gana-vadanam idam kavyam sa-jihvadharau*  
*ghrane saurabham aksini ruci-kulampani ca seva-sukham*  
*sri-radham anu vrndaka-vana-maharajyabhisekangatam*  
*ayatam bata janma-janmani yuvam avyajam avyad iha*

**“O my ears, lips, and tongue! May the words describing the abhiseka of Vrndavana’s queen protect you birth after birth and give you devotion to Radha and Krsna. O nostrils! May the fragrance of Radha’s divine abhiseka protect you! O eyes and hands! May the beauty and the happiness of service to the place of this abhiseka pastime nourish you!”**
