And is it not the greatest fortune to be counted amongst Your maidservants?”

The whole purpose of Dasa Gosvami’s life, indeed the conclusion of Gaudiya Vaisnavism, now rests in the balance of Radha’s answer. Thus Raghunatha Dasa asks again, “Devi! Tell me. Is it not true? Is this verse that I wrote to glorify Your lake not true?

*api jana iha kascid yasya seva-prasadaih*  
*pranaya-sura-lata syat tasya gosthendra-sunoh*  
*sapadi kila mad-isa-dasya-puspa-prasasya*  
*tad ati-surabhi radha-kundam evasrayo me*

**“‘The mercy obtained by serving Radha-kunda makes the celestial vine of pure love for the prince of Vraja, which is famous for bearing the flowers of service to my queen, sprout. May that very fragrant Radha-kunda be my shelter.’**

“And, is the verse of benediction (phala-stuti) I wrote to that prayer also not true?

*avikalam ati devyas caru kundastakam yah*  
*paripathati tadiyollasi-dasyarpitatma*  
*aciram iha sarire darsayaty eva tasmai*  
*madhu-ripur ati-modaih slisyamanam priyam tam*

**‘“To one completely dedicated to Queen Radha’s service, who happily reads these eight beautiful verses describing Her lake, even in this present body Lord Krsna shows His beloved as He happily embraces Her.”’**

No doubt Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami has presented a strong argument before Srimati Radharani, and it is now time for Her to give Her judgment. Summarising his reasoning, the acarya says,

**“O merciful one! If You do not give great mercy to this unhappy maidservant, who after so many years still longs for Your personal shelter, then what has been the value of her long years of service to Your lake and of her countless appeals for Your mercy?”**

As Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami sits in his cottage, the sound of lapping waves his only companion, a beautiful golden aura gradually fills his room and then beyond. The bliss swelling in his heart and body foretells the fulfilment of his ardent desire, and then, as if always there, Radha and Krsna stand before him, smiling, Their eyes overflowing with tears of love for Their peerless devotee.

Srimati Radharani says softly, “Rati! I have come.”

**Verse 104**

*ayi pranaya-salini pranaya-pusta-dasyaptaye*  
*prakamam api rodanaih pracura-duhkha-dagdhatmana*  
*vilapa-kusumanjalir hrdi nidhaya padambuje*  
*maya bata samarpitas tava tanotu tustim manak*

**“O abode of pure love! I pray that this Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, which I place at Your lotus feet, along with much weeping to attain Your mature loving service and a heart burning with pain, may give You a little pleasure.”**

Commentary: Finally, Radha and Krsna have appeared, and Their presence dispels Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s sorrow. Thakura Bhaktivinoda assures devotees that if they receive the mercy of Lord Caitanya, this vision will also be theirs:

*krsna-name anurag to ha'be he*  
*(takhon) anayase saphal ha’be jivera jivan*  
*krsiya-rati vina jivan to miche he*  
*(ese) brndabane radha-syamer pa’be darasan*  
*gaura-krpa ha’le he*

**“When attachment to the holy name of Krsna resides in the heart, a living being’s life very easily becomes successful. But without affection for Krsna, life is simply useless. \[And for those with such affection\] If you have the blessing of Lord Caitanya then at the end of life you will obtain the beautiful vision of Radha and Syama in Vrndavana.”**

After falling at the lotus feet of the divine couple, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami submits one last plea at Sri Radha’s lotus feet, “Pranaya-salini! You are the abode of love for Krsna, for Your girlfriends, for the cows, indeed for all living entities. Out of affection for this sad person You have come along with Your beloved and made me happy. Now, if You want to keep me in this state of bliss, please fulfil one final desire.”

Sweetly, Radha says, “Tell Me, what is there in your heart?”

Dasa Gosvami continues, “Give me the privilege of the kind of mature love (pratyaya) I need to serve You and Your beloved when You forget Your individual identities in the great ecstasy of love (pratyaya).’’

Srimati Radharani answers, “Rati! What you desire is rare because it is so difficult to attain.”

Baring his heart, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami persists, “By following the teachings of Your Rupa Gosvami, I have often seen the two of You meet within my heart. I have also seen my friend Rupa-manjari as she serves You when You have become languid from many passionate amorous pastimes, Your cheeks wet with perspiration, resting on the couch of Krsna’s chest. Now I too desire a similar service, one for which I have prayed many times before:

*pika-patu-rava-vadyair bhrnga-jhankara-ganaih*  
*sphurad-atula-kudunga-kroda-range sa-rangam*  
*smara-sadasi krtodyan nrtyatah sranta-gatram*  
*vraja-nava-yuva-yugmam nartakam vijayani*

**‘“I pray that I may fan the two young dancers of Vraja, who have become fatigued by happily dancing in Cupid’s arena in an incomparable forest grove filled with the instrumental music of the expert cuckoos and the humming songs of the bees.’”**

Radha says, “Rati! Again I tell you, such service is difficult to secure.”

Taking a deep breath, Dasa Gosvami replies, “Devi! I know how difficult it is. It is I who have spent my whole life crying for it, and it is I who have suffered as a result of my tears. But never mind! Whether I am alive or dead, I will continue to cry at Your feet until You consider me worthy.”

To gain the strength for what he is about to say next, Dasa Gosvami offers a silent prayer to beautiful Krsna, “May the splendid moon of Lord Krsna, which tirelessly dispels the great darkness of the demons, showers the nectar of pure love on the devotees, cools the white lotus of Sri Radha, and makes the flowers of Her breasts blossom with happiness, protect us.”

With a trembling voice, Dasa Gosvami says, “If You tell me to wait, to be patient, I will. But Goddess, know that I will be lamenting all the while, and my heart will be burning with agony!”

After a brief pause, Dasa Gosvami makes his last statement,

**“Just as mantras are chanted during the offering of flowers (puspanjali), the verses of this book are the mantras with which I offer the flowers of my tears and lamentations at Your lotus feet. If this offering brings You the slightest satisfaction, then all I’ve gone through has been worthwhile. That is all I have to say.”**

**\* \* \* \***

Radha and Krsna did not at once fulfil Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s prayers, but They did give him complete assurance that it would be done. There still remained some little service for the acarya to render in this world. Just as flowers, after having been offered, are showered on the assembled worshippers, the acarya would still have to distribute the teachings of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali by showing devotees how to cry for Radha and Krsna and how to leave this world while thinking of the divine couple in love. After that he could resume his eternal service as Rati-manjari. It only required a little more patience.

The verses of Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali comprise a textbook for devotees intent on learning how to cry for Srimati Radharani. Bhaktivinoda Thakura writes that devotees who, within their minds, want to follow in the wake of the Vraja gopis can find guidance in Sri Vilapa-kusuinanjali how to aspire for the gopis’ mood of devotion.

The first six verses of this work are Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s invocation, offered first as a follower of the Vraja-vasis, and then as a servant of Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Verses seven through seventeen explore the realms of separation from Sri Radha, and verses eighteen through ninety-five are meditations on different services rendered to Her. Verse ninety-six stands alone as the manjaris’ declaration of surrender and the anthem of Gaudiya Vaisnavas. And the concluding verses are the author’s final prayers for admittance into eternal service to Srimati Radharani.

Although Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami is an eternal associate of the divine couple, Caitanya Mahaprabhu has cast him in the role of a practising devotee, a sadhaka. From that position the acarya teaches by his personal example how to progress through the stages of pure devotional service, culminating with entrance into Krsna’s eternal pastimes. And above all, as attested to in the final prayers of this book, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami teaches devotees that they must be determined and patient to achieve perfection in devotional service.

While anchored by a body to this world, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami constantly meditates upon serving Radha and Krsna just as Rupa-manjari does. And as his meditations become increasingly mature, he becomes increasingly happy to enter, and sad to leave, the encounters he has in his eternal identity as Rati-manjari in the eternal unmanifest (aprakata) Vraja. Thus his life is immersed in constant hankering and lamenting for continual service to Srimati Radharani, and he tastes the intense bliss of service in separation.

When Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami comes to the doorstep of the tenth stage of separation, death, he is awarded the fulfilment of his desire: he goes back to Godhead. In the land of cintamani he again serves as Rati-manjari, shadowing Srimati Radharani wherever She goes and constantly enjoying the bliss of the divine couple’s company.

However, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s identity as an associate of Lord Caitanya is also eternal. After returning to Goloka Vrndavana, he continues to reside on the banks of Radha-kunda in an unmanifest sadhaka form. And as he did during his manifest presence, he continues to cultivate spontaneous devotion and to call out for eternal engagement in Sri Radha’s service. Thus, even today, pure-hearted Vaisnavas can go there to hear him sing the verses of Sri Vilapa- kusumanjali, just as he did long ago.

With the prayers of the previous acaryas I conclude this commentary on Sri Vilapa-kusumarijali, offering my obeisances to Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami in his eternal form as Rati-manjari, also known as Tulasi-manjari, and the devotional service that he taught by his words and example. May the Vaisnavas find Sri Vilapa-kusumanjali, and the present commentary, to be both of benefit and a source of pleasure!

*he sri-tulasy uru-krpady uta tarangini tvam*  
*yan-murdhni me carana-pankajam adadhah svam*  
*yac caham apy apibam ambu manak tadiyam*  
*tan me manasy udayam eti manoratho'yam*

**“O Tulasi! Compassionate goddess of auspiciousness! By my placing Your lotus feet upon my head and drinking a little water that washed Your lotus feet, the desire to render service in the aforementioned ways have arisen in my heart.”**

*kvaham para-sata-nikrty-anubiddha-cetah*  
*samkalpa esa sahasa kva sudurlabharthe*  
*eka krpaiva tava mam ajahaty-upadhi-*  
*sunyaiva mantum adadhaty agater gatir me*

**“Where am I, whose mind is a maze of hundreds of deceitful thoughts, and where are these very dear yet rarely attained desires that have sprung up within me? Still, because You do not count my offences, but offer me the refuge and destination of Your causeless mercy, am I able to conceive of such desires?"**

*radha-keli-nikunja-vithisu caran radhabhidham uccaran*  
*radhaya anurupam eva paramam dharmam rasenacaran*  
*radhayas caranambhujam paricaran nanopacarir muda*  
*karhi syam sruti-sekharopari carann ascarya-caryam caran*

**“When will I walk on the pathways of Radha’s pastime forests, chant the holy name of Radha, follow the religion of worshipping Radha, and happily serve Radha’s lotus feet in many ways? And when, walking on the heads of all the Vedas, will I serve Radha in the most sublime, intimateways?”**

## Appendix 26

**The Five Methods of Worshipping Lord Balarama**

(This appendix follows from chapter seventeen, in which Garga Muni gives to those gopis who were previously daughters of the snake king a method for becoming wives of Lord Balarama.)

This appendix will give a complete and detailed description of the five methods of worshipping Lord Balarama prescribed by Garga Muni for the naga-kanyas, as found in Sri Garga-samhita, Eighth Canto, chapters ten through thirteen. One thing we can learn from this elaborate description is how bothersome and complex any process for the awakening of Krsna consciousness can be, save and except nama-sankirtana. To that end, devotees may also benefit from this appendix by reciting the prayer (stotra) to Lord Balarama and by reciting the names (nama) of Lord Balarama on His appearance day.

There is a tendency amongst some ISKCON devotees to think that if they chant obscure mantras, equip themselves with kavacas, perform yajhas, and so on, they will somehow enhance the benefits gained from chanting Hare Krsna.

Actually, nothing could be further from the truth. The spiritualpractices adopted by great personalities — like the practices performed by the personified Vedas in their endeavour to become gopis — cannot be attempted by the lesser beings of this age. Spiritual practices cannot be taken up just because they are recorded in scripture. For a spiritual practice to bestow results it must either be the yuga-dharma, and therefore accessible to all souls in a given age, or it should at least be prescribed to a disciple by his guru. Spiritual practices cannot be taken up capriciously. Such behaviour is what Krsna refers to as “acting whimsically in lust” (kama-karatah), and it will only lead one to failure in his efforts, be those efforts spiritual or profane.

Furthermore, as is the case with the worship of Lord Balarama as outlined below, prescribed daily spiritual regimens often include the chanting of mantras that must be heard directly from a spiritual master who is connected to the chain of disciplic succession. Mantras haphazardly culled from books, no matter how devoutly intoned, will not yield perfection. This is the explicit conclusion of the Padma Purana, *sampradaya-vihina ye mantras te nisphala matah*: “A mantra will not bear fruit if it has not been received through disciplic succession.”

For readers who need to be further convinced, we urge them to carefully note the complexity of the following paddhati, mantra, stotra, kavaca, and sahasra-nama. Do devotees honestly think they have the time and determination to undertake these processes, processes that were — please bear in mind — not given to conditioned souls, but to those who were already associates of Lord Ananta?

Indeed, in the narrations that describe devotees who have achieved gopi-bhava by the rigid performance of some daily spiritual practice, we find only the likes of Lord Brahma, Lord Siva, Narada Muni, the personified Vedas, and the naga-kanyas, all of whom were either already liberated at the outset, or are eternal associates of Krsna. There is not a single example of an ordinary conditioned soul undertaking such elaborate spiritual practices in order to become a gopi.

In this age, however, it has become possible by the mercy of Lord Caitanya to approach the level of gopi-bhava through chanting Hare Krsna. Svarupa Damodara Gosvami confirms:

*anarpita-carim cirat karunayavatirnah kalau*  
*samarpayitum unnatojjvala-rasam sva-bhakti-sriyam*  
*harih purata-sundara-dyuti-kadamba-sandipitah sada*  
*hrdaya-kandare sphuratu vah saci-nandanah*

**“May the Supreme Lord who is known as the son of Srimati Saci-devi he transcendentally situated in the innermost chambers of your heart. Resplendent with the radiance of molten gold, He has appeared in the Age of Kali by His causeless mercy to bestow what no incarnation has ever offered before: the most sublime and radiant mellow of devotional service, the mellow of conjugal love.”**

Nonetheless, we will now present, for the edification of our readers, the detailed fivefold process for worshipping Lord Baladeva, once described to Duryodhana by Pradvipaka Muni. Duryodhana was a devotee of Lord Balarama and he enquired how the snake princesses of Patala-loka (naga-kanyas) had become gopis who then enjoyed the rasa dance with the Lord. In response the sage described, one by one, the paddhati, mantra, stotra, kavaca, and sahasra-nama that Garga Muni gave to the naga-kanyas.

**\* \* \* \***

The first of the five limbs of worship is the paddhati, or daily rites. Because Lord Balarama is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, He is not attained by any mechanical process but rather by the practitioner’s underlying mood of devotion. Therefore, to attract the attention of the Lord, these daily rites, as well as the other four limbs of His worship, must he performed with a devotional frame of mind. Such devotion can be obtained only through association with those who already possess it.

That said, the technicalities of the paddhati are as follows:

The sadhaka should rise before brahma-muhurta, chant the holy names of Lord Krsna and Lord Balarama, and how down before his guru. Only after having done these things can he place his feet on the ground. Then, in a secluded place the sadhaka should touch water, sit on a kusa grass mat, place his hands on his lap, and gaze at the tip of his nose. In this state he should meditate on Lord Balarama, whose complexion is fair and who is dressed in blue garments and decorated with a forest garland.

Wearing simple cotton clothing and sleeping on the ground, the sadhaka should control his senses and become free of the six enemies by drinking water twice in a day and by fasting from all but milk, which is taken only once. He should also meditate on Lord Balarama at sunrise, noon, and sunset with single-pointed concentration.

Accompanying this paddhati is the patala of Lord Balarama, the second limb of worship, which begins by chanting the mantra, *om klim kalindi-bhedanaya sankarsanaya svaha*. Brahma first gave this mantra to Narada, and sadhakas must vow to chant it one hundred and sixteen thousand times, after which they are qualified to attempt to perform the following fire sacrifice.

At a sacred place, draw a thirty-two-petalled lotus with five colours and a splendid whorl at the centre. In the centre of the whorl, place a beautiful golden throne, and upon that throne, a Deity of Lord Balarama.

One should then chant the mantra: om namo bhagavate purusottamaya vasudevaya sankarsanaya sahasra-vadanaya mahanantaya svaha. Then he should tie his sikha and bow to the Deity of Balarama as well as the directions.

Chanting the mantra om jaya jayananta balabhadra kama-pala talanka kalindi-bhanjana aviravirbhuya mama sammukho bhava, one should request Lord Balarama to appear. And while chanting another mantra — *om namas te ’stu sira-pane hala-musala-dhara rauhineya nilambara rama revati-ramana namo ’stu te* — one should offer a throne, padya, arghya, bath, madhuparka, incense, lamp, sacred thread, food, garments, ornaments, fragrant flowers, unbroken grains of rice, flowers, arati, and other services to the Lord.

At the conclusion of the first offering the sadhaka should chant another mantra, remembering the different names of the Lord as follows: *om visnave madhusudanaya vamanaya trivikramaya sridharaya hrsikesaya padmanabhaya damodaraya sankarsanaya vasudevaya pradyumnayaniruddhayadhoksajaya purusoctamaya sri-krsnaya namah*.

Then one should worship the limbs of the Deity of Balarama, beginning with His feet and progressing to His head, while chanting this mantra: *om pada-gulpha-januru-katy-udara-parsva-prsthi-bhuja-kandhara-netra-siramsi prthak prthak pujayami*.

After worshipping Lord Balarama in this way the sadhaka should worship the Lord’s paraphernalia and associates by chanting namah before their names (in the dative case). Thus one will worship Baladeva’s paraphernalia as follows: the conch shell, sankhaya namah; the disc, cakraya namah; club, gadayai namah; lotus, padmaya namah; sword, asaye namah; bow, dhanuse namah; arrows, banebhyah namah; plough, halaya namah; club, musalaya namah; Kaustubha jewel, kaustubhaya namah; forest garland, vanamalayai namah; Srivatsa mark, srivatsaya namah; yellow garments, pitambaraya namah; blue garments, nilambaraya namah; flute, vamsyai namah; stick, vetraya namah; chariot marked with the flag of Garuda, garudanka-rathaya namah; chariot marked with the flag of a palm tree, talanka-rathaya namah. And one will worship the Lord’s associates as follows: Daruka, darukaya namah; Sumati, sumataye namah;

*Kumuda, kumudaya namah*; *Kumudaksa, kumudaksaya namah*; and *Sridama, sridamaya namah*.

Following the worship of things and persons associated with Lord Balarama, one should place in their respective places in the lotus, Visvaksena, Vedavyasa, Durga, Ganesa, the planets, and the protectors of the directions, and then worship them accordingly. Then, sprinkling water and offering food cooked in an earthen pot, one should worship the sacred fire.

Again chanting the previously described mula-mantra, the sadhaka should offer 25,000 oblations to the sacred fire. And then, chanting the twelve-syllable mantra om namo bhagavate vasudevaya, one should offer 8,000 oblations. And finally, chanting the catur-vyuha maruta, one should again offer 8,000 oblations.

After circumambulating the sacred fire, one should bow down before his guru, worship him with daksina of valuable garments, gold ornaments, copper vessels, and cows with their newborn calves. And then, with much gold, the sadhaka must worship the brahmanas by offering them food and gifts. One should be careful not to neglect to feed the people of the city and bow down before his gurus.

Throughout all the above steps, sadhakas must not forget to meditate on Lord Balarama with love and devotion. This concludes the description of the second limb of Lord Balarama’s worship.

**\* \* \* \***

The third limb of worship consists of reciting a beautiful prayer to Lord Balarama. Only the translation will be reproduced here:

**“O master of the demigods! O Supreme Personality of Godhead! O Lord Ananta Sesa! O Lord Balarama! O fulfiller of desires, I offer my obeisances to You. O You who maintain the earth, who are the glorious Lord, perfect and complete, who hold a plough in Your hand, who have a thousand heads. O Lord Sankarsana, eternally I offer my obeisances to You!**

**“O Lord Balarama! 0 husband of Revati, elder brother of Krsna. O carrier of the plough, killer of Pralambasura. O Supreme Personality of Godhead, please protect me! O You of fair complexion and blue garments, who carry a palm-tree flag and who are the son of Rohini,**

**I offer my respectful obeisances unto You!**

**“You are the enemy of Dhenuka, Mustika, Kuta, and Balvala, and the killer of Rukmi, Kupakarna, and Kumbhanda. You scattered the Yamuna into many branches, dragged Hastinapura into its waters, and killed Dvivida. O king of the Yadavas! You are the ornament of Vraja. You killed Kamsa’s brothers, and although You are the supreme master, You went on pilgrimage. O Duryodhana’s guru! O master! Please protect me! Please protect me!**

**“O infallible Lord who are greater than the greatest! O Lord whose glories are heard in all directions without limit! Glory to You! Glory to You! Served by demigods, the kings of the sages, and the kings of the serpents, You hold a plough and a club. O powerful one! Obeisances unto You!”**

There is no indication in the Garga-samhita just how many times this prayer should be repeated, but because the phala-stuti mentions reciting it “regularly,” we can safely assume that it should be recited at least once a day.

The Balarama shield or armour (kavaca) is the fourth limb of worship. It is meant to protect one from enemies that lurk within and without, as well as any unfavourable circumstances that may obstruct one’s service to the Lord.

After bathing and then dressing in clean cotton garments, the sadhaka should sit on a kusa grass mat, purify his hands with mantras, bow down, and with fixed intelligence meditate on Lord Krsna’s elder brother, Lord Balarama, by reciting this prayer:

**“May Lord Balarama, the master of Goloka, the supreme controller of all controllers, whose fame is spotless, protect me. May Lord Balarama, who holds the earth on His head as if it were a single mustard seed, protect me in this world.**

**“May Lord Balarama protect me when I am surrounded by many armies. May He who holds a plough always protect me in battle. May the holder of the club always protect me in many fortresses, and may He who is the Supreme Personality of Godhead protect me in the forest.**

**“May Lord Balarama, who wears blue garments and who stopped the Yamuna, always protect me in fire, wind, and in the sky. And may He who is Lord Ananta Himself always protect me in the great ocean.**

**“May Lord Balarama, the son of Vasudeva, protect me on mountains. May He of a thousand heads protect me in great disputes. May the son of Rohini protect me from diseases, and may the one who fulfils desires protect me from catastrophes.**

**“May Lord Balarama, the enemy of Dhenukasura, always protect me from lust. May the killer of Dvivida always protect me from anger. May the enemy of Balvala always protect me from greed, and may the enemy of Jarasandha always protect me from illusion.**

**“May Lord Balarama, the best of the Vrsnis, always protect me at sunrise. May the king of Mathura always protect me in the morning. May the friend of the gopas always protect me at midday, and may He who is supremely independent always protect me in the afternoon.**

**“May Lord Balarama, who is the king of serpents, always protect me at sunset. May He who is greater than the greatest always protect me in the evening. May He whose power is invincible always protect me in the middle of the night and at every sunrise as well.**

**“May Lord Balarama, the master of Revati, protect me from every direction. May the enemy of Pralamba protect me from every direction. May the best of the Yadavas protect me from below, from above, from near, and from far. May Lord Balarama protect me everywhere.**

**“May Lord Balarama, the Supreme Lord, always protect me from within. May He who enjoys pastimes as the king of serpents protect me from without. May He who is the Supersoul residing in everyone’s heart, protect me always.”**

Like the preceding prayer to Lord Balarama, recitation of this kavaca should take place daily at the very least.

**\* \* \* \***

While reciting this kavaca— even in tandem with the paddhati, mantra, and stotra — may not be very time consuming, reciting the Balarama-sahasra-nama (the thousand names of Lord Balarama) certainly is. Moreover, like each of the aforementioned prayers, these thousand names must be pronounced perfectly in order to be effective.

Because of the length of the Balardma-sahasra-nama, only the first one hundred and eight names are included here. Devotees interested in reading them all may consult the Garga-samhita.

While chanting these names of Lord Balarama one should meditate on the Lord who fulfils all desires. He is decorated with a glittering crown, studded bracelets, and tinkling ornaments. He holds a club and a plough. Locks of black hair caress His cheeks, sparkling earrings frame His handsome face, and blue garments swathe His powerful frame just like dark clouds hover over a mountain of snow.

*om balabhadro ramabhadro ramah sankarsano 'cyutah*  
*revati-ramanu devah kama-palo halayudhah*

**“Lord Balarama is supremely powerful and happy (balabhadra), He is the supreme enjoyer (ramabhadra and rama), all-attractive (Sankarsana), infallible (acyuta), the lover of Revati (revati-ramana), the splendid Supreme Personality of Godhead (deva), the Lord who fulfils desires (kama-pala), and He who carries a plough-weapon (halayudha)**

*nilambarah sveta-varno baladevo ‘cyutagrajah*  
*pralambaghno maha-viro rauhineyah pratapavan*

**“He is dressed in blue garments (nilambara), fair-complexioned (sveta-varna), splendid and powerful (baladeva), the elder brother of the infallible Supreme Personality of Godhead (acyutagraja), the killer of Pralamba (pralambaghna), a great hero (maha-vira), the son of Rohini (rauhineya), and very powerful (pratapavan)**

*talanko musali hali harir yadu-varo bali*  
*sira-panih padma-panir lagudi venu-vadanah*

**“He bears the insignia of a palm tree (talanka), holds a club (musali), holds a plough (hali), takes away all that is inauspicious (hari), is the best of the Yadus (yadu-vara), is powerful (bali), holds a plough in His hand (sira-pani), has lotus hands (padma-pani), holds a club (lagudi), and plays the flute (venu-vadana)**

*kalindi-bhedano viro balah prabalah urdhvagah*  
*vasudeva-kalanantah sahasra-vadanah svarat*

**“He divided the Yamuna (kalindi-bhedana). He is heroic (vira), powerful (bala and prabala), exalted (urdhvaga), a plenary expansion of Lord Krsna (vasudeva-kala), and limitless (ananta). He has a thousand heads (sahasra-vadana) and is independent (svarat)."**

*vasur vasumati-bharta vasudevo vasuttamah*  
*yaduttamo yadavendro madhavo vrsni-vallabhah*

**“He is opulent (vasu), the goddess of fortune’s husband (vasumati- bharta), the son of Vasudeva (vasudeva), the best of the Vasus (vasuttama), the best of the Yadavas (yaduttama), the king of the Yadavas (yadavendra), the decendant of Madhu (madhava), and dear to the Vrsnis (vrsni-vallabha)."**

*dvarakeso mathureso dani mani maha-manah*  
*purnah puranah purusah paresah paramesvarah*

**“He is the king of Dvaraka (dvarakesa), the king of Mathura (mathuresa), generous (dani), noble (mani), noble-hearted (maha-mana), perfect (purna), the ancient Supreme Personality of Godhead (purana), the Supreme Person (purusa), the Supreme Master (paresa), and the Supreme Controller (paramesvara).”**

*paripurnatamah saksat-paramah purusottamah*  
*anantah sasvatah seso bhagavan prakrteh parah*

**“He is the perfect Supreme Person (paripurnatama), directly the Supreme Lord (saksat-parama), the Supreme Person (Purusottama), limitless (ananta), eternal (sasvata), Lord Sesa (sesa), the supremely opulent Lord (bhagavan), and beyond the world of matter (prakrteh para)**

*jivatma paramatma ca hy antaratma dhruvo ‘vyayah*  
*catur-vyuhas catur-vedas catur-murtis catus-padah*

**“He is the father of all living entities (jivatma), the Supersoul present in everyone’s heart (paramatma and antaratma), eternal (dhruva), imperishable (avyaya), the origin of the catur-vyuha expansions (catur-vyuha), the author of the four Vedas (catur-veda), the origin of the catur-vyuha (catur-murti), and the master of the four worlds (catus-pada)."**

*pradhanam prakrtih saksi sanghatah sanghavan sakhi*  
*maha-mana buddhi-sakhas ceto ‘hankara avrtah*

**“He is the material cause (pradhana), material nature (prakrti), the witness (saksi), accompanied by His associates (sanghata, sanghavan, and sakhi), noble-hearted (maha-mana), and the best counsellor (buddhi-sakha). He is consciousness (ceta), and ego (ahankara) and He is always surrounded by His associates (avrta).”**

*indriyeso devatatma jnanam karma ca sarma ca*  
*advitiyo dvitiyas ca nirakaro niranjanah*

**“He is the master of the senses (indriyesa), the Supreme Personality of Godhead (devata), the Supersoul (atma), knowledge (jnana), action (karma), auspiciousness (sarma), one without a second (advitiya), different from the individual living entities (dvitiya), a person whose form is not material (nirakara), and untouched by matter (niranjana)**

*virat samrat mahaughas ca dharah sthasnus carisnuman*  
*phanindrah phani-rajas ca sahasra-phana-manditah*

**“He is the entire universe (virat), the supreme monarch (samrat), a great flood (mahaugha), the maintainer of all (dhara), unmoving (sthasnu), going everywhere (carisnuman), the king of serpents (phanindra and phani-raja), and the serpent with a thousand hoods (sahasra-phana-mandita).”**

At the conclusion of this prayer it is stated that perfection is achieved by reciting this sahasra-nama one thousand times on the bank of the Yamuna. To become a great king, however, it should be recited ten times that.

**\* \* \* \***

The combination of these five limbs of worship creates a rather daunting spiritual routine that devotees should easily recognise to be beyond their abilities. In this age, when sadhakas often find it difficult to dedicate a few quality hours a day to chanting sixteen rounds and reading Bhagavad-gita, how will they possibly find the time for such an intensive spiritual regimen?

Aside from the time commitment this discipline requires, it is also absolutely necessary that it be performed without fault and with the utmost precision. In the fivefold worship of the naga-kanyas there is absolutely no room for error in pronunciation, ritual, or meditation. How then can people who are constantly prone to error by the influence of this age, which is known to he an ocean of faults (dosa-nidhi), make any progress in attempting to perfectly perform such paddhatis, mantras, statras, kavacas, and sahasra-namas? They simply cannot.

The purpose and conclusion of this appendix is clearly and succinctly reflected in the words of Sukadeva Gosvami:

*kaler dosa-nidhe rajann asti hy eko mahan gunah*  
*kirtanad eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet*

**“My dear king, although Kali-yuga is full of faults, there is still one good quality about this age. It is that simply by chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra, one can become free from material bondage and be promoted to the transcendental kingdom.”**

Devotees should therefore concentrate their time and energy on nicely chanting Hare Krsna, confident that by this one activity they can achieve perfection. If they so desire, on the strength of purely chanting Hare Krsna they may even become gopi associates of Radha and Krsna, as the naga-kanyas did by worshipping Lord Balarama.

It is clear: there is no other path to perfection in this age than chanting Krsna’s holy names. Devotees are not barred from paddhatis, mantras, stotras, kavacas, and sahasra-namas such as thoseoutlined above, but these ancillary spiritual practices should never minimise, but only enhance, the cultivation of the pure holy name as repeatedly mentioned.

Additional forms of worship, like reciting prayers and chanting mantras, can help to bridle the restless mind by providing helpful meditations and adding variety to one’s primary sadhana. For instance, at the conclusion of the Brhad-bhagavatamrta there is a special collection of prayers and verses that can help to direct one’s consciousness to Krsna in Goloka Vrndavana.While chanting Hare Krsna, devotees may meditate on these prayers and thus become more absorbed in their sadhana.

In short, devotees may practise any of the other eight limbs of devotional service in tandem with the ninth and main limb, nama-sankirtana. But they should never replace chanting Krsna’s names with any other devotional process. As Srila jiva Gosvami writes in his commentary to Srimad-Bhagavatam, *adyapyanya bhaktih kalau kartavya tada kirtanakhya bhakti-samyogenaiva*: “Even though in the Age of Kali one may perform the above eight branches of bhakti, nevertheless, one must perform kirtana as the principal way of advancing in sadhana-bhakti."

Sadhakas may therefore cultivate the other limbs of bhakti, such as smaranam, arcanam, vandanam, dasyam, or sakhyam, but they should do so only as support for kirtana. And as previously mentioned, the prayer to Lord Balarama and the recitation of His names may be incorporated as part of the observance of His appearance day, along with continuously chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra.

## Appendix 27

**How Sri Radha Is Revealed Through the Vedic Literature**

(This appendix follows from chapter seventeen, one of two chapters that glorify Radha-kunda, and confirms the Gaudiya Vaisnavas’ worship of Srimati Radharani as the Supreme Lord's topmost consort to be the authentic conclusion of the Vedic literature.)

Academics and religionists, generally speaking, do not share the view held by faithful adherents of Gaudiya Vaisnavism that Srimati Radharani is the personal feminine aspect of the Absolute Truth. Nor do they agree that loving service to Sri Radha, alongside Sri Krsna, is the ultimate goal of life as it is propounded by the Vedas. For sceptics such as these, Radharani’s infrequent appearance in sruti is taken to be convincing evidence that Radha could hardly be the Supreme Truth at which the Vedas ultimately arrive. Moreover, they insist that when Radha does appear in Smrti, in the Puranas in particular, such mention is either the result of philosophical interpolation or literary fancy.

Were this sort of scepticism to be succinctly expressed it would presumably sound something like this: “If Radha’s position in the Vedic pantheon is so philosophically significant, why is She not mentioned more prominently in the Vedas?” This appendix will address that challenge by showing that the Vedas do indeed speak of Sri Radha — as they do of Sri Krsna — but in a context relevant, and a manner most useful, to a sincere student of the Vedas.

The Skanda Purana confirms that Krsna — and by implication Radha, as we shall later see — is the constant focus of the Vedas:

*vede ramayane caiva purane bharate tatha*  
*adav ante ca madhye ca harih sarvatra giyate*

**“In the Vedic literature, including the Ramayana, Puranas, and Mahabharata, from the very beginning (adau) to the end (ante ca), as well as within the middle (madhye ca), only Hari, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is explained.”**

The Vedas also speak of Sri Radha, both directly through the scriptures themselves and through the writings of empowered acaryas who are faithful representatives of Vyasadeva, the original compiler of the Vedas.

To call into question Srimati Radharani’s apparent absence from the Vedas is both misleading and prejudicial. It is to imply that because She is not mentioned in the pages of the Vedic texts She cannot be relevant to the Vedic conclusion, and by extension, that the Gaudiya Vaisnava conception of Radha cannot be genuinely Vedic.

But there is an alternative explanation for the Vedas’ infrequent mention of Sri Radha. That explanation contends that Radha is actually the goal to which the Vedas ultimately point, but because it may not be advantageous for novices to directly approach the highest conception of the Absolute Truth, mention of Sri Radha in the Vedas remains indirect until spiritual aspirants have matured to the stage at which the position of Srimati Radharani can be fully appreciated. How that process of maturation is promoted in the Vedas will also be discussed in this appendix.

There is no logical reason why this second explanation should be dismissed outright. Indeed, to ignore its possible veracity indicates a priori bias. This appendix will show how this second explanation is harmonious with the philosophical presentation of the Vedas and the testimony of the great acaryas who have fully assimilated Vedic wisdom.

However, before delving more deeply into our explanation with all necessary supporting evidence, certain principles must first be established as axiomatic truths. These foundational principles could be fully verified at this point in the discussion. For the sake of brevity, and because they have already been brilliantly proven elsewhere, we will simply state them here.

Jiva Gosvami elaborates on these axioms in his Tattva-sandarbha. They are as follows:

(1) Sruti and Smrti are equally Vedic, the latter being an elaboration of the former.

(2) Srimad-Bhagavatam is the most perfect of all smrti scriptures. Consequently, it is the highest form of Vedic evidence.

(3) Srimad-Bhagavatam establishes that Krsna is the Absolute Truth and that He is described in the Vedas both directly and indirectly.

Objection and Refutation: Scholar of Sanskrit literature Barbara Stoler Miller voices a view common to sceptics when she writes,

**"Radha is one of the most obscure figures in early Indian literature. Until Jayadeva made her the heroine of his poem, she appeared only in stray verses scattered throughout various Puranas.” And a modern-day follower of Madhvacarya articulates similar sentiments, albeit with a palpable air of incredulity, “Even granting that one of the gopikas is called Radha as per Padma Purana, it is inconceivable how the supposedly highest layer of truth is found in Padma Purana (actually not even that, since the details of the pastimes are found primarily in writings of Gaudiya acaryas, not in Padma Purana either), and not in any of the standard texts on Vedanta.’’**

To summarise their argument: since Sri Radha’s name, much less Her glories and pastimes, are rarely if ever mentioned in the Vedas, Upanisads, and Vedanta, She could not possibly be relevant to the Vedic conclusion. It is even less plausible that She could be the original form of the Lord’s potency, adi-sakti.

Then how do sceptics explain the limited passages in sruti and the more abundant passages in smrti that do speak about Radha? And what do they say about the works of the acaryas that describe Her as Krsna’s divine counterpart?

Sceptics assert that the references in sruti are not only limited but inconclusive as well. Vaisnavas, they say, should not “construct fanciful etymologies for the word radha,’’ but see them in the context of the greater message of the Vedic scriptures, scriptures that, as they see it, are neither about Radha nor Krsna. In other words, they should be ignored.

As for the Puranic episodes found in smrti, sceptics deem them as inauthentic as they deem the Puranas themselves. According to such sceptics, the Puranas are non-Vedic, composed by many authors long after the compilation of sruti. They consider the authority of those authors to be dubious, and their literary output plagued by neologism and philosophical interpolation. In their minds, the Puranic passages dealing with Radha should also be ignored.

Finally, sceptics view the works of the Gaudiya acaryas and Vaisnava poets as no more than the popularisation of a theme introduced by Jayadeva, which romanticises the pastoral life of a Puranic deity, Krsna, with a completely fictitious figure, Radha, as His consort. The picture that the acaryas paint of Radha and Krsna troubles some of these sceptics enough for them to say, “The very thought of God falling in love with someone is something sickening \[and reminiscent of a legend\] pulled out of Greek mythology.”

The conclusion of the sceptics can be summarised as follows: Radha is not mentioned in the Vedas because She has no connection with their purpose. As A.W. Entwistle writes, “There is no indication of any personality comparable with Krsna’s Radha \[in the Vedas\]." Such sceptics are convinced that Radha is the product of a literary tradition incorporated into Bengali Vaisnavism during the fifteenth century, around which Caitanya’s followers developed an elaborate theology that has seen a worldwide revival over the last fifty years orso.

As mentioned in the opening paragraph, Gaudiya Vaisnavas reject the view of the sceptics, in which Radha’s importance is measured solely by the number of times Her name appears on the pages of Vedic texts. Such a quantitative assessment is not only misguided but also biased from the outset by the sceptics’ wholesale rejection of Puranic references on the grounds that the Puranas themselves are somehow not Vedic.

It should be noted that because Radha and Krsna are inextricably linked, the Gaudiya Vaisnava explanation of Srimati Radharani’s relevance to the Vedic literature directly addresses Krsna’s relevance as well. The Gaudiya view, therefore, refutes the attempts of sceptics to eject Krsna from the Vedic tradition along with Radha, in spite of the clear testimony of the Vedas themselves.

*srutir mata prsta disati bhavad-aradhana-vidhim*  
*yatha matur vani smrtir api tatha vakti bhagini*  
*puranadya ye va sahaja-nivahas te tad-anuga*  
*atah satyam jnatam mura-hara bhavan eva saranam*

**“When the mother Vedas \\sruti\] is questioned as to whom to worship, she says that You are the only Lord and worshipable object. Similarly, the corollaries of the sruti-sastras, the smrti-sastras, give the same instructions, just like sisters. The Puranas, which are like brothers, follow in the footsteps of their mother. O enemy of the demon Mura, the conclusion is that You are the only shelter. Now I have understood this in truth.”**

How does the Gaudiya Vaisnava view of the Vedic texts differ from that of the sceptics?

Gaudiya Vaisnavas envision the Vedas — Puranas included — as one cohesive body of work that gradually elevates its students through progressive stages of spiritual development from beginner through intermediate and all the way to the most advanced levels of realisation. In other words, like any educational system that starts with basic knowledge and systematically introduces more complex principles, the Vedic system admits students in their initial ignorance and gradually brings them to full realisation of the Absolute Truth. The Bhagavad-gita, for instance, summarises this Vedic system in which Krsna Himself prescribes successive stages of spiritual elevation.

In light of this systematic view, it is only logical that earlier Vedic texts would not give as much detail about the Absolute Truth as later ones, inasmuch as elementary students of maths are made to memorise their times tables before they are able to incorporate multiplication into the process of solving algebraic equations in the higher grades. As students become more accomplished in spiritual science, naturally more information can be made available to them. Not to follow this type of progressive approach would simply he poor pedagogy.

The successive stages of spiritual development just mentioned are three in number, corresponding to three grades of followers — the fruitive worker, the seeker of knowledge, and the worshipper — each exhibiting relative grades of purity from lowest to highest.

The fruitive workers (karmis) are still attached to enjoying this world, but instead of labouring blindly after material gain, they follow the system of Vedic rituals and regulations to ensure their sensual gratification. The actions of these future candidates for spiritual pursuit are guided by the four Vedas, which constitute the karma-kanda, or the ritualistic portion of the Vedic texts.

By following scriptural injunctions, performing sacrifices, and surrendering to the guidance of Vedic priests (brahmanas), these adherents of the Vedas gradually develop faith in spiritual authority, act according to the laws of nature created by God, and thereby become purified at heart. Their spiritual natures revived by being purified of material motivations, these souls become eager to know more about their eternal spiritual identities, the cause of their suffering, the universal laws that control them, and the ultimate controller of everything. Once persons have become thirsty for this kind of knowledge they are called jnanis, and the knowledge they seek is available in the Upanisads and Vedanta-sutra. These texts comprise the jnana-kanda portion of the Vedas, which deals with matters of philosophical enquiry.

Further purified by knowledge and austerity, aspiring transcen- dentalists eventually conclude that they should worship the cause of everything in the way that Krsna explains to Arjuna in Bhagavad-gita, *jnanavan mam prapadyate vasudevah sarvam iti*: “He who is actually in knowledge surrenders unto Me, knowing Me to be the cause of all causes and all that is.” These persons are devotees (bhaktas), and they follow the Puranas, which describe the personal aspect of God through historical narrations of His activities and the activities of His devotees. The Puranas are also known as the upasana-kanda portion of the Vedas.

Krsna declares in His instructions to Uddhava that people in general are ignorant of the progressive purpose of the Vedas in its threefold divisions:

*kim vidhatte kim acaste kim anudya vikalpayet*  
*ity asya hrdayam loke nanyo mad veda kascana*

**“In the entire world no one but Me actually understands the confidential purpose of Vedic knowledge. Thus people do not know what the Vedas are actually prescribing in the ritualistic injunctions of karma-kanda, or what object is actually being indicated in the formulas of worship found in the upasana-kanda, or that which is elaborately discussed through various hypotheses in the jnana-kanda section of the Vedas.”**

As the saying goes, quite often one can’t see the forest for the trees. It is therefore not surprising that the Vedic statements glorifying Radha and Krsna are so widely misunderstood.

Having outlined the process the Vedas prescribe for gradual spiritual elevation, let us now consider the ultimate goal of that process — direct realisation of the Absolute Truth. Substantially speaking, what is the nature of that Absolute Truth?

Two scriptural statements are relevant here. The Vedanta-sutra says, *ananda-mayo 'bhyasat*, which means that the Absolute Truth seeks pleasure by nature. And the Taittiriya Upanisad adds that the Lord is raso vai sah rasam hy evayam: “He Himself is rasa, the taste or mellow of a particular relationship.”

To synthesise these two statements: the Absolute Truth enjoys Himself through the variety of tastes found in relationships. Implicit in this conclusion is the fact that the Absolute Truth must be a person; how can a thing, inanimate or formless, taste or enjoy in a variety of relationships?

In short, the Absolute Truth must be a sentient living entity, and not a singular entity. As the sruti declares, tad aiksata bahu syam: “He becomes many.” Thus the Absolute Truth is not one, but two — the energetic source and His energies, the enjoyer and the enjoyed.

**\* \* \* \***

Let us consider the following:

If the Absolute Truth is manifest in dual aspects as the supreme enjoyer (purusa) and the supreme enjoyed (prakrti), then it stands to reason that so long as the tendency to enjoy independently of the supreme remains strong within the hearts of karmis, jnanis, and even neophyte bhaktas, then they should not hear any details regarding the enjoyment of the Absolute Truth. Hearing about the Lord’s transcendental enjoyment will only stoke the fires of material enjoyment burning within their hearts and hamper their spiritual progress.

With this danger in mind, the Vedic literatures do not elaborate on all aspects of transcendental knowledge, in all three stages of spiritual development, in all its texts. Therefore, in the karma-kanda portion of the Vedas neither Radha nor Krsna receive detailed, explicit mention. Instead, the need for basic religiosity is emphasised. In the jnana-kanda, Radha’s identity remains obscured, and while Krsna is spoken about in both impersonal and personal terms, His true identity is still not explicitly revealed. Only in the upasana-kanda, after followers of the Vedas have understood the nature of the individual self and of the Supreme Self and their relationship, is Krsna fully revealed along with His eternal consort, Srimati Radharani.

The methodology of the Vedas is to first introduce spiritual aspirants to a singular concept of God — a creator, a Lord of everything, an indwelling guide of everyone. Once devotees have accepted this conception of the supreme, they come to know Krsna as that Supreme Lord. Having developed strong faith in Krsna, they then become qualified to hear in detail of His amorous nature and His eternal consort.

In Srila Prabhupada’s words:

**“So we should not try to understand Krsna’s love with the gopis all of a sudden. It is very confidential Let us understand Krsna first of all. Of course, that is the aim, the higher understanding of Krsna. Gopi-bhava-rasamrtabdhi-lahari-kallola-magnau. But not all of a sudden. Try to understand Krsna first.... When you understand Krsna in that way, then, if you follow the footsteps of the acaryas, sri-rupa-raghunatha-pade haibe akuti, then you’ll be able to understand what is the loving affairs between Krsna and Radharani. Don’t try to understand all of a sudden… Then you’ll fall down.”**

The different sections of the Vedas, and the spiritual processes they recommend, are all for achieving Krsna, although the degree to whichthey reveal Krsna differs according to the methodology described above. The value of being situated somewhere within this Vedic process of gradual spiritual evolution, on the path to direct realisation of the Absolute Truth, as opposed to simply meandering in the meaninglessness of an unregulated life, is lauded by Krsna Himself.

*sri-bhagavan uvaca*  
*ya etan mat-patho hitva bhakti-jnana-kriyatmakan*  
*ksudran kamams calaih pranair jusantah samsaranti te*

**“The Supreme Personality of Godhead said; Those who give up these methods for achieving Me, which consist of devotional service, analytic philosophy, and regulated execution of prescribed duties, and instead, being moved by the material senses, cultivate insignificant sense gratification, certainly undergo the continual cycle of material existence.”**

It is important to note that for sincere spiritual aspirants the Vedic system of gradual elevation in pursuit of progressive revelation of the Absolute Truth is not optional. Adherents of the Vedas must worship according to their qualifications. That means they should not seek to know more about the Absolute Truth than their level of spiritual advancement qualifies them to know. The scarcity of information about Radha in the four Vedas and in the Upanisads is therefore not a defect; rather, it is within the grand scheme of the Vedic teachings, a scheme that demands aspirants not hear about Radha until they have developed the proper qualifications.

Krsna describes this principle in the following well-known verse:

*sve sve ’dhikare ya nistha sa gunah parikirtitah*  
*viparyayas tu dosah syad ubhayor esa niscayah*

**“Steadiness in one’s own position is declared to be actual piety, whereas deviation from one’s position is considered impiety. In this way the two are definitely ascertained.”**

From the discussion thus far it should be clear why only the Puranas speak about Srimati Radharani. But the reason why various Puranas speak about Radha in a variety of ways should also briefly be addressed. For instance, the Brahma-vaivarta Purana describes Radha as the wife of Krsna, the Brhan-naradiya Purana relates how She cursed Her brother over a disagreement, and Sri Garga-samhita describes Her as living amidst Vaikuntha-like opulence. Obviously, the composite picture these Puranas paint of Radha is not a homogeneous one. Why? Because Puranic literature is divided into three categories corresponding to three types of people: those under the influence of ignorance, those under the influence of passion, and those under the influence of goodness. Therefore, in order to appeal to different audiences, the ways in which the Puranas portray Radha vary.

But is it possible to harmonise these apparently contradictory images of Sri Radha?

Yes. In the same way one resolves which incarnation of Visnu can rightfully claim to be the Supreme Personality of Godhead: by turning to the pramanam amalam, the “spotless evidence” of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

The famous verse from the Bhagavatam’s First Canto, beginning *ete camsa-kalah pumsah*, clearly resolves that Krsna is the Absolute Truth. But what does it say about Sri Radha? Interestingly enough, as much as Srimad-Bhagavatam speaks about Krsna, even elaborately describing His pastimes with the gopis, it does not mention Srimati Radharani by name.

Why does Radha remain hidden in Srimad-Bhagavatam, even while She is explicitly spoken about in lesser Puranas?

The answer is that Srimad-Bhagavatam actually reveals the real Radha, while the lesser Puranas cover Her with veils made of the three modes. Srimad-Bhagavatam, however, is completely pure and transcendental and presents Radha as She is. The real Radharani is so chaste and so faithful to Krsna that She does not make Herself available to anyone else, even through the pages of Srimad-Bhagavatam.

Nevertheless, Srimati Radharani is made accessible in two ways. Firstly, through the indirect language with which Srimad-Bhagavatam refers to Her. Implicitly, Sukadeva Gosvami says, “If you are qualified to hear about Sri Radha, then you will understand and be pleasedwhen I speak of Her indirectly.” Krsna appreciates confidential, esoteric descriptions such as these, as He Himself says:

*veda brahmatma-visayas tri-kanda-visaya ime*  
*paroksa-vada rsayah paroksam mama ca priyam*

**“The Vedas, divided into three divisions, ultimately reveal the living entity as pure spirit soul. The Vedic seers and mantras, however, deal in esoteric terms, and I also am pleased by such confidential descriptions.”**

Simply put, those who are qualified can sec Radha in the pages of Srimad-Bhagavatam, hut those who are not qualified cannot. Thus on the basis of “one’s own position” (sve sve ’dhikare), Srimad-Bhagavatam makes Her accessible to those suitably qualified while it conceals Her from those who are not.

Secondly, Srimati Radharani is made accessible through the descriptions of Her personal associates, the gopis, who personally appeared as the most confidential followers of Caitanya Mahaprabhu.

Caitanya Mahaprabhu ordered Rupa Gosvami and Sanatana Gosvami, and through them, Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami, Jiva Gosvami, and Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami to disclose the truths of Vrndavana and its queen, Sri Radha. These saints are all accepted as incarnations of Srimati Radharani’s intimate gopi associates. What Vyasadeva did not directly reveal — or did reveal only indirectly— the Gosvamis fully revealed, by the explicit order of Krsna in His form as Caitanya Mahaprabhu. Books like Ujjvala-nilamani, Lalita-madhava, Brhad-bhagavatamrta, Stavavali, and others should therefore be seen as authorised appendices to Srimad-Bhagavatam. Devotees who are qualified to read these books may do so, but those who are not qualified must first become so.

It is for these reasons that Radha s name does not copiously and unequivocally appear in sruti and nyaya. The next section will attempt to illuminate some of the scriptural references to Srimati Radharani found in the Vedas. Careful readers will note the picture of Sri Radha that evolves with each successive quote, like a picture puzzle assembled piece by piece.

Vedic References: Up until the time of Laksmipati Tirtha, in the fifteenth century, the Brahma sampradaya worshipped Krsna alone, without Radha. But when Madhavendra Puri introduced the mood of service in ecstatic love, the Gaudiya branch of the sampradaya adopted the practice of worshipping Sri Radha alongside Sri Krsna. Later, the wife of Lord Nityananda, Jahnava-devi, embellished this established theological principle by adding to temple worship practical service to Radha and Krsna Deities. Because this method of worship was novel at the time, and because the scriptural understanding of Sri Radha was still not widespread, the Gaudiya Vaisnava sampradaya came under heavy criticism from different quarters, even from the disciplic succession of Madhva, to which it formally belongs.

In the eighteenth century, Baladeva Vidyabhusana wrote the first Gaudiya Vaisnava commentary on Vedanta-sutra in reply to an attack on the authenticity of the worship of Radha and Govinda in Jaipur.

A few hundred years earlier, in his book Ujjvala-nilamani, Rupa Gosvami had provided references from Vedic literature that describe the appearance of Srimati Radharani. Rupa Gosvami writes:

*maha-bhava-svarupeyam gunair ativariyasi*  
*gopalottara-tapanyam yad gandharveti visruta*  
*radhety rk-parisiste ca madhavena sahodita*  
*atas tadiya-mahatmyam padme devarsinoditam*  
*tatha hi*  
*yatha radha priya visnos tasyah kundala priyam tatha*  
*sarva-gopisu saivaika visnor atyanta-vallabha*

**“Srimati Radharani is glorified in all Vedic literatures. In the Gopala-tapani Upanisad, Uttara-kanda, She is addressed by the name Gandharva. In the Rg-veda-parisista She is addressed by the name Radha and described as the companion of Madhava. In the Padma Purana, Devarsi Narada sings Her glories: ‘Just as Srimati Radharani is dear to Lord Visnu, so Her lake, Radha-kunda is also dear to Him. Of all the gopis, Srimati Radharani is the most dear to Lord Visnu.’”**

Rupa Gosvami first refers to the Gopala-tapani Upanisad. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura and Baladeva Vidyabhusana have both stated in their commentaries on this text that it forms part of the Pippalada branch of the Atharva Veda. Thus there can be no reasonable argument that this reference is not Vedic. At the beginning of the Uttara-vibhaga portion, the text says:

*tesam madhye hy srestha gandharvety uvaca*  
*tam hi vai tabhir evam vicarya*

**“The leader of the gopis, named Gandharvi, had a quick discussion with Her friends and then questioned the sage.”**

The context is unmistakable. The story starts in Vraja. The gopis are speaking with Krsna — also addressed by the name Gopala — who sends them to Durvasa Muni. In this verse the leader of the gopis, Gandharvi, addresses that sage. The name Gandharvi is repeated twice more in the text. It is certainly difficult to interpret this reference in any way other than directly, which must lead one to conclude that Radha’s and Krsna’s pastimes are mentioned in the Atharva Veda.

Astute readers of the four Vedas will follow the clue given in this Upanisad by accepting Krsna as the Absolute Truth and Gandharvi as His primary consort. Students who are not so astute, however, will remain absorbed in chanting the hymns of the karma-kanda and aspiring to study the philosophy of the jnana-kanda.

Rupa Gosvami’s second reference comes from the Rg-veda-parisista, in which we find this oft-quoted verse:

*radhaya madhavo devo*  
*madhavena ca radhika*  
*vibhrajante janesva*

**“Madhava becomes especially beautiful by Radha’s side, in the same way that She is especially beautiful beside Him; together They outshine all others.”**

This verse has been quoted by acaryas like Jiva Gosvami, Dhyanacandra Gosvami, and Bhaktivinoda Thakura. As the name Radha is mentioned twice, there can be no argument that Her name is not present in sruti. Nonetheless, sceptics have provided a different interpretation of the word “Radha,” and of this verse itself. Authors like Barbara Stoler Miller would rather believe that “Madhava” refers to “the spring season” in which the “Radha star” is especially bright. In contrast, the acaryas mentioned at the beginning of this paragraph are unanimous in their opinion that the verse speaks not about heavenly bodies but about the divine couple. Of course, when forced to choose between the bona fides of the two disputants in this case, we side with the acaryas.

The third verse cited by Rupa Gosvami, although from smrti not sruti, will be presented here for the sake of continuity before we continue to examine more references to Sri Radha found in sruti. This verse is one of many verses in the Padma Purana that extol the virtues of Srimati Radharani. In praising the month of Karttika, that text says:

*yatha radha priya visnos tasyah kundam priyam tatha*  
*sarva-gopisu saivaika visnor atyanta-vallabha*

**“Just as Radha is most dear to Krsna, Her bathing pond is similarly dear. Of all the gopis, She is the most beloved of the Lord.”**

This verse is often cited by the Gaudiya Vaisnava acaryas to demonstrate the importance of Sri Radha. As the verse testifies, Radha is not simply dear to Krsna, She is the “most beloved” of all the gopis. Once again, the verse speaks for itself, yet academics boldly attempt to discredit it. Barbara Stoler Miller writes, “This section \[of the Padma Purana\] is noted several times in the attempts of the Gosvamins to fix Radha's place in established textual traditions, but the section itself seems to me a crude interpolation aimed at elevating Radha’s position in a more orthodox Visnu cult.”

Is this verse actually a “crude interpolation”?

Rather than answering that question from a linguistic, contextual, or logical standpoint, let us instead examine how Vaisnava scholars have dealt with this verse throughout the ages. At least from Caitanya Mahaprabhu Himself in the sixteenth century up to Srila Prabhupada in the more recent era, every acarya has accepted the validity of this verse and its source. No one has questioned its veracity. Considering that Miller neither defends nor explains her stance, there would seem little reason to accept her interpretation.

Even though this verse is not obscure, if it were the only verse in the Padma Purana to refer to Radharani, then it might be dismissed as solitary evidence. However, the Padma Purana is full of passages that glorify Radha as Krsna’s consort. Here is but one of the many: “O brahmana! One who worships Radha and Krsna becomes freed of all sins and returns to live with Them in the charming world of Goloka.” Here again, we find an unequivocal statement about the divine couple.

And if the Padma Purana were the only Purana or Smrti scripture to mention Radha, then sceptics might argue that it is the isolated opinion of one text, incongruent with the greater Vedic body of literature. However, Srimati Radharani is directly mentioned in numerous Puranas and other scriptures from smrti, and in all these texts She is presented as Krsna’s internal potency, most beloved, and eternal consort. It is hard to understand how sceptics can dismiss such a wealth of evidence as inconsequential, let alone non-existent. But unfortunately that has been the case.

The following are only some of the authorised smrti-sastras that mention Sri Radha directly: Bhavisya Purana, Brahmanda Purana, Brahma-vaivarta Purana, Garuda Purana, Naradiya Purana, Skanda Purana, Varaha Purana, Vayu Purana, Narada Pancaratra, Urdhvamnaya-tantra, Brhad-gautamiya-tantra, and so on.

This list, while by no means exhaustive, is still a formidable bank of evidence. One may object that some of the scriptures mentioned are not sattvika and thus their statements should not be considered authoritative. But it would be incorrect to argue that Puranas in the lower modes contain no valid knowledge. At the very least, they obviously give insight into Sri Radha’s presence in and relevance to the Vedas. Moreover, knowledge of Radha is also found in sattvika Puranas like the Narada, Garuda, Padma, Bhagavata, and Varaha.

And moreover, there are other references to Srimati Radharani found within the sruti-sastras. For instance, Baladeva Vidyabhusana argues, on the strength of the following reference, that the Upanisads describe Laksmi-devi, who is an expansion of Radha, as having many forms in order to accompany Visnu’s many incarnations.

*parasya saktir vividhaiva sruyate*

**“It is heard in the Vedas that Lord Visnu’s transcendental potency manifests in many forms.”**

And while Srimati Radharani’s name is not directly mentioned in this verse, Her identity as Visnu’s (or Krsna’s) original potency is inferred.

This quote is part of a lengthy, but unambiguous, description of the personal and physical qualities of the Absolute Truth, referred to in the Svetasvatara Upanisad as isvara, parama, and mahesvara. In Srila Prabhupada’s words, the Lord’s potencies mentioned in this revered text are “multifarious.” In context this implies that because they emanate from the Supreme Person, those potencies must also be persons. Baladeva’s translation assumes that parasya sakti means, “there is one supreme sakti that appears as many.”

The next line of the verse under discussion states, svabhaviki jnana-bala-kriya ca, which reinforces the idea that the potencies are persons. Why? Because this line says that the Lord, with the help of “many potencies” (svabhaviki), engages in “many pastimes" (bala-kriya). In light of the first two references Rupa Gosvami gives in the verse from Ujjvala-nilamani quoted earlier, these two lines from the Svetasvatara Upanisad can be read in the following way: “Madhava (Krsna) manifests His primordial energy in the form of Gandharvi(Radha), who expands into other gopi forms. Together, by engaging in pastimes and rendering different services, those gopis fulfil all the needs of the Lord.”

Baladeva Vidyabhusana then quotes the Purusa-bodhini Upanisad of the Atharva Veda. The Purusa-bodhini is the sequel to the Atharvana Upanisad, in which the Gopala-tapani forms the first six portions. The Purusa-bodhini is also called the Radha Upanisad. The third section of its first chapter begins, *gokuladhye mathura-mandale vrndavana- madhye / sahasra-dala-padme sodasa-dala-madhye*: “In the supreme abode of Gokula in the district of Mathura, Srimati Radharani and Srimati Candravali-devi stand at the left and right side of Lord Krsna.” And that, “Srimati Radharani expands Herself as Laksmi, Durga, and many other potencies of the Lord, which are all Her incarnations.”

Aside from the fact that this larger section of the Purusa-bodhini Upanisad of the Atharva Veda describes Gokula as the topmost abode, which is noteworthy in and of itself, it is amazing that the name Radha is mentioned four times, the name Radhika thrice, and Krsna’s name is mentioned twelve times. In addition, gopis like Candravali, Lalita, Syamala, and Bhadra are listed amongst those saktis who enrich Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes. Lesser expansions of Radha, like Laksmi, as well as the forests of Vraja and the associates and relatives of the divine couple are all mentioned as well. With that in mind, it is difficult to understand how one could say that Radha is neither mentioned in the Vedas, nor lauded by that same body of literature as Krsna’s primary consort in Vraja. In spite of the willful ignorance of some, it is clear that such evidence does indeed exist.

Combining all the previous information with these details gleaned from the quotes of the Purusa-bodhini, we get an increasingly vivid picture of Srimati Radharani, which includes Her role as the queen of Vrndavana and the beloved of the Supreme Lord.

**\* \* \* \***

Before presenting further scriptural evidence, let us consider a methodology for understanding the references we have discussed so far.

No doubt, there is relatively little mention of Srimati Radharani in the Vedas.As already mentioned, this is due in large to a general lack of qualification on the part of the students of these scriptures. However, we should not assume that qualified readers do not exist. Therefore, for those fortunate souls, certain passages of the four Vedas and Upanisads do contain references to Radha. When such qualified students come across these descriptions, they are inspired to search for more, and in so doing, piece together a more complete picture of Srimati Radharani’s identity, qualities, and pastimes. To that end, we are presenting these quotes not in isolation from one another, but as interconnecting texts.

Nonetheless, one may yet argue that the overall number of references is still too few to be able to paint a comprehensive picture. To this doubt we can only reply that for one who develops a genuine interest in Radha and Krsna, the Lord will give him or her the intelligence necessary to proceed in the right direction. This is Krsna’s guarantee in the Bhagavad-gita, *tesam satata-yuktanam bhajatam priti-purvakam / dadami buddhi-yogam tam yena mam upayanti te*: “To those who are constantly devoted to serving Me with love, I give the understanding by which they can come to Me.”

There are more references from sruti that could be given here, but the next quote will be the last before we cite evidence from Smrti. Acaryas like Jiva Gosvami, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, and Srila Prabhupada have all quoted the following verse from the Rg-veda-samhita:

*ta vam vastuny usmasi gamadhyai*  
*yatra gavo bhuri-srnga ayasah*  
*atraha tad urugayasya krsnah*  
*paramam padam avabhati bhuri*

**“We wish to go to Your \[Radha’s and Krsna’s\] beautiful houses, about which cows with large, excellent horns are wandering. Yet distinctly shining on this earth is that supreme abode of Yours that showers joy on all, O Urugaya \[Krsna, who is much praised\].”**

The features unique to this verse, which help to enrich the picture that has emerged so far, are two in number. Firstly, the abode where Radha serves Krsna is full of cows—it is a goloka — and secondly, the phrase usmasi gamadhyai (“we desire to attain”) implies not only that Radha’s and Krsna’s abode is attainable but also that spiritual disciplines exist which enable one to attain it.

In that sense, the significance of the phrase “we desire to attain” should not be minimised. Having come to accept Radha’s and Krsna’s joint supremacy over the spiritual world, a qualified student of the Vedas may well intelligently enquire, “How can I go there?” This verse replies that there is a way. But a detailed route is not given; it is left to the sincere student to find. If one with a pure desire to attain that divine abode enquires from the knowers of the Vedas, then as Caitanya Mahaprabhu tells Rupa Gosvami, *guru-krsna-prasade paya bhakti-lata-bija*: “By the mercy of both Krsna and the spiritual master, such a person receives the seed of the creeper of devotional service.” Thus, by Krsna’s grace the qualified student will be directed to a qualified spiritual master conversant in the subject of the student’s inquiries. By the merciful tutelage of his guru, the inquisitive soul will be given the seed of the creeper of devotional service. Then, having received that seed, he will embark on the process of sadhana-bhakti by hearing and chanting about the Lord. With much determination and perseverance, that quest will eventually lead to the gates of Goloka.

The verses from sruti quoted in this section form a clear picture of Srimati Radharani that is hardly obscure, and is certainly not at odds with what the Puranas or the acaryas have said about Sri Radha. The interpretive fancies of faithless sceptics have unnecessarily obscured that which, though admittedly sparse, is perfectly lucid. In one comment representative of this unfortunate trend, a present-day follower of Madhvacarya boldly proclaims that mere mention of Radha is “non-existent in Indian scriptures.” Not only is this misinformation but it is also poor scholarship. Unfortunately, because of speculations such as these the rumour of Srimati Radharani’s irrelevance to the Vedas has spread. This rumour should not be believed.

Puranic References: Having examined some of the evidence of Radha’s presence in the sruti, let us now study examples of evidence in the smrti.

In describing the slaying of Aristasura, the Varaha Purana glorifies the benefits of bathing in Radha-kunda by referring to it as a place where “Radha embraced tireless Krsna” (radha samaslisya krsnam aklistakaranam).

In the Brahma-vaivarta Purana, starting from the verse that begins with krsnasyardhanga-sambhuta, Garga Muni informs Nanda Maharaja about the secrets of Sri Radha’s identity:

**“Originally manifested from half of Lord Krsna’s body, Radha has now become the daughter of Vrsabhanu and Kalavati. She is the primordial goddess, the root of all nature, and although She stays always in Goloka, by Lord Krsna’s order She has come to this world without entering a mother’s womb—Radha embodies half the divine effulgence of Sri Krsna, and the irrefutable decree of the Vedas is that They are both one supreme truth appearing in two forms. He is Her husband and She is His wife. He is Her lover and She is His beloved. Their two forms are equal in splendour, beauty, virtue, power, intelligence, wisdom, and opulence; but because She came to this earth first, She is said to be a little older than He. He always thinks of Her and She always thinks of Him. She is made of His life breath and He is the form of Her life breath.”**

While this description of Radha is largely self-explanatory, one important phrase should be emphasised: bhedo vede 'nirupitah. In establishing these truths about Srimati Radharani, Garga Muni declares that what he is saying is not his opinion but, *bhedo vede ’nirupitah*: “The Vedas never say They are different from each other.” Thus this Purana states that its glorification of Radha is supported by all Vedic literature.

As is to be expected, Barbara Stoler Miller attempts to discount these statements of the Brahma-vaivarta Purana by alleging them to be insertions from “as late as the sixteenth century.” But of course she gives neither supporting evidence nor logical explanation for her assertion.

In the Matsya Purana, Sati describes to her father, Daksa, the different forms that she takes at holy places, *sivakunde Sivananda nandini devikatate / rukmini dvaravatyam tu radha vrndavane vane*: “At Sivakunda I am Sivananda, at Devikatata I am Nandini, at Dvaravati I am Rukmini, and in the forest at Vrndavana I am Radha.”This is an example of a Purana in which Radha is mentioned only once. Nonetheless, the reference is significant because of the order in which the goddesses are listed, the rule of order being that whomever is listed last is the most important. The rules of logic say, *purva-parayor madhye para-vidhir balavan*: “Between the former rule and the latter rule, the latter is more important.” Thus Radha is the original, and the others expand from Her in reverse order.

It is certainly noteworthy that the Linga Purana gives a Gayatri mantra for Radha, which authenticates Her as a Vedic deity. Once again, Barbara Stoler Miller can't help but object to such a conclusion, saying that the mantra is “in imitation of the Gayatri.”

The final quote in this section comes from the Brhad-gautamiya- tantra. It is referred to by many acaryas, but it specifically appears as a verse in the Sri Caitanya-caritamrta:

*devi krsna-mayi prokta radhika para-devata*  
*sarva-laksmi-mayi sarva-kantih sammohini para*

**“The transcendental goddess Srimati Radharani is the direct counterpart of Lord Sri Krsna. She is the central figure for all the goddesses of fortune. She possesses all the attractiveness to attract the all-attractive Personality of Godhead. She is the primeval internal potency of the Lord.”**

Indeed, the verses that follow serve as Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami’s commentary or analysis.

Aside from once again establishing Radha as Krsna’s counterpart, this verse proclaims Her to be the source of all goddesses of fortune, a fact that Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami corroborates in Caitanya-caritamrta. Kaviraja Gosvami specifically states that sarva-laksmi means Radha is the original source of all goddesses of fortune. He also says that sarva-kanti means those goddesses derive not just their existence, but also their beauty from Her.Therefore, if Radha is the origin of the Vedic deity Laksmi, the goddess of fortune, She must also be one Herself.

In this particular section of the Caitanya-caritamrta, Kaviraja Gosvami makes a statement that nicely summarises our discussion here, and provides a concluding thought regarding the relevance of Srimati Radharani in Vedic scripture:

*radha—purna-sakti, krsna — purna-saktiman*  
*dui vastu bheda nai, sastra-paramana*

**“Sri Radha is the full power, and Lord Krsna is the possessor of full power. The two are not different, as evidenced by the revealed scriptures.”**

While professional scholars and followers of other sampradayas may have their own interpretation of scripture, and therefore of Srimati Radharani’s relationship to the Vedas, the opinion of the Gaudiya Vaisnava acaryas is clear—according to genuine Vedic scriptures, the dual aspects of the Absolute Truth are Radha, as the full power, and Krsna, as the possessor of that power.

Srimad-Bhagavatam: In the references we have cited from sruti and smrti there are no disagreements regarding the ontology of Srimati Radharani.
