But had there been any points of contention, the Vedic system accepts the statements of sruti as the final word in such disputes. Nonetheless, we have not yet seen any Vedic statement that discredits the evidence we have presented to establish Srimati Radharani’s position in the Vedic tradition. Nor have the sceptics provided a reference that proclaims Radha to be anything other than what we have seen so far in this appendix.

The statements of Smrti have helped us to see a fuller picture of Radha by elaborating on the limited number of statements available in sruti. In particular, the Puranas give so much information about Srimati Radharani, but because the Puranas describe Sri Radha from the varied perspectives of the modes of nature, we require, from a transcendental vantage point, a synthesis of all the Puranic information. That synthesis, as with all topics of the Vedas, is found in Srimad-Bhagavatam.

But before presenting the higher perspective of Srimad-Bhagavatam, it should be noted that the Vedas cannot be understood solely through the study of scripture. Souls conditioned by the material energy suffer from four defects, one of which is the tendency to make mistakes (pramada), and thus they cannot fully or correctly understand the perfect, revealed knowledge of the Vedas, known as apauruseya (that which comes from a superhuman source). To understand Srimad-Bhagavatam one must seek the guidance of self-realised souls who are free from defects and in full contact with the Absolute Truth. The necessity of this approach is repeatedly stressed throughout the Vedas.

In the words of Yudhisthira Maharaja:

*tarko ’pratisthah srutayo vibhinna*  
*nasav rsir yasya matam na bhinnam*  
*dharmasya tattvam nihitam guhayam*  
*mahajano yena gatah sa panthah*

**“Dry arguments are inconclusive. A great personality whose opinion does not differ from others is not considered a great sage. Simply by studying the Vedas, which are variegated, one cannot come to the right path by which religious principles are understood. The solid truth of religious principles is hidden in the heart of an unadulterated, self-realised person. Consequently, as the Sastras confirm, one should accept whatever progressive path the mahajanas advocate.”**

Understanding Srimad-Bhagavatam’s synthesis of the Puranas is therefore only possible through the guidance of the acaryas. This guidance is available in two ways: through their direct commentaries on Srimad-Bhagavatam, and through the books they have written elaborating on its philosophy.

An honest study of this progressive path chalked out by the acaryas will neither minimise nor remove it from the Vedic system. To do so would be to follow “the logic of accepting half a hen” (ardha-kukkuti-nyaya). A.W. Entwistle’s logic fits into this category. For example, Entwistle states that when Gaudiya commentators say that Srimad-Bhagavatam speaks of Radha, but in esoteric terms, the acaryas do so because they “feel obliged to find a reference to her \[Radha\].” Statements such as this display the “logic of accepting half a hen” in that they, in effect, reject the basic directive and methodology given by the very scriptures they attempt to explain: to accept the authority of self-realised souls in order to understand “the solid truth of religious principles.”

Let us hear more about the esoteric language (paroksa-vada) with which the acaryas say Sri Radha is glorified in Srimad-Bhagavatam.

Srimad-Bhagavatam’s most famous reference to Srimati Radharani is made by the cowherd girls of Vrndavana, when, following Krsna’s footprints in the forest, they noticed that He was not alone but with an unnamed gopi. This is the cowherd girls’ comment on that gopi:

*anayaradhito nunam bhagavan harir isvarah*  
*yan no vihaya govindah prito yam anayad rahah*

**“Certainly this particular gopi has perfectly worshipped the allpowerful Personality of Godhead, Govinda, since He was so pleased with Her that He abandoned the rest of us and brought Her to a secluded place.”**

Of this verse, Srila Prabhupada says:

**“Sometimes the critics of Srimad-Bhagavatam find it difficult to find Radharani’s holy name in that book, but the secret is disclosed here in the word aradhita, from which the name Radha has come… This gopis worship of Krsna is topmost, and therefore Her name is Radha, or ‘the topmost worshipper.’”**

This verse is not only the most explicit reference to Radha found in Srimad-Bhagavatam but also the clearest explanation of Her ontological nature.Srila Prabhupada’s interpretation of it is supported by the commentaries of acaryas like Jiva Gosvami and Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura on the same verse.

As we will see below, Jiva Gosvami confirms Srila Prabhupada’s explanation that within the word aradhitah the name Radha is hidden. There should be no etymological dispute with this, though Entwistle does question whether that is the intent of Sukadeva Gosvami. Certainly the acaryas all side with Jiva. Taking the discussion one step further, Srila Prabhupada reveals the essence of aradhitah’s ontological significance when he writes, “This gopi's worship of Krsna is topmost, and therefore Her name is Radha, or ‘the topmost worshipper.’”

Practically from the outset, Srimad-Bhagavatam establishes that “Krsna is the original Personality of Godhead” (*krsnas tu bhagavati svayam*).Therefore, when Radha is referred to as His “topmost worshipper,” it establishes Her as the embodiment of His hladini-saka.

Why?

By definition “topmost worship” means worship in love. In the words of Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura,

**“The hidden meaning of this verse is that Sri Radha, who is indicated here by the word aradhitah, is the topmost maidservant and devotee of Sri Krsna, being the very crown jewel of devotion.”**

Only the embodiment of the Lord’s own internal potency can be said to be the topmost worshipper in love.

Jiva Gosvami asserts that the words anaya bhagavan aradhitah mean that Radha brought the Supreme Lord under Her control, specifically indicating that the words beginning with yan na mean that Krsna left all the other gopis and took Radha to a secluded place.The gopis worship Krsna with the most elevated and intimate devotion.Who, therefore, could make Krsna disregard such peerless worship and leave the gopis behind? Who could bring Krsna fully under control other than Krsna Himself? The conclusion must be that Srimati Radharani is the embodiment of Sri Krsna’s feminine energy, hladini-sakti.

Hence the verse under discussion is not only important in establishing that Radha was in the rasa dance — as well as in the pages of Srimad-Bhagavatam— but that She is Krsna’s energetic counterpart, the female aspect of the Absolute Truth, and the goal of the Vedas.

**\* \* \* \***

In the verses that follow, Sukadeva Gosvami continues to emphasise the unique singularity of the lone gopi in Krsna's intimate company.

Radha is next mentioned in chapter thirty-two, in which Krsna returns to the gopis. At the beginning of that chapter, Sukadeva Gosvami describes how each gopi welcomes Krsna differently. Although Sukadeva Gosvami does not give names to the gopis in his narration, the acaryas identify each gopi by her conduct. Sukadeva says:

*eka bhru-kutim abadhya prema-samrambha-vihvala*  
*ghnantivaiksat kataksepaih sandasia-dasana-cchada*

**“One gopi, beside herself with loving anger, bit her lips and stared at Him with frowning eyebrows as if to wound Him with her harshglances.”**

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura analyses the mood of the gopi described in this verse and explains that She displays jealous anger born of possessive love, characteristic of a quarrelsome, crooked nature full of contrariness. The Thakura furthermore asserts that these particular characteristics reveal the gopi to be Srimati Radharani.

One may reasonably wonder why Sukadeva Gosvami doesn’t simply list the gopis by name. One may also wonder why, in this verse in particular, he does not directly name Srimati Radharani. But for devotees who have carefully studied the principles of rasa, merely hearing of the gopis’ qualities automatically reveals their identities in a way that is more poetic and thus more pleasing.

In addition to playing a central role in the five chapters that describe the rasa dance, Srimati Radharani is given a prominent part in the Tenth Canto of the Bhagavatam, chapter forty-seven, entitled “The Song of the Bumblebee.” There Uddhava visits Vraja and delivers a message from Krsna to the gopis. Krsna’s words submerge the gopis in ecstatic thoughts of Him, and at one point, one particular gopi (kacit) speaks at length to a bumblebee. In Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Srila Prabhupada identifies Her in a very matter-of-fact way:

**“One of the gopis, namely Srimati Radharani, was so much absorbed in thoughts of Krsna by dint of Her personal touch with Him that She actually began to talk with a bumblebee which was flying there and trying to touch Her lotus feet.’’**

The testimony of Sanatana Gosvami, along with the testimonies of other acaryas, confirms that the gopi speaking in verses eleven through twenty-one of this chapter of the Bhagavatam can only be Sri Radha. Why must this soliloquy be attributed to Her alone? Because each of the ten comments to the bumblebee exemplifies one of the ten divisions of divine madness (divyonmada) expressed by ten kinds of speech in divine madness (citra-jalpa). These symptoms of madness occur only at the point of bewilderment, the highest stage of great divine love (mahdbhava). And because this degree of mahabhava is only displayed by the embodiment of mahabhava, Srimati Radharani, the speaker must be Krsna’s consort.

There are many other verses in Srimad-Bhagavatam that refer to Srimati Radharani, but the verses cited above should be evidence enough that She is indeed glorified in “the spotless Purana."

The first two verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam establish its purpose: to glorify Sri Krsna and the process of pure devotional service to Him, free from tinges of karma and jnana.

*om namo bhagavate vasudevaya*  
*janmady asya yato 'nvayad ttaratas carthesv abhijnah svarat*  
*tene brahma hrda ya adi-kavaye muhyanti yat surayah*  
*tejo-vari-mrdam yatha vinimayo yatra tri-sargo ’mrsa*  
*dharma svena sada nirasta-kuhakam satyam param dhimahi*  
*dharmah projjhita-kaitavo ’tra paramo nirmatsaranam satam*  
*vedyam vastavam atra vastu sivadam tapa-trayonmulanam*  
*srimad-bhagavate maha-muni-krte kim va parair isvarah*  
*sadyo hrdy avarudhyate ’tra krtibhih susrusubhis tat-ksanat*

**“O my Lord, Sri Krsna, son of Vasudeva, O all-pervading Personality of Godhead, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You. I meditate upon Lord Sri Krsna because He is the Absolute Truth and the primeval cause of all causes of the creation, sustenance and destruction of the manifested universes. He is directly and indirectly conscious of all manifestations, and He is independent because there is no other cause beyond Him. It is He only who first imparted the Vedic knowledge unto the heart of Brahmaji, the original living being. By Him even the great sages and demigods are placed into illusion, as one is bewildered by the illusory representations of water seen in fire, or land seen on water. Only because of Him do the material universes, temporarily manifested by the reactions of the three modes of nature, appear factual, although they are unreal. I therefore meditate upon Him, Lord Sri Krsna, who is eternally existent in the transcendental abode, which is forever free from the illusory representations of the material world. I meditate upon Him, for He is the Absolute Truth. Completely rejecting all religious activities which are materially motivated, this Bhagavata Purana propounds the highest truth, which is understandable by those devotees who are fully pure in heart. The highest truth is reality distinguished from illusion for the welfare of all. Such truth uproots the threefold miseries. This beautiful Bhagavatam, compiled by the great sage Vyasadeva \[in his maturity\], is sufficient in itself for God realisation. What is the need of any other scripture? As soon as one attentively and submissively hears the message of Bhagavatam, by this culture of knowledge the Supreme Lord is established within his heart.”**

What exactly is that “highest truth” that Srimad-Bhagavatam propounds?

Since we are already used to speaking in esoteric terms, it should come as no surprise that we will have to look deeper to unearth that highest truth.

The first verse of Srimad-Bhagavatam establishes unequivocally that Krsna is at the heart of Srimad-Bhagavatam and the truth it propounds. And Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes, elaborately described in the first thirty-nine chapters of the Tenth Canto, reveal Him in His fullness, in the original form at which the Vedas hint when they say:

*apasyam gopam anipadyamana ma ca para ca pathibhis carantam*  
*sa sadhricih sa visucir vasana a varivarti bhuvanesv antah*

**“I saw a cowherd, who never falls from His position, who is sometimes near, and sometimes far, who wanders on various paths, who is a friend, decorated with a variety of clothes, and who comes again and again to the material world.”**

Vaisnava scholars of Srimad-Bhagavatam agree that, of those thirty-nine chapters that describe Krsna’s pastimes in Vrndavana, the five that deal with the rasa dance reveal the personal feature of the Absolute Truth as He fully displays the mellows (rasas) of spiritual devotion. In other words, the original feature of Sri Krsna is revealed when He sports with the gopis. And amongst all of them, one special gopi controls Krsna with Her love and becomes the object of His service.

Therefore, the highest truth propounded by Srimad-Bhagavatam is found in the form of Radha and Krsna, who can be attained through pure devotional service. Not unlike the relationship between Radha and Krsna, pure devotional service itself occurs in two states—meeting (sambhoga) and separation (vipralambha)—as evidenced by Srimad-Bhagavatam’s description of the rasa dance, and Radha’s soliloquy to the bumblebee.

Works of the Gosvamis: The Six Gosvamis of Vrndavana were the most prolific authors amongst Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s followers. In their writings they explicitly describe the philosophical truths relating to Srimati Radharani. Thus their output is unique in the library of Vedic texts. Unlike sruti, the Gosvamis’ works speak of Sri Radha often; unlike the varied presentation of the Puranas, the Gosvamis’ writings are firmly fixed on the spiritual platform; and unlike Srimad-Bhagavatam, the Gosvamis’ language is explicit and direct.

In the way of true gurus, the Gosvamis made Srimati Radharani completely understandable to sincere students of the Vedas. That sceptics still find fault with the conclusive truths so expertly presented in the works of the Gosvamis is surely a symptom of this dark Age of Kali. As Srimad-Bhagavatam says about the Kali-yuga, panditye capalam vacah: “one who is very clever at juggling words will be considered a learned scholar,” and *satyatve dharstyam eva hi*: “one who is audacious will be accepted as truthful.”

An appropriate summary to this appendix may be found in Brhad-bhagavatamrta. In the following verse, Pariksit Maharaja gives advice to his mother, Uttara, after revealing the essence of Srimad-Bhagavatam to her.

*matar gopa-kisoram tam tvam ca rasa-rasambudhim*  
*tat-prema-mohitabhih sri-gopibhir abhito vrtam*  
*amusam dasyam icchanti tadrsa-prema-bhangibhih*  
*nityam bhajasva tan-nama- sankirtana-parayana*

**“Dear mother, you as well should always worship this young cowherd boy. He is the ocean that yields the nectar of the rasa dance, in which divine gopis fully surround Him, entranced by pure love. You should cherish the desire to be a servant of these gopis, you should constantly worship Him in pure love as they did, and you should dedicate yourself to the sankirtana of His names.”**

In closing, let us revisit the words of Rupa Gosvami, the acarya of Gaudiya Vaisnavas, and the words of Sri Krsna Himself, the compiler, knower, and goal of the Vedas.

*tatrapi sarva-gopinam radhikativariyasi*  
*sarvadhikyena kathita yat puranagamadisu*

**“Srimati Radharani is the best of all the gopis and Her superiority is described in the Puranas, Agamas, and other Vedic literatures.”**

And lastly, the words of Sri Krsna Himself:

*trailokye prthivi dhanya yatra vrndavanam puri*  
*tatrapi gopikah partha tatra radhabhidha mama*

**“O son of Prtha! In the three worlds this earth planet, where the town of Vrndavana is situated, is most fortunate because that is where the gopis stay, and amongst them is My beloved, who is named Radha.”**

## About the Author

Sivarama Swami was born in Budapest, Hungary in 1949, and bis family emigrated to Canada during the failed 1956 Hungarian revolution. He became a disciple of A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, the founder-acarya of ISKCON, in 1973 and entered the renounced order of life (sannyasa) in 1979. Sivarama Swami is well known for his deep knowledge of Vaisnava literature and has written many books about Gaudiya Vaisnavism, including the “Krsna in Vrndavana” series. He is a member of iskcon’s Governing Body Commission and is responsible for projects in Hungary, Turkey, and Romania. Although he travels and speaks internationally, he spends as much time as possible at New Vraja-dhama (Krishna Valley), a replica of Vrndavana and self-sufficient farming project in Hungary’s countryside.

***You are cordially invited...***

Dear reader, I hope that after reading this volume of Nava-vraja-mahima you have not only been enriched by the pastimes of Lord Krsna, but that you are inquisitive to see New Vraja-dhama, the epitome of His eternal abode.

Radha-Syamasundara’s home is open year-round to guests for a day visit to see their Lordships and major pastime places, or for a month-long pilgrimage to perform parikrama of the dhama and dive deeply into the service of Radha-Syama.

There are a number of guesthouses both in New Vraja-dhama and in adjoining Somogyvamos that offer a variety of accommodation according to the preference and budget of the pilgrim.

In addition, the residents of New Vraja-dhama are eager to introduce pilgrims to the “Radha-Syama experience” and to encourage guests to taste for themselves through chanting, hearing, and serving the dhama, the mellows of devotional service as they manifest in this part of the world through the grace of Srila Prabhupada and the divine couple.

Part of the vision of the Hungarian yatra is to beautify New Vraja-dhama with a grand temple for Radha-Syamasundara, with pavilions, kundas, ghatas, gardens, and markers for pastime places. In this way the dhama will one day fully reflectthe glory of Bhauma Vrndavana with the purpose of inspiring residents and pilgrims to return to Goloka.

As in the case of Bhauma Vrndavana, the development of New Vraja-dhama can be financially realised not by the local residents who live simply from the produce of the land, but by donors around the world who are touched by the magic of Radha-Syama and Their abode. That is how New Vraja- dhama has managed to develop to date.

Yet as all readers of this book will know, the development of New Vraja-dhama is dependent on meticulous service to Radha-Syama. And so the first and foremost project in further development is to ensure the perpetual maintenance of the Deities, Their worship, ornamentation, dressing, and Their servants—the pujaris. When Their Lordships are suitably served, then the rest of the dhama will flourish in all ways.This is what Srila Prabhupada did by personally establishing the Mayapur-Vrndavana Trust in order to ensure the perpetual worship of the Deities he installed in those holy places. We have also established the Radha-Syama Seva-puja Fund in order to have stable maintenance of the Deities’ worship that is independent of New Vraja-dhama’s day-to-day income or even the economic climate of Hungary or the world.

At present hundreds of people contribute towards the daily service of the Deities either in monthly instalments or in a single donation, and thus enjoy a connection with Radha- Syama and the benefits of Their blessings.

Yet we have far to go to fully maintain Their Lordships. Therefore readers who are also desirous of maintaining such a service connection with Radha-Syama may also sponsor one or more daily seva-puja by writing the head pujari at fopujari@ krisnavolgy.hu. And those people who also want to support the further development projects of New Vraja-dhama, like the construction of a new temple, may contact either me directly, or the leaders of the yatra at project@krisna.hu .

Some readers may wonder why I have included such a commercially oriented letter in a classical text exclusively devoted to spiritual topics. My answer is that I would be remiss in my service to New Vraja-dhama and to those most interested in Radha-Syama — you, my dear reader — if I were not to speak of the opportunities for participating in serving Their Lordships and Their abode. I have personally tasted the extraordinary benefits of such service. How, after glorifying such service in these pages, could I not inform you of such opportunities? I would be guilty of miserliness, and the purpose of this book would not have been realised — the congregational glorification of Radha-Syamasundara, sankirtana.King Vajra first developed Bhauma Vrndavana with the support of Pariksit Maharaja’s empire, meaning the whole world. The Gosvamis again redeveloped the dhama with the help of sympathetic kings and merchants from across India. And Srila Prabhupada constructed his three major centres in India — the Krsna-Balarama Mandira in Vrndavana, Sri Mayapur Candrodaya Mandira in Mayapur, and Sri Sri Radha-Rasabihari (Hare Krsna Land) in Bombay — with financial support from his International Society for Krsna Consciousness. Thus, with this letter I am also trying to humbly follow in the footsteps of my predecessors, for the service of my worshippable Deities.

Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami answered the question of how one can decide on a worshippable Deity without understanding through logic and argument by saying, “If you are indeed interested in logic and argument, kindly apply it to the mercy of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. If you do so, you will find it to be strikingly wonderful." (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi-lila 8.15) In the same way, in answer to the question of how I can solicit financial support for New Vraja-dhama in this book, my reply is, “If you are indeed interested in service to Radha-Syamasundara, kindly participate in Their seva-puja and in developing Their abode and you will find the personal results to be strikingly wonderful.” In short, I cannot resist offering you that nectar, the taste of which allays all doubts and answers all questions.

Thank you.  
Yours in the eternal service of Srila Prabhupada’s Radha-Syama,  
Sivarama Swami

## Reference

The Deity of the Lord is fully transcendental — Krsna Himself—appearing to conditioned souls in material elements. The Deity is therefore simultaneously present in both the material and spiritual worlds. He is a juncture between the two, as is the place where He stands. In addition, there are other meanings of Yoga-pitha, including the place where the divine couple meet and the whorl of the lotus of Krsna’s and Balarama's pastime places.

The descriptions of the Yoga-pitha in this chapter are adapted from the following sources: Padma Purana, Patala-khanda, chapters 69-71; Sanat-kumara-samhita; Brahma-samhita 5.2-5; Sri Govinda-lilamrta, chapter 21; and Sri Krsria-sandarbha 105.287-94.

Descriptions of the Yoga-pitha in scripture and the works of our acaryas vary in detail. These variances are horn from differences in transcendental perception that result from unique relationships with Radha and Krsna (and hence with the Yoga-pitha), as well as the inherently inconceivable nature of the Yoga-pitha itself. The description of the Yoga-pitha given in this chapter includes the most common and most basic features described by authorities. For the sake of brevity, I have avoided a more detailed description.

According to the Padma Purana, the Yoga-pitha of Lord Rama- candra in Ayodhya is also called Antahpuri.

Vraja-riti-cintamani 2.70.

The phrase “medium in size” is used to indicate that the temple, though very spacious, never appears so grandiose that it would inspire the type of awe more characteristic of Vaikuntha than Gokula.

An elaborate description of this hexagonal mandala and its esoteric meaning is found in Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati’s purport to Sri Brahma-samhita 5.3. In short, the mantra is klim krsnaya govindaya gopijana-vallabhaya svaha, consisting of eighteen transcendental syllables and six transcendental words: (1) krsnaya, (2) govindaya, (3) gopijana, (4) vallabhaya, (5) sva, and (6) ha. In Krsna-sandarbha Jiva Gosvami writes that the seed klim is at the centre of this hexagon.

The asta-sakhis are the eight principal and most confidential girlfriends of Srimati Radharani. Each of these sakhis has innumerable maidservants, but the manjaris mentioned here are the leading and thus most confidential ones.

Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi-lila 1.16.

In Goloka Vrndavana, which is the subject of this description, Krsna retains His eternally youthful age. He does not take birth at any time in that spiritual domain. But because Krsna’s pastimes are human-like, the idea that Krsna has taken birth must somehow be there, even if He has not done so in fact. To resolve this paradox, Yogamaya instils in the minds of the Vraja-vasis a “memory” of Krsna’s birth. Therefore, this stanza accommodates that spiritual reality by stating that Gokula is “said to be” the place where Krsna took birth.

Vraja-riti-cintamani (2.79) describes how at Vighnaraja-tirtha, Krsna appeared in the form of a deity of Ganesa that the gopis came to worship to remove any obstacle to their constant association with Krsna.

There are three places in Vraja where gopis bathed and had their clothes stolen by Krsna. The place mentioned in this stanza is one of the three and unlike the others is not situated on the banks of the Yamuna.

Setubhanda-kunda has been described in chapter 5 on the subject of Kamyavana, where Krsna showed the gopis His pastime of building a stone bridge to cross to Lanka.

Generally, the potencies Sri, Bhu, and Nila are associates of conditioned souls in the material world: Sri is the energy of Godhead who maintains the cosmic manifestation, Bhu is the energy who creates the cosmic manifestation, and Nila (or Durga) is the energy who destroys the creation. In his Bhagavata-sandarbha (23), Jiva Gosvami defines these energies in the same way. In addition, he refers to the Padma Purana, which describes that the original spiritual forms of these energies reside in Goloka; these spiritual forms are the forms referred to in this stanza.

Like the dhama and Krsna’s pastimes, the Yoga-pitha is seen according to the consciousness of the observer. For example, Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that by Yogamaya’s arrangement, the demigods in the mood of servitude could not see the gopis during the rasa dance, they could only see Krsna. Similarly, this and the stanzas that follow describe the various ways in which various devotees perceive the Yoga-pitha. For example, those who know Radha to he Krsna’s favourite gopi see the Yoga-pitha as the divine couple’s capital. Those whose realisation is not so specific but still know Krsna as the lover of gopis will see the Yoga-pitha as the place where He meets many gopis, without specifying the hierarchy amongst them. And those who know Krsna as the protector of the Vraja-vasis will see it as a place where He meets with gopas and gopis alike, without distinction. Thus, although in one sense the physical location of the Yoga-pitha is accessible to everyone, its full manifestation as the confidential meeting place of Radha and Krsna is accessible only to those whose consciousness is fully and purely attuned to the amorous pastimes of the divine couple. (Sarartha-darsini 10.33.3)

These two concentric circles of gopis are not be confused with the eight sakhis and eight manjaris already mentioned in the initial description of the Yoga-pitha.

The cowherd boys who are younger than Krsna and who act as His servants have the sense of servitude mixed with fraternity, while those who are older than Krsna have a touch of parental care along with their feelings of friendship. Neither of these relationships is considered pure, or unmixed, friendship. However, those cowherd boys, like Sridama, who arc about the same age as Krsna and who are free from feelings of servitude have relationships with Krsna based solely and wholly on the platform of friendship. For that reason they are called confidential friends (priya-sakhas).

The eight names of the Yoga-pitha can be translated as follows: Candravali-duradarsa— very rarely seen by Candravali; Radha-saubhagya-mandira— the auspicious temple of Radha; Sri Ratna-mandapa — the jewelled courtyard of Radha; Srngara-mandapa— the courtyard of paramour love; Saubhagya-mandapa— the courtyard of good fortune; Maha-madhurya-mandapa— the courtyard of supreme sweetness; Samrajya-mandapa— the emperor of all jewelled courtyards; Surata-mandapa — the courtyard of amorous delights.

The following narration of Arjuna’s transformation into a gopi named Arjuni or Arjuniya is adapted from the Padma Purana, Uttara-khanda, chapter 74.

Tripura-sundari is a form of Durga. And although it is unclear from the text of the Padma Purana where along the river Yamuna Krsna and Arjuna were conversing — Hastinapura, Mathura, or perhaps in Vraja itself—to give Arjuna entrance into Vraja, especially in the body of a gopi, Tripura-sundari must be a form of Yogamaya.

Balavidya refers to the knowledge (vidya) related to Tripura-sundari as a young girl (bala). However, more relevant to Arjuna’s quest is the knowledge pertaining to the moods of devotion of the young girls of Vraja. In the Gayatri-mantra by which Tripura-sundari is worshipped, the presence of the words klim and kama indicates that by worshipping her, devotees can obtain the transcendental kama by which the gopis serve Krsna.

When Priyamuda speaks about the gopis who “have always been milkmaids” she is referring to the eternally liberated, eternally perfect gopis.

In describing their love, Priyamuda introduces these gopis as servants of the “lord of Radha” to indicate that, like Lalita and Visakha, they are favourably disposed to Radha. They are part of Her group of gopis, and are in no way Her competitors. This will be borne out when they bring Arjuniya into Radha’s presence.

From the outcome of this pastime it will be obvious that Arjuna’s desire was not to become a gopi who has no direct physical contact with Krsna (a manjari), but to enter the realm of those gopis who do.

Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika (122-24) describes these three distinct personalities as existing within the one body of Ramananda Raya: “Some say that Ramananda Raya is the incarnation of Lalita-gopi, and others say that because Lord Caitanya directly told Ramananda

Raya’s father, Bhavananda Raya, that he was the incarnation of Maharaja Pandu, Arjuna’s father, therefore Ramananda Raya must he the incarnation of Pandava Arjuna. The most learned devotees say that Ramananda Raya is the incarnation of both the Pandava Arjuna, and a gopi named Arjuniya. This explanation is also supported by the statements of the Padma Purana, Uttara-khanda. From all this we may conclude that Ramananda Raya is the incarnation of Lalita-gopi, Arjuniya-gopi, and Pandava Arjuna.”

It should be noted that other sources, including Srila Prabhupada, say that Ramananda Raya was an incarnation of Visakha-devi. Srila Prabhupada writes, “Srila Ramananda Raya was an incarnation of the gopi Visakha. Since Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu was Lord Krsna Himself, there was naturally an awakening of love between Visakha and Krsna. Sri Krsna Caitanya Mahaprabhu is the combination of Srimati Radharani and Krsna, and the gopi Visakha is a principal gopi assisting Srimati Radharani. Thus the natural love between Ramananda Raya and Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu awakened and they embraced.” (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya-lila 8.2.3) Srila Prabhupada mentions these two opinions but does not give his own conclusion: “The Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika (120-24) states that Ramananda Raya was formerly Arjuna. He is also considered to have been an incarnation of the gopi Lalita, although in the opinion of others he was an incarnation of Visakha-devi.” (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi-lila 10.134)

In New Vraja-dhama the deities of Gopisvara and Yogamaya reside in their own temples from April to October. But for the remainder of the year, during the cold season that lasts from November to March, they stay in Vrnda-devi’s grove. That grove can currently be found in the Tulasi greenhouse situated on the bank of Malyahari-kunda.

When Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura visited Radha-kunda in 1932, he lectured there from Sri Upadesamrta of Rupa Gosvami. Following the example of our revered acarya, the stanzas up until the conclusion of this section summarise the eleven verses of Sri Upadesamrta.

Two types of devotees are qualified to think of Radha’s and Krsna’s eightfold daily pastimes: conditioned souls whose minds are purified by regulated devotional practice, and liberated souls who have realised their spiritual identities. Both types of devotees perform such meditation under the guidance of their superiors.

Since the courtyard representing Radha-kunda in New Vraja-dhama is not always filled with water, devotees only physically bathe there when the opportunity arises. Otherwise they bathe there mentally. Moreover, when devotees are away from either New Vraja-dhama or Bhauma Vrndavana, they can also mentally bathe in Radha-kunda.

The killing of Aristasura and the appearance of Syama-kunda and Radha-kunda are adaptations of excerpts taken from Sri Lalita- madhava 2.1.13-17; Ujjvala-nilamani 15.113; Sri Vraja-vilasa-stava 58; Sri Brhad-bhagavatamrta 2.6.255-62; Gopala-virudavali 36 and 37; Sri Garga-samhita 1.6.49-51 and 4.24.15-31; Srimad-Bhagavatam, Canto 10, chapter 36; and Sarartha-darsini 10.36.16.

This stanza is adapted from Srimad-Bhagavatam 10.36.7.

Sri Garga-Samhita describes the fight differently than Srimad-Bhagavatam. For instance, the Garga-samhita says that Krsna tossed the demon sixteen miles instead of eighteen steps, and that the two combatants also threw mountains at each other.

Sri Garga-samhita (4.24.23-30) tells that when the soul of Arista left his body, he assumed the from of a brahmana, who bowed before Krsna and with a choked voice related the events that led to him being cursed to accept birth as a demon. The brahmanas name was Varatantu, a disciple of Brhaspati, who had incurred his guru’s wrath by once sitting spreadeagled before him. Brhaspati became enraged and said, “Since you sit like a bull, I curse you to become a bull in East Bengal.” In bad company Arista developed a demonic mentality. He met Kamsa when the evil king was out conquering all directions. Kamsa defeated Arista in a long fight and made him an ally in Mathura. Now freed from the curse, the brahmana prayed, “Obeisances to Sri Krsna, the son of Vasudeva, Lord Govinda who destroys the sufferings of the surrendered devotees!” With that the brahmana bowed before Krsna and mounted a plane destined for the heavenly planets.

In the Brhad-bhagavatamrta (2.6.255-62), Sanatana Gosvami describes how Krsna reigns victorious over Arista and Kesi in Goloka Vrndavana as well. Those two demon servants of Kamsa appear from time to time in that all-spiritual realm, determined to upset the peaceful life of the Vraja-vasis much as they did here in Bhauma Vrndavana so many years ago.

On one such occasion both entered Vraja side by side: Arista in the form of a bull and Kesi a horse, as fierce as death personified. With ear-splitting roars they terrorised the gopas and made all other creatures fall to the ground, petrified. In fear, Krsna’s young friends ran to Him for protection, but He made light of the threat by flexing His arms and striking a number of confrontational poses to flaunt His heroic power.

First Kesi came running towards Him, but with a mere kick Krsna sent the demonic horse flying through the air far away. Then Krsna caught Arista, pierced his nose, and taking the ring in hand, dragged the bull-demon before the deity of Gopisvara to offer Lord Siva a ride. When Kesi attacked again, Krsna skilfully jumped on his back and subdued the bucking bronco like an expert rodeo rider. In hardly any time at all Krsna was ordering Kesi to go here and there, taking the gopas for rides.

With Arista and Kesi domesticated, Krsna bridled the horse and kept him as a pet for riding. He harnessed the bull and had him engaged in the useful service of pulling the Vraja-vasi’s carts.

Different accounts give different details regarding the original source of Radha-kunda’s waters. Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, in his commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam, asserts that Radha proposed for water to be brought from Manasa-ganga, although the text does not directly state such an effort was made. He adds that finally Syama-kunda was the only source of water for Radha-kunda. Other authorities say the water was first brought from either Manasa-ganga or Kusuma-sarovara, and that the water of Syama-kunda was later mixed in. This version of the pastime is the one narrated here.

**“At some holy places one becomes free from all sins, at others one becomes free from the bondage of karma, at others one attains Brahman happiness, and yet at others one attains residence in Visnuloka. *phulla-madhavi-rasala-nipa-kunja-mandale*

**“Krsna-kunda is surrounded by groves of mango, kadamba, and other trees, with many madhavi and other vines. There, the cakravakas, cuckoos, and bees make sweet music. At night millions of inconceivable fragrances sweeten the air. Let us glorify residence at Krsna-kunda.”**

*dola-keli-citra-rasa-nrtya-giti-vadanair*  
*nihnava-prasuna-yuddha-sidhu-pana-kautukaih*  
*yatra khelatah kisora-sekharau sahalibhis*  
*tatra krsna-kunda eva samsthitih stutastu nah*

**“With Their gopi friends, the two crowns of youth enjoyed many pastimes there. They sang, talked, played musical instruments, rode on a swing, and danced wonderful rasa dances. In a secluded place They eagerly drank the nectar of a flower-fight. Let us glorify residence at Krsna-kunda.”**

*divya-ratna-nirmitavatara-sara-sausthavais*  
*chatrika viraji caru kuttima-prabha-bharaih*  
*sarva-loka-locanati-dhanyata yato bhavet*  
*tatra krsna-kunda eva samsthitih stutastu nah*

**“With the beauty of its glistening jewel shores and the splendour of its canopies and mosaic pavements, it brings auspiciousness to whomever sees it. Let us glorify residence at Krsna-kunda.”**

*mathuram vikunthato 'pi janma-dhama durlabham*  
*vasakananam tato ‘pi panina dhrto girih*  
*sri-hares tato ‘pi yat param saro ‘ti-pavanam*  
*tatra krsna-kunda eva samsthitih stutastu nah*

**“The district of Mathura, Krsna’s birthplace, is more sacred and difficult to attain than Vaikuntha. The forest where He lived is more sacred still, and the hill lifted by His hand is even more sacred still. More sacred even than that hill is Lord Hari’s very purifying lake nearby. Let us glorify residence at Krsna-kunda.”**

*krsna-kunda-tira-vasa-sadhakam pathed idam*  
*yo ‘stakam dhiyam nimajjya keli-kunja-rajitoh*

**“May whoever reads these eight verses, which convince one to reside on the shore of Krsna-kunda, and which also plunges one’s mind in the lotus flowers of Sri Radha-Giridhari’s feet, quickly attain sincere love for Them.”**

Generally speaking, Radha and Krsna come to Radha-kunda and Syama-kunda at midday (10:48 AM to 3:36 PM) and to Govinda- sthali during the night (10:48 PM to 3:36 AM). Still, there are exceptions to this general rule; they may go to either of these places at any time of the day or night. Vaisnava scholars, however, refer to the two places in connection with pastimes at the two times of the day given above. (Asta-kaliya-lila-smarana-mangala-stotra)

Therefore the grove of Visakha is Visakhanandada-kunja, the grove of Citra, Citranandada-kunja, and so on.

In the Bhagavad-gita As It Is (4-11) Krsna makes it clear that different relationships with Him bring about different results. He says, “As all surrender unto Me, I reward them accordingly.” This principle applies equally as well for perfected souls as it does for conditioned souls. In the case of perfected souls, their surrender is their specific loving relationship (rasa) with Krsna, and their reward is the role

Krsna takes to reciprocate their love. In reciprocating His devotees’ love, Krsna also avoids revealing to them aspects of His nature or pastimes that would conflict with the mellow or mood of love those devotees share with Him. For example, Mother Yasoda, in her parental role, sees Krsna as her pre-pubescent son. Therefore, Yogamaya hides from Yasoda any traces of Krsna’s flirtatious pastimes with the gopis. Thus Yasoda’s love flows unobstructed along its parental course. According to His devotees’ inclinations, Krsna gives them corresponding visions of Himself.

This same principle is echoed in Sri Brahma-samhita (5.38), where Brahma says, “I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, who is Syamasundara, Krsna Himself, with inconceivable innumerable attributes, whom the pure devotees see in their heart of hearts with the eye of devotion tinged with the salve of love.” Again, applying this verse to different categories of perfected souls, their different types of prema will award them a vision of different attributes of Syamasundara.

The purport to verse 10.88.4 elaborates: “False ego transforms into the mind, ten senses (the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin, hands, feet, voice, genitals, and anus), and five physical elements (earth, water, fire, air, and ether). Lord Siva appears in a special linga form in each of these sixteen substances, which are worshipped individually as deities in various sacred locations of the universe. A devotee of Siva may worship one of his particular lingas to obtain the mystic opulences pertaining to it. Thus Lord Siva’s akasa-linga bestows the opulences of ether, his jyotir-linga bestows the opulences of fire, and so on."

Srila Prabhupada defines the term rupanuga in his purports to Sri Caitanya-caritamrta: “In Vrndavana there are prakrta-sahajiyas who say that writing books or even touching books is taboo. For them, devotional service means being relieved from these activities. Whenever they are asked to hear a recitation of Vedic literature, they refuse, saying, ‘What business do we have reading or hearing transcendental literatures? They are meant for neophytes.’ They pose themselves as too elevated to exert energy for reading, writing, and hearing. However, pure devotees under the guidance of Srila Rupa Gosvami reject this sahajiya. philosophy. It is certainly not good to write literature for money or reputation, but to write books and publish them for the enlightenment of the general populace is real service to the Lord. That was Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati’s opinion, and he specifically told his disciples to write books. He actually preferred to publish books rather than establish temples. Temple construction is meant for the general populace and neophyte devotees, but the business of advanced and empowered devotees is to write books, publish them, and distribute them widely. According to Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura, distributing literature is like playing on a great mrdanga. Consequently we always request members of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness to publish as many books as possible and distribute them widely throughout the world. By thus following in the footsteps of Srila Rupa Gosvami, one can become a rupanuga devotee.” (Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Madhya-lila 19.132, purport)

Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika (184) says that Gopala Bhatta was referred to as both Ananga-manjari and Guna-manjari. Srila Prabhupada also refers to this dual identity, but he does not comment on it. Since Ananga-manjari’s primary identity in gaura-lila is Jahnava-devi, it is generally accepted that the primary identity of Gopala Bhatta Gosvami is Guna-manjari, and that he is further empowered by the mercy of Radha’s younger sister, Ananga-manjari.

The word smrti means “to remember.” It also refers to those scriptures that give injunctions and codes of conduct in pursuance of the original sruti, the Vedas. The Manu-samhita, for example, is considered smrti. Vaisnavas have written various smrti texts for Deity worship, devotional practice, and so on. Because Gopala Bhatta Gosvami is credited with the original manuscripts of Hari-bhakti-vilasa — which outlines the rules of devotional service and was later edited and elaborated upon by Sanatana Gosvami—as well as the handbook for Deity worship called Sat-kriya-sara-dipika, he is known as the smrti-acarya. Those who are strict followers of Smrti are called smartas, and when their purpose in following the Smrti is sense gratification, then those smartas are considered deviants. The true smarta is one who follows smrti for the sake of purification and the pleasure of the Lord.

One may wonder how Ananga-manjari can appear in Lord Caitanya’s pastimes as two people. Just as Krsna expands into countless forms and incarnations, His eternal associates have a similar potency, albeit to a lesser degree — they too can expand themselves into multiple forms. For example, Lalita-devi appears as Ramananda Raya, as Gadadhara Pandita, and also as Dhruvananda Brahmacari. (Gaura-ganoddesa-dipika 124, 148-150, and 152 respectively) Expansions may be personal expansions — expansions of the devotee’s full personality — or empowered expansions — expansions of a particular potency of the devotee.

This is the first verse of Catu-puspanjali, which is part of Rupa Gosvami’s Stavamala. The Sanskrit reads,

*nava-gorocana-gaurim pravarendivarambaram*  
*mani-stabaka-vidyoti-veni-vyalangana-phanam.*

This stanza is adapted from Catu-puspanjali 24. The English translation of the work follows in its entirety.

**O Queen as fair as fresh gorocana, whose garments are as splendid as a blue lotus, whose braid, decorated with jewels and flowers, glisten like the hood of a serpent.**

**O Queen whose incomparably beautiful face crushes the pride of all other beautiful things, and whose beautiful forehead decorated with musk tilaka rebukes the crescent moon.**

**O Queen whose eyebrows defeat Kamadeva’s bow. O queen with dark, curling locks of hair, whose glistening eyes, decorated with mascara, are more beautiful than two splendid cakora birds.**

**O Queen, the tip of whose nose, which resembles a sesame flower, is decorated with a beautiful, splendid pearl. O Queen whose lips rebuke the bandhuka flowers and whose teeth are more charming than a row of jasmine buds.**

**O Queen who wears earrings of gold, jewels, and lotuses, whose chin is decorated with a dot of musk, and who wears a splendid jewel necklace.**

**O Queen whose splendid arms, like the stems of lotuses, are embraced by glistening armlets, and who wears tinkling sapphire bracelets.**

**O Queen, the fingers of whose lotus hands shine with jewelled rings, and on whose beautiful budding breasts a great necklace moves playfully.**

**O Queen whose necklace features a jewel that rests above the line of downy hairs on Your abdomen like the jewel on the head of a serpent, and whose graceful, slender waist is encircled by a vine of three folds of skin.**

**O Queen whose broad hips support a chain of small, jewelled bells, and whose two beautiful thighs stun charming golden plantain trees.**

**O Queen whose knees defeat a treasure chest filled with topaz, and whose feet and tinkling anklets are worshipped by lotus flowers in autumn.**

**O Queen whose toenails defeat in their splendour the beauty of millions of full moons, and whose transcendental form is agitated by the eight sattvika ecstasies.**

**O Queen who casts a sidelong glance at the transcendental body of Lord Mukunda, who is thus tossed about by the waves of amorous desire and who is Himself full of transcendental beauty and bliss. O Queen of Vrndavana, I bow down and offer my respectful obeisances to You.**

**O Queen whose heart is overcome by the sweetness of rising ecstatic love and who wonderfully displays the characteristics of all kinds of amorous heroines.**

**O Queen whose lotus feet are filled with all sweetness and the beauty of whose toenails is eagerly sought by the goddess of fortune.**

**O flower worn in the parted hair of the moon-faced girls of Gokula, and whose budding smile is the life of Lalita and Your other friends.**

**O Queen, a drop of the sweetness of whose restless sidelong glance maddens Lord Madhava. O moonlight of bliss for the white lotus of Your father’s fame.**

**O Queen, the lake of whose heart is filled with a never- ending flood of mercy, please be kind to this person who yearns to become Your servant.**

**When will I see the prince of Vraja beg with sweet words for the mercy of Your restless sidelong glance?**

**When, as artistic Madhava carefully decorates You with madhavi flowers, and You begin to feel a little uncomfortable, will I fan You ?**

**O Queen, when will You order this person to fix Your curling locks of hair, which have become disarrayed during Your pastimes?**

**O Queen whose lips are like bimba fruit, when will the prince of Vraja snatch away and enjoy the betel nuts as I place them in Your lotus mouth?**

**O jewel in the parted hair of the beloveds of the prince of Vraja, let the path of Your intimate friends be not far from me.**

**O Queen of Vrndavana, moment by moment I beg only for Your kindness. By Your kindness may this person become able to offer proper prayers to Lord Krsna, the enemy of Kesi.**

**May whoever reads this prayer to the queen of Vrndavana, a prayer that bears the name Catu-puspanjali (“A Handful of Prayer-flowers”), become the object of Her mercy.**

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura gives the following description of the twenty-four and a half moons on Krsna’s body and their effect on the universe: “In the Kama-gayatri there are twenty-four and a half syllables, and these form twenty-four and a half full moons. These full moons arise in Sri Krsna’s bodily form and thereby make the three worlds kama-maya (pervaded with His own transcendental lusty desire to sport). The sastras describe the identities of these moons amongst the syllables of the Kama-gayatri mantra: Krsna’s face is one moon; His cheeks are two; His forehead is a half moon; the tilaka on His forehead is a full moon; His fingernails are ten moons; and His toenails are ten moons.Thus intelligent authorities have revealed that all the twenty-four and one half syllables of the Kama-gayatri mantra systematically form the different moons which correspond to the moons of Sri Krsna’s bodily features.” (Mantrartha-dipika)

In Mantrartha-dipika, Cakravarti Thakura gives this example of Radha’s form being composed of twenty-five syllables, which implies that the twenty-five syllables are the syllables of the Kama-gayatri mantra. Because, in one sense, Radha and Krsna are not different, if Her body is composed of Kama-gayatri’s twenty-five syllables, His must be also.

Raghunatha Bhatta Gosvami’s remains were interred in the garden of the sixty-four samadhis near Radha-Govinda temple. Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami's remains were interred at the Radha-Damodara temple. And Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami’s remains were interred on the bank of Radha-kunda next to Jahnava-ghata.

All three saints left this world on the same day (Asvina-sukla dvadasi, during the month of Karttika) but in different years: Bhatta Gosvami in 1579, Kaviraja Gosvami in 1582, and Dasa Gosvami in 1583.

Rupa Gosvami formulated the principle of yukta-vairagya and its opposite phalgu-vairagya as follows, anasaktasya visayan yatharham upayunjatah nirbandhah krsna-sambandhe yuktam Vairagyam ucyate / prapancikataya buddhya hari-sambandhi-vastunah mumuksubhih parityago vairagyam phalgu kathyate: “When one is not attached to anything, but at the same time accepts everything in relation to Krsna, one is rightly situated above possessiveness. On the other hand, one who rejects everything without knowledge of its relationship to Krsna is not as complete in his renunciation.” (Bhakti-rasamrta-sindhu 2.255-256, as quoted in Bhagavad-gita As It Is 6.10, purport)

Raghunatha Dasa Gosvami offers his respects to Sanatana Gosvami in the following verse of Vilapa-kusumanjali (6), vairagya-yug-bhakti-rasam prayatnair apayayan mam anabhipsum andhamkrp / ambudhir yah para-duhkha-duhkhi sanatanas tam prabhum asrayami: “I was unwilling to drink the nectar of devotional service possessed of renunciation, but Sanatana Gosvami, out of his causeless mercy, made me drink it, even though I was otherwise unable to do so. Therefore he is an ocean of mercy. He is very compassionate to fallen souls like me, and thus it is my duty to offer my respectful obeisances unto his lotus feet.” (As quoted in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi-lila 5.203, purport)

According to some sources, Akbar’s visit was around 1570. F.S. Growse, for instance, places the date at 1573 and says that Akbar came to Vraja specifically to meet with Jiva Gosvami. (A Mathura Memoir, page 241)

The other three temples Akbar gave permission for were the temples of Madana-mohana, Gopinatha, and Yugala-kisora.

It is said that Caitanya Mahaprabhu visited Vrndavana in 1515 and Aurangzeb’s soldiers came to desecrate the temples of Vraja in 1669 or 1670.

Not all the Deities left Vrndavana to eventually arrive in Rajasthan. For example, the servants of Radha-ramana stayed behind with their Lord, thinking that He was small enough to hide. When the Mogul’s did come, they hid Radha-ramana beneath the waves of the Yamuna.

Conflicting accounts describe the length of time the Deities stayed at Radha-kunda — from three days to one year. Some say that when soldiers arrived at Radha-kunda the Deities were all safely submerged in Radha’s lake.

Devotees sometimes say the Deities went from Kaman directly to Jaipur, but Jaipur was founded in 1727; even if the Deities stayed for thirty-four years between Radha-kunda and Kaman, they would have reached Rajasthan in 1704. Therefore, the more logical conclusion is that the Deities first went to Amber (roughly 10 kilometres from Jaipur), and then when Jai Singh had established Jaipur, most of the Deities were relocated there. However, some went elsewhere, like Madana-mohana, who moved to Karoli.

Indra killed the brahmana Visvarupa, and so Visvarupa’s father, Tvasta, performed ritualistic ceremonies with the goal to kill Indra. While offering oblations to the sacrificial fire, he prayed, indra-satro vivardhasva ma ciram jahi vidvisam: “O enemy of Indra, flourish to kill your enemy without delay.” (Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.9.11) However, because Tvasta mispronounced the mantra, its meaning changed. In his purport to the preceding verse, Srila Prabhupada writes, “Tvasta intended to chant the word indra-satro, meaning, ‘O enemy of Indra.’ In this mantra, the word indra is in the possessive case (sasthi), and the word indra-satro is called a tat-purusa compound (tatpurusa- samasa). Unfortunately, instead of chanting the mantra short, Tvasta chanted it long, and its meaning changed from ‘the enemy of Indra’ to ‘Indra, who is an enemy.’ Consequently instead of an enemy of Indra’s, there emerged the body of Vrtrasura, of whom Indra was the enemy.” One who was an enemy to Indra would have killed that king of the demigods; instead, one to whom Indra became an enemy was killed by the king of heaven. And so it was with the great devotee Vrtrasura.

Diti, the mother of Hiranyaksa and Hiranyakasipu, blamed Indra for her sons’ deaths. She pleased her husband Kasyapa Muni in many ways, and so he gave her a ritualistic process by which she would get a son who could kill Indra. Nonetheless, the sage warned his wife as follows, “My dear gentle wife, if you follow my instructions regarding this vow for at least one year, you will surely get a son who will be able to kill Indra. However, if you deviate from this vow of following the Vaisnava principles, you will get a son who will be favourable to Indra.” (Srimad-Bhagavatam 6.18.45) Fortunately for Indra, Diti once made the slight mistake of not cleansing her mouth after eating and thus received the opposite of what she had hoped to gain from her austerities. Thus the forty-nine Maruts were born.

Srila Prabhupada explains this same principle in relation to approaching both Lord Caitanya and Lord Krsna: “And after finishing respectful obeisances to the spiritual master and the Gosvamis, then we approach Lord Caitanya. Lord Caitanya is also approached with His associates. Savadhutam, sadvaitam. Sa means ‘with.’ Advaita, Advaita Gosai. And avadhuta means Nityananda. So with Advaita and with Nityananda, the offering goes to the Lord, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu. So after finishing all these obeisances one after another, according to the system, then sri-rddha-krsna-padan, then we approach Radha and Krsna. Radha-Krsna is also associate. Krsna is associated with Radharani, and She is associated with Her immediate companions like Lalita, Visakha, and others. So this is the process of offering respectful obeisances to the Deity. We cannot approach Radha-Krsna directly. We have to approach through the spiritual master, through the Gosvamis, through the associates of Lord Caitanya. Then we approach Radha, then Krsna. If one approaches Krsna through this channel of disciplic succession, his efforts become successful. Otherwise, if he wants to approach Krsna directly, it will he futile endeavor.” (Purport to the Mangalacarana Prayers, Los Angeles, 8 January 1969)

Caitanya-bhagavata, Adi-khanda 9.166. Some controversy exists over whether or not Lord Nityananda was an initiated disciple of Madhavendra Puri. A verse in Bhakti-ratnakara indicates that Laksmipati Tirtha, the guru of Madhavendra Puri, gave Lord Nityananda diksa. (Bhakti-ratnakara 2306.) However, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura highlights the following verse in his commentary to Caitanya-bhagavata (Adi-khanda, 9.188): “Nityananda considered Madhavendra to be His guru and nothing else.” While Lord Nityananda may have been initiated by Laksmipati in the ways of regulated devotion according to the Tattvavada line, the Lord considered Madhavendra Puri to be His guru in the ways of worship in ecstatic love. In short, Madhavendra Puri was Lord Nityananda’s siksa-guru, and in the Lord’s pastime He accepted Madhavendra Puri as His main guru.

The stage of love of God wherein devotees are qualified to constantly see Krsna and enter into His pastimes is called anuraga. This platform is unattainable in one’s material body, therefore our acaryas explain that a devotee thus qualified acquires a spiritual body on a planet in the material world where Krsna is personally performing His pastimes. There one is able to directly see Krsna and His associates, who further train that devotee in the ways of loving devotion. (See Raga-vartma-candrika 2.7 for one example.) But that begs the question, “What is meant, then, when it is said that in this life perfected souls may see Krsna?” It means that one may have a brief vision (darsana) of Krsna like Narada Muni or Dhruva Maharaja had.

What does the phrase “love...cultivates itself’ mean? When the first stage of love (prema) appears, one’s devotional activities are both saturated with and caused by love. As a result of those loveladen devotional activities — mostly chanting and hearing about Krsna — love progresses through further stages (like sneha, mana, pranaya, raga, anuraga, and so on). Because the means of cultivating love is the process of loving devotion itself, it is said that “love cultivates itself.” And it must be so, for like Krsna, who is purchased only by love, love for Krsna is also acquired only by love.

The material elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether; their corresponding sense objects are touch, taste, form, smell, and sound respectively; and the sense organs for acquiring knowledge are the skin, tongue, eyes, nose, and ears. The meaning of this mantra is “I offer my respectful obeisances to Lord Sankarsana, the thousand-headed Lord Ananta, and the son of Vasudeva.”

The meaning of the first mantra is “O Lord Balarama! O Lord Ananta! O fulfiller of desires who carries a palm-tree flag and who diverted the course of the Yamuna, all glories to You! O Lord, please appear before me.” The meaning of the second mantra is “O Lord who holds a plough and a club! O Balarama, son of Rohini and husband of Revati, who is dressed in blue garments, I offer my obeisances to You!"

The meaning of this mantra is “I worship the Lord’s feet, ankles, knees, thighs, hips, belly, sides, back, arms, shoulders, eyes, and head.”

The catur-vyuha mantra is om namo bhagavate tubhyam-vasudevaya saksine / pradyumnayaniruddhaya namah sankarsanaya ca.

This prayer concludes with the following blessing (phala-stuti): “A person who regularly recites this prayer attains Lord Hari’s transcendental abode. All the strength in the universe is his. He crushes his enemies and attains great wealth and a great dynasty.”

This kavaca concludes with the following blessing: “This kavaca of Lord Balarama is the best of armours. It destroys the fears of the demigods and demons. It is a blazing fire that burns up the fuel of a host of sins. It is the death of a host of obstacles and it is the abode of spiritual perfection.”

These are the technical details associated with this mantra: the sage is Garga Muni, the meter is anustup, the Deity is Lord Balarama, the seed (bija) is Balahhadra, the energy (sakti) is Revati, the support (kilaka) is Ananta, and the purpose for chanting these names is to please Lord Balarama.

This explanation of upasana-kanda is simplified for the sake of brevity. Technically, upasana-kanda begins with worship of demigods and is perfected when it culminates in worship of Krsna. However, Srila Prabhupada would also sometimes equate upasana-kanda with bhakti, as he does in the following statement: “...three departments of human knowledge disseminated by the Vedas, namely fruitive work (karma-kanda), transcendental knowledge (jnana-kanda), and devotional service (upasana-kanda)...” (Srimad-Bhagavatam 2.9.42, purport) For the purposes of this appendix, therefore, upasana-kanda should be considered synonymous with bhakti.

The above statement of the Chandogya Upanisad implies that Krsna expands not just into two, but into many. “Many” specifically means personal expansions (visnu-tattva), energetic expansions (sakti-tattva), and marginal expansions (jiva-tattva). According to the principles of rasa, Krsna’s greatest enjoyment comes from His relationship with His original sakti expansion, Sri Radha. Thus the highest and most complete feature of the Absolute Truth can be found in Radha and Krsna.

One may wonder if it is obligatory to systematically study the Vedas and gradually advance through the stages of selfless work, philosophical speculation, and functional deity worship before readingSrimad-Bhagavatam and the other works of the Gosvamis. The answer is no. In the same way that Isvara Puri considered his disciple, Lord Caitanya, unqualified to read the Vedas, people of this age are unable to follow the language, ritual, and philosophy of the four Vedas, the Upanisads, or even other Puranas. Nor are they able to persevere through the gradual elevation prescribed by the Vedic system.

How then can they possibly become qualified to read the highest Vedic evidence, Srimad-Bhagavatam, and hear about Srimati Radharani?

By chanting Hare Krsna.

Chanting Hare Krsna gives one the qualification required to successfully hear Srimad-Bhagavatam from pure devotees. When one’s chanting becomes free of offence, Srimati Radharani is revealed through the pages of the Bhagavatam. Narada Muni describes that chanting the holy name of the Lord is equivalent to passing gradually through the progressive stages of the Vedic system, trayo vedah sad-angani chandamsi vividhah surah / sarvam astaksarantah-stham yac canyad api vah-mayam / sarva-vedanta-sararthah samsararnava-taranah: “The essence of all Vedic knowledge — comprehending the three kinds of Vedic activity \[karma-kanda, jnana-kanda, and upasana-kanda\], the chandah or Vedic hymns, and the process for satisfying the demigods — is included in the eight syllables Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna. This is the reality of all Vedanta. The chanting of the holy name is the only means to cross the ocean of nescience.” (Narada-pancaratra, as quoted in Sri Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi-lila 7.76, purport.)

Regarding Sri Radha’s “quantitative” absence from sruti, it is commonly accepted that what currently exists of non-Puranic literature is roughly six percent of what was originally written by Vyasadeva. Given that fact, it can be reasonably assumed that the existing references to Srimati Radharani also comprise only six percent of what Vyasadeva originally intended his audience to read. While that does not make a percentile difference, it does speak to the charge of quantitative paucity.

Although the following verse does not directly mention Radha by name, because Thakura Bhaktivinoda quoted it so often, and because it directly names Krsna while making reference to Radha, it also deserves to be mentioned. Moreover, Srila Prabhupada quoted it in his 1936 Vyasa-puja homage to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta. Because the word sabala indicates Krsna’s internal potency, the overall meaning of the verse, and its relevance to Radharani, is self-evident. The Chandogya Upanisad (8.13.1) says, syamac chabalam prapadye / sabalac chyamam pradadye: “For receiving the mercy of Krsna, I surrender unto His energy \[Radha\], and for receiving the mercy of His energy, I surrender unto Krsna.”

A man decides that the head of the hen is costly because he always has to spend money to feed it, whereas the back end of the hen is profitable because it is giving eggs that can be sold at market. At the conclusion of part one of Brhad-bhagavatamrta (1.7.158), Sanatana Gosvami gives another reason why Sukadeva Gosvami avoided speaking the names of the gopis, especially the name of Sri Radha. Sanatana explains, through the words of Maharaja Pariksit, that the gopis’ love for Krsna is like a flame burning in their hearts, which like any fire can burn one who comes too close. Because Sukadeva Gosvami is already so closely attuned to the gopis’ moods, if he were to mention them by name he would become overwhelmed by the ecstasies of their love for Krsna and lose control of himself. With only seven days to recite Srimad-Bhagavatam to his disciple Pariksit Maharaja, Sukadeva could not risk losing time to his ecstasies. Therefore he refrained from mentioning the gopis by name.
